en: The First Chapter of the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, composed by the venerable great sage Vedavyāsa.
Having attained this auspicious beginning, which is capable of destroying the fear and suffering of existence for yogis, and which has been highly praised by those whose minds are utterly secluded;
May that pair of lotus feet of Hari purify you—
feet by which the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar were successively transcended as they manifested.
May he protect you— he who is skilled in shattering all sins,
whose form rests upon the coils of the serpent within the belly of the ocean of milk,
and who is formidable with the droplets of water shaken from his breath.
The Sindhu river dances as it were because of its association with him.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
O Blessed One, the narrative called the Bhārata was spoken by the high-souled Vyāsa;
it is complete, stainless, radiant, and a compendium of various scriptures.
It is endowed with purity of lineage, adorned with excellent words,
and possessed of the establishment of both prima facie arguments and final conclusions.
As Viṣṇu is among the thirty gods, as the Brāhmaṇa is among bipeds, and as the crest-jewel is the best among all ornaments; 1.4.
Just as the thunderbolt is among weapons and the mind is among the senses,
so too is the Mahābhārata the supreme among all scriptures here on earth.
In this work, wealth, virtue, pleasure, and liberation are described—
both their mutual interconnections and each of them individually.
This is the preeminent treatise on dharma, this is the supreme treatise on artha,
this is the foremost treatise on kāma, and likewise it is the most excellent treatise on mokṣa.
O highly fortunate one, this means for establishing the conduct and stability of the duties of the four stages of life has been proclaimed by the wise Vedavyāsa.
In this manner, dear father, this was indeed accomplished by Vyāsa of noble deeds,
so that this great scripture, being pervaded [by it], is not overcome by contradictions.
By the flood of Vyāsa’s words— which sweeps away the tree of fallacious reasoning and descends upon the mountain of the Vedas— the earth has been made free from dust.
The great lake of the Vedas concerning Kṛṣṇa has the sound of the *kalaśa* as its great swan, the *Mākhyāna* as its supreme lotus, and the narrative as its expansive waters. (MarkP 1.11)
This narrative called the Bhārata contains many meanings and is an extensive expansion of the Vedas;
O Blessed One, desiring to know it in its true essence, I have approached you.
Why did Janārdana Vāsudeva, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, assume human form even though he is devoid of [worldly] qualities?
And why was that single daughter of Drupada, Kṛṣṇā, made the queen of the five sons of Pāṇḍu? For here we have a great doubt.
Why did the exceedingly powerful Baladeva, whose weapon is the plow, undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords as a remedy for the sin of killing a Brahmin?
And how did those sons of Draupadī, those great chariot-warriors who had not yet taken wives,
though having the high-souled Pāṇḍu as their protector, meet their death like those who are protectorless?
"You ought to explain all of this to me here in detail;
for you are always the ones who awaken those of dull intellect."
Having heard these words of his, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya,
free from the eighteen defects, began to speak.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of sages, this time for action has arrived for us;
even when there is much to be told, this is not the time praised for such discourse.
But those who shall speak, O Jaimini, I will speak to you today;
and thus these birds will leave you with your doubts dispelled.
Piṅgākṣa, Vibodha, Suputra, and Sumukha were the sons of Droṇa; they were the best of birds, knowers of reality, and contemplators of the scriptures.
Having approached and questioned those whose intellect is unimpeded in understanding the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, even while they dwell within the caves of the Vindhya mountains.
Thus addressed then by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya,
that tiger among sages replied, his eyes wide with wonder.
Jaimini said: "O Brahmin, this is most wonderful, like human speech issuing from a bird,
that those birds have attained such knowledge as is exceedingly difficult to obtain."
If they were born in the womb of animals, from where did their knowledge come?
And how is it that the sons of Droṇa are called "birds"?
And who was this renowned Droṇa, whose four sons were born endowed with virtues and possessed of knowledge of dharma, those great-souled ones?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen attentively to what occurred long ago in the Nandana grove,
during the meeting of Śakra, the Apsarases, and Nārada.
In the Nandana grove, Nārada saw Śakra, the sovereign lord of the gods, standing in the midst of a throng of unchaste women, his eyes fixed upon their faces.
As soon as he was seen by that most excellent of sages, the Lord of Śacī rose up and respectfully offered him his own seat.
Seeing that slayer of Bala and Vṛtra risen, the celestial women bowed down,
and they stood before the divine sage, humbled by modesty.
Then, having been honored by them, once Śatakratu was seated,
he engaged in delightful conversation with them after exchanging appropriate greetings.
Śakra said: Then, in the course of their conversation, Śakra spoke to that great sage:
"Grant permission for these to dance—whichever among them is to your liking."
Whether it be Rambhā or Karkashā, or Urvaśī or Tilottamā,
or Ghṛtācī or Menakā, or whoever else may be to your liking.
Having heard these words of Śakra, Nārada, the best of the twice-born,
reflected and spoke to the Apsarases who stood there bowed in humility.
"Among all of you here, she who considers herself superior in beauty, nobility, and virtue—let her dance before me. (MarkP 1.35)
For one devoid of the qualities and forms [of the art], there is indeed no accomplishment in drama;
dancing with a beautiful foundation is true dancing, while any other dancing is mere mockery.
And at the very moment of those words, each one of them bowed down and said, "I am superior in virtue, not you; nor are you," and so spoke the others as well.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beholding their agitation, the Blessed Lord Pākaśāsana said, "Let the sage be questioned; he shall tell you who among you is superior in virtue."
O Jaimini, hear from me that speech which Sanātana, together with Nārada, then spoke when he was questioned by those women who followed the will of Śakra.
I consider her to be superior in merit among you all— she who forcibly disturbed Durvāsas, the best of sages, as he was performing austerities while dwelling upon the king of mountains.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard those words of his, they all, with their necks trembling, spoke these words: "This is impossible for us."
There, an Apsaras named Vapuḥ, proud of her power to disturb sages, replied:
"Today I shall go to where that sage is staying."
Today, I shall make that driver of the body— who has yoked the horses of the senses—
into a wretched charioteer, with the reins slipping from his grasp due to the weapons of the God of Love.
Whether it be Brahmā, Janārdana, or even Nīlalohita,
I shall today make even him one whose inner being is wounded by the arrows of desire.
Having spoken thus, that body then departed for the Snowy Mountain,
an hermitage where wild beasts had been pacified by the power of the sage’s asceticism.
While that great sage remained there, sweet as the song of the male cuckoo,
a choice celestial nymph stood at a distance of one *krośa* and sang.
Hearing the sound of that singing, the sage, his mind filled with wonder,
went to the place where that girl of beautiful countenance was staying.
Seeing her, whose every limb was beautiful, the sage steadied his mind;
perceiving that she had come to disturb him, he was filled with anger and indignation.
Then that great seer of mighty asceticism spoke these words to her.
"O sky-dweller intoxicated with pride, you have come here for my own sorrow, as an obstacle to this ascetic merit earned through suffering."
Therefore, O you of impure intellect, defiled by my wrath, you shall take birth in the Suparṇa lineage for sixteen years.
Abandoning her own form and assuming the shape of a bird,
that lowly Apsaras shall give birth to those four sons.
And failing to find pleasure among them, you shall, purified by the sword, obtain a dwelling again in heaven; you must not speak a word of reply under any circumstances.
Having made that proud woman hear these unbearable words, her eyes bloodshot with anger and her bracelets jingling,
the Brahmin abandoned the earth, which was as restless with its waves.
They proceeded to the celestial Gaṅgā, which possesses a vast multitude of renowned virtues.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Curse on the Body," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Two.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The son of Ariṣṭanemi was the king of birds named Garuḍa;
Garuḍa’s son was the renowned Sampāti.
He too had a son, the heroic Supārśva, whose prowess was like that of Vāyu; Supārśva’s son was Kunti, and Kunti’s son was Pralolupa.
He too had two sons, Kaṅka and Kandhara.
On the peak of Kailāsa, Kaṅka beheld a Rākṣasa follower of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), known as Vidyudrūpa, whose eyes were like lotus petals.
He was intent on drinking, wearing a stainless garland and garments,
seated with his wife upon a pure and auspicious stone slab.
As soon as Kaṅka saw that Rākṣasa filled with rage, he said to him: "O lowest of birds, why have you come here?"
"Why do you approach me as I stand in the company of women? This is not the conduct of the wise regarding matters to be accomplished in secret."
Kaṅka said:
This king of mountains is common property; as it is yours, so it is mine, and so it is for all other living beings as well. What sense of ownership do you have in this matter?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: While Kaṅka was speaking thus, the Rākṣasa cut through his sword with [his own blade],
which was quivering and unconscious, loathsome with flowing blood.
Hearing that Kaṅka had been slain, Kandhara, the lord of birds, overcome with rage,
quickly set his mind upon the slaughter of Vidyudrūpa.
Having gone to the mountain peak where Kaṅka lay slain,
that sky-goer performed the funeral rites for his eldest brother,
his eyes wide with rage and indignation, hissing like a lordly serpent.
Then he went to where that Rākṣasa, the slayer of his brother, was staying,
shaking the great mountains with the mighty wind from his wings.
Scattering masses of clouds with speed, his eyes bloodshot from rage,
he destroyed his enemies in an instant and leaped over mountains with his two wings.
There he saw that night-stalker, his mind addicted to drink,
with a face and eyes copper-red, reclining upon a golden couch.
His crest was filled with garlands, he was adorned with yellow sandalwood paste,
and his most terrible face had teeth resembling the inner petals of the *ketakī* flower.
And he beheld his long-eyed wife named Madanikā, who rested upon his left thigh and possessed a voice as melodious as that of the male cuckoo.
Then Kandhara, his soul overcome with rage, spoke to him who was staying in the cave: "O you of wicked soul, come and fight with me! (MarkP 2.17)
"Since you have killed my eldest brother while he was trusting you,
therefore I shall send you, while you are still intoxicated, to the abode of Yama."
Slain by me today, you shall go to all those hells reserved for the slayers of the trusting and for the murderers of women and children.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the lord of birds had spoken thus in the presence of the woman,
the Rākṣasa, overcome with rage, replied to the bird.
If your brother has been slain, then indeed your manliness has been displayed;
today I shall slay you as well with this sword, O sky-walker!
"Stay a moment! You shall not depart from here alive, O lowest of birds!
Having said this, he took up a stainless sword that shone like a mass of collyrium.
Then there occurred an incomparable battle between the king of birds and the warrior-lord of the yakṣas, like that between Garuḍa and Śakra.
Then, out of rage, that rākṣasa brandished his sword with great force and hurled it at the lord of birds; it blazed like extinguished embers.
And the lord of birds, having leaped slightly from the ground,
then seized that sword with his beak, just as Garuḍa seizes a serpent.
Having shattered it with his mouth and the soles of his feet, he then caused an incomparable agitation;
when that sword was broken, a hand-to-hand struggle ensued.
Then, having been attacked on the chest by the king of birds, the Rākṣasa was swiftly deprived of his hands, feet, arms, and head.
When he had been slain, that woman, seized with some fear, sought refuge with the bird and said, "I shall become your wife."
Taking her, the best of birds returned once more to his own home;
having gone there, he performed the funeral rites for his brother who had been struck down by a lightning bolt.
And having reached the palace of Khandava,
that fair-browed daughter of Menakā, assuming any form at will, took on the shape of Suparṇī.
Then he begot upon her a daughter named Tārkṣī, whose body had been scorched by the fire of a sage’s curse; she was the most excellent of the Apsarases. The bird then gave her the name Tārkṣī.
And the sons of Mandapāla were four of immeasurable intellect,
beginning with Jaritāri and ending with Droṇa, O best of the twice-born.
Among them, the youngest, a righteous soul who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
married that auspicious daughter of Tārkṣya with the consent of Kandharā.
Then, after some time, Tārkṣya conceived a child;
when the embryo was seven days old, she went to Kurukṣetra.
While the most terrible battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas was taking place,
she entered into the midst of the fray because of the destined nature of the event.
There he then beheld the battle between Bhagadatta and Kirīṭin;
the sky was filled without interval by arrows, as if by locusts.
The broad-headed arrow, dark as a buffalo, released from Pārtha’s bow with extreme velocity,
severed the skin of her belly.
When his abdomen was split open, four eggs, resembling the crescent moon, fell upon the ground;
because some of his life-force still remained, they fell like a heap of cotton.
And at the very moment of his fall, a great banner fell from the excellent elephant Supratīka,
its fastenings severed by arrows.
Having reached the surface of the earth from all sides, she pierced through it and remained there,
covering the eggs of birds that lay upon the flesh.
And while that king Bhagadatta, the lord of men, was being slain,
the battle between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas continued for many days.
When the battle had ended and the son of Dharma had gone into the presence of the son of Śantanu,
[the sages remained] in order to hear all the dharmas from the high-souled Bhīṣma as he spoke them.
O best of the twice-born, while the eggs remained there for six years,
the self-restrained sage named Śamīka arrived at that place.
There he heard the sound "cicīkucī" being uttered by those whose speech was indistinct due to childhood, even though their consciousness was otherwise fully developed.
Then the seer, accompanied by his disciples, having uprooted the plantain tree in amazement,
beheld the young birds whose wings were neither mother nor father.
Seeing them there upon the ground in that manner, the venerable sage Śamīka was filled with wonder and spoke to the brahmins who followed him.
This was rightly said by the foremost of the twice-born, Śukra Uśanas himself,
upon seeing the army of the Daityas, oppressed by the gods, intent on flight.
"You must not go; turn back! Why do you flee like cowards?
Having abandoned valor and fame, where have you gone? Will you not die?"
Whether one is perishing or fighting, life lasts only so long as the Creator did not previously ordain it, and for no longer than is desired by the mind.
Some die in their own homes, while other people perish even as they flee; likewise, some have met their end while eating food and drinking water.
Likewise, other playful lovers,
free from disease and with their limbs unhurt by weapons, have fallen under the power of the King of the Dead.
Others, devoted to asceticism, were led away by the followers of the King of the Dead;
and others, intent on the practice of yoga, did not at all attain immortality.
In ancient times, the thunderbolt was hurled at Śambara by the wielder of the vajra;
though struck in the heart by it, the asura did not die.
Indeed, by that very thunderbolt, wielded by Indra, the Dānavas were slain when the time had come;
the Daityas met their destruction at that very moment.
Having understood this, they should not feel terror; for [the danger] will turn back.
Then those Daityas turned back, having abandoned the fear born of death.
Thus, the truthful words of Śukra have been fulfilled by these best of birds,
who did not meet their death even in that superhuman battle.
O Brahmins, where is the falling of reeds, and where is the simultaneous falling of bells? And where is the act of covering the ground with flesh, fat, and blood? ||| MarkP_2.57 |||
"O Brahmins, these are by no means ordinary birds;
rather, it is the favor of destiny that reveals great fortune in this world."
Having spoken thus and looked at them, he spoke these words again:
"Return! Go to the hermitage, taking the young birds with you."
Where there is danger from cats or mice, let birds be stationed there for these egg-born creatures, so that they may not fall prey to hawks or even mongooses.
O twice-born ones, why are you being slain by your own deeds with such great effort,
while all living beings are protected just like these young birds?
Nevertheless, men must exert effort in all their undertakings;
for by performing human endeavor, one does not incur the censure of the virtuous.
Thus urged by the best of sages,
those sons of the sage then took hold of those birds and the swarms of bees perched upon the branches of the tree.
Then they went to their own hermitage, which was delightful for ascetics.
And he too, having taken with his mind the forest roots, flowers, fruits, and kusha grass that he desired,
performed [the worship] of the wielder of the discus, Rudra, and the Creator.
Surendra, Vaivasvata, and Jātavedas.
O best of the twice-born, [the offerings] for the Lord of Waters, the Lord of Cows, the Guardian of Wealth, as well as for Vāyu,
Dhātṛ, and Vidhātṛ, and then those pertaining to the Viśvedevas.
But the various ritual acts prescribed by the Vedas are indeed meritorious deeds.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Origin of the Sparrow," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Three.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Day after day, O best of Brahmins, that most excellent of sages provided them with nourishment consisting of milk and likewise protected them.
In just a month, they traveled along the path of the sun’s chariot,
watched by the sons of sages with eyes restless with curiosity.
Having seen the earth, together with its cities, oceans, and great rivers,
reduced to the size of chariot wheels, they returned once more to their hermitage.
Those great-souled ones, born not from a womb, had their inner selves weary with fatigue;
yet, by their power, knowledge became manifest to them there.
Having circumambulated the sage as he spoke this determination of the Dharma out of compassion for his disciples, they all bowed down at his feet.
And they said: "O Sage, we have been liberated from a terrible death by you;
you are our provider of shelter, food, and water—our father and our teacher."
The mothers of those staying in the womb have died, and they were not even protected by their fathers;
you have granted us life, since we infants have been protected by you.
On earth, you whose splendor remains unimpaired even as others wither like worms,
uprooted the elephant-bell and brought about the destruction of Duḥkhara.
"How shall these weak ones grow? When shall I see them standing in the air?
When shall I see them, having reached the trees from the earth, moving from one tree to another?"
When will my innate luster be destroyed by the dust raised by the wind from their wings as they move about near me? (MarkP 3.10)
"O father, while you were thus reflecting, we were protected by you; now that we have grown up and awakened, what should we do? (MarkP 3.11)
Having heard their words, which were clear and refined,
the seer, surrounded by all his disciples and accompanied by his son Śṛṅgin, [departed].
Becoming filled with curiosity and covered by a cloth of horripilation, he said:
"Tell me truly the cause of these words that have proceeded."
"By whose curse has this supreme transformation of both form and speech been incurred by you? You ought to tell me that."
The birds said:
"In former times there was a most excellent sage known as Vipulaśravas.
To him were born two sons, Sukṛṣa and Tumburu."
We four sons of that self-controlled Sukṛṣa have always been bowed down by our discipline, conduct, and devotion toward that ṛṣi.
At that time, for him who was intent on the practice of austerity and whose senses were being restrained,
we provided whatever he desired.
All the sacrificial fuel, flowers, and so forth, as well as whatever is used for food—
such were the provisions for those of us dwelling there in that forest.
The lord of the gods, having assumed the form of a bird, arrived— of massive stature, with broken wings and overcome by old age, his eyes copper-red and his body frail.

Desiring to know that best of sages—whose conduct was characterized by truth, purity, and forbearance, and whose mind was exceedingly noble—and wishing also for the removal of the curse upon us; ||| MarkP_3.20 |||
The bird said: "O lord of the twice-born, you ought to protect me here, for I am overcome by hunger;
O illustrious one, become my incomparable refuge for the sake of being eaten."
Standing on a peak of the Vindhya mountains, O illustrious one, I was indeed blown down by the wind, driven by the force of the wings of birds, with extreme velocity.
Overcome by delusion, I remained there on the ground for seven days without consciousness;
on the eighth day, I regained my senses.
Having regained consciousness, overcome by hunger and devoid of joy, I have come to you for refuge with a heart tormented by the desire for food.
Therefore, O one of pure intellect, form a firm resolve to save me;
O brahmin-sage, give me food sufficient for my sustenance.
Thus addressed, he spoke to Indra in the form of a bird:
"I shall give you whatever food you desire for the sake of sustaining your life."
Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born asked him once more:
"What kind of food should be prepared by me for your sake?
And he replied: "My supreme satisfaction comes from human flesh."
The sage said:
"Childhood has passed for you, and youth too;
O bird, the decline of age surely now prevails over you."
Since in him all the desires of every man are completely stilled,
why are you so cruel-hearted even in your old age?
Where is human flesh, and where is your final age?
In every way, the pacification of those with wicked dispositions is not possible.
Or rather, what need is there for me to say this?
Our minds have long been resolved that whatever has been promised must always be given.
Having spoken thus to him and being resolved that "so be it," that best of brahmins quickly summoned us and praised us for our virtues.
With an agitated heart, the sage spoke these very harsh words to all of them, who were bowed in humility, filled with devotion, and joined their palms in reverence. (MarkP 3.33)
O best of the twice-born, you who have perfected your souls are bound to me by debts;
for you have produced excellent offspring, just as I have, O brahmins.
If you consider your supreme father to be worthy of worship as a guru,
then carry out my word with a heart free from guile.
And at the very moment those words were spoken by us with reverence,
whatever you shall say— let it be understood that it has already been accomplished.
The sage said:
"This bird, overcome by hunger and thirst, has come to me for refuge,
so that his hunger may indeed be satisfied for a moment with your flesh."
"And let the destruction of our craving be accomplished quickly by means of passion.
Then we, deeply distressed and trembling with fear, cried out, "Alas! Alas! and said, "We shall not do this."
How could a wise man destroy or cause the destruction of his own body for the sake of another's body? For as is one's self, so is one's son.
Indeed, it is the son who discharges the debts owed to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings that have been declared; it is not merely the one who provides a body who is called a son.
Therefore, we shall not do this which was practiced by those of old;
for as long as one lives, one attains blessings, and while living, one performs meritorious deeds.
Upon death, there is the destruction of the body as well as the cessation of dharma and other duties;
those who know the dharma say that the self must be protected from all sides.
Having heard these words of ours, the sage, as if blazing with anger,
spoke to us once more, as if burning us with his eyes.
"Since you will not carry out this word which I have promised, therefore,
consumed by my curse, you shall go to the womb of an animal."
Having spoken thus, he then said to that bird:
"After you have performed my funeral rites and the post-mortem ceremonies according to the scriptures..."
"O best of the twice-born, eat me here with full confidence;
I have offered this body of mine to you as food."
This alone is declared to be the true Brahminhood of a brahmin:
as long as he protects his own truth, like the foremost among the species of birds.
O Brahmins, that great merit which is obtained by the protection of truth cannot be attained through sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, nor by any other action.
Having heard these words of the Ṛṣi, Śakra, who was then bearing the form of a bird, filled with inward wonder, replied to the sage at that time.
"O best of brahmins, resorting to yoga, you should cast off this body of yours;
for as long as I am alive, O best of brahmins, I shall never eat a living creature."
Having heard those words, the sage became absorbed in yoga;
and Śakra, knowing his resolve, spoke while assuming his own body.
"O eminent Brahmin, awaken! O wise one, whose nature is consciousness, understand that which is to be understood.
O sinless one, this offense was committed by me against you for the sake of inquiry."
Therefore, forgive this, O lady of pure intellect; whatever desire you have, let it be fulfilled.
Because of your protection of your word of truth, my affection for you is supreme.
"From this day forward, the knowledge of Indra shall manifest within you;
as you practice asceticism and dharma, no obstacle shall arise for you."
When Śakra had departed after saying this, our father, filled with anger,
bowed his head and spoke these words to the great sage.
O dear one of great intelligence, you ought to forgive us who are terrified of death and wretched; for we hold life dear.
Where there is a mere heap of skin, bone, and flesh, filled with pus and blood, no pleasure should be found; yet therein lies this pleasure of ours.
And listen, O highly fortunate one, how the world is deluded,
rendered helpless by powerful enemies in the form of defects such as desire, anger, and the like.
It is joined with the rampart of wisdom, has bones for its pillars, is most vast,
possesses a great enclosure with skin for its walls, and is plastered with flesh and blood.
It has nine gates, is vast in extent, and is bound on all sides by sinews;
and there, O King, dwells a conscious person.
His two ministers, intellect and mind, being at odds with one another,
both strive against each other to destroy their mutual enmity.
Four enemies desire the destruction of that king:
lust, anger, greed, and delusion as the fourth foe.
But when that king remains with those gates closed,
he always becomes one whose strength is well-established and who is free from fear.
Having become filled with affection, he is not overcome by his enemies.
But when he opens all the gates,
then the enemy called passion seizes the gates of the eyes and other senses.
The Great Path is all-pervading and enters through five gates;
following its course, that truly terrible triad of enemies enters as well.
Then, having entered there through the gates known as the senses,
passion enters into union with the mind and with the others.
Having brought the senses and the mind under control, he becomes difficult to overcome;
and having brought the gateways under control, he then destroys the rampart.
Seeing his mind thus dependent [on her], his intellect perished at that very moment;
he was there deprived of his ministers and likewise abandoned by the body of citizens.
A king who provides an opening for his enemies meets with destruction;
in this same way, passion, delusion, greed, and likewise anger [lead to ruin].
Evil-minded beings, who cause the loss of human memory, prevail;
from passion (rāga) arises anger (krodha), and from anger greed (lobha) is born.
From greed arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory comes the destruction of the intellect; and from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.
O best of beings, show favor toward those whose intellects are thus ruined, who follow after passion and greed, and who are full of craving for life.
O best of sages, may this curse bestowed by the Blessed One not come to pass; may we not go to a miserable, dark destination.
"O sons, that which has been spoken by me shall never become false; my speech has not uttered an untruth even until this very day."
"In this matter, I consider destiny supreme; fie on useless human effort, by which I have been forcibly compelled to perform an unthinkable and improper act!"
And because I have been propitiated by you with prostrations,
therefore, even though you have fallen into the state of animals, you shall attain supreme knowledge.
Having been shown the path by knowledge and having shaken off the impurity of the afflictions,
you shall, through my grace, attain supreme perfection free from doubt.
"O Blessed One, we were thus cursed by our father in the past through the power of fate;
then, after a long time, we entered into another womb."
"O best of the twice-born, having been born in the midst of battle, we were indeed protected by you; thus have we attained the state of birds.
There is no one here in this world who is not afflicted by destiny."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the venerable sage Śamīka,
the highly fortunate one, replied to the twice-born who were standing nearby.
I have already declared this in your presence:
these are not ordinary birds; they are some of the best of the twice-born, who did not meet their death even in that superhuman battle.
Then, permitted by that high-souled and joyful one,
they went to the Vindhya, the best of mountains, which was covered with trees and creepers.
As long as the birds of Dharma remain today upon that mountain,
devoted to austerity and sacred study, and firmly resolved in meditative absorption.
Thus, having received hospitable treatment from the best of sages,
those sons of the sage attained the state of birds in the dense forest of the great mountain,
where the waters are exceedingly pure.
With disciplined minds, they dwell upon the slopes of the Vindhya mountains.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Vindhya," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Four.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus those sons of Droṇa became wise birds;
they dwell on the Vindhya mountain—attend upon them and question them.
Having heard these words of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya, Jaimini went to the peak of the Vindhya mountains where those birds of dharma were located.
And having come near that mountain, Jaimini heard the sound of those reciting; and having heard it, overcome with wonder, he reflected: MarkP_4.3 //
It is recited by the best of the twice-born with excellence of posture, with breath controlled, without pause, clearly articulated, and free from defects.
"I consider it a marvel that even these young sons of sages, though born from a non-human womb, do not abandon their eloquence."
Having abandoned one's circle of kinsmen, as well as friends and whatever else is dear in the home, all those depart; but Sarasvatī does not leave one.
Reflecting thus, he entered a mountain cave;
having entered, he saw the twice-born ones seated upon stone slabs.
Then, observing them all reciting without any defect in their pronunciation,
he addressed them all with both sorrow and joy.
"May it be well with you, O best of the twice-born! Know me to be Jaimini, the disciple of Vyāsa, who has arrived here, longing for a sight of you."
One should certainly not harbor anger toward one’s father, even if he is exceedingly angry;
those who were cursed have attained the state of birds—it was entirely destiny.
It is said that some high-minded men were born into families of abundant wealth;
yet when their wealth was lost, those best of the twice-born were thoroughly consoled by a Śabara.
Having given, men beg; others are killed after having killed;
and having caused others to fall, they themselves are made to fall, due to the exhaustion of their ascetic merit.
This has been seen by me many times in its various forms;
the world is perpetually agitated by the constant fluctuations of existence and non-existence.
Reflecting thus in your minds, you ought not to grieve;
for such is the fruit of knowledge: invincibility against both sorrow and joy.
Then they all honored Jaimini with water for his feet and the arghya offering;
having prostrated before the great sage, they inquired after his well-being.
Then all the sky-goers spoke to the disciple of Vyāsa, that treasure-house of asceticism,
who was seated comfortably at rest, his fatigue dispelled by the wind from their wings.
The birds said:
"Today our birth has become fruitful and our life well-lived,
since we behold these two lotus-feet of yours, which are worshipped by the gods."
O Brahmin, that fire of our fathers' anger which was ignited and resides within our bodies has today been extinguished by the water of your sight.
"O Brahmin, is all well with you in this hermitage among the deer and birds,
the trees, the creepers, the shrubs, the bamboos, and the various kinds of grass?"
Or rather, this was not said correctly by us who hold you in high regard;
for how could there be any misfortune for those who have association with you?
"Show us your favor here and tell us the reason for your arrival.
Your company is like that of the gods; it is a great blessing. By what weighty fortune of ours have you been brought within the range of our vision?"
Jaimini said:
"Listen, O tigers among the twice-born, to the reason why he has come here to this beautiful cave of the Vindhya, which is sprinkled by the drops of the waters of the Revā."
I have gone to the land of Bhārata to ask about those doubts regarding the scripture.
Having approached the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, who was formerly born in the lineage of Bhṛgu,
I questioned him regarding my doubts concerning Bharata.
And being questioned by me, he said: "On the great mountain Vindhya there are high-souled sons of Droṇa; they will explain the matter in full detail."
"And because he was addressed by those words, I have come to this great mountain;
listen to that in its entirety, and having heard it, you should explain it."
The birds said:
"Since there is a matter at hand, we shall speak; listen to it without hesitation.
How could we not speak that which falls within the scope of our own understanding?"
For indeed, in all four Vedas, in the Dharmaśāstras, in all their auxiliary branches (aṅgas), and in whatever else is authoritative as equal to the Veda; ||| MarkP_4.27 |||
O best of brahmins, these are within the range of our intellect; nevertheless, we are not able to mount the vow itself. (MarkP 4.28)
Therefore, speak with confidence regarding whatever is doubtful concerning Bhārata;
O knower of dharma, we shall explain it to you, provided that no delusion arises.
Jaimini said:
"O you who are pure, listen to those matters concerning the *Bhārata* that are doubtful to me; having heard them, you should explain them."
Why did Janārdana, Vāsudeva— the support of all and the cause of all causes— descend to human status, even though he is devoid of [worldly] qualities?
And why was that single daughter of Drupada, Kṛṣṇā, made the queen of the five sons of Pāṇḍu? There is great doubt regarding this matter.
Why did the immensely powerful Baladeva, whose weapon is the plow, undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords as a remedy for the sin of killing a Brahmin?
And how did those sons of Draupadī, great chariot-warriors who had not yet taken wives,
though having the high-souled Pāṇḍu as their protector, meet their death like those who have no protector?
"Tell me all of this regarding the Bharatas, for it is a matter of doubt;
by which means I may achieve my purpose and go happily to my own hermitage."
The birds said: Having paid homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of gods, the all-powerful,
the Supreme Person, the immeasurable, the eternal, and the immutable.
To him who consists of the fourfold manifestation, who possesses the three qualities yet is beyond qualities; who is most excellent, most venerable, most desirable, and immortal.
Because there is nothing subtler than he, because there is nothing greater than he,
by whom this entire universe is pervaded— by that unborn one who is the beginning of the world.
They say that this which was created is distinct from appearance and disappearance, from the seen and the unseen; likewise, at the end, it is withdrawn.
Having paid homage with meditative absorption to Brahmā, the primordial god,
he purifies the three worlds by emitting the Ṛg and Sāman verses from his mouths.
Having prostrated before Īśāna in that manner, [he described] how the sacrifices of the performers of rites are destroyed by hosts of asuras who have been conquered by him with a single arrow.
We shall proclaim the entire doctrine of Vyāsa, whose deeds are marvelous,
by whom dharma and the other goals of life were revealed through the Mahābhārata.
The waters were called *nārāḥ* by the sages who perceive the truth;
because they were his first place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
That divine Lord Nārāyaṇa, the all-pervading and omnipresent,
exists in four forms, O Brahmin, both with attributes and likewise without attributes.
The wise perceive that one form as indefinable and white;
with her limbs enveloped in a garland of flames, she is the supreme goal of yogins.
Whether situated far away or standing nearby, she who transcends all qualities is to be known;
she, designated as Vāsudeva, is perceived through the state of "mine-lessness."
Its forms, colors, and so forth are not real entities, being merely products of conceptual construction;
it exists eternally as pure, firmly established, and of a single nature.
The second, known as Śeṣa, supports the earth from below with his hoods;
he is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasī) and is situated in a horizontal position.
The third [form] performs action, being intent on protecting her subjects; she should be known as one overflowing with *sattva*, the establisher of righteousness (*dharma*).
The fourth [form] dwells in the midst of the waters, reclining upon a bed of serpents;
her quality is rajas, and she indeed constantly effects creation.
That third form of Hari, which is intent upon protecting the subjects,
establishes dharma on earth with constancy.
He slays the upraised asuras who cause the destruction of dharma;
he protects the gods and other virtuous ones who are devoted to the preservation of dharma.
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Jaimini,
and a rise of unrighteousness, then he creates himself.
Formerly, having become a boar,
he thrust aside the waters with his snout and uprooted the earth with a single tusk, like a lotus plant.
Having assumed the form of Narasiṃha, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain,
and other Dānavas, headed by Vipracitti, were struck down.
I am not able here to enumerate his other incarnations, such as Vāmana and the rest;
however, this present one at Mathurā is indeed an incarnation of him.
Thus that Sāttvika form indeed effects incarnations;
she is known as Pradyumna, established in the work of protection.
Established in the state of a deity, a human, or an animal,
she always assumes that very nature by the will of Vāsudeva.
Thus has been fully explained to you why the Lord Viṣṇu, though having accomplished all his purposes, assumed a human state; now hear further concerning this.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Incarnation of the Fourfold Vyūha," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Five:
The Birds said:
O Brahmin, when the son of Tvaṣṭṛ was previously slain, Indra,
overwhelmed by the sin of brahmin-murder, suffered a supreme downfall of his vital energy.
Then he entered that Dharma; however, due to the departure of Śakra’s splendor, Śakra became devoid of luster once that splendor had issued forth from the Dharma.
Then, having heard that his son had been killed, Tvaṣṭṛ, the Prajāpati, became enraged; plucking out a single lock of matted hair, he spoke these words: MarkP_5.3 //
Today let the three worlds, together with the gods, behold my prowess;
and let that evil-minded slayer of a Brahmin, Indra, behold it as well.
"By him, who delights in his own deeds, my son has been brought to ruin.
Having said this, with eyes reddened by anger, he offered that matted lock into the fire.
Then the great asura Vṛtra rose up, garlanded with flames,
possessing a massive body and large fangs, with a luster like a heap of crushed collyrium.
Indraśatru, of immeasurable soul and augmented by the splendor of Tvaṣṭṛ,
grew day by day, that one of great strength, like the flight of an arrow.
Seeing the great asura Vṛtra for his own destruction, Śakra,
afflicted by fear and desiring peace, dispatched the seven ṛṣis.
Then the sages, whose minds were filled with joy and who were devoted to the welfare of all beings, formed a friendship with him and likewise established an agreement with Vṛtra.
When Vṛtra was slain by Śakra after he had transgressed the established agreement, Indra’s strength then shattered, overwhelmed as he was by the sin of slaughter.
Falling from the body of Śakra, that power entered the wind,
which is all-pervading, unmanifest, and the presiding deity of strength itself.
And when Śakra, assuming the form of Gautama, violated Ahalyā,
the lord of the gods, his own form then diminished.
Then, leaving behind the wicked lord of the gods, the two Nāsatyas went away, taking with them that exceedingly beautiful charm of his major and minor limbs which was so captivating to the mind.
Knowing that the Lord of the Gods had been deprived of his dharma and splendor, rendered powerless and formless, the Daityas made an effort to conquer him.
O great sage, among the families of kings of exalted valor who desired to conquer the Lord of the Gods, Daityas of exceeding strength were born.
Then, after some time, the earth, oppressed by its burden,
went to the summit of Mount Meru, where the assembly of the celestial dwellers was held.
Oppressed by a heavy burden, she spoke to them regarding the cause of her own distress arising from the Daityas, the sons of Danu.
These asuras of vast power, who were slain by you,
have all been born in the world of men within the households of kings.
"For there are many akṣauhiṇīs; oppressed by their weight, I am sinking down.
O gods, act in such a way that peace may be mine."
The birds said:
Then the gods descended from heaven to the earth with portions of their splendor,
for the sake of benefiting living beings and for the removal of the burden of the world.
The bull [Dharma] himself released that splendor born from Indra’s body;
from that was born the highly resplendent King Yudhiṣṭhira from Kuntī.
Then the Wind released his strength, from which Bhīma was born;
and from half of Śakra’s virility, Pārtha Dhanañjaya was born.
Two twin sons of great splendor, resembling Śakra himself, were born to Mādrī;
thus did the blessed Lord Śatakratu descend in five forms.
To him was born a highly fortunate wife, Kṛṣṇā, from the sacrificial fire.
She is the wife of Śakra alone and not of anyone else;
for masters of yoga can create even many bodies.
This matter concerning the five brothers sharing a single wife has been told to you;
now hear how Baladeva also went to the Sarasvatī.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "The Transformation of Indra," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
The sixth chapter begins with the birds saying:
Knowing Pārtha’s supreme devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, Rāma,
the wielder of the plow, reflected in many ways on what deed might be considered well-done.
Indeed, without Kṛṣṇa, I will not go into the presence of Duryodhana;
nor, having sought refuge with the Pāṇḍavas, how could I [go] to King Duryodhana? (MarkP 6.2)
"I shall cause the death of the lord of men, who is both my son-in-law and my disciple;
therefore, I will go neither to Pārtha nor to King Duryodhana."
"I shall immerse myself in sacred fords by my own effort until the end of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas is brought about."
Having thus addressed Hṛṣīkeśa, as well as Pārtha and Duryodhana,
Śauri departed for Dvārakā, surrounded by his own army.
Having arrived at Dvāravatī, which was crowded with happy and well-fed people, Rāma,
whose weapon is the plow, drank wine in preparation for the holy bathing sites he was to visit the following day.
Then, having drunk the yellow liquor, he went to the prosperous Raivata garden,
taking by the hand the intoxicated Revatī, who resembled an apsaras.
Standing in the midst of a group of women, the hero went along intoxicated, stumbling at every step;
and he beheld a most excellent and delightful forest.
Abounding in fruits and flowers of every season, crowded with troops of monkeys,
it was a meritorious great forest containing lotus groves and ponds.
He heard many auspicious sounds, sweet and very melodious, pleasing to the ear, uttered from the mouths of birds, which were delightful and intoxicating with joy.
There he saw trees rich with the weight of fruit in every season, radiant with blossoms of every season, and made resonant by the songs of birds.
Mangoes, hog-plums, bhavya fruits, coconuts along with sinduka fruits,
as well as bilva, cumin, pomegranates, and citron fruits.
[He saw] jackfruit trees, lakucas, plantains, and most enchanting nīpas;
also pārāvatas, kaṅkolās, nalinas, and amlavetasas.
Bhallātaka, āmalaka, tinduka with its large fruits, iṅguda, karamarda, harītakī, and vibhītaka; 6.14.
The joy of the Yadus beheld these and other trees,
as well as the aśoka, punnāga, ketakī, and bakula.
Campakas, saptaparṇas, karṇikāras along with mālatīs,
pārijātas, kovidāras, mandāras, and likewise badaras;
[He saw] lovely *pāṭala* trees in full bloom, as well as *devadāru* trees,
*sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, along with excellent *kiṃśuka* and *vañjula* trees.
With *cakora* birds, *śātapatra* birds, *bhṛṅgarāja*s, as well as parrots, cuckoos, sparrows, green pigeons, and *jīvajīvaka* birds; ||| MarkP_6.18 |||
It was also inhabited by *cātaka* birds with their beloved young, as well as various other birds,
all warbling very sweetly and pleasing to the ear.
And there were delightful lakes with clear waters,
adorned with white water-lilies, lotuses, and beautiful blue lotuses.
They were covered on all sides with white water-lilies and lotuses,
as well as with *kādamba* ducks, ruddy geese, and water-fowls.
It was strewn on all sides with water-fowls, ducks, swans, tortoises, cormorants, and various other aquatic creatures.
Thus, gazing upon the delightful forest in due order, Śauri proceeded,
followed by the women, toward an unsurpassed bower of creepers.
There he saw twice-born men who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—
Kauśikas, Bhārgavas, Bhāradvājas, and Gautamas.
And he saw the best of the twice-born, born into various lineages,
seated upon great thrones and eager to hear the sacred narratives.
Upon seats made of black antelope skins, upon kuśa grass, and upon vṛṣī mats,
the Sūta sat in their midst, recounting auspicious stories.
Having seen Rāma, whose eyes were reddened by the drinking of honey-wine, all the twice-born ones [recited] the ancient stories concerning the deeds of the primordial celestial sages.
Thinking, "This one is intoxicated," they rose up with haste,
honoring the wielder of the plow, with the exception of that one born of the Sūta lineage.
Then the mighty wielder of the plow, his eyes rolling with rage and having agitated all the Dānavas, struck down the charioteer.
When that son had been struck down, he ascended to the state of Brahman;
and all those twice-born ones, clad in black antelope skins, departed from the forest.
Considering himself thus to be an Avadhūta, Halāyudha reflected: "A very great sin has been committed by me."
For this charioteer, having been struck down, has indeed gone to the realm of Brahmā;
for thus all these twice-born ones have departed upon seeing me.
And the odor of my body is as unpleasant as that of iron;
I perceive myself to be as loathsome as a slayer of a Brahmin.
Fie upon indignation, as well as intoxication, excessive pride, and fearlessness,
by which I, being possessed, have committed this very great sin!
For the sake of its destruction, I shall observe a twelve-year vow,
performing the supreme atonement that makes my own deed known.
Now, this pilgrimage to the sacred fords which I have just undertaken,
I shall perform by traveling along the Sarasvatī in its reverse direction.
From there, Rāma went to the Pratilomā Sarasvatī;
after that, hear this account concerning the Pāṇḍaveyas.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Brahman-slaughter of Baladeva," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Seven:
The Birds of Dharma said:
In ancient times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a royal sage named Hariścandra;
he was a righteous protector of the earth, of supreme excellence and resplendent fame.
While that king was ruling, there was neither famine nor disease, nor untimely death among men; nor did the citizens take pleasure in unrighteousness.
People did not become intoxicated by the pride of wealth, heroism, or asceticism;
nor were any women born who had not attained their youth.
Once, while that mighty-armed one was pursuing a deer in the forest, he repeatedly heard the cry of a woman: "Save me! (MarkP 7.4).
Leaving the deer behind, the king said, "Do not fear!
While I rule, who is this person of wicked intellect and unjust conduct?"
Following that cry and intent on obstructing all undertakings, the fierce King of Obstacles reflected within himself during that interval: MarkP_7.6 //
This powerful Viśvāmitra, having undertaken incomparable austerity, while observing his vow,
is now mastering the sciences that were previously unattainable by others.
Being tormented by him—who is self-restrained through patience, silence, and mental discipline—they cry out, afflicted by fear: "How can this task be accomplished by me?"
The illustrious Kauśika is the foremost, while we are very weak;
these women cry out thus in fear, and it seems to me that this place is difficult to cross.
"Or else, this king has arrived; do not be afraid," he said repeatedly.
"Entering right here, I shall quickly accomplish my desire."
Having reflected thus, the king was then possessed by the fierce Vighnarāja; and overcome by him, he spoke these words in anger.
"What evil-doing man is this who binds fire to the hem of his garment, while I, my husband, stand present, blazing with the power of my fiery splendor? (MarkP 7.12)
Today, with all his limbs pierced by arrows that illuminate the quarters of the sky as they are released from my bow, he shall enter into long sleep.
Then Viśvāmitra, having heard those words of the king, became enraged;
as that best of sages grew angry, those sciences perished in an instant.
And that king, seeing Viśvāmitra, the treasure-house of asceticism,
trembled violently with fear, like a leaf of the holy fig tree suddenly shaken by the wind.
When the sage said, "O evil-minded one!
Stay! the king then prostrated himself out of humility and spoke.
"O Blessed One, this is my duty; it is no fault of mine, O Lord.
You ought not to be angry with me, O Sage, for I am devoted to my own dharma."
A king who knows the Dharma must both give and protect;
he must draw his bow and fight in accordance with the teachings of the Dharmaśāstras.
Viśvāmitra said:
"To whom must things be given, who are to be protected by whom, and with whom must you fight, O King?
Explain this quickly, if you have fear of unrighteousness."
Hariścandra said:
"Gifts must be given to the foremost of Brahmins and to others who are of meager means;
those who are afraid must always be protected, and war must be waged against adversaries."
Viśvāmitra said: "If you, O King, truly observe the duties of a king,
then I, a Brahmin desiring to be invested with office, shall receive my desired sacrificial fee."
The birds said:
Having heard these words of the king, with a heart filled with joy,
he considered himself as if born again and spoke to Kauśika.
"O Blessed One, let that which is to be given to you be spoken without hesitation;
know that it is already given, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (MarkP 7.23)
Gold or fine gold, a son, a wife, one's own body, life-breaths, a kingdom, a city, fortune, or whatever else is desired by oneself— [all these were given].
Viśvāmitra said: "O King, this gift which was given to you has been accepted;
first, however, bestow the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) pertaining to the Rājasūya."
The king said:
"O Brahmin, I shall indeed give even that to you as a sacrificial fee;
O tiger among the twice-born, let that which is desired by you as a gift be chosen."
Viśvāmitra said:
"O hero, [accept] this entire earth with its oceans, along with its mountains, villages, and cities,
as well as the whole kingdom teeming with chariots, horses, and elephants."
"O sinless one, [give me] your storehouse, your treasury, and whatever else you possess, as well as your wife, your son, and even your own body."
And whoever follows the Dharma that leads to the knowledge of all dharmas—what is the use of saying more? Let all this be given.
The birds said:
Having heard those words of the ṛṣi, that king, with a joyful mind and an expression of face free from change, replied "So be it" with palms joined in reverence.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O royal sage, even if my entire possessions— the kingdom, the earth, the army, and the wealth— have been given away,
over whom does sovereignty belong while I, an ascetic, remain established in the kingdom?"
Hariścandra said:
"O Brahmin, at the very time when the earth was given by me, you were already my master; how much more so now that I am the lord of the world?"
Viśvāmitra said: "O King, if the entire earth has been given by you to me,
then you ought to depart from that portion of my domain over which I hold sovereignty."
Having cast aside his entire collection of ornaments, including his waist-bands and other finery,
he donned garments of tree bark together with his wife and son.
The birds said,
"So be it," and having spoken thus and performed [the ritual], the king set out to go together with his wife Śaivyā and his young son.
Then, blocking his path as he was departing, he said to that king:
"Where will you go without giving me the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the Rājasūya?"
Hariścandra said:
"O Blessed One, this kingdom has been given to you, with all its thorns removed;
O Brahmin, what remains for me today is only this triad of bodies."
Viśvāmitra said:
"Nevertheless, you must indeed give me the sacrificial fee;
for what is promised but not given, especially to Brahmins, destroys [the giver]."
O King, the sacrificial fee for the Rājasūya should be given only to the extent that it brings satisfaction to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having given your promise, you must fulfill it; you must fight against those who would do you harm, and likewise, you must protect the distressed, for this was promised by you previously.
Hariścandra said:
"O Blessed One, at present I have nothing; in the course of time I shall give to you.
O Brahmin-sage, show me favor, taking into account my sincere devotion."
Viśvāmitra said:
"O lord of men, for how long a time must I wait for you?
Tell me quickly, otherwise the fire of my curse will consume you."
Haricandra said:
"O brahmin-sage, I shall give you the wealth for the sacrificial fee in one month;
at present I have no riches, so you should grant me permission."
Viśvāmitra said:
"Go, go, O best of kings; uphold your own duty.
May your path be auspicious, and may there be no adversaries."
The birds said:
"Permitted to go, depart," [said they]; and the lord of the earth departed. His beloved followed him on foot, though it was not proper for her to travel on foot.
Seeing that best of kings departing from the city with his wife and sons,
the citizens and the king’s followers cried out in lamentation.
"Alas, Lord! Why will you abandon us, who are tormented by constant suffering?
O King, you are devoted to righteousness and likewise intent on showing favor to your citizens."
O royal sage, if you have regard for dharma, do not lead us away; O Indra among kings, wait but a moment to behold the lotus of your face.
When shall we drink [of him] with the bees that are our eyes, and when shall we behold him again—
he before whom kings walk as he departs, and behind whom they follow?
His wife follows him, carrying their young son;
for when he sets forth, his servants who were stationed in the groves go before him.
This very Hariścandra, the lord of kings, now goes on foot;
alas, O King, your face was so delicate, with beautiful eyebrows, smooth skin, and a prominent nose!
"What will your face look like, soiled by the dust of the road?
Stop, stop, O best of kings; observe your own duty!"
Compassion is the supreme duty, especially for Kṣatriyas.
O Lord, what is the use of wives, sons, wealth, or even grain?
Having abandoned all this, we have become like shadows following you; O Lord, O Great King, O Master, alas, why do you abandon us?
