As soon as he has gone there, he beholds Yama in the midst of Death, Time, the Ender, and the others— his eyes excessively red and possessing the luster of a mass of crushed collyrium.
The Lord had a face made terrible by fangs and a form formidable with a frown;
he was surrounded by hundreds of diseases and possessed faces that were deformed and terrifying.
To that great-armed and most terrifying being, who is armed with a staff and holds a noose in his hand,
the creature then goes to the destiny— whether auspicious or inauspicious— that has been assigned by him.
The man who gives false testimony as a witness, or who is a liar, goes to Raurava;
listen now as I describe the nature of that Raurava.
Indeed, Raurava is two thousand yojanas in extent;
beyond that is a chasm, knee-deep in depth, which is very difficult to cross.
There, it was made level with the earth and covered with heaps of burning coals,
being scorched by the intensely blazing ground of glowing embers.
In the midst of that, the followers of Yama release the evildoer;
burning with intense fire, he runs about there.
At every step, his foot withers and decays again;
by day and night he proceeds, lifting his foot and setting it down.
Having thus crossed a thousand yojanas, he is liberated;
thereafter, for the sake of purifying other sins, he goes to a similar hell.
Then, having passed through all those states, the sinner experiences the condition of an animal among worms,
insects, moths, beasts of prey, mosquitoes, and the like.
Having gone into births among elephants, trees, and the like, as well as among cows and horses, and indeed into other sinful wombs that grant suffering; MarkP_10.87 //
Having attained human birth, he may be born as a hunchback, or one who is despised, or even a dwarf; or he is born among the wombs of Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, and other such low castes.
Endowed with whatever remaining demerit and merit he possesses,
he then enters a higher birth as a Śūdra, Vaiśya, king, or the like.
Even the state of being a lord of gods among Brahmins may at some point lead to a descent;
thus do those of evil deeds fall downward into the hells.
Listen as I explain to you how those who have performed meritorious deeds proceed;
those men go to the auspicious destination ordained by Yama.
Multitudes of Gandharvas sang forth, throngs of Apsarases appeared, and there were supreme ornaments, beautified by necklaces, anklets, and the sound of cymbals.
Resplendent with various divine garlands, celestial chariots depart quickly;
from there, they fall for kings and other great-souled beings.
They are born into that family as upholders of virtuous conduct;
they attain intense enjoyments and thereafter go upwards, or otherwise [they do not].
Having reached the Avarohaṇī, human beings proceed as before.
All this has been told to you regarding how a living being perishes;
now listen, O brahmin-sage, to how it enters the womb.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Father and Son," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
The eleventh chapter begins with the son saying:
When the seed of men has reached the menses of women during conception,
it immediately departs from hell or even from heaven.
Overpowered by that, O Father, those two seeds attain stability;
they then become the *kalala*, the *budbuda*, and subsequently the *peśī*.
Just as a minute seed within a grindstone is said to be the sprout,
so too is the arising of the five limbs described according to their respective portions.
The secondary limbs— the fingers, eyes, nose, mouth, and ears—
as well as the nails and so forth, likewise emerge from those primary limbs.
Thereafter, body hair and head hair grow upon the skin;
it attains equal prosperity through that very source of its arising.
Just as a coconut fruit increases while still encased in its husk,
so too does this [being] attain growth while remaining downward-facing within its shell.
But in that [other posture], having placed his hands on the sides of his knees, he grows;
likewise, the two thumbs are placed upon the tops of the knees, as are the fingers.
Likewise, the knees, the back, the eyes, the middle of the knees, the nose,
the buttocks, the two heels, and the arms and shanks are situated on the outside.
In this way, the living being situated within the womb of a woman undergoes gradual growth;
its state within the belly of another creature is according to the form of that being.
Hardness is produced by fire; it lives by what is eaten and drunk.
Thus, the state of a living being within the womb consists of a substratum of merit and demerit.
The channel named Āpyāyinī is attached to his navel;
likewise, it becomes attached within the cavity of the intestines of women.
Just as the food and drink consumed by women pass into the womb of the fetus,
so too this living being, his body nourished by them, indeed attains growth.
Many realms of saṃsāra come to his memory;
thus, being tormented here and there, he arrives at world-weariness.
"Once I am released from this womb, I shall never act in such a way again; I will strive so that I may not enter a womb once more."
Thus he reflected, recollecting indeed hundreds of sufferings of birth—
those which were previously experienced and those which were caused by fate.
Then, in the course of time, the creature turns head-downwards;
for it is in the ninth or tenth month that it becomes fully formed.
As he is being expelled by the wind belonging to Prajāpati,
he is tormented by suffering in his heart and departs while wailing.
Having emerged from the belly, he falls into an unbearable faint;
and endowed with the touch of the wind, he regains consciousness.
Then the deluding Māyā of Viṣṇu seizes him;
his mind being utterly bewildered by that, he suffers a fall from knowledge.
Then, with his knowledge fallen away, the creature enters the state of childhood;
from that, it passes through the stages of infancy, youth, and even old age.
Furthermore, just like that, a human being undergoes death and birth;
consequently, he is whirled around in this wheel of saṃsāra like a waterwheel.
At one time a man attains heaven, and at another time he reaches hell;
indeed, having died, he may experience both hell and heaven at different times.
Sometimes, having been born again right here, he experiences his own karma;
sometimes, having exhausted his karma, he passes away after a short time.
O best of the twice-born, at other times, one is born here in the heavenly world or in hell as a result of even small auspicious and inauspicious deeds, and there one mostly experiences their fruits.
This is a great suffering in the hells, O dear one, that those dwelling in heaven see the denizens of hell being cast down while they themselves rejoice.
Even in heaven there is incomparable suffering, for from the very moment of ascent, this thought dwells in the mind: "I shall fall."
Beholding the denizens of hell and experiencing great suffering,
I am restless day and night, thinking, "I shall go to this very destiny."
There is great suffering in dwelling in the womb, as one is born from the birth canal;
and for one who has been born, there is suffering in the absence of strength and likewise in old age.
In youth, there is the connection with desire, envy, and anger, which is exceedingly difficult to endure;
old age consists mostly of suffering, and at death, there is the ultimate misery.
For one who acts wickedly, there is falling into the hells of Yama;
and again, there is the womb, then birth, death, and likewise hell.
Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, living beings are whirled around like a water-wheel;
bound by natural fetters, they are tormented again and again.
"There is no happiness at all here, O dear one, in this world crowded with hundreds of sufferings;
therefore, for one striving for liberation, how could the three Vedas be practiced by me? (Markandeya Purana 11.32)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Father and Son," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Twelve.
The father said:
Excellent, my child!
You have described the supreme density of saṃsāra,
which, by relying upon it, yields great fruit born from the bestowal of knowledge.
In that regard, all those hells have been described by you just like Raurava; explain them in detail, O Mahāmati.
The son said:
"O father, I have first described to you Raurava;
now hear about the hell named Mahāraurava."
It extends for seven thousand and five thousand yojanas all around;
there the ground is made of copper, and beneath it is fire.
Scorching all directions with its heat, possessing a radiance like that of the rising moon,
it appears exceedingly fierce in its sight, touch, and other qualities.
Bound there by the followers of Yama with both hands and feet,
the evildoer is released from the midst as he rolls along.
Being devoured by crows, vultures, wolves, owls, scorpions, and mosquitoes, as well as by vultures, he is swiftly dragged along the path.
Being consumed by fire, agitated and distressed, he cries out repeatedly, "O father! O mother! O brother! O dear one!
and finds no peace.
Thus, liberation from that [suffering] is indeed attained by men who have transcended it,
even those evil-minded ones by whom sins were committed for tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years.
Likewise, another is named Tamas; it is by nature extremely cold, as vast as Mahāraurava, and similarly enveloped in darkness.
Afflicted by the cold, men running there in the dreadful darkness encounter one another, embrace, and seek refuge together.
And their teeth break as they tremble from the affliction of cold;
there, hunger and thirst are intense, as are other such calamities.
The cruel wind, carrying fragments of snow, shatters their bones;
consequently, those afflicted by hunger devour the marrow and blood that have flowed out from them.
Licking [the ground] as they wander together in mutual encounter,
even so there is great suffering for men there in the darkness.
O best of brahmins, one reaches this state until the exhaustion of one's evil deeds;
beyond that is another, most excellent hell known as Nikṛntana.
O father, upon those [mountains] potter’s wheels revolve incessantly;
there, men are placed and cut asunder with the Kālasūtra.
O best of the twice-born, by means of the Yama-anuga [mantra] residing on the fingers, [the poison spreads] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head; yet no loss of life occurs for them.
Their bodies are cut into hundreds of pieces and then joined back together;
in this manner, those who have committed evil deeds are dismembered for thousands of years.
Listen as I describe that unstable hell, until indeed that sin has been entirely exhausted. (MarkP 12.19)
The hell-beings remaining here experience unbearable suffering;
those very same things which are elsewhere wheels and water-wheels.
Certain men who have committed evil deeds and are the cause of suffering for others are mounted upon wheels and made to whirl there.
Their stay lasts for as many as thousands of years, with no interval in between,
just like a water-pot bound within a water-wheel.
Men wander about again and again, vomiting blood,
with weapons issuing from their mouths and eyes dripping with tears.
They undergo sufferings that are unbearable for living beings;
hear now of another hell named Asipatravana.
There, for a thousand yojanas,
the ground is strewn with blazing fire and heated by the fierce rays of the sun, which are exceedingly and most dreadful.
Sentient beings dwelling in hell always fall there,
and in the midst of it, a beautiful forest with glossy leaves appears.
O best of the twice-born, the leaves there are the blades of swords and the fruits are [the scabbards];
and there, powerful dogs, appearing in tens of thousands, bark.
With large mouths and large fangs, they were as terrifying as tigers;
then, having beheld that forest ahead, which offered cool shade.
There, living beings go, tormented by intense thirst, crying out "O mother! O father!
in extreme distress.
As they go there, their pair of feet are scorched by the fire situated upon the earth;
for them, the wind there brings down a rain of sword-blades.
By that wind they are blown so that their swords fall upon them;
then they fall to the ground upon a mass of blazing fire.
And while he is being licked elsewhere, his entire body covered by them,
dogs then quickly tear at him from his flesh.
The many limbs of those weeping ones are exceedingly terrifying; O dear one, this Asipatravana has thus been described by me to you.
Beyond this, learn from me of the Taptakumbha hell, which is even more terrifying.
On all sides are heated cauldrons enveloped in flames of fire.
Filled with blazing heaps of fire and iron powder mixed with oil,
those of evil deeds are indeed cast headfirst into them by the servants of Yama.
They are boiled, their limbs bursting open and fouled by marrow dripping from them,
while their skulls, eyes, and bones quiver as they are hacked apart by terrifying beings.
Torn apart by vultures, they are released again only to be seized with great force by those very same birds;
once more they are crushed with a *sima-sima* sound and reduced to a single mass by oil.
Then, their heads, limbs, sinews, flesh, skin, and bones having been liquefied,
they are swiftly stirred with a ladle by the men of Yama.
In the Kṛtāvarta hell, where there is great oil, evildoers are churned;
this Taptakumbha hell has been described by me to you in detail, O Father.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Hells such as Mahāraurava," in the dialogue between the father and son within the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirteen.
The son said:
Born indeed into a Vaiśya family, seven births ago in this very life, I formerly caused the obstruction of cattle at a watering place.
As the ripening of that karma, he reached a most dreadful hell,
terrifying with flames of fire and filled with iron-beaked birds.
It was a mire produced by streams of blood from limbs crushed by machines,
and it was filled with the tumultuous sounds of the cries of evildoers being slaughtered as they fell into them.
While being cast down there, a full hundred years passed for me,
scorched by the pain of great heat and consumed by the burning of thirst.
There, a breeze that was immediately refreshing and pleasantly cool came upon me as I stood amidst the jars of sand mixed with parched grain.
Through contact with him, no torment remained for all those men;
and for me, too, there was supreme bliss, just like that of the gods in heaven.
And with eyes fixed wide in wonder and joy, we beheld nearby that unsurpassed jewel among men, wondering, "What is this? (MarkP 13.7).
And the terrible messenger of Yama, with staff in hand and radiant as a thunderbolt, appeared before him, showing the way and saying, "Come! MarkP_13.8.
Then that man, seeing the hell crowded with hundreds of torments,
spoke with compassion to that servant of Yama.
The man said:
"O messengers of Yama, tell me what evil deed I have committed,
by which I have reached this supreme hell of terrifying torments?"
I was born in the lineage of the Janakas as one renowned as Vipaścit,
a king who properly protected men in the realm of Videha.
I have performed many sacrifices, and the earth has been protected according to dharma;
I have never shirked battle, nor have I ever turned away a guest.
I have never failed in my service to my ancestors, the celestial rishis, or my dependents;
nor have I ever entertained desire for the wives or the wealth of others.
At the times of the festival-parvans the ancestors come, and at the times of the lunar days the deities;
they approach a man of their own accord, like cows to a watering trough.
Since those householders depart with their faces turned away and sighing,
therefore both their *iṣṭa* (sacrificial rites) and *pūrta* (charitable works) perish.
The divine breath of a father undoubtedly destroys the merit accumulated over seven lifetimes,
as well as that produced during three lifetimes.
Therefore, I was always constantly diligent in rites for the gods and the ancestors;
how have I, such as I am, fallen into this most dreadful hell?
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Father and Son," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fourteen.
The son said:
Thus questioned then by that high-souled one as we listened,
the messenger of Yama, though terrible, spoke these flowing words.
Yama’s servant said:
"O Great King, it is exactly as you have said; there is no doubt in this matter.
However, I shall remind you of a very small sin that was committed by you."
"Vaidarbha, she who was your wife, known by the name Pīvarī—
formerly you rendered her fertile season barren."
Because you were then attached to the beautiful Kaikeyī, you fell,
due to the transgression of the seasons, into such a terrible hell.
Just as fire awaits the pouring of clarified butter at the time of the oblation,
so does Prajāpati await the casting of the seed during the fertile season.
But that righteous soul who, having transgressed it, becomes attached to sensual desires,
shall incur sin from his debt to the ancestors and fall into hell.
"O King, your evil is only this much; nothing else whatsoever exists [within you]. Therefore, come, go now for the enjoyment of your merits."
The king said:
"I shall go, O follower of the gods, wherever you lead me.
I ask you something; you ought to tell it to me as it truly is."
These crows with adamantine beaks steal away the eyes of men;
indeed, their eyes are restored again and again in that same manner.
Tell me what loathsome deeds they have committed,
such that their tongues are snatched away as they are being born anew.
Why are these beings so exceedingly miserable, being split apart with other blades?
They are roasted upon sands of burning embers, submerged in oil.
Tell me, what kind of beings are these who are dragged away by iron-beaked birds,
crying out with great shrieks from the pain of their dismembered bodily bonds?
Why are these men, suffering from wounds on all their limbs caused by the falling of iron beaks,
tormented day and night by those who do what is undesirable?
These and other torments are seen for those who have committed evil deeds;
tell me in their entirety that which results from the ripening of such karma.
Yama’s servant said:
"O protector of the earth, as for what you ask me regarding the arising of the fruit of sinful karma,"
That I shall declare to you in brief, exactly as it is.
For a person experiences merit and demerit in alternation;
as one enjoys them, whether it be demerit or merit, they come to exhaustion.
But there is no merit or any other action, whether sinful or otherwise, that purifies a human being except through experience;
indeed, the exhaustion [of karma] arises from experience.
Understand from me that he abandons both merit and demerit along with worldly enjoyments;
just as one famine leads to another famine, one affliction to another affliction, and one fear to another fear.
From the dead, those who have died—poor ones and evildoers—go to various kinds of destinies; living beings go [to these states] due to the bondage of their karma.
Those who possess faith, who are peaceful, who give wealth, and who perform auspicious deeds, go from festival to festival, from heaven to heaven, and from happiness to happiness.
Fierce beasts, elephants, and inaccessible terrains, as well as the terrors of snakes and thieves—sinners, struck down by their own evil, go [to these]; what could be more than this?
In the same way, the merit and demerit of men, accumulated through the collection of many hundreds of thousands of births, gives rise to the sprouts of happiness and suffering.
Just as a seed, O protector of the earth,
depends upon water,
so too does [the fruit] depend upon merit and demerit, as well as time, place, other actions, and the agent.
Even a very slight evil committed by a person, when brought about by the influence of place and time,
yields suffering like that caused by a thorn stepped upon while walking.
That produces even more abundant and gross suffering arising from stakes and spikes,
as well as unbearable suffering such as diseases of the head and so forth.
Just as indigestion, fasting, cold, heat, fatigue, fever,
and so forth depend upon one another to produce their effects, so too do sinful deeds depend on one another at the time of the ripening of their fruits.
In this way, great sins indeed result in transformations such as long-term diseases and the like,
as well as in the fruits of suffering from weapons, fire, torture, imprisonment, and so forth.
One who offers even a very small amount of merit, a pure fragrance, or with ease provides touch, sound, taste, or even form— MarkP_14.29—
In the same way, that which arises after a long time, even if it is very great and born of a long duration, [is experienced];
and thus indeed are pleasures and pains produced by merit and demerit.
Experiencing [the fruits] arising from many cycles of existence, he remains here,
subject to births restricted by place, as well as the fruits of knowledge and ignorance.
There, men who are disciplined never at any time or place manifest [their true nature] toward themselves by means of mere outward signs, nor through their body, mind, or speech.
Whether performing evil karma or abiding in merit, whatever suffering or even happiness a person encounters, [it is the result of that]. (MarkP 14.33)
Whether it be abundant or very small, if it causes a transformation of the mind,
to that extent there is merit or demermer for him, or otherwise.
Through their experience [of suffering], they go to destruction, like food being consumed;
thus these [beings] endure great sin through agonies day and night.
Just so, O King, men who revolve within the terrible hells exhaust their [sins],
and likewise the immortals in the heavenly world exhaust their merits.
In the states of gods, humans, and animals, they experience auspicious and inauspicious results through the songs and other enjoyments of gandharvas, siddhas, and apsarases.
O King, as for what you ask me regarding the torments of evildoers: one experiences the results arising from merit and sin, characterized by pleasure and pain.
"By what [means] and by what [sin]? I shall tell you that in its entirety."
The wives of others were gazed upon with wicked eyes by the lowest of men,
and the property of others was coveted with a wicked mind.
Those birds with diamond-tips snatch away their eyes;
moreover, the rebirth of these eyes occurs for them again and again.

For as many moments as it takes for these men to blink their eyes while committing evil, for that many thousands of years they shall indeed experience the fruit of their deeds in the presence of Netra.
But those men by whom instructions contrary to the sacred scriptures were given, and by whom they were counseled,
acted for the destruction of right view, even if it were that of their enemies.

Those by whom the scripture has been proclaimed otherwise, those by whom improper speech has been uttered, and those by whom revilement was directed toward the Vedas, the gods, the twice-born, or the guru; ||| MarkP_14.43 |||
Their tongues are pulled out again and again as they are born; for that many years, these beings, with diamond-beaks and ever-terrible, continue to devour them.
Likewise, the sowing of dissension between father and son, between kinsmen, between the patron and the preceptor, or between mother and her son who lives with her; ||| MarkP_14.45 |||
And those lowest of men who created dissension between wife and husband—
behold them, O King, as they are being sawn apart with a saw.
Those who cause suffering to others and those who obstruct the joy of others [are reborn as] those who steal the breeze from palm-leaf fans and the fragrance of sandalwood and ushira root.
Those base ones who inflict life-ending torment upon the innocent—
these partakers of evil now dwell amidst the sand of boiling gruel.
But that man who, having been invited by one person, eats at another's *śrāddha*,
whether for the sake of the gods (*daiva*) or the ancestors (*pitrya*), is torn asunder in two ways by birds.
But those birds remain there, unimpeded, piercing with their beaks that man who cuts the vital organs of the virtuous with wicked words.
He who practices slander, speaks with malicious intent, and possesses a distorted mind—
his tongue is thus split in two by sharp razors.
Those who, being arrogant, have shown contempt for their mother, father, and teachers,
these very people sink head-first into a pit of pus, excrement, and urine.
Those who eat while the deities, guests, living beings, servants,
and visitors have not yet eaten, as well as those who eat before the ancestors, the sacred fires, and birds, [commit a sin].
Those wicked ones, who feed on the exudation of pus and have needle-like mouths, are born with the stature of great mountains; behold what kind of men they are!
Those who feed a Brahmin or one born of another caste unequally in a single row in this world are eaters of excrement, just like these.
Those who eat their own food while abandoning a man traveling with them in the same caravan who is destitute and seeking wealth— they are eaters of phlegm.
O Lord of Men, those by whom cows, Brahmins, or fires were touched while they were impure from eating leftovers—
their hands are cast into jars of fire and forced to lick them.
For those by whom the sun, the moon, and the stars have been looked upon while they were impure from eating,
fire is placed in their eyes by the men of Yama and it blazes up.

Cows, fire, one's mother, a learned Brahmin, an elder brother, a father, a sister, female relatives, teachers, and the elderly— those men by whom these have been touched with their feet [are to be purified].
With their legs bound by iron shackles heated by fire, they stand in the midst of heaps of glowing coals, burning up to their knees.

The eyes of those sinners who have eaten milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, goat-meat, or whatever foods are fit for the gods, without having first performed the consecratory rites (saṃskāra), shall be [plucked out].
Behold, as they lie cast upon the surface of the earth with upturned eyes staring,
they are then dragged from their mouths by the Yama-attendants using pincers.
By those lowest of men who have listened to the censure of gurus, gods, the twice-born, and the Vedas, and who take delight in sins; (63)
These messengers of Yama repeatedly drive iron spikes, raining fire,
into the ears of those who are even then wailing.

While they are thus wailing repeatedly, the exceedingly cruel servants of Yama strip away their skin from their bodies with these sharp weapons.
Those men who void urine upon cows, Brahmins, the sun, or on the path—
their entrails are dragged from their anus by crows.
Having given his daughter to one man, he gives her to a second;
thus severed in many ways, he is carried away in the river of alkaline water.
But that man who, intent on nourishing himself alone, abandons his sons, servants, wife, and other circle of kinsmen when they possess nothing; ||| MarkP_14.69 |||
Even during a famine or a time of upheaval, he likewise eats his own flesh, which has been cut off and placed in his mouth by the servants of Yama, due to his hunger.
He who, out of greed, abandons those who have come for refuge and depend upon him for their livelihood,
is likewise tormented by the servants of Yama with the crushing of machines.
Those men who bestow the merit they have performed throughout their entire lives are ground with stone-grinders, just like these evildoers.
Those men who have stolen deposits are bound with fetters on all their limbs and are devoured day and night by worms, scorpions, and crows.
Emaciated by hunger, their tongues falling from their palates due to thirst,
those sinners who engage in sexual intercourse during the day and those who enjoy the wives of others suffer from intense agony.
In the same way, behold the silk-cotton tree (śālmali) with its long iron thorns; those whose limbs are pierced by them stand there, drenched and fouled by the profuse flow of their blood.
O tiger among men, behold also these men, who were intolerant of others' wives, being destroyed by the servants of Yama within the crucibles.
That man who, having placed his teacher beneath him, haughtily receives instruction—
whether it be sacred learning or a craft— he too shall thus carry a stone upon his head.
Bearing his burden, he suffers great affliction on the road of worldly existence;

Those by whom urine, phlegm, and excrement were cast into the water have now gone to this hell, foul-smelling with phlegm, feces, and urine.
Driven by hunger, they will devour one another's flesh;

But those by whom the Vedas have been cast aside and who have abandoned their sacred fires—
these are repeatedly hurled down from the tip of the Śāla peak.
Furthermore, those kings who remain alive until they are worn out by old age—
having fallen into the state of worms here, they are devoured by ants.
By accepting gifts from outcasts, by officiating at sacrifices for them, and by constantly serving them,

While his circle of servants, friends, and guests look on,

O King, because he devoured the back-flesh of people, his own back is constantly being consumed by terrifying wolves. (MarkPurāṇa 14.85)
Blind, deaf, and mute, this man wanders about afflicted by hunger—

This ungrateful man, who harms his friends and is of evil mind, falls into a vessel of heated iron; from there, he shall go to the grinding mill.
From that [comes] the sand of boiling gruel; from that, the crushing by machines;

Having undergone the Kālasūtra hell, as well as cutting and many other torments, I do not know how he will ever find release from this.
The Brahmins assembled at the *śrāddha*, rising up against one another,

The thief of gold, the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—

They remain for many thousands of years,

A cow-killer goes to hell for a longer duration than that, and likewise for all minor offenses (upapātaka); such is the certainty.
Listen as I describe those various wombs into which those who have fallen from hell go, according to the specific sins they have committed.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Yama’s Servant and Jaḍa," in the Jaḍopākhyāna of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

Yama’s Servant said:
A twice-born man who accepts wealth from an outcast shall go to the womb of a donkey;

A creature who insults his parents is born as a donkey;

One who treats his brother’s wife with contempt attains the state of a pigeon;

He who consumes the food provided by his master but does not perform the service desired by him,

One who steals a sacred deposit (nyāsa) is reborn as a worm after being released from hell;

From violating another's wife, one is born as a large-mouthed mouse resembling a brown mongoose,

A worm, an insect, a moth, a bird, an aquatic creature, or a wild beast; and having attained the state of a cow, or even the loathsome condition of a Caṇḍāla or Pukkasa.

Therefore, O King, the wind that comes from contact with your body bestows delight;

The father said:

Whatever consciousness exists there is not found elsewhere;
O dear one, this [teaching] is the supreme remover of all doubts even for the wise.

Those men who are firm in their resolve attain godhood, the status of lord of the immortals, or the state of being worshiped by them, or whatever else they desire.

This best of horses, capable of traversing the entire circle of the earth without fatigue,

O best of the twice-born, that wicked one, the lowest of dānavas, who torments you day and night— he too shall be slain after you have mounted him.

In that same way, I shall give a name to your fourth son.
"O knower of dharma, this younger son of yours shall attain fame in the world as Alarka, and he shall be wise."

Having heard that name given to his son by his mother, the lord of the earth laughed and then spoke these words, which were inconsistent with the name "Alarka": MarkP_26.14: "Having heard that name given to his son by his mother, the lord of the earth laughed and then spoke these words, which were inconsistent with the name 'Alarka'."
The king said:
"O auspicious lady, what is this name that has been given to my son by you?
Why is it so incoherent; what is its meaning, Madālasā?"
Madālasā said:
"O Great King, this is a conceptual construction; it has been made for the sake of worldly convention."
O King, hear now the meaninglessness of those names created by you.
Wise men declare that the Puruṣa is all-pervading, since "krānti" (striding) is defined as the movement from one place to another. 26.17.
"Since the Lord of the body is all-pervading and does not go anywhere,
this designation 'Vikrānta' (the Strider) is, in my view, meaningless."
O Lord of the Earth, that name "Subāhu" which was given by you to this other son of yours is likewise meaningless, because the Puruṣa is formless.
As for the name "Arimardana" given to the third son, I consider that too to be inappropriate; hear now the reason for this as well.
When the Puruṣa is indeed one and the same within all bodies,
then, O King, who here is considered his enemy, or who is his friend? (MarkP 26.21)
Beings are crushed by beings; how can that which is formless be crushed?
Since anger and the other [afflictions] exist as distinct entities, this conceptualization is meaningless.
If a non-existent name is devised for the sake of conventional usage,
why do you consider the name "Alarka" to be devoid of meaning?
Jaḍa said:
Having been thus addressed by that virtuous queen, that lord of the earth,
possessed of great intelligence, said "So be it" to his beloved wife who spoke the truth.
And that fair-browed woman spoke to that son as she had to her previous sons, words that produce awakening; to her, the king then said: MarkP_26.25 //
"What are you doing, O fool, by providing this wicked understanding for my lineage’s destruction, just as you did previously toward my sons? (MarkP 26.26)
If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, and if my word is to be accepted,
then establish this son on the path of spiritual practice.
"O Goddess, the path of karma will not thus come to an end;
nor, O virtuous lady, will there be a cessation of the ancestral offerings."
The ancestors dwelling in the world of the gods, as well as those who have entered the state of animals,
likewise those who have attained human status and those established among the classes of elemental beings— [all these are sustained by that].
A man established in his duty, by the offering of morsels of food and water, [delivers] both those with merit and those without merit who are emaciated by hunger and overwhelmed by thirst.
O fair-browed one, it is always nourished;
likewise, it is nourished by gods, guests,
humans, ancestors, spirits, and guhyakas.
A human being alone is sustained by birds, worms, and insects;
therefore,
O slender-limbed one, that which must be done for a son by those born of the Kṣatriya caste— [that you must do].
Please duly bestow that fruit which pertains to both this world and the next.
Jaḍa said:
Thus addressed by her husband, that excellent woman Madālasā spoke to her son named Alarka with playful words.
"O son, grow strong; gladden the heart of my husband with your deeds, for the benefit of your friends and for the destruction of your enemies."
O son, you are fortunate indeed, for you alone shall long protect the earth free from enemies;
from that protection, may there be the enjoyment of happiness.
And from dharma you shall obtain the fruit of immortality.
On festival days, you should gratify the gods and ancestors;
you should fulfill the desires of your kinsmen;
and you should contemplate the welfare of others in your heart.
You should turn your mind away from the wives of others.
Constantly gratify the gods with numerous sacrifices, the twice-born with wealth, and those who depend upon you,
as well as women, for a long time with incomparable objects of desire.
And by battles, O hero, you shall satisfy your enemies.
A child delights his kinsmen;
likewise, a youth delights his teacher through acts of service;
and a young man delights women who are ornaments of noble families.
O child, he is an old man dwelling in the forest among those who roam the woods.
While ruling the kingdom, O dear one, you should gladden your friends by protecting the virtuous;
you should perform sacrifices with offerings.
O child, for the sake of cows and Brahmins, you should meet death in the midst of battle by smelling the breath of wicked enemies.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Instruction to the Son," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
The twenty-seventh chapter begins with Jaḍa saying:
Thus being addressed day after day by his mother,
that boy named Ālarka grew in both age and intelligence.
Then, having reached his youth and having been initiated, that wise son of Ṛtadhvaja prostrated himself and spoke to his mother.
Tell me everything that I, bowing with humility, ought to do here for the sake of happiness in this world and the next.
Madālasā said:
"O child, a king who has been consecrated to the kingdom must, from the very beginning, act to delight his subjects without contradicting his own dharma."
Having abandoned the seven vices that destroy the very root,
one must protect oneself from enemies by keeping secret counsel from leaking outward.
Just as a chariot meets with eightfold destruction because of its wheels,
so too a king undoubtedly perishes when his counsel leaks out to the outside.
One should discern which ministers are wicked and which are not by means of their enemies' faults;
likewise, spies should be diligently sought out through the spies of the enemy.
A king should not place trust in friends, acquaintances, or kinsmen;
rather, O lord of men, he should place his trust even in an enemy when it serves his purpose.
A lord of men must be one who knows the increase and decrease of his positions, whose self is refined by the sixfold policy, and who does not act under the sway of desire.
First, the king must conquer himself and his ministers, then his servants;
immediately after that, the citizens, and finally he may contend with his enemies.
But he who seeks to conquer these enemies without first conquering himself— though his ministers may be subdued— is oppressed by the host of his foes.
Therefore, my son, desires and the like must first be conquered by the sovereign;
for when they are conquered, victory is certain, but a king defeated by them perishes.
Lust, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, and likewise exhilaration—
these are indeed the enemies that lead to the destruction of kings.
Just as he turned back Pāṇḍu, who had been struck down after remembering himself to be addicted to sensual desire,
so too should he turn back Anuhrāda, whose son has been slain, from his wrath.
Hatamaila was killed by greed, Vena by pride, the twice-born by arrogance, Anāyuṣa by anger, and Purañjaya by joy.
When these have been conquered, everything has been conquered by the high-souled Marutta;
therefore, having reflected on this, a lord of the earth should avoid these faults that belong to himself.
A king should emulate the conduct of the crow, the cuckoo, and the bee; of the deer, the serpent, and the peacock; and of the swan, the cock, and the iron [ore]. (Markandeya Purana 27.17)
The lord of men should employ measures against insects;
at the proper time, the king should also take action against ants.
The king should understand the sparks of the fire of the knowable and the activity of the seed of the silk-cotton tree (śālmali) in the form of the moon and the sun for the sake of political policy.
Wisdom should not be accepted from a harlot, a lotus, a śarabha deer, a trident, the breasts of a pregnant woman, nor likewise from the wife of a cowherd, O King.
Likewise, for the sake of the task of protecting the earth, the lord of the earth should assume the five forms of Śakra, Arka, Yama, Soma, and Vāyu.
Just as Indra nourishes the earth with the release of water for four months,
so should the lord of the earth nourish the world with acts of remission.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays over the course of eight months,
so too should a king collect taxes and other dues by subtle means.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come,
so should the king be impartial toward the liked and the disliked, and toward the wicked and the virtuous.
Just as a man becomes filled with joy upon beholding the full moon,
so too is that the Śaśivrata, wherein all subjects find their fulfillment.
Just as the wind moves hidden within all living beings,
so should a king move among his citizens, ministers, and kinsmen by means of spies.
O child, that king whose mind is not dragged away by others through greed, desire, or worldly gain, attains heaven.
That king who establishes on their own duty those men who are deluded, who have taken to wrong paths,
and who have strayed from their own dharma, attains heaven.
O child, he in whose kingdom the duties of the castes and the stages of life do not decline attains eternal happiness both in this world and in the hereafter.
This is the supreme duty of a king, and likewise the means to achieve success:
the establishment of men in their own dharma, for they are led astray by those of evil intellect.
By the very protection of living beings, the lord of the earth fulfills his duty;
as a proper protector, he diligently obtains a share of the merit of dharma.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Discrimination of the Self," in the dialogue between father and son within the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Chapter Twenty-Eight.
Jaḍa said:
Having heard those words of his mother, Alarka again questioned his mother regarding the duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) and the duties pertaining to the stages of life (āśramadharma).
Alarka said:
"O highly fortunate lady, this which you have related concerns the administration of a kingdom."
I wish to hear that Dharma which consists of the system of social classes and stages of life.
Madālasā said:
"Giving, study, and sacrifice are considered the threefold duty of a Brāhmaṇa;
there is no other fourth duty for him except in times of distress."
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts—
this threefold livelihood of his has been correctly described.
Giving, study, and sacrifice—this threefold duty is declared for the Kṣatriya as well;
the protection of the earth and living by the sword are his means of livelihood.
Giving, study, and sacrifice—these three duties belong to the Vaiśya as well;
moreover, trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are his means of livelihood.
Giving, sacrifice, and service to the twice-born— these three have been explained by me as the duty of the Śūdra, as well as his livelihood through manual crafts.
In the same way, service to the twice-born, nourishing them, and buying and selling—these are declared to be the duties of the castes;
now hear those pertaining to the stages of life (āśramas).
A man attains perfection by adhering to the duties of his own caste and does not fall away from it;
however, by practicing what is forbidden, he goes to hell after death.
But as long as the initiation ceremony is not performed for the twice-born,
my son, he remains subject to acting, speaking, and eating according to his own desires.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, let the student dwell properly as a celibate in the house of his teacher;
listen to me as I describe the dharma pertaining to him there.
Vedic study, service to the sacred fire, bathing, and likewise wandering for alms—
these should always be performed after offering that food to the guru and with his permission.
One should be diligent in the service of the guru and properly provide him with satisfaction; when summoned by him, one should study with that as one's sole purpose, without a distracted mind.
Having received one, two, or even all the Vedas from the mouth of a guru,
he should then, being permitted by him, pay homage and offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru.
One who desires the stage of the householder should dwell in the householder's stage;
or he may enter the forest-dweller's stage, or the fourth, according to his own inclination.
Or, in that very place, namely in the house of the guru, the twice-born man shall attain completion;
in the absence of the guru, he may do so with the guru’s son, or with his disciple, provided there is no son of the guru.
Desirous of learning and free from pride, he should dwell in the stage of the student (brahmacarya);
then, having returned from that stage, he may desire the stage of the householder (gṛhastha).

Then, for the sake of entering the householder stage of life, he should lawfully marry a wife who is of a different lineage from his own Ṛṣi-family, of equal status, healthy, and free from physical defects.
Having acquired wealth through his own labor, he should properly satisfy the ancestors, the gods, and guests with devotion, and likewise support those who depend upon him.
Then, by giving food according to their capacity, they [honored] servants, children, sisters, as well as the poor, the blind, the fallen, birds, and likewise animals.
This is the duty of a householder: approaching his wife during her season, as well as not neglecting the performance of the five sacrifices according to his ability.
After the ancestors, gods, guests, and kinsmen have eaten, a man himself should eat the remains with his dependents, respectfully and according to his means.
This stage of life for the householder has been declared by me in brief;
now I shall describe the duty of the forest-dweller—let it be heeded.
Having seen the continuity of his offspring and having subdued his senses,
a wise man should enter the stage of the forest-dweller for the sake of his own purification.
In that regard, there is the enjoyment of forest-dwelling, the drawing [of the self] through austerities,
sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and the performance of rites for the ancestors, the gods, and guests.
Performing fire oblations, bathing three times a day, wearing matted hair and bark garments, constant practice of yoga, and subsisting on forest oils.

Thus, this stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) serves for the purification of one’s sins and is beneficial to oneself; therefore, it is the final and other [distinct] stage for the mendicant (bhikṣu).
Now hear from me the true nature of the fourth stage of life,
O dear one, which has been declared as its specific duty by the great-souled ones who know the dharma.
The renunciation of all attachments, the practice of celibacy, freedom from anger,
restraint of the senses, and not dwelling for long in a single residence.
Likewise, abstaining from worldly undertakings, subsisting on alms-food taken only once a day,
the desire for the awakening of self-knowledge, and the contemplation of the Self.
This dharma for the fourth stage of life has been declared by me to you;
now hear from me that which is common to the other castes and to the other stages of life.
Truthfulness, purity, non-violence, lack of envy, as well as forbearance,
benevolence, lack of miserliness, and contentment is the eighth quality.
These duties for the various classes and stages of life have been declared to you in brief;
one should remain entirely established in these respective duties of one's own.
Any man who, transgressing his own duty defined by his caste and stage of life,
should act otherwise, must be punished by the king.
Furthermore, when men commit evil by abandoning their own duty,
the merit of the king’s sacrifices and charitable works perishes if he neglects them.
Therefore, with diligent effort, the king should ensure that all social classes proceed according to their own duties;
otherwise, they are to be punished and established once more in their respective tasks.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Words of Madalasa," in the *Putrānuśāsana* (Instruction to the Son) section of the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. Chapter Twenty-nine:
Alarka said:
That which is the duty of men who follow the householder stage of life,
wherein there would be bondage through non-performance and the attainment of elevation through its performance.
Tell me, as I ask you, exactly what should be done for the benefit of men and what should be avoided by a virtuous man in his home, and how it is to be performed.
Madālasā said:
"O child, by adopting the householder's state, a man nourishes this entire world; through that, he conquers the desired worlds."
The ancestors, sages, gods, beings, and likewise humans;
as well as worms, insects, moths, birds, animals, and asuras.
Householders depend upon him, and from that they attain satisfaction;
they gaze upon his face, wondering indeed, "Will he give us something? (MarkP 29.5).
"O child, this cow consisting of the three Vedas is the support of all;
upon her the entire universe is established, and she is considered the cause of the universe."
She has the *Ṛgveda* as her back, the *Yajurveda* as her middle, and the *Sāmaveda* as her mouth and neck;
she has sacrifices and charitable works as her horns, and the hymns of the virtuous as her body hair.
Consisting of feces, urine, and the elements of peace and nourishment, established upon the earth as its color and foundation, it is the sustenance of all worlds; inexhaustible, it does not diminish.
O son, the utterances Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ,
and Hanta constitute her four breasts.
The gods and the ancestors made the *svāhākāra* their breast consisting of *svadhā*,
while the sages and the beings other than gods and spirits made the *vaṣaṭkāra* theirs.
Humans drink the *hantakāra* offering and constantly suckle at the breast;
in this way, O child, this cow consisting of the three Vedas nourishes them.
And that man who is an exterminator of them, being an evildoer of the utmost degree,
sinks into the Andhatāmisra, the Tāmisra, and the Tamasa hells.
And that man who causes this cow to drink with her own calves— the gods and others— at the proper time, he attains heaven.
Therefore, my son, a human being must nourish daily the gods, sages, ancestors, men, and elemental spirits, just as one nourishes one's own body.
Therefore, having bathed and become pure, one should, being composed, perform at the proper time the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as those to Prajāpati and the Ādityas.
Having worshipped the gods with *sumana* flowers and fragrant blossoms,
a person should then perform the satiation of the fire and likewise offer oblations (*bali*).
One should offer the bali-oblation to Brahmā in the middle of the house, and likewise to the Viśvedevas;
and dedicated to Dhanvantari, one should cast the bali toward the north-east.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Śakra in the east, to Yama in the south,
to Varuṇa in the west, and then to Soma in the north.
One should offer an oblation to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the door of the house;
then one should offer it to Aryaman outside, and to the household deities on all sides.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the nocturnal spirits from the sky,
and one should likewise present it to the ancestors while standing facing the south.
The householder, becoming intent upon that with a well-composed mind,
should then take water from those very vessels for the purpose of sipping (ācamana).
The wise man should place [the offerings] in their respective places, designating them for various deities.
Having thus performed the domestic bali offering, the master of the house remains pure within his home.
For the nourishment of all beings, he should respectfully perform the ritual offering;
he should scatter food on the ground for dogs, for outcastes, and for birds.
For this is indeed called the Vaiśvadeva rite, prescribed for both evening and morning;
having sipped water (ācamana), the wise man should then perform the inspection of the door.
Even one who appears for only an eighth part of a muhūrta should be regarded as a guest;
when such a guest arrives there, he should be honored with food, drink, and water.
One should worship [the deity] according to one's ability with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
however, one should not treat a friend or a resident of the same village as a guest.
One whose family and name were unknown, who had arrived at that moment,
hungry, weary, begging, and possessing nothing.
They say that a Brahmin is a guest; he should be honored by the wise according to their ability.
A learned man should not inquire about his lineage, his Vedic school, or even his private study.
One should regard that Prajāpati as having both beautiful and ugly forms;
because he remains impermanent, he is therefore called a guest.
When he is satisfied, the householder is released from the debt arising from the sacrifice to men;
therefore, the man who eats by himself without having given [to him] is merely a consumer of sin.
He who has a guest turn back from his house with hopes frustrated eats only sin and excrement in another birth.
Having given that evil deed to him, he departs taking away the merit;
even by the gift of water or vegetables, or whatever he himself eats.
A man should honor a guest with due respect according to his ability;
and he should perform the *śrāddha* rite day after day with food, drink, and water.
One should feed the Brahmins with the ancestors in mind, or indeed a single Brahmin alone;
having set aside the first portion of the food, one should present it to that Brahmin.
And he should give alms to wandering mendicants and students;
an alms-meal should be the size of a mouthful, and four such mouthfuls constitute a full meal.
The best of the twice-born say that the *agra* (first portion) multiplied by four is the *hantakāra*;
or rather, the *hantakāra* is a meal, or else it is the *agra*, or even alms (*bhikṣā*).
One should not eat without having first given according to one's means to beloved guests, kinsmen, relatives, and those who seek assistance. (MarkP 29.37)
One should feed those who are physically impaired, children, the elderly, and likewise the sick,
as well as any other person destitute of food whose soul is overcome by hunger.
When one has the means and wealth available, a kinsman should be fed;
for that kinsman who suffers while a wealthy relative is present [is a great loss].
Whatever has been done by one who is sinking [in distress], he partakes of that very sin;
furthermore, the evening rite must be performed there, and the guest brought by the setting sun [must be honored].
One should honor him according to one's ability with beds, seats, and food;
thus, my dear, does one carry the burden of the householder’s life that has been undertaken.
In the *Skandha* [Purāṇa], the Creator, the gods, the ancestors, and the great seers—
all of whom shower down blessings— as well as guests and kinsmen, are likewise described.

The herds of beasts and flocks of birds, as well as other minute insects, were satisfied; and here, O highly fortunate one, Atri himself sang these verses: MarkP_29.43: "O highly fortunate one, Atri himself sang these verses here."
Listen to that, O highly fortunate one:
those established in the householder stage of life,
having duly honored the gods, the ancestors, guests, and likewise their kinsmen.
A householder who possesses wealth should give food on the ground even to his sister's sons, to his teacher,
to dogs, to outcastes (śvapacas), and to birds.
For this is indeed called the Vaiśvadeva; one should perform it both in the evening and during the day.
Whatever meat, grain, or vegetables has been prepared in the house, he must not eat that himself until he has offered it according to the rule.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Madālasā," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty.
Madālasā said:
Listen, my son, to that which is the duty of the householder: the daily rite, the occasional rite, and likewise the daily-occasional rite. // MarkP_30.1 //
That which has been described to you as the perpetual [duty] based on the five sacrifices, as well as the occasional [rites], such as the ceremonies for the birth of a son and so forth; 30.2.
The wise should understand that the *nitya* (obligatory) and *naimittika* (occasional) rites include the *parva-śrāddha* and others;
therein, I shall describe to you the occasional *śrāddha* for prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Whatever rite is to be performed by men at the birth of a son, equal to the *jātakarman*,
and that which is to be done at marriage and other occasions— all that has been correctly described.
And here the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas are to be honored;
one should offer them rice-balls mixed with curd and combined with barley.
Facing either north or east, the sacrificer, with a concentrated mind—
some men maintain that such [an offering] is devoid of the Vaiśvadeva rite.
In this rite, an even number of twice-born men should be engaged, and they are to be honored by circumambulation from left to right;
this is the occasional rite for prosperity, as well as other rites pertaining to the deceased.
Now listen to that which must be performed on the anniversary of the death: the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
it should be performed without [invoking] the gods, and likewise with only a single sacred grass ring (*pavitraka*).
One should not perform the invocation (āvāhana), as it is devoid of the fire-offering (agnaukaraṇa);
one should offer a single pinda for the deceased in the vicinity of the remnants of the meal.
And the water with sesame seeds, poured with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) while recollecting the name of the deceased,
[is offered] with the words "May it be inexhaustible for so-and-so," at the point where the Brahmins are dismissed.
One should say, "May you take pleasure [in this]," and they should reply, "We do take pleasure.
This should be performed by men every month for the duration of a year.
Now, when a full year has passed, or whenever it is performed by men, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite must be carried out; its procedure is now being declared.
And that [offering] as well, being devoid of the divine [invocation], consisting of a single *arghya* and a single *pavitraka*,
has no *agnaukaraṇa* there, and it is likewise devoid of the *āvāhana*.
There too, one should feed an odd number of twice-born men with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
furthermore, there is another specific distinction there: an additional rite performed every month.
Listen with one-pointed attention as I describe it:
there, four vessels filled with sesame seeds, scented water, and other offerings [should be prepared].
O son, one should perform three offerings for the ancestors and one for the deceased;
one should pour the water of honor (arghya) from the vessel of the deceased into the three vessels.
Reciting "ye samānā," he should perform the remainder as previously described;
this same Ekoddiṣṭa rite is declared to be for women as well.
The sapindikarana rite for those women does not exist in the absence of a son;
rather, men should perform the ekoddista rite for a woman every year.
On the anniversary of the day of death, according to the rule prescribed here for men,
the sapinda relatives perform the rites in the absence of sons, and in their absence, the sodaka relatives.
The sapinda relatives of the mother, as well as those who are her sodaka relatives, should properly perform this rite for one who has no son; even a grandson may do so.
In this same manner, the sons of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should likewise perform [the rites] for their maternal grandfather;
those known as dvaimātura (sons of two fathers) should perform them for both their maternal and paternal grandfathers.
They should perform worship according to the rule, both with regular and occasional *śrāddha* rites;
in the absence of all [male relatives], women should perform it for their own husbands without mantras.
And in the absence of such persons, the king shall cause all the rites, beginning with cremation, to be properly performed by his own householders or by men of that same caste.
Since the king is the kinsman of all social classes, these rites,
O child, have been described to you as both daily and occasional.
Now hear of another rite based on the *śrāddha*, which is both regular (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*).
In that case, the new moon (*darśa*) is indeed the occasion, and the time consists of the waning of the moon;
furthermore, the fixed time indicates its status as a regular duty.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Occasional Śrāddhas and Others," in the *Alarkānuśāsana* section of the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-one. Madālase said:
After the sapindikarana rite, the great-grandfather of the father becomes a recipient of the lepa (the smearings of the offerings) and passes away,
having been severed from the ancestral pinda.
Among them, the fourth is he who eats the food smeared for the son;
he too, due to that connection, obtains a diminished enjoyment.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
these three men are to be known as those connected by the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
And other relatives connected by asceticism (tapas), beginning from the great-grandfather, are said to be three; with the sacrificer himself, they constitute seven.
Thus has this ancestral lineage been declared, extending for seven generations;
starting from the sacrificer and ascending upwards, those who partake of the unguents are likewise included.
Then all his other ancestors, those others who dwell in the hells,
those who have entered the state of animals, and those who exist as spirits and the like— [all these were liberated].
O child, listen to that by which the sacrificer, performing the śrāddha according to the rules, causes all of them to swell with nourishment. MarkP_31.7 //
Whatever scattering of food is performed on the earth by human beings,
by that those who have fallen into the state of Piśācas attain satisfaction.
O son, whatever water falls upon the ground from the bathing cloth produces satisfaction for those who have attained the state of trees.
And those droplets of water from his body that fall upon the surface of the earth provide nourishment for those who have attained divinity within their family.
Then, when the rice-balls have been lifted up, those who have fallen into the state of animals or entered a low family receive nourishment from the grains of food that remain on the ground.
Those children in the family who are uneducated, immature, unfit for ritual action,
and unconsecrated, perish by consuming the scattered food and the water used for sweeping.
And by the water that the Brahmins sip after eating, as well as by the water used for washing their feet,
others indeed attain satisfaction.
Thus, whatever scattering of water or food there may be from the sacrificer or from those twice-born ones— whether it be pure or even impure remnants— [is not defiling].
Therefore, O child, others born into that same family who have entered various other wombs attain nourishment through those who perform the śrāddha rites correctly.
The śrāddha that is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means satisfies those born in such wombs as the caṇḍālas and pukkasas.
In this way, my child,
for many kinsmen here,
nourishment arises through the performance of a śrāddha by scattering drops of food and water.
Therefore, a man should perform a śrāddha with devotion, even if only with vegetables, according to the prescribed rules;
for one who performs the śrāddha, no one in his family shall suffer.
I shall describe its times, consisting of the regular and the occasional;
learn from me the rule by which it is performed by men.
The śrāddha rite must be performed on the new moon day every month when the moon has waned, as well as during the aṣṭakās; now learn from me the times for optional performance.

O son, [one should perform this] upon meeting a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, during solar and lunar eclipses, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, at the sun's transition into a new zodiac sign, and during the Vyatīpāta yoga.
Upon obtaining materials suitable for a śrāddha, as well as upon seeing an evil dream,
or when one's birth star is afflicted by malefic planets, one may perform a śrāddha according to one's desire.

One who is distinguished, a learned scholar of the Vedas, a yogi, a knower of the Vedas, a singer of the Jyeṣṭha-sāman, one who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire, one who knows the three sweets, one who knows the Tri-suparṇa hymn, and a knower of the six auxiliary sciences.
A daughter’s son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, a sister’s son, a father-in-law, one devoted to the five-fire ritual, one devoted to austerity, and likewise a maternal uncle; MarkP_31.24 //
Furthermore, those devoted to their parents, as well as disciples, relatives, and kinsmen—
these best of the twice-born are all worthy of being invited to a śrāddha ceremony.
One who has spilled his seed, as well as one who is diseased, one with a missing limb or an extra limb,
one born of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, a *kuṇḍa*, a *gola*, and likewise a son [of such a union].
One who betrays a friend, one with deformed nails, a eunuch, one with black teeth, one who has been expelled from his caste,
one who is slandered by his father, a backbiter, and a seller of Soma— these are excluded.
One who defiles a maiden, a physician, one who abandons his guru or father, a teacher for hire, an enemy, and likewise the husband of a woman previously married to another; MarkP_31.28 //

Furthermore, those who have abandoned the Vedas, those who have renounced the sacred fires, those defiled by being the husbands of low-caste women (vṛṣalīs), and other twice-born men engaged in improper occupations must indeed be excluded from rites for the ancestors.
On the day before, one should invite the best of the twice-born as previously described;
for the rites dedicated to the gods and those dedicated to the ancestors, one should prepare them in that same manner.
Those female ascetics must remain self-restrained; and as for whoever shall perform a *śrāddha*—if, after giving or consuming the *śrāddha*, one engages in sexual intercourse, [he incurs sin].
But for those two, the ancestors lie within that semen for a month;
this applies to both he who eats at a śrāddha after having approached a woman, and he who approaches a woman after having eaten at a śrāddha.
For that month, the ancestors of those two subsist on food made of feces and urine;
therefore, a wise person should first extend an invitation to them.
On that day, even when food has not been obtained, those who are devoted to women must avoid ascetics and self-controlled mendicants who have arrived at the proper time for the sake of alms.
One should feed them with prostrations and other marks of respect, having propitiated them with a restrained mind;
for just as the dark fortnight is indeed dearer to the ancestors than the bright fortnight.
Likewise, the afternoon is considered superior to the forenoon for the ancestors;
having honored these twice-born who have arrived at his home with a welcome, [he should proceed].
With the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand, he should seat those who have sipped water on their seats—
the odd number of the best of the twice-born for the ancestors as desired, and an even number for the gods.
Or, according to one's own ability, one may perform the rite for each of the ancestors and the gods individually,
as well as for the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva offering equally for all.
Likewise, some other men maintain that these two [rites] are separate;
one should perform the rites intended for the gods facing east, and those for the ancestors facing north.
In the same manner, the wise have declared the rule for the maternal grandfathers:
having offered *kuśa* grass for the purpose of seats and having honored them with the *arghya* offering and other rites, the learned man should proceed.
Having offered the sacred grass-filters (pavitraka) and other items to them, and having obtained their permission,
the wise twice-born man should perform the invocation (āvāhana) of the gods with mantras.
Likewise, having offered the arghya for the Vaiśvadeva rite with barley-water, and having properly presented perfumes, garlands, water, incense, and a lamp; ||| MarkP_31.42 |||
One should arrange everything for the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
having given them double-folded darbha grass and having obtained their permission, one should proceed.
A wise person should perform the invocation of the ancestors preceded by the recitation of mantras;
likewise, he should offer the water for the hands (arghya) with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), and substitute sesame seeds for the barley.
"O illustrious one, being devoted to the gratification of the ancestors, you may perform the rite in the fire as authorized by the twice-born, who have said: 'Do so! (Markandeya Purana 31.45)
One should offer food, excluding condiments and salts, according to the prescribed rule;
"Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāha" is the first oblation.
One oblation should likewise be for Soma accompanied by the ancestors with "Svāhā," and there is a third oblation for Yama, the lord of the departed, with "Svāhā. (MarkP 31.47)
One should give the remnants of the oblation into the vessels of the twice-born;
having touched their vessels, one should offer the food according to the prescribed rule.
One should say, "Eat as you please, sir," in a gentle manner;
then they too, being focused on that and observing silence, shall eat happily.
Whatever is most desired by them, that very food a man should give without haste, without anger, and enticing them with hospitality.
One should mutter mantras that destroy Rākṣasas and scatter the earth with sesame seeds and white mustard for the sake of protection; for the Śrāddha rite is indeed full of deception.
When those who have been questioned and satisfied respond, "Are you satisfied? and say, "We are satisfied," the man, having received permission, should scatter food on the ground on all sides.
In the same way, he should offer water for the purpose of sipping once each time;
then, having obtained permission, he should remain with his speech, body, and mind restrained.
Then, O son, one should offer morsels of food mixed with sesame using the left hand upon *darbha* grass near the remains of the meal, intending them for the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
O Prince, with a concentrated mind, the sacrificer, out of devotion, should offer water to them by means of the *pitṛtīrtha*,
designating the ancestors.
In the same manner, having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the maternal grandfathers according to the rule,
he should then offer water for sipping (ācamana) accompanied by perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Having given according to his ability, he should say to the carpenters, "May there be a good svadhā!
And when they have replied, "So be it," being satisfied, he should cause those belonging to the Vaiśvadeva rite to recite the prayers.
One should utter, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased; may there be blessings upon you. When the brahmins have replied, "So be it," one should then request their benedictions.
Having spoken pleasant words and having prostrated with devotion, he should dismiss [the guest];
he should follow him as far as the door and return only after seeing him off with joy.
Then one should perform the daily rites and likewise feed the guests;
some excellent authorities maintain that the daily rite for the ancestors should also be performed.
Likewise for the ancestors; others should perform the remainder as previously described.
Others say it is not with a separate cooking, while some say the preceding part is to be done as before.
Then that man, together with his servants and others, should eat that food;
thus should the knower of dharma, being composed, perform the ancestral śrāddha.
Or rather, just as the satisfaction of the foremost of the twice-born is produced, there are three purifiers at a śrāddha: a daughter’s son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds.
And they say, O chief of Brahmins,
that anger, traveling on a road, and haste are to be avoided;
likewise, a silver vessel is commended for śrāddha rites, my son.
Likewise, silver should be used for the ritual act, whether for viewing or for giving;
for it is heard that the earth was milked by the ancestors as their own *svadhā*.
Therefore, silver is desired by the ancestors and increases their satisfaction.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha," in the *Alarkānuśāsana* section of the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-two.
Madālasā said:
Henceforth, my son, listen with devotion to this which has been brought forth for the pleasure of the ancestors— both that which should be avoided and that which causes them joy.
Satisfaction for the ancestors lasts for one month through offerings of sacrificial food (haviṣya);
through fish and meat, the grandfathers attain satisfaction for two months.
The meat of the deer is to be known as providing satisfaction to the ancestors for three months;
however, the flesh of the hare nourishes the ancestors for four months.
Flesh of birds for five months, pork for six months,
goat's flesh for seven months, and the meat of the eneya deer for eight months.
The flesh of the ruru deer indeed provides satisfaction for nine months; of this there is no doubt.
The meat of the gavaya provides satisfaction for ten months.
Likewise, mutton for eleven months grants satisfaction to the ancestors;
as does cow's milk, or even milk-rice (pāyasa), for a full year.
The meat of the vādhrīṇasa, iron, kālaśāka, honey, the meat of a daughter’s son, and whatever else is offered by those born of one's own lineage; ||| MarkP_32.7 |||
O son, the son of Gaurī likewise bestows infinite satisfaction upon the ancestors through the Gāyā-śrāddha; of this there is no doubt.
Śyāmāka, rājaśyāmāka, likewise prasātikā,
nīvāra, and pauṣkala— these grains serve for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Barley, rice, wheat, sesame, mung beans, mustard seeds, millet,
kovidāra, and flat beans are exceedingly auspicious.
Monkeys should be avoided at a śrāddha, as well as kidney beans and small grains;
those who eat like vultures and lentils are censured in the performance of the śrāddha rite.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and radishes; gruel,
and whatever other foods are deficient in taste and color.
Gāndhārika, bottle-gourds, salts, saline soils, those resins which are reddish, and salts visible to the eye; // MarkP_32.13 //
These indeed are to be avoided at a śrāddha: whatever is not praised by word of mouth, whatever is obtained through bribes and the like, and whatever is acquired from outcasts and the like.
In this [age], wealth obtained through the improper payment of a bride-price is censured;
likewise, water that is foul-smelling, frothy, or very scanty is condemned.
That food where a cow finds no satisfaction, that which is brought at night,
that which is not offered from all available portions, and that which is unfit for consumption because it comes from a watering place— [these should not be eaten].
O dear one, water from those [sources] should always be avoided in ancestral rites; as well as water from the roads,
from sheep, from camels, and all that comes from animals with uncloven hooves.
"Give me for the sake of my ancestors the flesh of a buffalo, a yak, a cow, and even one that has not passed ten days since calving; and whatever else has been brought forth," he said. (MarkP 32.18)
The wise should always avoid that water in the performance of the śrāddha rite;
likewise, ground containing living creatures, parched ground, and ground scorched by fire should be avoided.

In this rite, there are undesirable and wicked sounds and fierce, foul odors; those who bring disgrace upon their families and those who destroy their lineages are excluded from the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*).
The naked, those guilty of mortal sins, a eunuch, one who has been cast off, a cock, and a village pig— these would destroy the ancestral rite by their very sight.
A dog indeed destroys *śrāddha* rites, as do *yātudhānas* by their mere sight;
therefore, one should give [the offerings] well-restrained, scattering sesame seeds over the ground.
In this way, O dear one, protection will be established for both at the funeral feast (śrāddha),
as well as for those touched by impurity from death or birth, and by those afflicted with chronic diseases.
One does not nourish the ancestors with offerings that are fallen or defiled;
likewise, such things must be avoided at a *śrāddha*, as well as the sight of a woman in her courses.

The practice of shaving the head or drinking liquor [is forbidden] by the sacrificer out of respect; likewise, food contaminated by hair or insects, or that which has been looked upon by dogs, [is unfit].
That which is putrid, stale, or fermented from vārtāka,
as well as anything struck by the wind from a garment, must indeed be avoided at a śrāddha.
When that which is given with supreme faith, mentioning the names and lineages of the ancestors,
becomes their food according to what they have been born to eat, then it attains the state of being their food.
Therefore, one who possesses faith and desires the satisfaction of the ancestors should give what is prescribed for the ancestral rite to a worthy recipient, and indeed in the proper manner.
And yogins should always be fed at a śrāddha by the wise man;
for the ancestors have yoga as their support, therefore one should always honor them.
If a yogi, even if he eats only leaves, were to offer them to thousands of brahmins,
he would ferry across the sacrificer and the eaters like a boat upon the water.
Furthermore, the verses concerning the ancestors are sung here by those who discourse on Brahman—
those very verses which were formerly sung by the ancestors to King Aila.
When shall there be born in our lineage a preeminent son who,
on this earth, will offer us funeral cakes made from the food consumed and dried by yogins?
Or at Gayā, one should offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) consisting of rhinoceros meat as a great oblation,
or potherbs with black śāka and abundant sesame, or rice cooked with sesame (kṛsara), for the satisfaction [of the ancestors] for a month.
The Vaiśvadeva and the Soma sacrifice, with rhinoceros meat as the supreme oblation—
by obtaining a hornless rhinoceros, may we enjoy these until the sun’s end.

One should offer the śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day and under the Maghā asterism according to the prescribed rule; likewise, during the southern solstice, one should offer milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter.
Therefore, O son, a man desiring all his wishes and liberation from sin should worship his ancestors with devotion. (MarkP 32.36)
The ancestors of human beings, when gratified by the śrāddha rite, please the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, as well as the lunar mansions, the planets, and the stars.
The ancestors, when gratified by the śrāddha offering, bestow longevity, wisdom, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and pleasures, as well as sovereignty.
