This, my son, has been told to you regarding the ancestral rites (śrāddha) as they have been declared; now hear, dear child, concerning those rites performed for specific desires (kāmya).
The proclamation of the lunar days for the ancestral rites (śrāddha).
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Ritual for Śrāddha," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-three.
Madālasā said:
The first [night] leads to the acquisition of wealth; the second bestows bipeds;
the third is for one seeking boons; and the fourth destroys enemies.
On the fifth day one attains prosperity; on the sixth, a man becomes worthy of honor;
on the seventh, lordship over the Gaṇas; and on the eighth, supreme growth.
On the ninth day, one obtains women; on the tenth, the fulfillment of all desires;
and on the eleventh, one devoted to ritual action attains all the Vedas.
On the twelfth day, the worshiper of the ancestors obtains victory and gains offspring,
intelligence, cattle, prosperity, independence, and supreme nourishment.
A man devoted to faith who performs a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day attains long life and sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
Provided with the excellence of a *śrāddha* performed according to his means,
he for whom the young ancestors have died or were slain by a weapon [attains success].
Therefore, a pure man desiring their satisfaction should diligently perform the śrāddha rite on the fourteenth day or on the new moon day.
One obtains all desires and enjoys infinite heaven;
by worshipping the ancestors during the Kṛttikās, a human being attains heaven.
One desiring offspring shall obtain them under Rohiṇī;
one obtains vigor under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras); one attains heroism under Ārdrā; and land and other such things under Punarvasu.
By always worshipping [the deity] during the Puṣya asterism, one gains nourishment; during Āśleṣā, excellent sons;
during Maghā, preeminence among one's kinsmen; and during the Phālgunīs, good fortune.
A man who gives offerings at a śrāddha under the Uttarās becomes generous by nature and blessed with offspring; he attains preeminence and truthfulness, and holds [the fruit] in his hand.
One will obtain beautiful offspring under Citrā;
Svāti bestows profit from trade, and Viśākhā grants the desire for sons.
Those performing [rites] under Anurādhā attain the status of a wheel-turning monarch;
under Jyeṣṭhā, sovereignty; and under Mūla, supreme health.
Under Āṣāḍhā there is the attainment of fame; under the Uttarās, freedom from sorrow;
under Śravaṇa, auspicious worlds; and under Dhaniṣṭhā, great wealth.

One becomes a knower of the Vedas under Abhijit; let one achieve success as a physician under Śravaṇa; one finds goats and sheep under Proṣṭhapada, and likewise cattle under the following one (Uttarā).
Likewise, by performing a *śrāddha* under the Revatī asterism, one obtains base metals; under the Aśvinī asterism, horses; and under the Bharaṇī asterism, one attains excellent longevity.
Therefore, the knower of reality should perform rites for specific desires under these asterisms.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Optional Śrāddhas," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-four.
Madālasā said:
Thus, my son, a householder must worship the deities and the ancestors with *havya* and *kavya*, as well as guests and kinsmen with food.
All beings— servants, animals, birds, and even ants—
as well as mendicants who beg and others who dwell in one's house.
O dear one,
even a virtuous householder who follows the conduct of the righteous incurs sin if he neglects his obligatory and occasional rites.
Alarka said:
"O Mother, you have described to me that which is daily and occasional;
indeed, human action is threefold: daily, occasional, and [special]."
"O delighter of your family, I wish to hear about virtuous conduct—
that by practicing which a human being attains happiness both in this world and in the next."
Madālasā said:
A householder must always maintain the observance of proper conduct;
for one devoid of proper conduct finds no happiness either in this world or in the next.
Sacrifices, gifts, and ascetic penances exist here for the welfare of a man who acts in accordance with right conduct;
they do not belong to one who proceeds by transgressing it.
For a man of evil conduct does not attain a long life in this world;
one should always exert effort in good conduct, for good conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
O son, I shall describe the nature of that virtuous conduct;
having heard it from me with a one-pointed mind, you should observe it accordingly.
A householder should exert effort in accomplishing the three aims of life;
for when these are fully realized, the success of the householder is achieved both in this world and in the next.
A self-possessed man should set aside one-quarter of his wealth for the sake of the hereafter;
with another half, he should provide for his own maintenance, including both regular and occasional obligations.
One should increase the root of deceit for one's own sake;
O son, for one who acts in this way,
wealth deserves to be fruitful.
In the same way, for the sake of warding off evil, dharma should be practiced by the wise;
likewise, another kind of dharma is performed for the sake of the next world, while yet another yields fruit in this very life.

Desire is said to be twofold according to its non-contradiction with the three aims of life: that which arises from the fear of transgression, that which is for the sake of specific rewards, and another which is non-contradictory.
And hear from me concerning those qualities, such as dharma and the rest, which are linked in a continuous succession.
Dharma has the purpose of following after further dharma; dharma does not obstruct one's own interest.
Desire is of two kinds with respect to both of these, and therefore those two are again twofold.
One should awaken during the *muhūrta* known as Bāhya and reflect upon dharma and artha;
having risen, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), facing the east, self-controlled, and pure.

One should perform the morning twilight devotion while the stars are still visible and the evening twilight devotion while the sun is still present, according to the prescribed rule; one should not abandon these except in times of distress.
One should avoid idle chatter, falsehood, and harshness of speech;
and one should avoid false scriptures, false debate, and the service of the wicked, my son.
In the evening, having returned, one who is self-restrained should likewise perform the fire-oblation;
he should not gaze upon the orb of the sun at either its rising or its setting.
Grooming the hair, looking into a mirror, cleaning the teeth,
and the libations to the deities— these should be performed only in the forenoon.
One should not void excrement or urine on the road to a village, a dwelling, or a sacred ford, nor in a field, nor in a ploughed area, nor in a cow-pen.
One should not look at another man’s wife naked, nor should one even glance at one’s own; the sight, touch, and likewise conversation with a woman in her courses must be avoided.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or engage in sexual intercourse in water;
nor should one stand upon excrement, urine, hair, ashes, or potsherds.
A wise person should likewise not step upon husks, charcoal, bones, fragments, ropes, garments, and so forth, whether on a path or on the ground.
Having performed the worship of the ancestors, the gods, humans, and living beings according to his means, the householder may then eat.
Facing either the east or the north, having sipped water for purification, restrained in speech, and pure,
a man should always eat his food with his mind focused on it and his hands placed between his knees.
A wise person should not proclaim the fault of another unless it has been witnessed;
one should avoid food that is visibly salty as well as food that is excessively hot.
A self-controlled person should not discharge feces or urine while walking or standing;
nor should he perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) or consume anything at all [in that state].
Being impure from remnants of food, one should not speak anything at all and should avoid Vedic recitation;
likewise, one should not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or one's own head.
One should not intentionally look at the sun, the moon, or the stars;
likewise, one should avoid a broken seat, a bed, and a vessel.
One should offer a seat to one's gurus, honoring them with rising from one's seat and other marks of respect; likewise, one should engage in agreeable conversation preceded by a formal salutation.
In that manner one should follow [the teacher], and should not act contrary to him;
one should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform the worship of the deities.
A wise man should not drive away Brahmins, nor should he void excrement into the fire;
a man should never bathe naked, nor should he ever sleep naked.
One should not scratch one's head with both hands,
nor should men wash their heads frequently without a specific reason.
Having bathed his head with oil, he should not touch any part of his body;
and during all periods when study is forbidden, he should avoid the private recitation of the Veda.
One should never urinate toward a Brahmin, a wind, a cow, or the sun;
during the day one should discharge waste facing north, and at night facing south.
In times of illness, one may act according to necessity regarding the voiding of urine and feces;
one should not speak of the teacher's faults, and if he is angry, one should appease him.
One should not listen to the slander of others even when they are speaking it;
the path must be yielded to Brahmins, to a king, and to one suffering from disease.

For one who is superior in learning, for a pregnant woman, for one oppressed by a heavy burden, for a younger person, and for those who are mute, blind, deaf, intoxicated, or insane; ||| MarkP_34.40 |||
One should avoid the house of an unchaste woman, one who has committed an act of enmity, a child,
and an outcast, as well as a temple attendant, a sacred tree, and likewise a crossroads.
A wise person should circumambulate a teacher who is superior in knowledge as if he were a god;
he should not wear shoes, clothing, garlands, or other items already worn by others.
One should avoid the sacred thread, ornaments,
and the water-pot on the fourteenth day, the eighth day, the fifteenth day, and on other festival days.
One should avoid anointing with oil, as well as luxury and women;
a wise man should never stand with his feet and shanks dangling.
One should not toss one's feet about, nor should one step with one foot upon the other;
one should avoid striking vital points, verbal abuse, and slander.
A wise person should not associate with those who are hypocritical, arrogant, or harsh,
nor with fools, the insane, the addicted, the deformed, or the deceitful.
One should not mock those with missing limbs or extra limbs with derisive laughter;
nor should one wield a rod against another, except for the purpose of instructing a son or a pupil.
In that same way, a wise man should not sit down after treading upon his seat with his foot;
nor should he prepare saṃyāva, kṛsara, or meat for his own sake alone.
Having performed the worship of guests, one should eat in the evening and in the morning;
facing either the east or the north, and remaining silent, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
O child, one should always act thus: one should avoid plants that are forbidden to be avoided;
a man should never sleep with his head toward the north, nor with his head toward the west.
Having placed Agastya upon his head, he should then lie down with Purandara;
however, he should not bathe in waters containing fragrance, nor should he do so at night.
It is declared that bathing is mandatory on the day following an eclipse;
one should not wipe the limbs with garments or hands without having bathed.
A wise man should never shake his hair, nor should he shake his garments; likewise, he should never apply ointments without having first bathed.
One should not wear dyed garments, nor those that are variegated or black;
one should not commit a reversal of the order of the two garments, nor should one do so with ornaments.
One should avoid a garment that has been bitten by a rat, one that is excessively worn out,
one infested with hair or insects, one that has been crushed, or one that has been looked upon by dogs.

O son, one should avoid meat that has been licked by others, meat that has fallen [to the ground], meat from which the vital essence has been extracted, meat from the back (pṛṣṭhamāṃsa), meat not offered in sacrifice (vṛthāmāṃsa), and meat that is forbidden.
One should never eat foods containing visible salt; moreover,
my son, one must avoid food that has been kept for a long time or that has become stale.
O prince, you should avoid preparations made from flour, vegetables, sugarcane,
and milk, as well as preparations of meat, even if they have been kept for a long time.
At the rising and setting of the sun, one should avoid lying down;
likewise, a man should not study while unclean, nor while reclining, nor with a distracted mind.
Nor while lying down, nor while seated on the ground, nor in a place with noise; nor wearing only a single garment, nor while speaking, nor without having given to those who look on.
A man, having bathed, should eat according to the rule both morning and evening;
a wise man must not approach the wife of another.
For men, approaching another's wife destroys their merit from sacrifices and charitable works, as well as their lifespan;
indeed, nothing else in this world is so detrimental to longevity.
Just as a man’s violation of another’s wife in this world is [a grave offense],
so too are the worship of the gods, the fire-rituals, and the salutation of one’s teacher.
Having sipped water properly, one should likewise perform the act of eating food with care,
using water that is free from foam, odorless, and clear.
"Drink water for purification, my son,
with auspicious waters while facing either east or north;
[avoiding water] from within a body of water, from a dwelling, from an anthill, or from a mouse-hole."
One should avoid the five types of earth remaining after purification;
having washed both hands and feet and sprinkled oneself with water, one should remain composed.

Likewise, one should sip water while keeping the hands between the knees; one should drink water three or four times, and after wiping the corners of the mouth twice, as well as the sense-orifices and the head.
Having sipped water properly, one should indeed perform the ritual acts with purity,
diligently for the sake of the deities, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors.
Having become composed in mind, a man should always perform [his duties];
after sneezing, spitting, or changing his clothes, a wise man should sip water for purification (ācamana).
Upon sneezing, licking, vomiting, or spitting and similar acts,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), touch the back of a cow, and look at the sun.
One should also make an offering to the right ear;
indeed, this should be done according to one's means, and in the absence of the former, the latter follows.
When that which was previously mentioned is absent, the attainment of the subsequent state is desired;
one should not grind one's teeth nor strike one's own body.
One should avoid sleeping, studying, and eating during the two twilights;
likewise, one should avoid sexual intercourse and setting out on a journey at twilight.
O dear one, one should perform the worship of the gods in the forenoon, that of humans at midday,
and likewise the worship of the ancestors with devotion in the afternoon.
Having bathed his head, he may perform rites for the gods or for the ancestors;
he should also have his beard and hair trimmed while facing either the east or the north.
One should avoid a girl who has a physical deformity, even if she is born of a noble family, as well as one who is diseased,
deformed, tawny-eyed, talkative, or universally disparaged.
A man who desires his own welfare should always marry such a maiden— one who is free from physical defects, possesses a beautiful nose, and is endowed with auspicious marks.
One should marry a woman who is at least fifth in descent from one's father and seventh in descent from one's mother;
one should protect one's wife, abandon envy, and avoid sleeping during the day and sexual intercourse.
One should avoid actions that cause harm to others and inflict suffering upon living beings;
a woman in her courses must be avoided by members of all castes for four nights.
To avoid being born as a woman, one should also avoid the fifth night;
thereafter, O son, one should approach on the sixth night, for that is the best among nights when the women are in union.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights;
therefore, a man seeking a son should always approach his wife on even nights.

O son, those who follow contrary practices [should not bathe] during the day known as the forenoon, nor at the time of twilight, nor after shaving, nor after vomiting, nor after sexual intercourse with a woman.
If he possesses a cloth, the wise man, having gone to a place made of straw, should bathe for the sake of the gods,
the Vedas, the twice-born, and the virtuous, truthful, and high-souled ones.
O son, you must not engage in slander or even in jest against your guru, devoted wives, sacrificers, or ascetics.
One should never listen to those who are undisciplined while they are acting [thus];
nor should one sit upon a superior bed or seat with someone of inferior status.
One should not have an inauspicious appearance, nor should one utter inauspicious speech;
rather, one should be clothed in white garments and adorned with white flowers.
A wise man should not cultivate friendship with those who are agitated, insane, or deluded, nor with the undisciplined, nor with the immoral, nor with those defiled by theft and similar vices.
Nor by those who are excessively wasteful, nor by the greedy, nor by enemies; nor by unchaste women, nor by the lowly, nor likewise by the husbands of unchaste women.
One should not associate with those who are powerful, nor with those who are inferior, nor with those who are censurable;
nor with men who are constantly suspicious of everything, nor with those who are devoted solely to fate.
One should cultivate friendship with the virtuous who adhere to right conduct— those who are wise, free from malice, capable, and devoted to diligent effort in their tasks.

One should also honor friends, consecrated kings, those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), fathers-in-law, and the six classes of officiating priests and others worthy of the arghya offering when they have arrived at one's home.
O son, according to his means,
he should untiringly honor twice-born men who have resided for a year with the madhuparka offering at the appropriate time.
Desiring their welfare, the best of the twice-born should remain steadfast in their teaching;
he should not dispute with them, even when he is constantly reviled by them.
Having performed the proper worship of the household deities in their respective places and in due order,
one should then fully honor the fire and offer oblations in sequence.
One should give the first [offering] to Brahmā, then to Prajāpati;
the third indeed to the Guhyas, and likewise another to Kaśyapa.
Then, having offered [the oblation] to Anumati, one should give the domestic bali-offering,
which was previously described by me to you in the procedure for the performance of the daily rites.
At the end, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva; hear from me regarding that, how one should separately dedicate offerings to the gods according to their respective places.
One should offer three *māṇakas* to Parjanya, the supporter of the earth;
and to Vāyu, and to the directions, starting from the east, in due order.
To Brahmā, to the intermediate space, and to Sūrya in due order;
and likewise to all the gods and to all the elemental spirits.
Then, one should give [the offering] to Uṣas and Bhūtapati in the north;
having said "Svadhā, obeisance," one should also offer to the Pitṛs in the south.

Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one desiring the remnants of the food should offer water from the vessel toward the northwest, saying "O Yakṣman, this for you," according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having set aside the first portion of the food and prepared the *hantakāra*,
one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa according to the prescribed rule and in the proper manner.
One should perform one's ritual acts according to the specific sacred part (tīrtha) of the hand appropriate for each, following the prescribed rule;
likewise, one should perform the act of sipping water (ācamana) for the gods and others using the portion belonging to Brahmā.
The line on the palm of the right hand that runs above the thumb is known as the *brāhma* tīrtha for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamana*).
The space between the forefinger and the thumb is declared to be the ancestral (paitrya) tīrtha;
with that one should offer water and other substances to the ancestors, except for those who are nāndīmukha.
Likewise, the divine (daiva) [tīrtha] is at the tip of the finger; by that, the ritual procedure for divine acts is performed.
The [tīrtha] of Prajāpati is at the base of the little finger; by that, the bodily (kāya) [rite] is performed.
Thus, one should always perform one's duties at these sacred fords (tīrtha) together with the gods and the ancestors, and never by means of any other ford.
Sipping water (ācamana) with the *brāhma* [tīrtha] is recommended; that with the *paitrya* [tīrtha] is always for ancestral rites;
for the gods, it is with the *daiva* [tīrtha]; and for Prajāpati, with the *nijam* [tīrtha].
A wise man should perform the offering of rice-balls and water for the Nāndīmukhas using the Prājāpatya tīrtha, as well as whatever else pertains to Prajāpati.
A wise person should not simultaneously hold both water and fire;
likewise, one should not stretch out one's feet toward a teacher or a deity.
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one drink water with cupped hands;
this applies during all occasions of purification, whether they be great or small.
One should not delay for the sake of purification, nor should one blow on a fire with the mouth. My son, one should not dwell in a place where these four things are not present.
Where there is a lender of loans, a physician, and a learned Vedic scholar; where there is a river with abundant water;
and where the king has conquered his enemies and is powerful and devoted to righteousness.
A wise person should dwell there permanently; for how can there be happiness under a bad king?
Where the king is invincible and where the earth is rich with grain.
Where the citizens are well-restrained and always abide by justice,
and where the people are free from envy, there residence brings about happiness.
In that kingdom where the farmers are generally not overly indulgent in their enjoyments,
and where all medicinal herbs are found in abundance, there a wise man should dwell.
In that regard, my son, you must not dwell where these three things are always present:
a person seeking victory, an old enmity, and people who are constantly celebrating.
A wise person should always dwell among those of virtuous conduct who live together;
this, my son, has been told by me out of a desire for your welfare.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the *Alarkānuśāsana* section of the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
[Chapter Thirty-Five] Madalasa said:
Henceforth, listen to you regarding the practice of what is to be avoided and what is not;
food that has been kept overnight is fit to be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been stored for a long time.
Furthermore, preparations made from wheat, barley, and cow's milk are devoid of fat;
so too are the rabbit, the tortoise, the iguana, the porcupine, the rhinoceros, and the *putraka*.

For these are indeed fit for consumption; likewise, village pigs and cocks are to be avoided, as is the remnant of offerings to the ancestors, gods, and others at a śrāddha ceremony, unless desired by the Brahmins.
One does not incur fault by eating meat that has been consecrated with sprinkling or intended for medicinal purposes;
nor does one incur fault regarding conch-shells, stones, gold, silver, ropes, or garments.
And likewise for vegetables, roots, and fruits; for split bamboo, leather, gems, diamonds, corals, and pearls.
The purification of the limbs of human beings is prescribed with water,
just as that of iron is with water and that of stone is by scrubbing.
The purification of vessels containing oily substances is by means of hot water;
likewise for winnowing baskets, grain, skins, pestles, and mortars.
For garments that are gathered together, purification is prescribed by sprinkling;
for a heap of all kinds of bark garments, purification by water and earth is required.
The purification of grass, wood, and medicinal herbs is held to be by sprinkling;
likewise, all woolen products and hair are considered pure.
Furthermore, O dear one, by means of a paste of white mustard seeds or a paste of sesame seeds mixed with water,
it always becomes effective for those who have been afflicted.
Likewise, the purification of cotton products is by means of water and ashes;
for wood, ivory, bone, and horn, purification is held to be by means of planing.
Furthermore, earthen vessels become pure through re-firing;
alms-food, the hand of an artisan, merchandise, and likewise the mouth of a woman, are pure.

That which has come from the street and is unrecognized, that which has been brought by a group of servants and the like, that which is directed by a crooked command, that which is long past, and that which is separated by many intervals— this is light [in weight].
Excessive wealth, children, the aged, the sick, and those who are inactive; workshops, charcoal pits, and women with nursing infants—these are to be avoided.
Likewise, pure waters that are free from odor and bubbles purify themselves by flowing;
and the earth is purified over time by burning, sweeping, and the treading of cattle.
Through plastering, scraping, sprinkling water, sweeping the house, and worship;
and when hair or insects have fallen in, or it has been smelled by a cow, or is infested with flies.
O dear one, for the sake of purification, earthenware should be sprinkled with earth, water, and ashes;
those made of udumbara wood with sour liquid; and those of tin and lead with alkaline solution.
The purification of bell-metal vessels is by means of ashes and water, as is that of liquids through straining;
for those smeared with impurities, it is by means of earth and water, and by the removal of the odor.

And for others, water that remains in its natural state when it has reached the earth is pure, provided it does not steal away the color or fragrance of those substances and is sufficient to satisfy a cow.
Likewise, my dear, meat fallen from a *caṇḍāla*, a carnivorous beast, or the like,
as well as clothing and such that has come onto the road,
is declared pure by virtue of the wind.
Dust, fire, a horse, a cow, shade, rays of light, wind, the earth,
droplets, flies, and the like are not considered defiled by contact with the wicked.
A goat and a horse are pure at the mouth; neither is the face of a cow nor that of a calf.
The flow from a mother's udder is pure, as is a bird when it causes fruit to fall.
A seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, and grass on the road—
these are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind, just like merchandise.
After descending onto a street, bathing, sneezing, drinking, performing acts that cause fatigue,
and after changing one's clothes, one should sip water for purification according to the prescribed rule.
Even when touched by refuse, mud, or water from a ditch,
things constructed of baked brick become pure through contact with the wind.
Having set aside and discarded the first portion from abundant food that has been defiled,
one should sprinkle the remainder with water after sipping water (ācamana) and likewise with earth and water.
One who eats food from a wicked person should observe a fast for three nights;
however, if it was done unknowingly, the expiation for that fault consists in the restoration of knowledge.

Having touched a woman in her courses, a horse, a jackal, and the like, or a woman who has recently given birth, an outcaste, or those carrying a corpse, one should bathe for the sake of purification.
Having touched a human bone that still contains marrow, a man becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is devoid of marrow, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or beholding the sun.
Likewise, one should not leap over blood, nor should one spit or rub the body;
a wise person should never stay in gardens or similar places at improper times.
One should not converse with a woman who hates people or one who lacks heroic virtue;
nor should one cast out from the house the remnants of food, feces, urine, or water used for washing the feet.
Having offered five lumps of food, one should not bathe in the water of others;
one should bathe in natural pools, in the lakes of the Gaṅgā, and in rivers.
Having touched or conversed with those who revile the deities, the ancestors, the true scriptures, sacrifices, mantras, and so forth,
one becomes pure by looking at the sun.

Having likewise observed a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a fallen corpse, one who follows a heterodox path, a woman who has recently given birth, a eunuch, a naked person, and a low-caste man; 35.34.
Those who are charioteers, those who lead horses, and those who take pleasure in the wives of others—
this indeed is the purification that the wise must perform for themselves.

One who knows the Dharma should avoid the food of those who have recently given birth, eunuchs, cats, rats, dogs, and cocks, as well as those who have fallen from their caste, those who are pierced by arrows, outcastes, and those who carry corpses.
By bathing after physical contact, a woman in her courses, a village pig,
and likewise two men defiled by the impurity of childbirth, are purified.
He whose daily domestic rites decline day by day,
and who is abandoned by the Brahmins, is a sinner and the lowest of men.
One should never neglect the performance of obligatory rites;
for by failing to perform them, one is bound solely to the cycle of death and rebirth.
A Brāhmaṇa should remain for ten days, abstaining from giving gifts, performing fire-oblations, and other such rites;
a Kṣatriya for twelve days, and a Vaiśya for half a month.
A Śūdra, however, should remain for one month abstaining from his own duties;
thereafter, all should perform their respective duties as prescribed.
Having cremated [the body] outside, the kinsmen should offer water on the first day,
as well as on the fourth, the seventh, and the ninth.
The collection of ashes and bones should be performed by the kinsmen on the fourth day;
after that collection, the touching of their limbs is prescribed.
After the collection of the bones, all rites must be performed with water;
likewise, on the day of death, the touching [of the corpse] by the sapindas belongs to both [the giver and the receiver].
One should avoid [the following] one by one: bears, weapons, water, hanging, fire, poison, precipices, and so forth, as well as death by fasting (prāya) and self-immolation (anāśaka).

When a child, one residing in another country, or likewise one who has gone forth as a renunciant has died, there is immediate purification; however, others have declared that the period of impurity lasts for three days.
If a sapinda dies while another sapinda is already deceased,
the funeral rites for the latter should be performed on the same number of days designated by the duration of the prior period of impurity.
This very same rule is seen to apply even at birth during a period of impurity (sūtaka),
for the sapinda relatives among sapinda relatives, and likewise among those related by water (sodaka).
When a son is born, bathing with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father;
even in that case, if another son should be born after the first has been born.
Even in that case, purification is prescribed for one who possesses [the memory of] a previous birth after the passing of ten,
twelve, half a month, or a full month’s number of days.
All the social classes (varṇas) should perform their respective ritual duties according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, the ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed in honor of the deceased.
Wise men should indeed give gifts to the Brahmins—
whatever is most beloved in the world and whatever is most cherished in the home.
One who desires that very gift to be inexhaustible should give it to one possessed of those respective qualities;
then, when the days are complete, having touched water, a vehicle, and a weapon.
Likewise, the goads and staffs, the castes properly performing their rites,
and the acquisition of goods as prescribed by the duties of one's own caste, as well as their respective activities.
All these, when performed with purity, bestow prosperity both in this world and the next;
the triple Veda should be studied constantly, and one must become wise.
O son, wealth should be acquired through righteous means, and one should strive diligently to perform sacrifices; furthermore, whatever you do, it should not cause your own self to feel reproach.
That which should not be hidden from great men must be done without hesitation;
for a man who lives in the house acting in this manner, my child, [there is no fear].
Through the attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, there is excellence both in this world and in the next.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Things to be Avoided and Not Avoided," in the *Alarka-anuśāsana* section of the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-Six.
Jaḍa said:
Having been thus instructed and having reached youth with his mother, he,
the son of Ṛtadhvaja, duly took a wife.
The powerful lord begot sons and also performed sacrifices with rituals;
and at all times, he carried out his father’s commands.
Then, after a long time, having reached his final years,
Ṛtadhvaja performed the consecration of his son upon the kingdom.
The righteous-souled lord of the earth, a highly fortunate great Rākṣasa, descended [from heaven] together with his wife, desiring to go to the forest for ascetic penance.
And Madālasā spoke these final words to her son,
for the sake of his renunciation of the pursuit of sensual enjoyments.
Madālasā said:
"When your suffering— born from separation from dear kinsmen, or arising from the oppression of enemies, or produced by the loss of wealth— is unbearable," *MarkP* 36.6.
For one who relies on the duties of a householder and performs the work of ruling a kingdom, there will be [only suffering];
for a householder whose basis is the sense of "mine" (mamatva) is indeed a locus of suffering.
Then, my son, having extracted from this the ring given by me, you must deliver my command inscribed in minute characters upon the tablet.
Jaḍa said:
Having spoken thus, he gave him a golden ring and also such blessings as were appropriate for one who dwells in the house of Paruṣa.
Then that Kubalayaśva and Queen Madālasā,
having bestowed that kingdom upon their son, departed for the forest to practice asceticism.
The thirty-seventh chapter.
Jaḍa said:
That Alarka, too, [ruled] according to the law, while his subjects were as joyful as if toward their own sons.
The righteous-souled one protected those who were established in their respective duties.
Inflicting punishment upon the wicked and providing proper protection for the virtuous,
he attained supreme joy and performed great sacrifices.
And sons were born to him, endowed with great strength and prowess,
righteous-souled, high-minded, and obstructors of the path of the wicked.
He pursued wealth through righteousness, or again, righteousness through wealth;
and without the conflict between these two, he also enjoyed the objects of the senses.
Thus, as he protected the earth for many years,
being devoted to virtue, wealth, and pleasure, those years passed for him like a single day.
Dispassion did not arise in him as he enjoyed his beloved sense-objects,
nor was he capable of acquiring merit or wealth.
His brother, named Subāhu, who lived in the forest, heard that he was thus intoxicated by the indulgence of pleasures and had not conquered his senses.
Then, desiring to awaken him, that lord of the earth reflected for a long time and concluded that the king's welfare lay in taking refuge with his enemy.
Then that skillful man, having repeatedly sought refuge with the King of Kāśī— who possessed a vast army and mounts— came to him in order to regain his own kingdom.
That king also made preparations for military force against Alarka and dispatched a messenger, saying, "Let the kingdom be restored to him."
Knowing his own duty, Alarka did not wish to grant that request even after it had been commanded;
he replied to the messenger of the King of Kāśī: MarkP_37.11 //
"Let my elder brother come to me alone and beg for the kingdom out of affection;
I will not grant him even a small piece of land through force or fear."
Then the wise Subāhu also made no request;
for he thought, "This is not the duty of a Kṣatriya," since his wealth consists solely of his own prowess.
Then, surrounded by his entire army, the Lord of Kāśī marched forth to invade the kingdom of King Alarka.
Immediately thereafter, having come into contact with those who were close by,
he was attacked by some of their servants and brought under their control.
Without afflicting his vassals with the oppression of their territories,
he likewise brought under his control the fortress-guards and the forest-dwellers.
He brought some kings under his control by means of bribery, others by sowing dissension, and still others by conciliation alone— those who remained loyal to him in secret.
Then that king, possessing little strength and oppressed by a foreign army,
suffered a great depletion of his treasury and had his city besieged by his enemy.
Thus being oppressed day by day, his treasury exhausted,
he fell into extreme despondency and agitation of mind.
Having reached the height of distress, he remembered that ring,
on account of which his mother Madalasa had previously spoken to him.
Then, having bathed and become pure, and having caused the best of the twice-born to recite auspicious prayers,
he extracted the edict from it and beheld it with its letters clearly visible.
Right there, the king read what was written by his mother;
his body bristling with visible horripilation, his eyes blossomed wide with great joy.
Attachment should be abandoned with one's whole being; if it cannot be abandoned, it should be practiced with the virtuous, for the company of the virtuous is indeed the medicine.
Desire should be abandoned with one's whole being; yet if it cannot be abandoned, then the desire for liberation must be directed toward that [desire], for that alone is its remedy.
Having recited [the scriptures] many times, she resolved, "How may there be welfare for men? It must be through the desire for liberation," since that [welfare] arises from association with him.
Then that lord of the earth, reflecting upon the company of the virtuous and being in great distress,
went to the highly fortunate Dattātreya.
Having approached that high-souled one, who was stainless and unattached,
he prostrated himself, honored him according to the prescribed rites, and spoke.
O Brahman, show me favor; be a refuge for me who seek refuge.
Remove my suffering, for I am afflicted by pain and yearn for liberation.
"O King, I shall remove your suffering this very day.
Tell me the truth, O lord of the earth: for what reason do you suffer?"
Jaḍa said:
Having been addressed thus by that wise man, the king reflected upon himself as the locus of all three kinds of suffering.
Having reflected for a long time, the noble-minded and steadfast king laughed at himself by means of his own self and then spoke these words.
I am neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor wind, nor space; rather, happiness is sought by uniting with that which is embodied.
In this group of five, pleasure and pain undergo increase and decrease;
if such were the case, why would it not also occur when they reside elsewhere within that same [self]?
In that which is eternally abundant and real, there is no depression or elevation due to deficiency or excess;
likewise, when "mine-ness" is abandoned, no distinction whatsoever is perceived.

For one who perceives the subtle state established in the mere elements (tanmātra) and likewise the true nature of the primary elements (bhūta) within the third part, what is there in the body that is pleasant or unpleasant?
Whatever mental suffering or happiness is situated in the mind,
because of that [it belongs to the mind], there is no suffering or happiness for me, for I am not the mind.
Since I am neither ego, nor mind, nor intellect,
how can that suffering born of the internal organs— which belongs to the "I"-notion— be mine?
I am neither the body nor the mind, since I am distinct from both the body and the mind; therefore,
let [these notions] reside in the mind or even in the body.
What do pleasures and pains matter to me in this regard?
If his elder brother desires sovereignty over this body which is a mere aggregate of the five elements,
what concern have I with that, since it proceeds from my own qualities?
Abiding in that, both he and I am distinct from the body.
For one whose hands and all else are entirely without flesh, and whose bones are not even distinguishable,
what need has he for stores of elephants, horses, chariots, and the like?
Even a very slight connection exists here for a person.
Therefore, I have no enemy, nor do I have suffering;
I have neither pleasure, nor a city, nor a treasury; nor do I possess an army of horses, elephants, and so forth. Nor does he [possess these].
Nor does it belong to anyone else whatsoever, nor even to me.
Just as the single space contained within a water-clock, a jar, and a water-pot is seen as many,
so too are Subāhu, that King of Kāśī, and I.
And upon the bodies as garlands, through the destruction of their physical forms.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Discrimination of the Self," in the dialogue between father and son within the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Jaḍa said:
Then, having prostrated before the brahmin Dattātreya, that king, bowing low with humility, addressed these words to the high-souled one: MarkP_38.1 //
O Brahmin, for me who perceives correctly,
there is no suffering whatsoever;
those who do not perceive correctly are always submerged in the ocean of misery.
Whatever object a man’s intellect becomes attached to,
from that very thing it seizes hold [of him] and bestows nothing but sufferings.
The grief felt when a domestic cock is eaten by a cat is not the same as that felt for a sparrow or a mouse when they are devoid of the sense of "mine."
Thus, I am neither miserable nor happy, since I am beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
for that which is overcome by the elements and consists of the elements is indeed characterized by pleasure and pain.
Dattātreya said:
"O tiger among men,
it is exactly as you have spoken."
"Mine" is the root of suffering, and "not mine" is the root of nirvāṇa.
It is solely from my question that this supreme knowledge has arisen in you,
by which the notion of "mine" has been cast away like the down of a silk-cotton tree.
The sprout "I" has arisen; it possesses the great trunk of the "mine," with high branches of house and field, and leaves of sons, wife, and so forth.
It has great leaves of wealth and grain, grows continuously at all times,
bears the foremost flowers of merit and demerit, and yields the great fruit of happiness and suffering.

Therein, the great tree of knowledge regarding what ought to be done has its roots spreading throughout the path to liberation; it is watered by contact with the deluded and is richly adorned with swarms of bees that are the desires to act.
For those who, exhausted by the path of saṃsāra, have taken refuge in its shade,
and who remain dependent on the pleasure of deluded cognition— how could there be ultimate [liberation] for them?
But those by whom the tree of possessiveness has been cut down with the axe of knowledge, sharpened on the stone of association with the virtuous, have gone by that path.
Having reached the cool forest of Brahman, which is free from passion and thorns,
the wise, devoid of worldly activity, attain supreme bliss.
O King, neither you nor I am composed of the gross elements and the senses;
neither of us consists of the subtle elements (tanmātras), nor do we have the internal organs as our essence.
Whom, O Indra among kings, shall I behold?
This is the primary essence of us both;
for beyond that is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), while this aggregate is composed of the qualities (guṇas).
Just as there is a distinction between a gnat, a fig tree, a blade of grass, a reed, a fish, and water,
even though they exist as one, so it is, O King, with the field and the Self.
Alarka said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, this supreme knowledge has been revealed to me—
such as it is, which effects the discernment between primordial matter (pradhāna) and consciousness (cit-śakti)."
But here, my mind is assailed by sense objects and possesses no steadiness; nor do I know how I might be liberated from this bondage to primordial nature.
How may I not be born again, and how may I attain the state beyond qualities? And how indeed may I reach oneness with the eternal Brahman?
Therefore, O Brahmin, O one of great wisdom, please explain that yoga correctly to me, who am bowed before you and making this request.
For association with the virtuous is indeed beneficial to human beings.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Questions," in the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between father and son; [and also concerning] what kind of seat is prescribed for one who is constantly engaged in yoga.
Having assumed the lotus posture, the half-lotus posture, or likewise the svastika posture,
one should practice yoga, placing the *praṇava* within the heart.
Having become even and seated on a level seat, having drawn together both feet,
with the mouth likewise closed, and having firmly pressed the thighs together in front.
Standing with self-restraint, he should touch his penis and testicles with his two heels;
with his head slightly raised, he should not let his teeth touch one another.
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the directions,
he [overcame] the activity of passion by means of darkness, and likewise the activity of passion by means of goodness.
Having covered [the senses] and remaining within the stainless being, the knower of yoga should practice:
he should withdraw the senses from their objects, as well as the vital breaths and the mind itself.
Having restrained [the senses] through their collective withdrawal, one should undertake the practice of pratyāhāra;
for he who withdraws all desires just as a tortoise draws in all its limbs.
Always delighting in the Self and established in solitude, he should master the self within the self;
having accomplished both external and internal purification from the navel to the throat.
Having filled the body, the wise one should begin the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra);
ten and two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) are said to constitute one retention (dhāraṇā).
Two types of concentration (dhāraṇā) are taught in yoga by yogis who perceive reality:
indeed, for the yogi thus engaged in yoga, whose self is restrained, [these two are prescribed].
All defects perish and he becomes healthy;
he beholds the supreme Brahman and perceives the primal qualities (guṇas) as distinct from one another.
In this manner, the yogi, restrained in diet and devoted to breath control, [perceives] the atoms of space and so forth, as well as the stainless Self.
One should ascend the ground, stage by stage, slowly, as if climbing into one's own house; for the earth remains unconquered when it is overrun by faults, diseases, and delusion.
One should not ascend to a stage that has not been conquered;
therefore, it is traditionally known as *prāṇāyāma* because of the restraint of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
This is called "retention" (dhāraṇā) because the mind is retained in such a way that the senses,
which have been set in motion toward sound and other objects, are restrained by those of self-controlled mind.
They are withdrawn by means of yoga; therefore, it is known as *pratyāhāra*.
This method has been taught here by the yogis and supreme sages.
By this, indeed, no defects such as diseases arise for the yogin;
just as one seeking water obtains it gradually through mechanical contrivances, pipes, and the like.
In that manner, the yogi who has conquered fatigue should inhale the air;
first at the navel, then in the heart, and thirdly likewise in the chest.
In the throat, the mouth, the tip of the nose, the eyes, between the eyebrows, on the crown of the head,
and furthermore, beyond that— concentration (dhāraṇā) upon these is declared to be supreme.
Having attained these ten dhāraṇās, one attains equality with the Imperishable;
one is neither bloated, nor hungry, nor fatigued, nor is one's mind distracted.
O Indra among kings,
a yogi, being diligent for the sake of success, should practice yoga neither when it is too cold nor too hot, nor in the presence of dualities, nor where there is a prevailing wind.
One intent on meditation should not practice yoga during these times:
when there is noise, near a fire or a web of smoke, in a dilapidated cow-pen, or at a crossroads.
On a heap of dry leaves, in a river, in a cemetery infested with reptiles, on the bank of a well where there is danger, or on a heap of ruins or an anthill; MarkP_39.49 //
In these places, one who knows reality should avoid the practice of yoga;
and when the presence of pure beings is lacking, one should avoid that place and time.
In yoga, there is no vision of that which is non-existent; therefore, one should avoid it.
Indeed, he who practices yoga while disregarding these places due to delusion [is mistaken].
Listen to me as I explain the defects that arise from smelling it:
deafness, dullness, loss of memory, muteness, and blindness.
And fever arises immediately for that practitioner of ignorance;
if these faults of the practitioner arise through negligence, this is the treatment.
Learn from me that which must be performed by a yogin for their destruction:
having eaten very hot, unctuous gruel, one should retain it right there.
For the sake of pacifying wind-induced abdominal tumors (vātagulma), as well as upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and abdominal enlargement (udara),
one should likewise administer gruel or a wind-dispelling decoction to counteract the wind-knot (vāyugranthi).
Likewise, when there is trembling, one should fix the mind upon a great mountain;
in the case of an obstruction of speech, upon speech; and in the case of deafness, upon the faculty of hearing.
Just as one afflicted by thirst might meditate on a mango fruit when the sense of taste is active,
so too should one [meditate] upon that which is beneficial for whatever part of the body is in pain.
One should maintain the concentration (dhāraṇā) that is cooling when it is hot, and burning when it is cold;
having placed a peg upon the head, one should strike wood with wood.
By that means, memory is immediately restored to the yogin whose memory has been lost;
he should also practice concentration on the pervasive heaven and earth, as well as wind and fire.
These afflictions arising from non-human beings or from living creatures are to be treated medically;
however, if a non-human being should enter into the interior of the yogin, [the following applies].
By means of the *vāyvagrī* concentration, one should utterly consume that which resides within the body;
thus, O King, protection must be performed by the knower of yoga with his whole being.
Since the body is the instrument for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
and because the practitioner's consciousness dissolves through the disclosure of activities characterized by worldly engagement, such activities must be kept secret.
Freedom from agitation, health, lack of harshness, a pleasant odor, scanty urine and feces,
radiance, clarity, and gentleness of voice.
For this is indeed the first sign of the commencement of yoga.
A devoted person proclaims the virtues [of the deity] in his absence;
he does not cause living beings to suffer—this is the supreme sign of success.
For one who experiences no affliction from the most intense cold, heat, and so forth,
and who feels no fear of others, accomplishment has arrived.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Yoga," in the Legend of Jaḍa within the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
The fortieth chapter begins:
Dattātreya said:
For when the Self has been seen, afflictions arise for the yogin;
those which occur, I shall explain to you in brief—learn them from me.
Likewise, through rites performed for specific desires, one seeks human desires:
women, the fruit of giving, knowledge, magical power, base metals, wealth, and heaven.
The state of divinity, the lordship over the immortals, the various elixirs and ritual practices, leaping into the wind, performing sacrifice, and likewise entering into water and fire; 40.3.

The fruits and likewise the rules for all gifts given during ancestral rites (śrāddha), as well as those arising from fasting, from works of public utility (pūrta), and even from the worship of deities; 40.4.
Afflicted by various such actions, the mind thus proceeds; the yogi should turn it back from this state with effort.
Making his mind one with Brahman, he is liberated from calamities;
once these calamities have been conquered by him, further calamities [no longer arise].
Yogins proceed according to their qualities—sāttvika, rājasa, or tāmasa.
Their powers are the intuitive (prātibha), the auditory (śrāvaṇa), the divine (daiva), as well as the two others beginning with delusion (bhrama).
These five— the meanings of the Vedas, the meanings of poetic treatises, and all branches of knowledge and arts— arise as bitter obstacles to the yoga of practitioners.
That which appears to him is intuitive; such is the intuitive knowledge of the yogin, by which he knows all words and their meanings and indeed grasps the word itself.
He is said to be audible from thousands of yojanas away;
when he, like a deity, gazes all around, he sees eight [yojanas].
The wise say that even fate is subject to adverse conditions when the mind of a yogi wanders without support due to its own defect, like one who is insane.
That is proclaimed as delusion (bhrama) which arises from the total collapse of right conduct;
it is like an eddy in water, a whirlpool of knowledge that is agitated and confused.
The whirlpool destroys the mind; that is called an obstacle.
By these, all those born of divine origin have their yoga destroyed.
Because of most terrible afflictions, they revolve again and again;
therefore, the yogi should wrap himself in the white, mind-made blanket.
Having made his mind inclined toward it, the yogi, ever engaged in yoga, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses, should contemplate the Supreme Brahman.
There are seven subtle concentrations (dhāraṇās), beginning with Earth; the yogi should fix them at the crown of the head.
By fixing on the Earth-element, the yogi attains its subtlety.
He considers himself to be the earth and abandons its odor;
just as there is a subtle taste in water, so too is there form in fire.
In the same way, by maintaining the concentration on that wind, he likewise abandons touch;
and by [maintaining] the subtle activity of space, he likewise abandons sound.
When, through the mind, one enters into the minds of all beings while maintaining mental concentration (dhāraṇā), the mind becomes subtle.
In the same way, the knower of yoga, having attained the unsurpassed subtlety of intellect, reaches the intellect of all beings and then relinquishes it.
The knower of yoga who, having correctly understood them, abandons these seven subtle things— O Alarka— has no further rebirth.
Having repeatedly observed the subtlety of these seven concentrations, the self-possessed one, having abandoned each [lower] perfection as he attains it, shall proceed to the supreme state.
O Lord of the Earth, toward whichever being one directs passion,
having become attached to that very being, one comes to ruin.
Therefore, having understood these subtle things which are mutually attached,
the embodied soul who renounces them shall attain the supreme state.
But referring specifically to these seven subtle elements, O King,
detachment from the primary elements and the rest leads to liberation for one who knows their true nature.
Having become deeply attached to fragrances and other such objects, O King, he perishes; he returns once more to a state that is neither Brahman nor human.
O Lord of Men, having transcended these seven concentrations, whatever the yogi desires, he attains absorption into that very subtle element.
He enters into dissolution within the bodies of gods, asuras, gandharvas, uragas, or rakshasas, yet he never incurs attachment to anything.
Aṇimā, laghimā, and mahimā, as well as prāpti;
likewise prākāmya, īśitva, and furthermore vaśitva.
O tiger among men, one attains these eight divine qualities, which indicate supreme nirvāṇa, including the power of determining the fulfillment of desires at will.

Subtlety is the quality of being subtler than the subtlest and more minute; lightness is the quality of swiftness; greatness arises from being worthy of worship by all; and attainment is that which nothing is unattainable for him.

Because he is all-pervasive, he possesses the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*) and lordship (*īśitva*); because he is free from attachment, the seventh quality of the yogi is called mastery (*vaśitva*).
Wherever one desires to go, and wherever one has mastery over the dissolution of one's will—
at these causes of sovereignty, the power of the yogin is said to be eightfold.
O King, it is the supreme Nirvāṇa of the self, which indicates liberation;
therefore, it is neither born, nor does it grow, nor does it perish.
Nor does it undergo destruction, nor does it undergo transformation;
nor does it suffer cutting, moistening, burning, or drying from the earth and the other elements.
One does not obtain [anything] from the group of elements, nor is one carried away by sound and the other sense objects;
for these sense objects do not exist for him, and as their enjoyer, he is not joined with them.
Just as a piece of gold, O King, when its impurities have been burnt away by fire, becomes one with another piece of gold; so it is with the soul.
In that same way, the ascetic, having his defects burnt away by the fire of yoga, attains oneness with Brahman and no longer perceives any distinction.
Just as fire cast into fire follows after its identity due to their equality, having become one with it,
it cannot be perceived as distinct.
O Lord of the Earth, having attained oneness with that Supreme Brahman and having burnt away all impurities,
the yogi never again undergoes a state of separation.
Just as water poured into water attains oneness with it,
so the self of the yogi attains identity within the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, named "The Attainment of Yoga," in the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
The forty-first chapter begins:
Alarka said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear in truth about the conduct of the yogin, so that the yogin, following the path of Brahman, does not falter. (MarkP 41.1)
Dattātreya said: These two— honor and dishonor— which cause agitation to men,
become the very causes of success for the yogin when their meaning is reversed.
These two, honor and dishonor, are said to be poison and nectar;
therein, dishonor is the nectar, while honor is a most dangerous poison.
One should set foot down purified by the sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak speech purified by truth; and one should contemplate that which is purified by the intellect.
A knower of yoga should never go to householder’s rites of hospitality, śrāddha ceremonies, sacrifices, divine processions, festivals, or even to great assemblies for the sake of personal success.

When the people have all finished eating, when the cooking is over, when the smoke has cleared, and when the embers have subsided, the knower of yoga should wander for alms; he should not do so constantly from only three houses.
Just as people thus despise and treat one with contempt,
so should the yogi conduct himself, not defiling the path of the virtuous.
He should wander for alms among householders and among the houses of Yāyāvaras;
this first mode of life is taught as the most excellent for him.
Then the ascetic should always move among householders who are modest, full of faith, self-controlled, learned in the Vedas, and high-souled.
From this point forward, even among those who are neither corrupt nor fallen,
the practice of begging alms from those of low appearance is considered the lowest mode of livelihood.
Alms-food, rice-gruel, buttermilk, milk, or even barley-meal; or fruit, roots, millet, or the flour of grain-husks and oil-cake.
These auspicious foods bring about success for the yogi;
therefore, the sage should employ them with devotion and supreme meditative concentration.
Having first sipped water once, remaining silent and composed, the first oblation for him is prescribed as "To Prāṇa. (MarkP 41.13)
The second is for apāna, another is for samāna;
the fourth should be for udāna, and the fifth for vyāna.
Having separated the remainder by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he may eat it at will;
then, having sipped water once more and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), he should touch his heart.
Non-stealing, celibacy, renunciation, and likewise non-attachment—
these five vows of the mendicants are indeed supreme through their commitment to non-violence.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and daily study of the Vedas— these are proclaimed as the five observances (niyamas).
One should attend to that knowledge which is essential and effective for accomplishing one's purpose;
for this multiplicity of knowledges is indeed an obstacle to yoga.
He who wanders about thirsting with the thought, "This is to be known, this is to be known," will not attain what is to be known even in thousands of eons.
Having abandoned attachment, conquered anger, eating light food, and subdued the senses,
one should close the doors [of the senses] with the intellect and fix the mind in meditation.
In empty spaces, in caves, and in forests,
the yogi, ever-disciplined, should always properly undertake meditation.
The staff of speech, the staff of action, and the staff of mind—these three are his;
he whose staffs are thus restrained is a great ascetic, a *tridaṇḍin*.
For him for whom this entire world— whether existent or non-existent— is composed of the Self,
and who consists of both qualities and their opposites, O King, who is dear and who is not dear?
With purified intellect, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, and being equanimous toward all beings,
he attains the supreme, eternal, and imperishable state.
For having realized the Supreme, one is not born again.
From the Vedas come all sacrificial rites;
from sacrifice comes silent recitation and the path of knowledge; from silent recitation comes meditation, free from attachment and desire.
When that has been attained, there is the perception of the eternal.
Concentrated, devoted to the Brahman, heedful, pure, dwelling in solitude, and with senses subdued—
the great-souled one shall attain this yoga.
Then, through his own yoga, he attains liberation.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Conduct of Yogis," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Two.
Dattātreya said:
Thus, the yogi who proceeds in this way, being correctly established in yoga,
cannot be turned back even by hundreds of future births.
And having beheld the Supreme Self directly, in his universal form— the Lord of the universe, the creator of the universe, whose feet, heads, and necks are the universe itself.
To attain that, one should mutter the single-syllabled "Om," which is a great merit;
for him who hears its supreme nature, that itself constitutes his study.
The syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*—
these three syllables are indeed the three measures (*mātrā*), characterized by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Free from qualities, accessible to yogis, and situated above the half-mora,
she is to be known as Gāndhārī, taking her support from the Gāndhāra note.
A sensation like the movement of ants, when applied, is perceived on the crown of the head;
just as a glowing coal, when applied, passes out through the crown of the head.
Likewise, the yogi who consists of the syllable Oṃ becomes imperishable within the Imperishable.
The vital breath is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is the unsurpassed target to be pierced.
One who is heedful should pierce [the target] like an arrow and become absorbed in that;
"Om"—this is the three Vedas, the three worlds, and the three fires.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara, as well as the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas,
together with the three and a half measures (mātrās), are to be known as the ultimate reality.
In that regard, the yogin who is disciplined shall attain absorption in that;
the letter *a* is the world of *bhūr*, and the letter *u* is said to be *bhuvaḥ*.
The letter *ma*, together with its consonant, is conceived as the heavenly world (*svarloka*);
the first vowel is manifest, while the second is designated as unmanifest.
The third measure is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), and the half-measure is the supreme state;
by this very sequence, these stages of yoga are to be understood.
By the utterance of "Om," everything that exists and does not exist is grasped;
its first measure is short, while the second is endowed with length.
And the third is called the half-pluta; that is not within the range of speech.
This is the imperishable Brahman, designated as the supreme Oṃkāra.
But the man who knows this correctly, or likewise meditates upon it,
having cast off the wheel of saṃsāra, abandons the threefold bondage.
Having known death through the signs of its approach, even one whose bonds of karma are not yet exhausted attains dissolution into Brahman, the supreme Self.
By recollecting [this] at the time of departure, one attains the state of a yogin once again;
therefore, whether by means of unaccomplished yoga or accomplished yoga,
one should always know the omens so that one does not falter at the moment of departure.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Chapter on Oṃkāra," in the Yoga-dharma section of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
The forty-third chapter begins with Dattātreya saying:
O Great King, listen as I describe to you those omens of death,
by the sight of which the knower of yoga recognizes his own approaching demise.
That man who does not see the path of the gods, Dhruva, Śukra, the shadow of the moon (Chāyā), and Arundhatī, shall not live beyond a year.
Having seen the sun's disk without rays and the fire garlanded with flames,
a man does not live beyond eleven months.
He who, in a dream, sees gold or silver being directly placed upon vomit, urine, or excrement, shall live for ten months.
Having seen pretas, piśācas, and the like, as well as cities of the gandharvas and trees of golden hue, he lives for nine months.
He who suddenly becomes stout or thin, or thin and then stout,
and turns away from his natural constitution, has a lifespan of eight months.
He whose foot is fractured at the heel or at the tip of the toe will live for seven months amidst dust and mud.
If a vulture, a pigeon, a crow, a raven,
or even a blue carnivorous bird alights upon one's head, it indicates that one has six months to live.
A man who sees his own shadow as something other than itself, or is struck by rows of crows or a shower of dust, shall live for four or five days.
Having seen lightning in a cloudless sky occurring in the southern direction,
or even a rainbow at night, one's life remains for only two or three months.
He who sees his own body without a head in ghee, oil, a mirror, or water,
does not live beyond a month.
O King, for that yogin whose body has a fragrance like that of a ram or even like that of a corpse,
his life should be known to last for half a month.
Even for one whose heart and feet are completely parched while drinking water, such a person lives for ten days.
When his vital points (marmasthāna) are cut by the agitated wind and he does not experience horripilation upon contact with water, death has arrived for him.
He who, traveling in a dream toward the southern direction while riding upon a bear or a monkey and singing, does not meet death; time does not claim him.
If a woman wearing red and black garments leads a man toward the southern direction while singing and laughing in a dream, he does not live.
If one sees in a dream a single, naked Kṣapaṇaka of great strength, laughing and leaping about, one should know that death has arrived.
Furthermore, that man who sees himself submerged up to the surface of his head in an ocean of mud in a dream dies immediately.
Having seen hair, charcoal, ashes, serpents, or a river without water in a dream, death occurs after ten days on the eleventh day.
A man who, in a dream, is struck with stones by terrifying, hideous, and black men with uplifted weapons, shall meet death immediately.
If at sunrise a jackal goes toward a person, howling,
whether in the opposite direction or surrounding them, that person meets with immediate death.
He whose heart is oppressed by hunger immediately after eating, and who experiences grinding of the teeth, has reached the end of his life; of this there is no doubt.
He who does not perceive the scent of a lamp, who trembles both by day and by night,
and who does not see his own reflection in the eyes of others— he does not live.
Seeing Indra’s weapon at midnight or the host of planets during the day,
one who knows himself should consider his own life to be exhausted.
He whose nose becomes crooked, whose ears undergo depression and elevation,
and whose left eye weeps— his life has departed.
When the face becomes reddish or the tongue turns dark,
then the wise man should recognize that death is near for himself.
He who travels toward the southern direction in a dream by means of a camel or a donkey vehicle should be known as one facing immediate death; of this there is no doubt.
Covering his ears, he does not hear the internal sound;
the light of his eyes perishes—he too shall not live.
If, while falling into a pit in a dream,
one's exit is blocked and he does not emerge from the abyss, his life has reached its end.
The gaze is upward-turned and finds no rest;
it is bloodshot and rolling about;
there is heat in the mouth and a hollowing at the navel.
They declare that this is another body for men.
He who enters fire in a dream and does not emerge again,
or likewise enters water, his life ends there.
And that man who is struck by wicked spirits, whether by night or by day,
will undoubtedly meet his death at the end of seven nights.
If a man sees his own garment— which was previously stainless and white— as red or black,
one should indeed declare that death is near for him.
The reversal of one's own nature and the inversion of one's innate character— these, they say, are always near to men as Yama and Antaka.
Those whom he has constantly disciplined and who are considered his most venerable, he treats with contempt and reviles.
He does not worship the gods, nor does he honor the elders, teachers, or Brahmins; he fails to show respect to his mother and father, and he treats his sons-in-law with contempt.
When the time has arrived, that which is to be known by the wise— namely, for yogins who possess knowledge, for others, and for great-souled ones— should be understood by the discerning.
O Lord of the Earth, yogis must constantly and diligently observe the omens;
at the end of the year, their results should be known as they manifest day and night.
O Lord of Men, having observed this clearly visible and most terrifying succession of their fruits, you must recognize in your mind that the time has come.
Having correctly understood that time and having taken refuge in the state of fearlessness,
the yogi should apply himself to yoga so that this time does not become fruitless for him.
Having thus perceived the omen of death, the yogi abandons the fear born of dying;
having then beheld its true nature, he remains until the appointed time has arrived.
The knower of yoga should likewise apply himself to yoga during the divisions of that day—
in the forenoon, the afternoon, and also at midday.
Or rather, during whichever part of the night that ill omen was observed,
one should remain engaged in that very state until that day has arrived.
Then, having abandoned all fear and having conquered that time,
the self-possessed one remained in that very dwelling, or wherever his own steadfastness lay.
Having conquered the three qualities (guṇas), one should practice yoga within the Supreme Self;
becoming absorbed in that through the self, one should even abandon the activity of consciousness (cid-vṛtti).
Thereafter, he attains that supreme nirvāṇa which is beyond the senses, not within the range of the intellect,
and which cannot be described.
All this has been fully explained to you, O Ālarka,
according to the truth;
now learn from me in brief that by which you shall attain that Brahman.
Just as the moonstone releases water through contact with the rays of the moon,
yet does not do so unreasonably— that is remembered as the analogy for the yogin.
And just as the sun-gem, though not by itself, manifests fire through contact with the rays of the sun—
that too is a simile for the yogin.
Ants, mice, mongooses, house-lizards, and francolins dwell in a master's house like the master himself; when it is ruined, they depart from there for elsewhere.
But there is suffering when the master is destroyed; for them, there is nothing [of consequence] regarding that house, O King of Kings—
this is the analogy for the attainment of yoga.
Even with a body as light as a soft grass mat and a mouth as minute as a fine hair,
the instruction of that yogin creates a heap of earth.
Having seen a tree laden with leaves, flowers, and fruits being plundered by beasts, birds, humans, and others, yogins attain success.
Observing the tip of the horn of a young ruru deer, which has the shape of a *tilaka* mark,
and growing together with it, the yogi shall attain perfection (*siddhi*).
Having taken up a vessel filled with liquid and ascending a high path from the earth,
what was not perceived by the yogi upon beholding it from above?

Having understood in truth that exertion of a man which, even when all his possessions are buried underground, is sufficient for his livelihood, the yogi attains the state of having accomplished all that was to be done.
That is one's home where one dwells; that is food by which one lives;
and that is wealth by which one’s purpose is accomplished—this is happiness. What attachment can there be to these?
Just as one performs a task with instruments even when requested by others,
so too should the yogi accomplish the supreme goal by means of the intellect and other faculties that belong to another.
Jaḍa said:
Then, having prostrated before the son of Atri, that lord of the earth, Alarka, bowing low with humility and filled with great joy, spoke these words.
Alarka said: "By good fortune, O Brahmin, this [calamity] arising from the defeat by enemies has been brought about by the gods."
Thus was brought about an exceedingly fierce danger that cast doubt upon his very life.
"By good fortune, the King of Kāśī, who possesses great strength, wealth, and prowess, has been destroyed; for it is through his destruction that I have come here to be in your company."
"By good fortune I am of feeble strength; by good fortune my servants have been slain;
by good fortune the treasury has reached exhaustion; and by good fortune I have come to fear."
By good fortune, the pair of your feet has come within the range of my memory;
by good fortune, all your words are established in my heart.
"By good fortune, knowledge has arisen within me through my meeting with you;
and by good fortune, O Brahmin, compassion has been shown toward me by you."
Even misfortune becomes a source of benefit for a man when his fortune rises,
just as this calamity of yours has become a means of assistance through your meeting with me.
O Lord, that Subāhu was a benefactor to me, as was the King of Kāśī;
it is for their sake, O Master of Yoga, that I have come into your presence.
Thus, with the stain of ignorance burnt away by the fire of your grace,
I shall strive in such a way that I may never again become a vessel for such suffering.
Having obtained permission from you, a high-souled giver of knowledge, I shall renounce the state of a householder, which is a forest of trees in the form of suffering.
Dattātreya said:
Go, O Indra among kings;
may it be well with you, according to what has been told to you by me.
Free from "mine-ness" and free from egoism, conduct yourself in that manner for the sake of liberation.
Jaḍa said:
Having been addressed thus, he bowed to him and returned in haste to where the Lord of Kāśī was, along with his elder brother Subāhu.

Leaping up before Subāhu, that Alarka spoke to the heroic king of Kāśi, whose arms were great, as if laughing: MarkP_43.71: "Leaping up before Subāhu, that Alarka spoke to the heroic king of Kāśi, whose arms were great, as if laughing."
"O King of Kāśī, you who desire the kingdom, enjoy this powerful realm;
or, if it pleases you likewise, bestow it upon Subāhu."
The King of Kāśī said:
"Why have you abandoned your kingdom, Alarka, without engaging in battle? This is not the duty of a kṣatriya, and you are one who knows the dharma of the kṣatriyas."
Having conquered his circle of ministers and abandoned the fear of death,
the king should discharge his arrow, aiming it at the enemy as his target.
Having conquered him, the king may enjoy excellent pleasures as he desires;
for the sake of supreme success, he should perform great sacrifices.
Alarka said: "O hero, such was the state of my mind as well in former times."
Now hear also the cause for this contrary result.
Just as this physical body is composed of the elements, so too is the internal organ of men;
likewise, all qualities exist in every single living being without exception.
O King, when this power of consciousness alone exists and nothing else whatsoever exists, then what room is there for the states of friend, enemy, lord, or servant based on knowledge?
