Therefore, O lord of men, having experienced that supreme suffering born of fear of you,
I have obtained knowledge through the grace of Dattātreya.
But one who has conquered the group of senses, having abandoned attachment entirely and fixing the mind upon Brahman, achieves the supreme victory in conquering that [mind].
Since there is nothing else to be accomplished for the sake of that attainment,
one restrains the senses and thereby secures success.
Thus, I am not your enemy, nor are you my foe; this Subāhu is not one who does me harm.
I have seen all this as being just like myself.
"O King, let another enemy be sought out by you."
Thus addressed by him, King Subāhu rose up delighted and,
greeting his brother with the words "By good fortune!", rejoiced.
The Lord of Kāśī spoke these words.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of Ariṣṭa," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-four: Subāhu said:
O tiger among kings,
that for which I have come to you for refuge has been entirely attained by me; I shall depart, so may you be happy.
Kākhirāja said:
"For what reason have you come, and what is the purpose you have accomplished, O Subāhu?
Tell me that, for my curiosity is great."
"Having conquered me—who am possessed of a great ancestral kingdom that has been invaded by the sun of impurity—you have urged me on, saying, 'Give [the kingdom] back! (MarkP 44.3)
Therefore, having seized the kingdom from this younger brother of yours, I have brought this army of yours; enjoy it, for it is appropriate for your own lineage.
Subāhu said: O King of Kāśī, listen to the purpose for which this exertion was undertaken by me,
and for which you yourself were made to exert yourself so intensely.
"This brother of mine is attached to vulgar pleasures, though he knows the truth;
my two elder brothers are both deluded and enlightened."
O Lord of the Earth, just as a small amount of mother’s milk was placed in the mouths of those two and myself during our childhood, so too has awakening been instilled in our ears.
O King, those categories of objects which are recognized by men as belonging to those two and to me have been brought to light by my mind; they are not [limited] to his measure alone.
O Lord of the Earth, just as when one among those traveling toward a single goal falls into distress, so too does sorrow arise for the virtuous; such is our grief.
O Lord of Men, while this body is sinking, fallen into the delusion of household life, its kinsmen maintain the notion that it is their brother.
Then, having reached a firm decision, I resolved that the cultivation of detachment from suffering would come about, and I applied myself with effort toward the end of this existence.
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, his detachment from suffering has arisen through perfect awakening;
the task is accomplished. May it be well with you; I shall depart.
"O King, having drunk from my breast while languid with passion within my womb, let them not follow the path traveled by the sons of other women. (MarkP 44.13)
Having reflected upon all this, I have performed it with you as my refuge;
that too has been accomplished, and I shall now proceed again for the sake of success.
O Lord of Men, those by whom one's own kin, relatives, and friends are neglected when they are sinking into distress—
I do not consider them to possess their senses; for they are indeed deficient.

If one who has a friend, kinsman, or relative capable of helping should nevertheless suffer, the blame lies with those [who do not assist] regarding virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; but it does not lie with that person.
"O King, through association with you, this great task has been accomplished by me.
May it be well with you; I shall now depart. O best of men, may you become a possessor of knowledge."
The King of Kāśī said:
"A great service has been rendered by you to the virtuous Alarka;
why do you not likewise direct your mind toward doing me a favor?"
Since the association of the virtuous with the virtuous is fruitful and never without result,
it is therefore fitting that I have attained this exaltation through my reliance upon you.
Subāhu said: "Regarding the four aims of human life known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—
among these, dharma, artha, and kāma are all abandoned by that other [aim]."
I shall explain that to you in brief; listen here with a focused mind.
Having heard it and having reflected upon it correctly, O King, strive for your own welfare.
"O King, you should not entertain the notion 'I am' nor the notion 'mine.
For having reflected thoroughly, one sees that dharma indeed has no support in the absence of dharma."
Having reflected with your own self during the latter parts of the night, you should consider: "To whom does this notion 'I' belong? and examine both the internal and the external.
That which begins with the unmanifest and ends with the specific elements is changeless and insentient;
you should know both the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as who it is that knows them—namely, me.
Within this very consciousness, everything has been understood by you;
to perceive a self in that which is not-self is a delusion as empty as space.
Thus, O King, I am omnipresent according to worldly convention;
having been asked all this by you, I shall now depart.
Having spoken thus, the wise Subāhu departed from the King of Kāśī;
and the King of Kāśī, having honored Alarka, returned to his own city.
Alarka also, having consecrated his eldest son as the lord of men,
went to the forest for the sake of his own spiritual perfection, having completely renounced all attachments.
Then, after a long time, free from dualities and without possessions,
having attained incomparable perfection in yoga, he reached supreme nirvāṇa.
Beholding this entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans,
bound by the snares consisting of the qualities (guṇas) and being constantly bound anew.

Drawn by the senses— which are conditioned by notions of "son" and so forth, "brother's son" and so forth, or "one's own" and "another's"— the soul is afflicted by suffering and possesses a fragmented vision.
The Great-Minded One, having himself crossed over and not being submerged within the mire of ignorance, sang this verse: MarkP_44.32 //
"Alas, what suffering it was that we formerly exercised sovereignty!"—
thus was it later understood by me through yoga, that there is no happiness higher than this.
Jaḍa said:
"O father, practice this supreme yoga for the sake of liberation;
by means of it you shall attain that Brahman, reaching which you no longer grieve."
Then I too shall depart; what need have I for sacrifices or for muttering prayers?
For one who has accomplished his purpose, such action conduces to the state of Brahman.
Having obtained your permission, free from dualities and without possessions,
I shall strive for liberation in such a way that I may attain final bliss.
The birds said:
Having spoken thus to his father and obtained his permission,
O Brahmin, that wise one departed, having renounced all possessions.
His father as well, being of great intelligence, likewise gradually entered the fourth stage of life after having established himself in the forest-dweller’s stage.
There, having encountered his own son and abandoned his bonds such as the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth,
that wise man attained supreme perfection, having gained realization at that very moment.
This has been told to you, O Brahmin, which we were asked by you;
it has been explained at great length and according to the truth. What else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Jaḍa," in the Dialogue between Father and Son within the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Five.
Jaimini said:
"O best of the twice-born, you have correctly explained to me this twofold Vedic action: that which is engaged in worldly activity (*pravṛtta*) and that which is withdrawn from it (*nivṛtta*)."
"Oh, by the grace of your father, you possess such knowledge that even having attained this state of an animal, your delusion has been dispelled! (MarkP 45.2)
Blessed are you, for since your minds remain established in the prior state for the sake of perfection,
they are not shaken by the delusions arising from sense objects.
By good fortune, you have been described by that wise Bhagavān Mārkaṇḍeya as those who most effectively remove all doubts.
In this extremely perilous cycle of existence where humans wander,
association with those such as you does not arise for those who have not practiced austerities.
If, having encountered you whose vision is wisdom,
I were not to achieve my purpose, then surely I would find no fulfillment elsewhere.
I consider your intellect regarding both active and withdrawn knowledge and action to be stainless, as it is not that of anyone else.
O best of the twice-born, if your minds are inclined toward showing me favor,
then you ought to explain this to me in its entirety.
O virtuous ones, how did this world of moving and non-moving beings arise,
and how will it go again to its dissolution at the time of the end?
And how do the lineages originate from the gods, sages, ancestors, and elemental beings?
What are the Manvantaras, and what is the history of the dynasties?
Whatever creations there are, as well as whatever dissolutions; how the divisions of the kalpas occur, and what the duration of the manvantaras is.
And how the configuration of the earth is, and what the measurement of the world is;
and how the oceans, mountains, rivers, and forests are situated.
The host of worlds beginning with Bhūrloka up to Svarloka has its support in Pātāla;
likewise, it is the path for the sun, the moon, and the other planets, constellations, and luminaries.
I wish to hear all this regarding the dissolution at the end of the eon,
and what will remain in this world once it has been withdrawn.
The birds said:
"O best of sages, this incomparable burden of questions which has been asked by you—we shall explain that to you; listen to it here, O Jaimini."
Just as it was told of old by Mārkaṇḍeya to Krauṣṭuki—
the son of a twice-born, who was peaceful, protected by his vows, and wise.
O Lord, Krauṣṭuki questioned the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, who was seated with the best of the twice-born, regarding that which he had previously asked.
And we shall relate to you with pleasure that which the sage, the descendant of Bhṛgu, told him; listen to it, O best of the twice-born.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, the Grandfather born from the lotus,
who exists as the source of the universe— abiding in the form of Viṣṇu during its maintenance,
and as the fierce Rudra in the form of the Destroyer at the time of dissolution.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Long ago, as soon as Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, had come into being,
this Purāṇa and the Vedas issued forth from his mouths.
The supreme ṛṣis composed numerous Purāṇa-saṃhitās,
and they also divided the Vedas into thousands of parts.
Knowledge of the Dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty belong to that Great-Souled One;
indeed, this fourfold set is not accomplished without his instruction.
From him, the mental sons of the seven ṛṣis received the Vedas;
and the ancient mental sons of that [Brahmā], the munis, received the Purāṇa.
This was told by Cyavana in the presence of Bhṛgu;
and it was also proclaimed to Dakṣa by those high-souled sages among the twice-born.
This was also told to me by Dakṣa at that time;
today I shall relate it to you, for it destroys the defilement of the Kali age.
"O highly fortunate one, listen to all this from me through my meditative concentration,
just as it was previously heard by me as Dakṣa was speaking, O Sage."
Having prostrated before the source of the world, the unborn, the undecaying refuge,
the creator of the moving and unmoving universe, and the supreme state;
To Brahmā, the primal person, who is the incomparable cause for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world],
and in whom everything is established.
Having bowed down to that wise Hiraṇyagarbha, the sustainer of the worlds, I shall correctly explain the unsurpassed category of beings.
Beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), it possesses all varieties and characteristics;
it is accessible through the five means of valid cognition and endowed with six streams.
"O highly fortunate one, listen with supreme concentration to that which is eternally presided over by the Puruṣa, yet appears as if it were non-eternal."
O great seers, that which is the primary cause, called the Unmanifest (avyakta), which they call the subtle, eternal Prakṛti, consisting of both being and non-being; 45.32.
It is eternal, imperishable, ageless, and immeasurable; it does not depend on anything else, and it is devoid of smell, form, taste, sound, and touch.
Without beginning or end, the source of the world, from which the three qualities arise and into which they dissolve,
inconceivable and unknowable, Brahman existed in the beginning.

Following that dissolution, O sage, this entire universe was pervaded by it; then, from that state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), [the creation proceeds] presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Then again, at the time of creation, from that [state] in which the qualities were being manifested,
the principle of Pradhāna emerged and enveloped the Mahat.
Just as a seed is covered by its husk, so too is the Great Principle (mahat) enveloped by the unmanifest;
it is declared to be threefold: consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
From that, indeed, the threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) was born:
the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi, which is characterized by darkness (tamas).
And that Great One (Mahat), being enveloped by that which is indeed intensely passionate, undergoes transformation;
from that, the source of the elements (bhūtādi) produces the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra).
From the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), he emitted space, which is characterized by sound;
then the source of the elements (bhūtādi) enveloped that space, which consists of sound alone.
In this world, the subtle element of touch alone is born; of this there is no doubt.
From it, the powerful wind is born, and touch is considered its quality.
And Vāyu, undergoing transformation, indeed produced the subtle element of form (rūpa-mātra);
light is born from Vāyu, and it is said to have the quality of form.
Vāyu, consisting of the subtle element of touch alone, indeed enveloped the subtle element of form;
and light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste.
From that, water indeed came into being, and it was composed of the essence of taste;
that water, consisting of the element of taste, then enveloped the element of form.
And the waters, undergoing transformation, produced mere fragrance;
from that, the aggregate is born, and therefore fragrance is considered its quality.
In each of those [subtle elements], there is only that [specific quality]; therefore, they are known as "tanmātras" (merely-that).
And because they denote nothing other than their own specific quality, they are consequently called "aviśeṣas" (undifferentiated).
They are neither peaceful nor terrible, nor are they deluded, for there is no distinction among them;
this creation of the elements and subtle essences proceeds from the tamasic ego.
From the *vaikārika* ego, which is characterized by the predominance of *sattva*,
that *vaikārika* creation proceeds simultaneously.
There are exactly five organs of perception and five organs of action;
they say these ten organs are the Taijasa (fiery) deities, while the Vaikārika (modifying) ones are [the other ten].
The eleventh there is the mind; the deities known as the Vaikārikas are said to reside therein.
The ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth [are the organs].
For the sake of attaining sound and the other objects of sense, those endowed with intelligence will be described:
the feet, the anus, the generative organ, the hands, and speech shall be the fifth.
Motion, emission, bliss, craftsmanship, and speech—these are its functions;
space, being merely sound, entered into the mere quality of touch.
The wind arises as twofold; touch is considered its quality.
As it enters [the next stage], form likewise appears, and both sound and touch become its qualities.
Fire, possessing sound, touch, and form, was twice as great as that;
and sound, touch, and form entered into the subtle element of taste.
Therefore, water should be known as possessing four qualities; it consists essentially of taste.
Sound, touch, form, and smell enter into taste.
United by the mere quality of smell, they enveloped this earth;
therefore, earth is seen among the elements as possessing five qualities and being gross.
They are known as the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded because of their specific distinctions;
through mutual interpenetration, they support one another.
Within the earth, indeed, is all this world, veiled by dense clouds;
and the specific objects perceivable by the senses are remembered as such because of their fixed nature.
Each subsequent one acquires the quality of each preceding one;
these seven, possessing diverse potencies and existing separately, [are ineffective] without their union.
Being unable to create living beings without coming together entirely,
they met one another in mutual union and became dependent upon one another.
And having attained complete unity, they possess the single mark of the aggregate,
both because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest.
Indeed, those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg;
there, it gradually attains growth like a bubble in water.
O one of great intelligence, from the elements arose the cosmic egg,
which rested upon the vast waters;
having grown within that primordial egg, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) became known as Brahmā.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa.
As the primordial creator of all beings, Brahmā appeared at the beginning.
By him all this triple world, including the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded;
from him Meru was produced, as were the mountains and the fetal membrane (jarāyu).
The waters of the womb gathered within that egg of the Great-Souled One;
within that egg was the entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans.
From that [Mahat] arise the lamps and so forth, the mountains, the oceans, the kingdom, the luminaries, and the collection of worlds;
then, from water, wind, fire, and space, [arise the elements] starting with the primary matter (bhūtādi) on the outside.
The layer of clarified butter (vṛta-maṇḍa) is ten times [the thickness of the previous layer], and it is again surrounded by each of those [elements] individually,
increasing in magnitude by that same measure.
Accompanied by all of them and enveloped by the Unmanifest (Avyakta),
the cosmic egg is surrounded by these seven primordial coverings.
And those eight primal natures (prakṛtis) remain covering one another;
this is that eternal primal nature within which that Puruṣa resides.
That which is called Brahmā has been described to you in brief; now listen again to it, just as someone submerged in water might emerge from that very water.
Brahmā pours forth the water, and so does the all-pervading Prakṛti;
the unmanifest is designated as the field (kṣetra), while Brahmā is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).

One should know all this as the characteristic of the field and the knower of the field. Thus, this primordial creation, presided over by the Knower of the Field, appeared spontaneously for the first time, like a flash of lightning.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Origin of Brahmā," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa,
composed by the venerable great sage Vedavyāsa.
The glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
(Second Part) Chapter Forty-Six.
Krauṣṭuki said:
O Blessed One, the birth from an egg has been correctly described to me;
likewise, the birth of the high-souled Brahmā within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) has been told.
O descendant of Bhrigu’s lineage, I wish to hear from you this:
when the dissolution of all things has occurred at the end of time and everything has been withdrawn, does the creation of beings exist or does it not? (MarkP 46.2)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When this entire world goes to dissolution into its primordial nature (prakṛti), then the learned call this the elemental reabsorption (prākṛta-pratisañcara).
When the manifest has subsided into its own self and all modification has been withdrawn,
both Prakṛti and Puruṣa remain in a state of similarity.
Then tamas and sattva were established in a state of equilibrium—
neither excessive nor deficient— and they were mutually dependent upon one another.
Just as oil exists within sesame seeds or clarified butter resides in milk,
so too does passion (rajas) abide pervading darkness (tamas) and goodness (sattva).
The period from the creation of Brahmā until the end of his lifespan—two parārdhas—is one day for the Supreme Lord;
his night is equal in duration to that.
Awakened at the break of day, he is the beginning of the world, yet himself without beginning;
the cause of all, of inconceivable nature, supreme, and beyond all further action.
Having swiftly entered both Prakṛti and Puruṣa,
the Supreme Lord, the Master of the World, agitated them through his supreme yoga.
Just as intoxication takes hold of young women, or as the spring breeze enters them,
so did he, possessing a form of yoga, enter to cause agitation.
But when Pradhāna was being agitated, that god known as Brahmā emerged,
situated within the shell of the cosmic egg, just as I have described to you.
He alone is the agitator who was previously the object of agitation, the Lord of Prakṛti;
he remains in the state of Pradhāna through both contraction and expansion.
Having come forth as the source of the world, although devoid of qualities, he proceeds with creation while assuming the state of Brahmā and experiencing the quality of rajas.
Having created the subjects while in the state of Brahmā, he then, possessing an abundance of *sattva*,
attains the state of Viṣṇu and performs their protection through righteousness.
Then, intensified by the quality of tamas, having withdrawn the entire universe into the state of Rudra,
he who is both endowed with the three qualities and yet devoid of qualities, sleeps over the three worlds.
Just as he was previously the pervasive field, the protector, and the reaper,
so too does he come to assume the designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
In the state of Brahmā, he creates the worlds; in the state of Rudra, he even withdraws them;
and in the state of Viṣṇu, he remains indifferent—these are the three states of the Self-Existent One.
Rajas is Brahmā, tamas is Rudra, and sattva is Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World;
these alone are the three gods, and these alone are the three qualities (guṇas).
For these are mutual mates and likewise mutually dependent;
there is no separation between them for even a moment, nor do they ever abandon one another.
Thus Brahmā, the first in the world, the four-faced god of gods,
having resorted to the quality of rajas, established himself in the role of creator.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the first of the gods, though beginningless by way of metaphorical designation,
was born at the beginning of creation, situated upon the pericarp of the earth-lotus.
The maximum lifespan of that great-souled one is indeed one hundred years;
learn from me its reckoning according to the measurement of Brahmā himself.
Ten *nimeṣas* are said to be one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* are indeed one *kalā*;
thirty such *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*.
A day and night of humans is traditionally reckoned as thirty muhūrtas;
and thirty such days and nights constitute two fortnights, which is called a month.
By those six [months] is a year; there are two solstices, the southern and the northern.
That is a day and night of the gods; among them, the northern solstice is the day.
The four yugas, known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, consist of twelve thousand divine years; hear from me their respective divisions.
The Kṛta age is said to consist of four thousand years;
its morning twilight consists of four hundred years, and its evening twilight is of the same duration.
The Tretā age consists of three thousand divine years and three hundred;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) is equal to that, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is likewise.
The Dvāpara age consists of two thousand and two hundred years;
its dawn is said to be two hundred years, and its twilight is likewise two hundred years.
O best of the twice-born, Kali lasts for a thousand divine years;
its dawn (sandhyā) and twilight (sandhyāṃśa) are each declared to be one hundred [years].
This period of twelve thousand years is designated as a "yuga" by the poets;
a thousandfold of this is declared to be a day of Brahmā.
O Brahman, during the day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus;
they exist in their respective portions, and that [day] is divided into a thousand such parts.
The gods, the seven ṛṣis, Indra, Manu, and his sons, the kings,
are created together with Manu and withdrawn as before.
The number of four yugas is indeed seventy-one and more;
learn from me the calculation of that manvantara in terms of human years.
O twice-born one, thirty full crores have been calculated by number,
as well as sixty-six other millions (niyutas) by calculation.
Twenty thousand years, plus a little more—
know from me that this is declared to be a manvantara in divine years.
Eight thousand years according to divine reckoning,
along with another fifty-two thousand years in addition.
For this period of fourteen guṇas is remembered as a day of Brahmā;
at its conclusion, O Brahmin, a dissolution is declared by the wise to be the "occasional" (naimittika) one.
The Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and Svarloka are perishable;
likewise they come to destruction, while Maharloka remains.
Even those dwelling there depart for Janaloka due to the heat;
and when the three worlds have become a single ocean, Brahmā indeed sleeps during the night.
The night is of the same duration as that day; at its end, [the world] is created again.
In this manner, one year of Brahmā passes, and that consists of one hundred such years.
Indeed, one hundred of his years is called a *parama*;
likewise, fifty such years is proclaimed as a *parārdha*.
In this manner, O best of the twice-born, one half of a *parārtha* passed away;
at its conclusion occurred the great aeon (*mahākalpa*) renowned as the Pādma.
O twice-born one, this first Kalpa of the current second Parārdha is designated as Vārāha.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Measurement of Brahmā’s Lifespan," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Seven.
Krauṣṭuki said:
Tell me in detail how the blessed Brahmā, the original creator, the lord of creatures and the divine master, indeed brought forth the progeny.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Brahmin, I shall now tell you how the Lord,
the eternal creator of the world, brought forth the entire universe, both the stationary and the moving.
At the end of the lotus, at the time of dissolution, the Lord Brahmā arose from the womb of Night; then, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), he beheld the world as a void.
In this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, the god whose nature is Brahman, the source and the dissolution of the world: MarkP_47.4 // [Verse follows]
"We have heard that 'nārāḥ' and 'tanavaḥ' are indeed names for the waters;
because he lies within them, he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa."
Having awakened in that water and perceived through inference that the earth lay within it, he then desired to effect its extraction from the ground.
Just as in former ages at the beginning of the kalpas he assumed other bodies such as those of the fish and the tortoise, so too did he take on the form of a boar.
Having assumed a divine form composed of the Vedas and sacrifices, the all-pervading Lord, the source of all and omnipresent, entered the waters.
And having lifted the earth from the netherworld (pātāla), he released it into the waters;
while the Lord of the World was being meditated upon by the Siddhas residing in Janaloka.
Above that flood of water, the earth stands like a great ship;
yet, because of the vastness of its body, the earth does not sink into submersion.
Then, having leveled the earth,
he created mountains upon it after the previous creation had been consumed by the Saṃvartaka fire.
By that fire, those mountains were shattered on all sides upon the earth;
the rocks sank into the single ocean, and the waters were condensed by the wind.
Wherever they settled, there they became immovable;
having thus divided the earth, it was adorned with seven continents.
He fashioned the four worlds, beginning with Bhūr, as before;
and as he contemplated creation at the beginning of the kalpas, just as in the past.
Therefore, that which consists of darkness (tamas) appeared without being preceded by conscious intent;
it is known as tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra.
This fivefold ignorance arose from the Great-Souled One;
as he meditated, the unawakened creation manifested in five ways.
Lacking light both inside and out, its nature concealed and consisting of mountains—
since the primary [beings] are called "mountains" (naga), this is therefore known as the Primary Creation (mukhya-sarga).
Seeing that creation to be imperfect, he thought of another once more;
as he meditated upon that creation, the flow of animals (tiryak-srotas) indeed came into being.
Because their movement is horizontal, they are known as the "horizontal-streamers" (tiryak-srotas);
these are renowned as the beasts and so forth, for they consist mostly of darkness and lack knowledge.
Adhering to the wrong path, they consider their ignorance to be knowledge;
possessed of egoism and self-conceit, they consist of twenty-eight types.
All of them were luminous within, yet they were mutually obscured;
considering even that to be ineffective, another arose from him as he meditated.
The third, however, was the Ūrdhvastrotas, who were characterized by sattva;
they abounded in happiness and joy, and were unobstructed both internally and externally.
Radiant both externally and internally, arising from the upward stream, the third is the divine creation (devasarga), which is characterized by contentment. Thus it is remembered.
When that creation was completed, Brahmā then felt satisfaction;
thereafter, he meditated upon another, supreme creation to be accomplished.
As he was thus meditating with truthful intent,
there then emerged from the Unmanifest the "downward-streaming" (arvāk-srotas) practitioner.
Because they turned back from that point onward, they are called the arvāk-srotas (those with downward currents);
they abound in light, yet are dominated by darkness and excessive passion.
Therefore, those humans who perform [the rite] repeatedly are full of suffering;
they are manifest both externally and internally, and they are practitioners.
The fifth is the creation of favor (anugraha-sarga), which is established as fourfold:
through error (viparyaya), through attainment (siddhi), as well as through tranquility (śānti) and contentment (tuṣṭi).
Furthermore, they know the objects that have passed away as well as those currently existing;
this is called the sixth creation of the beings beginning with the elements (bhūtas).
All those who are possessive, as well as those who delight in sharing,
those who are inciters, those who lack moral conduct, and those such as the Bhūtas and so forth— these are to be known [as the classes].
The first creation is to be known as that of Mahat from Brahmā; the second is the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātras), which is called the creation of the gross elements (bhūtasarga).
The third creation, however, is known as the Vaikārika, which pertains to the senses;
thus is this Prākṛta creation, produced preceded by the intellect.
The fourth is indeed the primary creation (mukhya-sarga), and the immobile beings are known as the primary ones;
that which is called the horizontal-stream (tiryak-srotas) is the fifth, consisting of those born of animal wombs (tiryag-yoni).

Likewise, the sixth creation of the gods is said to be that of the *ūrdhva-strotas* (those who flow upwards); thereafter, the seventh creation is that of the *arvāk-strotas* (those who flow downwards), which is the human race.
The eighth is the creation of grace, which is both characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and darkness (tāmasa).
These five are known as the secondary creations (vaikṛta), while three are considered primary creations (prākṛta).
The Prākṛta, the Vaikṛta, and the Kaumāra is recorded as the ninth;
thus indeed are these nine creations of Prajāpati fully described.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Primary and Secondary Creation," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Eight:
Krauṣṭuki said:
The creation of the gods and others has been correctly described to me by your lordship in brief, O Brahman; now tell it to me in detail.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Brahmin, she was conditioned by her previous deeds, both auspicious and inauspicious.
For they are thus known as being unreleased, yet withdrawn at the time of dissolution.
O Brahman, at that time, as Brahmā was performing the act of creation, the fourfold classes of beings, beginning with the gods and ending with the immovable, were born from his mind.
Then, desiring to create the fourfold [beings]— the gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans—
he joined his own self to these waters.
From Prajāpati, whose self was disciplined, the quality of darkness (tamas) became predominant;
from his loins, as he desired to create, the Asuras were first born.
Then he cast off that body whose nature was composed of the quality of darkness (tamas);
once discarded by him, that body immediately became night.
Assuming another body, he who desired to create attained joy;
then, from the abundance of the quality of purity (sattva), the gods were born from his mouth.
And that all-pervading Lord of Beings cast off that body as well;
once discarded, it became a day characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva).
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of sattva;
as he regarded it as his father, his ancestors were born from him.
Having created the ancestors, that Lord cast off even that body;
and once cast off, it became the twilight (saṃdhyā), situated between day and night.
Then that Lord assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of rajas;
from that, human beings were born, originating from the quality of rajas alone.
Having created human beings, the Lord then cast off that body;
it became the moonlight which appears at the end of the night and at the break of day.
O twice-born one, these are the bodies of that wise God of gods:
they are known as night, day, twilight, and moonlight.

Likewise, the twilight of the stars consists of the three qualities in their state of pure goodness (sattva); night consists of the quality of darkness (tamas). Therefore, it is indeed called the "three-watch" period.
Therefore, the gods are powerful by day, while the asuras are powerful at night; likewise, humans are powerful when the moonlight appears, and the ancestors during the twilight.
They become powerful and invincible to their adversaries; of this there is no doubt.
But by encountering the opposite of that, they meet with the opposite result.
Moonlight, night, day, and twilight— these four, O Lord,
are indeed the bodies of Brahmā, which are supported by the three qualities (guṇas).
Having produced these four, Prajāpati,
overcome by hunger and thirst, assumed another body composed of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) during the night.
In that darkness, the unborn Lord created beings who were deformed and bearded, emaciated by hunger; and they began to devour that body.
O twice-born one, those others who said "We shall protect" became the Rākṣasas; and those who said "We shall devour" became the Yakṣas, because of their act of devouring (yakṣaṇa).
Upon seeing them, the hair of that Creator fell out in displeasure;
yet those hairs did not re-grow upon the head of Brahmā.
Because of their gliding (*sarpaṇa*), they became serpents (*sarpāḥ*); because of their deficiency (*hīnatva*), they are known as *ahayaḥ*.
Then, seeing the serpents, he, whose nature is anger, created beings from his wrath.
Those fierce beings who were flesh-eaters were tawny in color;
then, as he meditated upon the earth (gā), the Gandharvas were born as his sons.
As they drank the speech, they were born as Gandharvas; for that reason, they are so called. When these eight divine origins had been created, that Lord [proceeded further].
Then he created other birds and cattle from his own body;
he created goats from his mouth and sheep from his chest.
And from his belly he created cows, and from his two sides he brought forth Brahmā;
and from his feet he created horses, elephants, donkeys, hares, and deer.
Camels, mules, and various species of diverse forms,
as well as medicinal herbs bearing fruits and roots, were born from his body hair.
Having thus created the animals and the plants, the omnipresent Lord performed a sacrifice in the ritual;
that was at the beginning of the Kalpa, at the onset of the Tretā Yuga.
The cow, the goat, the man, the sheep, the horse, the mule, and the donkey—these they call domestic animals; now learn from me those that are wild.
Wild beasts, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth;
aquatic creatures as the sixth class of animals, and reptiles as the seventh.
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī meter, the Ṛgveda hymns, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Soma-juice, the Rathantara-sāman, and the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice among all sacrifices.
From his southern mouth, he emitted the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, the Pañcadaśa stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and likewise the Uktha.
From his western face, he fashioned the Sāman chants, the Jagatī meter, the fifteen-fold Stoma, the Vairūpa, and the Atirātra sacrifice.
From his northern mouth, he created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāmaṇa, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Svarāja.
At the beginning of the kalpa, the all-pervading Lord created lightning, thunderclouds, red clouds, rainbows, and birds.
High and low beings were born from the limbs of that [Being], after he had first created the fourfold progeny: the gods, asuras, and ancestors.
Then he created all beings, both stationary and moving—
yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of apsarases.
Nagas, kinnaras, rakshasas, birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents;
that which is imperishable and that which is perishable—all this, whether stationary or moving.
Whatever actions those beings performed prior to creation,
those very same actions they undertake again and again as they are created once more.

Whether violent or non-violent, mild or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, truthful or false—impregnated by those very qualities, they enter into them; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which accords with it.
Regarding the senses, their objects, the elements, and bodies, that Lord,
the Creator himself, ordained their diversity and their specific functions.
In the beginning, he created from the very words of the Veda the names and forms of all beings, the expansion of their activities, and [the names] of the gods and others.
He bestows the names of the seers and those creations among the gods that were produced at the end of the night, as well as those of others.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear again and again in their regular succession,
so too do these same states of being recur at the beginnings of the Yugas.
Such creations indeed arise at the end of every night for Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
as he awakens in every kalpa.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manner of Creation," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-nine:
Krauṣṭuki said:
O Brahman, you have described that which is the downward-streaming human being; tell me in detail how Brahmā created it.
And furthermore, O Mahāmati, tell me how he created the castes and their qualities,
and what the traditional duties are said to be for the Brahmins and the others.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O sage, as Brahmā was formerly creating while meditating upon the Truth,
he then emitted from his mouth a thousand pairs of beings.
For those who were born were endowed with goodness and possessed their own splendor;
he then produced another thousand pairs from his chest.
All of them were dominated by the quality of rajas, full of vigor, and impatient;
moreover, he created another thousand pairs from his thighs.
Those who were dominated by rajas and tamas are remembered as being of a striving nature;
he also created another thousand pairs from his two feet.
Overwhelmed by darkness, all were indeed devoid of splendor and possessed small intellects;
thereafter, those living beings, produced through the union of pairs, began to rejoice.
Possessed by mutual desire, they proceeded to engage in sexual union;
from that time forth, indeed, was the origin of pairs in this kalpa.
The monthly menstrual flow that women normally experience did not occur for them then;
therefore, they did not give birth, even though they engaged in sexual intercourse.
At the end of their lifespan, they give birth to pairs at once;
from that time forward, indeed, was the origin of pairs in this kalpa.
Through meditation and the mind, a pure object—sound and so forth—arises simultaneously for those beings; each such object possesses five characteristics.
Thus was this human creation of Prajāpati in the beginning;
from his lineage were born those by whom this world was filled.
In that age, they indeed roam among rivers, lakes, oceans, and even mountains, where the cold and heat are mild.
O Mahāmati, having attained natural satisfaction regarding sense objects,
they experience no obstruction, nor hatred, nor even envy.
Dwelling indeed upon mountains and by the ocean, they were entirely without fixed abodes;
moving about free from desire, their minds were ever joyful.
Piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as envious people, beasts,
birds, crocodiles, fish, and reptiles— MarkP_49.16.
For those who are egg-born are indeed obstructors; they are born of unrighteousness.
They do not produce roots, fruits, or flowers, nor do they yield seasonal crops for years.
The time was pleasant in every season, with neither excessive heat nor cold;
as time passed, their various accomplishments were achieved.
And so, although they were not satiated in the forenoon and at midday,
their satisfaction was achieved without effort as they desired it once again.
And as they desired, such exertion arose in their minds;
consequently, those waters attained subtlety and the accomplishment of various shimmering flavors.
And another [woman] was born who grants all desires;
those subjects, with bodies not subject to the [usual] processes of refinement, remained in perpetual youth.
Without sexual union, offspring are born from them as pairs;
they are equal in birth and appearance, and they die together as well.
Free from desire and aversion, they dwell together with one another;
all are equal in form and lifespan, devoid of inferiority or superiority.
The lifespan is four thousand human years, and they live without misfortunes caused by the afflictions.
Yet in some places and at other times, the earth remained fortunate in every respect; however, as time passed, it went to destruction just like all living beings.
In that manner, those accomplishments (siddhis) gradually perished everywhere;
when all of them had vanished, men fell from the sky.
For the most part, those wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) have come to be designated as "houses," and from them all their various enjoyments arise.
At that time, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, they produced offspring from them;
then, in the course of time, passion suddenly arose within them.
Because menstrual flow occurs month after month, there is repeated conception of embryos;
because passion arises from that, those trees are designated as "houses" for them.
O Brahmin, for others, however, the branches of trees fell down,
and garments as well as ornaments were produced from their fruits.
In those very [trees], there arises for them honey, endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor;
it is without bees, possesses great potency, and is found in every single blossom-cup.
Or rather, they subsisted upon it during the mouth of the Tretā-yuga;
then, after a certain period of time, they were once again possessed by greed.
Possessed by the sense of "mine," they took possession of those trees;
yet, because of that transgression, even those trees perished for them.
Then, pairs of opposites indeed arose, such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst;
to ward off the affliction caused by those pairs, they first built cities.
In the desert wastes, in difficult terrains, on mountains, and in caves,
they take refuge in fortresses— whether in trees, on mountains, or by the water.
And having measured out artificial fortresses according to their own fingers' breadth,
they first established those measurements for the purpose of standardization.

The atom (paramāṇu) is the ultimate subtle; then the mote of dust in a sunbeam (trasareṇu), the particle of earth-dust (mahīrajas), the tip of a hair (bālāgra), the nit (likṣā), the louse (yūkā), and then the belly of a barley grain (yavodara).
They say that eight *yavas* in succession make one *aṅgula*;
six *aṅgulas* constitute a *pada*, and twice that is known as a *vitasti*.
Two *vitastis* likewise constitute a *hasta*, which measures from the *brāhmya-tīrtha* [the tip of the thumb] to the end;
four *hastas* are a *dhanus*, a *daṇḍa*, and also a pair of *nāḍikās*.
Two thousand bows make one *gavyūti*, and four times that is declared by the wise to be a *yojana*; this is the ultimate measure for the purpose of calculation.
Then, regarding the four types of fortresses, they diligently constructed three from their own materials and the fourth as an artificial fortress.
O twice-born one, a *pura*, a *kheṭaka*, likewise a *droṇīmukha*, a *śākhānagaraka*, as well as a *karvaṭaka* and a *drama*; MarkP_49.42.
He established a village with a well-arranged settlement of houses, containing separate dwellings for them, surrounded on all sides by high ramparts and walls and encircled by a moat.
The city should have a width of one and a half yojanas and a length eight times that;
it is recommended to slope toward the east and north, with its lineage of pure descent extending outward.
A *kheṭa* is half of that, and a *karvaṭa* is a quarter of it;
a *droṇīmukha* is smaller than that by one-eighth part. Thus it is said.
A city devoid of walls and moats is called a *kharvaṭa*;
another type is a branch-city (*śākhānagaraka*) which belongs to the administration of a minister or a feudal lord (*sāmanta*).
Likewise, a settlement known as a village consists of a majority of Śūdra people, primarily cultivators who subsist on their own wealth, situated amidst lands fit for cultivation and enjoyment.
That dwelling which is constructed by men with a specific purpose in view, such as from another city or similar place, should indeed be understood by men as a *vasati*.
One who is mostly wicked, who wanders upon the lands of others without his own fields, and who is powerful, is known as a *dramī* in the village; he relies on the favor of the king's favorites.
With goods loaded upon carts, without a marketplace, and with herds of cows,
the settlement was like a cowherd camp whose dwellings were established wherever they pleased.
Having thus constructed cities and other settlements for their own residence,
they indeed built dwellings as abodes for the pairs of humans.
Just as the trees had previously stood there in the form of houses,
those creatures, recollecting all of that, constructed their dwellings accordingly.
Just as the branches of a tree extend in such a manner and others extend in another,
some bent and others raised, even so did they fashion the branches.

O best of the twice-born, those very branches that formerly belonged to the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) became the branches of houses; for that reason, they possess the nature of "śāla" among them.
Having thus brought about mutual destruction,
they ceased to consider the means of livelihood once the *kalpavṛkṣa* trees had entirely perished along with the honey.
Those creatures, indeed, were agitated by despair and afflicted by thirst and hunger;
then, at the beginning of the Tretā age, spiritual success (siddhi) appeared to them.
For other rains are not produced by these [elements], but rather rain falls from them according to their desire;
indeed, whatever waters of rain fall here upon the lowlands belong to them.
By the rain that had been withheld, the streams, channels, and rivers were filled;
those drops of water which had previously reached the surface of the earth [now surged forth].
Then, through contact with the earth,
fourteen types of medicinal herbs— both cultivated and wild— arose spontaneously, without being ploughed or sown.
Trees and shrubs were born bearing flowers and fruits according to the seasons; this was the first appearance of medicinal herbs during the Tretā age.
O sage, in the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsist on medicinal herbs;
at that time, passion and greed arise among people quite unexpectedly.
Then they traversed rivers, fields, and mountains,
as well as trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, according to their own power and strength.
Because of that fault, O twice-born one, those medicinal herbs perished while people looked on;
O high-minded one, those herbs were then devoured by Bhūri all at once.
When those [plants] had perished once more, those creatures, bewildered and afflicted by hunger, went for refuge to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
And having understood in truth that the earth was then being swallowed up,
the blessed and all-pervading Lord made Sumeru his calf and milked her.
Then, from that milk of the cow, crops were produced upon the surface of the earth;
those seeds, moreover, became both cultivated and wild.
The medicinal herbs, which end with the ripening of their fruit, are recorded as seventeen groups:
rice, barley, wheat, millet, and sesame; 49.67.
For there are fine priyaṅgu grains, as well as koradūṣa and cīnaka; and there are māṣa, mudga, masūra, niṣpāva, and kulattha.
Āḍhakas and caṇakas are recorded as the seventeen groups;
these were formerly the species of cultivated plants.
And there are fourteen highly esteemed medicinal plants, both cultivated and wild:
rice, barley, wheat, millet, and sesame; 1.70.
These seven are indeed headed by priyaṅgu, while the eighth consists of kulattha;
furthermore, there are śyāmāka, nīvāra, tila, and gavedhuka.
The kuruvinda, the markaṭaka, and those which are veṇuyava—
these are remembered as the fourteen medicinal plants belonging to both cultivated and wild varieties.
When the plants that had been sown did not sprout again,
he then devised a means of livelihood for their growth.
Then the blessed Brahmā, the Self-Existent One, [attained] the accomplishment of the hand born of karma;
from that time forth, medicinal herbs grew upon being ploughed.
When their livelihood had been successfully established, the Lord himself then laid down the boundaries of conduct for them, according to what was right and according to their respective qualities.
O best of the upholders of dharma, [tell me] the duties of the social classes and the stages of life,
and of all the worlds belonging to every class who properly protect dharma and worldly prosperity.
The station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas who perform their ritual duties;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not flee in battles.
The station of the Maruts belongs to the Vaiśyas who follow their own dharma;
that of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who follow the duty of service.
The very same abode that is prescribed for the eighty-eight thousand sages who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is also for those who dwell with their teacher.
The place remembered for the Seven Sages is indeed that of the forest-dwellers; that of the householders is the realm of Prajāpati; for renunciants it is the abode of Brahmā;
and for yogins it is the immortal station—such is the arrangement of the stations.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the Section on Creation of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, as he was being divided, mental offspring were born from him,
together with those effects produced from his body along with their respective causes.
From the limbs of that wise one, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) emerged;
all those who were previously mentioned by me emerged from him.
From the gods down to the stationary beings, all are recorded as being within the domain of the three qualities (guṇas).
Thus were created both the stationary and the moving entities.
When all those creatures of that wise one did not multiply,
he then created other mind-born sons who were like himself.
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise Aṅgiras;
Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha, who was born of his mind.
"These nine Brahmās are established as such in the Purāṇas;
thereafter, Brahmā again created Rudra, who was born from his own self through anger."
He [established] both volition and dharma, which were the first-born even of the ancients— namely,
Sanandana and the others who were previously created by the Self-existent One.
Not clinging to the worlds, they are free from worldly concern, composed in mind;
all of them possess knowledge of the future, having transcended passion and being devoid of envy.
When they remained thus indifferent toward the creation of the world, a great wrath arose within the high-souled Brahmā; there, a fire resembling the sun was produced.
Then that Puruṣa, possessing a body half-female and half-male and endowed with an exceedingly vast form,
said, "Divide yourself," and thereupon vanished from that place.
Thus addressed, he indeed separated his female nature and likewise his male nature;
he divided that male nature into ten parts and also into one.
Through those who were gentle and ungentle, as well as those who were peaceful, that Lord, the God, divided masculinity and femininity in many ways by means of men who were dark and fair.
Then, O twice-born one, the Lord, the protector of creatures, having fashioned from himself the first Manu, Svāyambhuva, who was born of Brahmā and was his own equal, [established him as ruler].
And the powerful Lord Svāyambhuva Manu took that woman Śatarūpā, whose impurities had been cleansed by austerity, as his wife.
And from that Puruṣa, Śatarūpā gave birth to two sons,
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, who became renowned for their own deeds.
Then the father gave two daughters, Ṛddhi and Prasūti;
he formerly gave Prasūti to Dakṣa and Ṛddhi to Ruci.
O highly fortunate one, Prajāpati took hold of that pair; from them was born a son, Yajña, together with Dakṣiṇā,
as a couple consisting of a male and female.
From the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the sacrifice, twelve sons were born;
they are known as the Yāmas, the gods in the period of Svāyambhuva Manu.
The sons of that Yajña were the Sabhāsvaras, born of Dakṣiṇā; and from Prasūti, Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters.
He created daughters; hear from me their names correctly:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and Kriyā.
The Lord Dharma accepted the daughters of Dakṣa as his wives for the sake of marriage: Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapuḥ, Śānti, Siddhi, Kīrti, and the thirteenth, Trayodaśī.
From them, eleven younger daughters of beautiful eyes remained:
Khyāti, Satī, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and likewise Kṣamā.
Santati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā;
and Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, and the sage Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise the sages;
Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and likewise Agni, as well as the Pitṛs, in their proper order.
The most excellent sages took these daughters: Khyāti and others took Kāma; Śraddhā took Darpa; and Śrī took Niyama as her son, Dhṛti.
From contentment arose satisfaction, and from that, greed; from greed arose nourishment, as well as intelligence, sacred learning, ritual action, punishment, policy, and discipline.
Buddhi gave birth to Bodha, as well as Lajjā, Vinaya, Vapu, and Ātmaja;
Vyavasāya was born from her, and Śānti gave birth to Kṣema.
"Bliss, success, glory, and fame—these are the sources of dharma.
From desire, she gave birth to Atimuda, the grandson of Dharma, who was full of joy and exultation.
Violence was the wife of Adharma; from her were born Untruth, and a daughter, Nirṛti. From her two sons were born: Naraka and Bhaya.
Māyā and Vedanā—this pair constitutes a couple;
from them was born Māyā’s son, Death (Mṛtyu), the destroyer of living beings.
Then from Raurava were born Feeling, Self, and Son, as well as Suffering;
and from Mṛtyu were born Disease, Old Age, Sorrow, Thirst, and Anger.
For all these are known to arise from suffering and are characterized by unrighteousness;
they have neither wife nor son, for they are all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
O Sage, Nirṛti and another named Alakṣmī became the wives of Mṛtyu;
and from that Alakṣmī, fourteen sons were born to Mṛtyu.
For these are the sons of Alakṣmī, the executors of Death's commands;
they seize men at the times of destruction—listen to who they are.
Abiding thus in these ten sense-faculties as well as in the mind,
they indeed join a man or a woman to their respective objects.
Then, O twice-born one, having assailed the senses of men with passion, anger, and the like,
they cause them to suffer loss through unrighteousness and other such evils.
One [type of man] is possessed by egoism, while another is established in intellect;
relying on great passion, they strive for the destruction of women.
Likewise, there was another in the house of men, renowned by the name Duḥsaha;
he was emaciated by hunger, with his face cast down, naked, clad in rags, and possessing a voice like a crow.
That storehouse of darkness was created by Brahmā to devour all beings;
it was exceedingly terrifying, with its mouth wide open and its fangs formidable.

To him who desired to eat that, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, pure, consisting of all the Brahman, and the imperishable cause of the universe, said this: MarkP_50.40: "I am the one who is to be eaten by you; do not eat me. Having spoken thus, he vanished right there. Then, having lost his appetite, the Grandfather (Brahmā) went to the world of Viṣṇu. There, the Grandfather saw the Lord of the World seated upon Garuḍa, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O Lord of the World, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon. The Lord of the World said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "Let me be invincible to all beings. The Lord of the World said, "Except for those born from my own body. He chose that very boon. Then, having obtained it, the Grandfather went to the world of Śiva. There, the Grandfather saw the Lord of Creatures (Śiva), the source of the three worlds, seated upon Nandin, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O Lord of Creatures, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon. The Lord of Creatures said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "Let me be invincible to all beings. The Lord of Creatures said, "Except for those born from my own body. He chose that very boon. Then, having obtained it, the Grandfather went to the world of Indra. There, the Grandfather saw the Thousand-eyed One (Indra) seated upon Airāvata, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O Thousand-eyed One, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon. The Thousand-eyed One said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "Let me be invincible to all beings. The Thousand-eyed One said, "Except for those born from my own body. He chose that very boon. Then, having obtained it, the Grandfather went to the world of Yama. There, the Grandfather saw the God of Death (Yama) seated upon his buffalo, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O God of Death, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon. The God of Death said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "Let me be invincible to all beings. The God of Death said, "Except for those born from my own body. He chose that very boon. Then, having obtained it, the Grandfather went to the world of Varuṇa. There, the Grandfather saw the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) seated upon his makara, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O Lord of Waters, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon. The Lord of Waters said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "Let me be invincible to all beings. The Lord of Waters said, "Except for those born from my own body. He chose that very boon. Then, having obtained it, the Grandfather went to the world of Soma. There, the Grandfather saw the Lord of the Night (Soma) seated upon a chariot drawn by horses, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O Lord of the Night, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon. The Lord of the Night said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "Let me be invincible to all beings. The Lord of the Night said, "Except for those born from my own body. He chose that very boon. Then, having obtained it, the Grandfather went to the world of Agni. There, the Grandfather saw the Lord of Fire (Agni) seated upon his ram, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O Lord of Fire, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon. The Lord of Fire said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "Let me be invincible to all beings. The Lord of Fire said, "Except for those born from my own body. He chose that very boon. Then, having obtained it, the Grandfather went to the world of Vāyu. There, the Grandfather saw the Wind-god (Vāyu) seated upon his deer, surrounded by hosts of gods, and spoke these words: "O Wind-god, I have been deceived by you through a trickery; therefore, grant me a boon."
Brahmā said:
"O you who have devoured this world, abandon your anger and attain tranquility;
cast off this tamasic disposition and discard the portion of rajas."
Duḥsaha said: "O Lord of the World, I am emaciated by hunger,
thirsty, and weak."
O Lord, how may I attain satisfaction?
How may I become powerful?
Tell me what my support shall be, and where I may abide in peace.
Brahmā said:
"O child, for men, your refuge is their home and unrighteous people are their strength; you bring nourishment through the neglect of daily rites."
He will go.
And those who snap their fingers in vain— to you I give clothing and food that is torn,
infested with insects, and likewise looked upon by dogs.
Likewise, food that has been broken by the breath, or pacified by the breath from the mouth, as well as that which is leavings, uncooked, undercooked, licked, or unconsecrated; ||| MarkP_50.45 |||

Food eaten while sitting on a broken seat, or when it has just arrived, or facing an intermediate direction, or during the two twilights, or amidst the clamor of dancing and musical instruments; MarkP_50.46 //
Food defiled by a woman in her courses, or even that which has been looked upon by such a woman,
as well as any food or drink that is otherwise contaminated— [these should not be consumed].
I give these and other things as well for the sake of your nourishment;
[but know that] what is offered or given without faith, or by those who have not bathed, or with contempt, is of no avail.
That which was thrown away without water, that which was rendered useless, that which was discarded after being displayed, and that which was given out of extreme astonishment; ||| MarkP_50.49 |||
O Yakṣa, that which is given by one who is wicked, angry, or afflicted, shares in its fruit;
and whatever subsequent rite for the sake of the next world a person performs, [that too bears fruit].
And that woman who leads to rebirth is a yakṣī;
for your satisfaction,
she attends to financial transactions as a means of securing a bride-price.
Likewise, O Yakṣa,
those practices based on false treatises performed for the sake of nourishment, and whatever has been studied that is devoid of purpose and not rooted in truth; [all these are in vain].
Therefore, I grant you all the time periods for your success:
in approaching a pregnant woman and in the omission of the twilight devotions and daily obligatory rites.
And among those men corrupted by false scriptures, improper actions, and evil speech,
your power to overcome them will always be irresistible.
Your dwelling shall be among those who break the ranks of the assembly, those who cook in vain, those who cook out of turn, and those who are constantly engaged in domestic quarrels.
Likewise, when servants, draft oxen, and other such animals are not nourished;
when the house has not been sprinkled during the twilight hours; and at such times, men shall have fear of you.
O Yakṣa, when there is affliction from the stars and planets, or when the three kinds of portents appear, you shall overcome those men who are intent on non-peaceful rites.
Those mortals who fast in vain, who are always addicted to gambling and women, who merely offer you empty words, and those who follow the "vow of the cat" (vaiḍālavratika); [these go to hell].

Study performed by one who does not lead a life of celibacy, a sacrifice offered by one who lacks knowledge, and likewise ascetic practice in a penance grove by those who enjoy village pleasures and have not conquered their own selves— all these are in vain.
The conduct of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have fallen from their own duties and desire to attain the next world; MarkP_50.60 //
"O Yakṣa, all the fruit that belongs to her shall be yours.
Furthermore, I grant you another boon for the sake of your nourishment; listen to it."
At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, they will offer you a powerful oblation (bali), preceded by the utterance of your name, saying, "This is for you."
He who eats refined food according to the rules, being pure within and likewise without,
free from greed and having conquered his lust for women— abandon his house.
The deities and the ancestors are honored there with offerings to gods and manes,
as are the sisters and guests; therefore, O Yakṣa, avoid that house!
Avoid that house as well where there is no loving-kindness toward children, the elderly, women, and men, nor among one's own kinsmen.
O Yakṣa, avoid that house where women are unrestrained, have no desire to go outside, and are always possessed of modesty.
O Yakṣa, in whichever house there are beds and foods suitable for our age, that house must be avoided by you at my command.
O Yakṣa, you should abandon that house where compassionate ones, ever established in virtuous deeds and provided with common utensils, reside.
O Yakṣa, you should always avoid that house where those who are seated— namely the teacher, the elders, and the twice-born— do not remain standing when they are present.
If the foundation of a man's house has not been pierced by young trees, shrubs, and the like, or if there is no breach in its vital points, that dwelling is auspicious for you; otherwise, it is not.
Abandon the house of that man who provides for the gods, the ancestors, his dependents, and guests with food remaining from his own meal.
O Yakṣa, you should abandon such men as these: those who speak the truth, who are patient by nature, who do no harm, who feel no remorse, and who are free from envy.
Abandon that woman who is devoted to serving her husband, who avoids the company of unchaste women,
and who is nourished by the food remaining from the family and her husband.
Abandon that twice-born man whose mind is always intent on sacrificing, studying, practicing, and giving, and who makes his livelihood by officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts.
Abandon that Kṣatriya who is ever-intent on giving, study, and sacrifice, yet is difficult to endure; he shall provide you with wages from his livelihood of weapons and legitimate taxes.
Abandon that stainless Vaiśya who is endowed with the three aforementioned qualities and has obtained his livelihood through cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture.
O Yakṣa, abandon him who is intent on giving gifts and service to the twice-born,
as well as the Śūdra who supports his livelihood through service to Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
The householder, having established his livelihood in accordance with the Śruti and Smṛti, remains at home;
and wherever he may be, his wife follows him with her whole being.
Where a son offers worship to his teacher, to the gods, and likewise to his father,
and where a wife honors her husband, how could there be any fear of misfortune there?
O Yakṣa, you are not able even to look upon this house, which is constantly anointed, sprinkled with water during the twilights, and provided with offerings of flowers.
Houses that have beds visible from the sun, where fire and water are always present,
and where lamps are kept for the purpose of beholding the sun— such houses are the vessels of prosperity.
Where there is a bull, sandalwood, a lute, a mirror, honey, clarified butter,
poison, ghee, and copper vessels— that house is not a refuge for you.
Where there are thorny trees, where there is the niṣpāva creeper,
and where the wife is a remarried woman— such an anthill is your abode, O Yakṣa.
In that house where there are five men, three women, as many cows,
darkness, fuel, and fire— that house shall be your dwelling.
O Yakṣas, quickly wither this house: one goat, two calves, three oxen, five buffaloes, six horses, and seven elephants.
Likewise, their spades, sickles, baskets, and vessels such as cooking pots,
wherever they were thrown down, would provide you with shelter.
The pestle and mortar are the mouth of women, as is the udumbara tree;
and the privy is the place for counsel—O Yakṣa, this has been done for your benefit.
Just as grains, both ripe and unripe, are trampled where they lie in a house, so too are the scriptures there; O Duḥsaha, conduct yourself therein as you please.
Wherever fire is placed upon the lid of a cooking pot or with the back of a ladle,
that house becomes the refuge for all manner of misfortunes.
O Yakṣa, wherever human bones are found in a house, where there is the state of death day and night,
there is your dwelling, as well as that of other Rākṣasas.
Those men who eat the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and the water-offering of a kinsman without having first given [these] themselves—
unite with those people at that time, O sapiṇḍas and sodakas.
Abandon that house where Padmā, Apahā, Padmā, Surabhi, Mokāśinī, Vṛṣabhā, and Airāvatī are consecrated.
Where deities who are unarmed are conceived by men as being armed even without a battle, and are thus worthy of worship— abandon that temple.
Do not frequent that house where the citizens and country-folk perform their long-established great festivals as they did before.

Go to those whose auspicious marks have been destroyed by bathing with the wind from a winnowing basket, with water from a jar, with droplets of water from a garment, or even with the water on the tips of their fingernails.
The customs of regions, conventions, the duties of kin, recitation, oblation, auspicious rites, worship of the gods,
proper purification according to rule, and worldly maxims— [he should know these].
But let there be no attachment for you toward a man who acts thus.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to Duḥsaha, Brahmā vanished on that very spot;
and he (Duḥsaha) likewise carried out the command of the Lotus-born One.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Instruction of the Yakṣas," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-one:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Duḥsaha had a wife known by the name Nirmārṣṭi;
she was born from Kala’s wife during her season through the sight of a Caṇḍāla.
From those two were born sixteen offspring who pervaded the world:
eight Kumāras and likewise eight most terrifying daughters.
Tantākṛṣṭi, Tathokti, Parivarta, Aṅgadhruk, Śakuni, and Gaṇḍaprāntarati; // MarkP_51.3 //
Another was Garbhahā, and another Sasyahā; they had sons named Kumāra and Tanaya, and likewise eight other daughters—listen to their names from me.
The first is indeed the Impeller (niyojikā), and likewise another is the Obstructer (virodhinī);
then the Self-Stealer (svayaṃhārakarī), the Wanderer (bhrāmaṇī), and the Season-Stealer (ṛtuhārikā).
And there were two other daughters of those two, exceedingly cruel, who robbed one of the seed of memory;
and the eighth daughter was named Vidveṣaṇī, who brought fear to the world.
I shall describe the rites for these [goddesses] and that which pacifies their defects;
listen, O best of the twice-born, regarding the eight Kumāras as well. (MarkP 51.7)
The "teeth-drawer" (dantākṛṣṭi), residing in the teeth of sleeping children,
causes them to grind their teeth, desiring to bring about an unbearable arrival [of death].
Its pacification should be performed for one who is asleep by scattering white mustard seeds upon the bed and over the teeth of the human [patient].
By bathing with the *suvārccalā* medicinal herb, by reciting the true scriptures, and by wearing camel-thorn, rhinoceros bone, and linen garments; (MarkP 51.10)
But the other prince remained, repeatedly saying, "So be it";
he joined men to good and evil fortune, for what was spoken by him cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, the wise should always speak what is auspicious and free from fault;
when something evil has been heard or spoken, Janārdana should be praised.
Brahmā, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, is the family deity of whomsoever;
he always causes other embryos to revolve within his own womb.

If one obtains pleasure from a statement that is quite different from what the speaker intended to say, this is known as *parivartaka*; for that as well, [one should perform the rite] with white mustard seeds.
The knower of reality should provide protection through the recitation of mantras that destroy demons;
furthermore, he should perform for men the rite known as *sphuraṇa* on their limbs, which is like the wind.
It declares auspicious or inauspicious results through the striking of his limbs with kuśa grass;
another method involves [the bird] perching on a crow or other bird, or even entering onto a limb of the dog or other animal.
Furthermore, another youth, Śakuni, speaks of both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
in that case as well, if it is unfavorable, there is distraction and the abandonment of the undertaking.
"O best of the twice-born, Prajāpati has declared that in an auspicious moment one must act with extreme haste; however, when situated at the junctions of the Gaṇḍas, another half-muhūrta remains."
O twice-born one, the prince devours all undertakings, those who speak ill of their teachers, those who are envious,
those who utter insults against Brahmins, those who praise deities improperly, and those who uproot plants.

Through bathing with cow urine and mustard seeds, through the worship of those respective planets, and furthermore through the performance of the *Dharmopaniṣad* and the study of the scriptures; ||| MarkP_51.20 |||
Without [the deity's] permission, one afflicted by a tumor reaches a state of pacification at birth;
likewise, another [afflicted] in the womb of women experiences a most terrible destruction of the fetus.
His protection must always be ensured by constantly practicing purity,
by inscribing well-known mantras, and by wearing consecrated garlands and other such items.
O twice-born one, likewise, another who destroys the grain— that is, one who causes the ruin of the harvest— suffers from the same lack of effort regarding his pure home and dwelling.
One should also provide protection for that [place] by wearing worn-out sandals,
by walking with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), and by the entrance of a Caṇḍāla.
And by offering external oblations and by the recitation of the *Soma* and *Ambu* [mantras],
one protects men from [the sins of] violating another's wife, seizing property, and so forth.
And that maiden, acting as an instigator, enjoins others as well;
through her recitation of the purifying text and her avoidance of anger, greed, and the like.
She urges me on and causes me to avoid those things that are disagreeable;
even when reviled by another or struck, she considers herself the one who has instigated it.
Thinking, "It yokes this [mind]," the wise man should not fall under its control—
neither his own mind nor his very self— in association with the wives of others and the like.
"A wise man should reflect: 'She is directing me toward this [sin],' for she creates discord between a husband and wife who are in love. (MarkP 51.29)
That hostility which arises toward kinsmen, friends, parents, sons, and those of the same lineage— one should counteract that by performing the rite of offerings (balikarman).
Likewise, from enduring harsh speech, from following the conduct prescribed by the scriptures,
and from gleaned grain, from the house, from cows, milk, and likewise clarified butter— these are the other [sources of merit].
A maiden who steals away prosperity from one possessed of abundant wealth is called a *svayaṃhārikā*; she is constantly intent upon making herself invisible.
He always eats together with those eating, whether the food is half-prepared in the kitchen, situated in the dining hall, or being served.
O twice-born one, Durharā carries off the remnants of human food and their sustenance from the workshops, houses, and halls, taking away their perfected prosperity.
She always carries milk from the breasts of cows and women;
she takes curd, ghee, oil from sesame seeds, and likewise liquor from a tavern.
She takes the dye of safflower and other such things, as well as cotton and thread;
she is known as Swayamhārikā, O twice-born one, and she steals incessantly.
One should create an artificial woman for the sake of protection, forming a pair with a peacock;
furthermore, protective diagrams should be drawn in the house, and likewise, the state of being left-over from food (ucchiṣṭatā) must be avoided.
The purification of vessels containing milk and other such substances should be performed with the smoke, ashes, and [remnants of] the sacrificial fire-deity; thus is their protection prescribed.
That maiden who is said to cause agitation to a man living in one place is called Bhrāmaṇī.
Then, one should perform protection for him with scattered white mustard seeds,
wherever that man sits— on his seat, his bed, or on the ground.
And a man should reflect: "This sinful and wicked-minded woman repeatedly causes me to wander from my meditative concentration while I am reciting the *Bhūḥ-sūkta*. (MarkP 51.41)
Another woman steals the menstrual flow of women;
that girl, however, who steals it while it has already begun its course, should be known as a dauḥsahā, a thief of the ṛta.
One should perform ablutions at sacred fords, temples, shrines, mountain peaks, river confluences, and excavated pools; by that, such [suffering] is pacified.
