O twice-born one, at the junctions of time and at dawn, the physician who knows the mantras, understands the principles,
and is skilled in medical treatment, [should act] with well-administered, excellent medicines.
Another [demoness] steals away the memory of women; she is the "Memory-stealer.
Through frequenting solitary places, her pacification occurs.
There is another, most terrifying female spirit who steals the seed of both men and women;
her pacification occurs through the consumption of pure food and ritual bathing.
The eighth [night] is named Dveṣaṇī, a maiden who brings fear to the world;
she makes either a man or a woman hated by the people.
For the sake of pacification, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds smeared with honey, milk, and ghee;
and by performing the Mitra-vindā sacrifice, that [calamity] is likewise pacified.
O best of the twice-born, these youths and maidens had thirty-eight offspring; hear their names from me.
From the extraction of the teeth were born the daughters Vijalpā and Kalahā;
Vijalpā was characterized by contempt, falsehood, and evil speech, and [the other] for her pacification.
The wise man should contemplate that very [truth] and live as a householder with self-restraint; for quarrels incessantly provoke further quarrels among men in the home.
She is the cause of the destruction of one's family; listen now to the means for her pacification:
in the rite of offering (balikarma), one should use sprouts of dūrvā grass smeared with honey, ghee, and milk.
One should scatter [the offerings] and likewise offer oblations into the fire,
while invoking Mitra together with the Mothers of all beings, for the sake of the peace of children.
May they always grant me peace regarding sciences and austerities, as well as self-restraint and discipline, and in agriculture and the profits of trade.
Having been honored according to the rule, may they all attain satisfaction—
both the Kuṣmāṇḍas and the Yātudhānas, and whoever else are designated as hosts.
By the grace of Mahādeva and by the will of Maheśvara,
may all these [deities] quickly grant eternal satisfaction to those men.
Being satisfied, may they all cast away every ill-deed and misdeed,
everything arising from the Mahāpatāka [sins], and whatever else causes obstacles.
By their very grace, may all obstacles perish in every way, indeed,
in all marriages and in rites for prosperity.
In the performance of meritorious deeds, in the service of gurus and gods,
in the rites of recitation and sacrifice, and on pilgrimages— these are the fourteen [auspicious days].
May they always grant peace for my body’s health, for the enjoyments of wealth that bestow happiness, and especially for the elderly, children, and the sick.
From Soma and Ambupa was born Ambhodhi, and from Savitṛ were born Anila and Anala;
from their union was born Kālajihva, whose son was Tālaniketana.
O twice-born one, he afflicts those wicked ones upon whom his tongue is positioned; however, his two sons, Parivarta and Suta, are both deformed and hideous.
Taking refuge in the tops of trees, moats, ramparts, and the ocean, those two,
while moving about with their pregnant mother, supported her with their feet and hands.
O Krauṣṭuki, there may be a change for the embryo from one womb to another;
yet it cannot pass through a tree, nor a mountain, nor a wall, nor the great ocean.
Or a weak woman carrying a fetus might step into a moat;
she who harms her own body will obtain a son known by the name Piśuna.
He devours the strength of men who have not conquered their selves, reaching even into their bones and marrow;
he also devours his own sons in the forms of hawks, crows, pigeons, vultures, and owls.
Śakuni obtained five [of them], which the gods and asuras seized;
Mṛtyu seized the hawk, and Kāla seized the crow.
Nirṛti seized the owl, which is exceedingly terrifying;
Vyādhi, the lord of disease, seized the vulture; and Yama himself seized the pigeon.
And it is said that these very beings are employed for the production of evil;
therefore, if hawks and other such creatures should alight upon one's head.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should perform rites for peace sufficient for self-protection; likewise, their birth in one's house or their nesting within it [requires such measures].
O twice-born one, one should avoid a house occupied by a man who has died there, as well as one whose roof is perched upon by pigeons;
for the hawk, the pigeon, the vulture, the crow, and the owl [are ill-omened] in a house.
Having entered, one should report the end [of the lifespan] to those dwelling in that house;
a wise man should thus abandon such a home and perform rites for peace.
For even in a dream, the sight of a pigeon is not praised;
likewise, six offspring are said to result from one who delights in the side of the cheek.
Listen to me regarding the duration of the menstrual flow in women and its respective periods:
the first four days, and likewise another thirteen.
Likewise, on another day, he had eleven offspring;
on yet another day, by approaching [his wife], and similarly on another day, by performing a śrāddha offering.
Furthermore, on other festival days (parvan), these should be avoided by the wise:
a son born to a woman who caused an abortion, and a daughter born to one who was under a delusive influence.
One enters the womb and devours [the embryo], while another, having consumed it, causes delusion;
from that delusion, snakes, frogs, and tortoises are born.
Or other crawling reptiles, or even excrement;
for six months she shall eat the flesh of an unrestrained woman who is pregnant.
At night, she should take refuge in the shade of a tree or at a triple or quadruple crossroads,
standing upon the ground of a cemetery or a place for funeral mats, and divested of her upper garment.
Then, at midnight, while she is weeping,
that one called Kṣudraka by name— who is a destroyer of crops— shall likewise enter that woman.
Listen to how he always destroys the abundance of crops by finding a vulnerability:
he who sows while unsatisfied and at the commencement of an inauspicious day.
He indeed effects an entry into the fields that are associated with the end;
therefore, on a highly auspicious day, having worshipped the Moon, [one should perform] the ritual (kalpa).
One who is joyful, contented, and well-supported by companions should undertake an enterprise and sow seeds;
such is the maiden I have described as "Niyojikā" for the sake of Duḥsaha.
To her were born four daughters known as Pracodikā;
they were always intoxicated, mad, and heedless toward men and women alike.
They enter [the body] for its destruction and incite here what is terrible:
unrighteousness in the form of righteousness, and desire in the form of non-desire.
Those who are ill-disciplined and lack purity show what is harmful as having the form of benefit, and liberation as having the form of non-liberation, to men who are separated [from truth].
By their entering, men fall away from the goals of human life;
and their entry occurs when the sky is reddened by the twilight.

The transition [of the moon] occurs among nine women, and their offspring are born quickly;
for Virodhinī, there are three sons: Codaka and likewise Grāhaka.

There is another, darkness, which is a concealer; hear from me its true nature regarding a wicked person who is defiled by association with the sons of Diti and has transgressed like a lamp [extinguished] by contact with smoke.
Wherever there were pestles and mortars, sandals, or women's seats, and wherever there were winnowing baskets, sickles, and the like, he likewise dragged them along with his feet.
There, the sons of Virodhinī, being incited, prevail;
among men and women, there is one who speaks falsehood as truth upon his tongue.
He who incites discord in the household is called a slanderer;
another, being of very wicked mind, stands listening with full attention.
But that evil-minded one, having assailed the minds of men and shrouded them in darkness, becomes the grasper who seizes hold of those words.
He who gives rise to anger is one who is shrouded by darkness;
he himself shall take away the three sons born [to him] through theft.
They take away everything, they take away half, and likewise they take away one's vigor;
these [demons] dwell in houses where food has not been formally offered and in houses where conduct is lax.
When those who have not washed their feet enter the kitchen, or when there is malice in threshing floors, cow-pens, or indeed in those houses; ||| MarkP_51.98 |||
Among them, all dwell and take delight according to their respective rights;
however, there is one son of Bhrāmaṇī known as Kākajaṅgha.
Possessed by him, no one in the city indeed finds pleasure,
even while eating, singing, or laughing, O Maitreya.
O twice-born one, he enters the man who has sexual intercourse at twilight,
as well as the woman who has borne three daughters and the girl who suppresses her menses.
One maiden is named Kucāharā, another is Vyañjanahārikā,
and the third is declared to be the maiden Jātahāriṇī.
If for any woman the entire marriage rite is not performed,
or if it is performed after the proper time has passed, a single woman seizes away her pair of breasts.
Furthermore, having failed to perform the funeral rites with proper faith and likewise failing to honor his mother,
he seizes the dowry of a married maiden.
Likewise, in a lying-in chamber that is devoid of fire and water, lacking incense,
without lamps, weapons, or pestles, and destitute of *bhūti* ashes and mustard seeds;
Having entered [the womb], O twice-born one, she carries away the child born of her own self; then, giving birth for only a moment, she abandons the infant right there.
She is named Jātahāriṇī, a most terrible eater of flesh;
therefore, one must take great care to protect [the child] in the lying-in chamber.
And for those who are heedless, her son named Pracaṇḍa by name destroys their memory through frequenting empty houses.
From his grandsons were born hundreds of thousands of worlds,
as well as eight Caṇḍāla wombs, most terrifying with their staffs and nooses.
Then those beings, overcome by hunger and born from the womb of Caṇḍālas,
rushed at one another, desiring to devour each other.
But Pracaṇḍa, having restrained those various beings born of the Caṇḍāla womb, established them in their respective duties; hear now what kind [of duties] they were.
"From this day forward, whoever shall provide a dwelling for the worlds,
I will undoubtedly inflict an incomparable punishment upon him."
Whichever woman of the Caṇḍāla womb shall give birth in this dwelling,
her previous existence shall end, and she herself shall perish instantly.
She gave birth to two daughters who steal the seed of both women and men:
Vātarūpā and Amarūpā; these two are her weapons.
At the conclusion of the ritual union, she who casts her son toward one whose form is like the wind—
that man, or even the woman herself, becomes possessed of seminal fluid like the wind.
In the same way, for one who goes [to the river] immediately, there is a loss of seed through the formless [state];
likewise, a man who eats without having bathed, as well as one who eats meat, [is similarly affected].
But that maiden who is hostile, her face contorted with a frown,
shall have two sons who manifest malice toward men.
A man or a woman who is devoid of purity becomes seedless;
likewise, one who delights in slander, is fickle, and associates with the wicked [reaches the same state].
And these two do not remain upon a man who hates people;
they do not persist when he is surrounded by mother, brother, friends, beloved ones, kinsmen, or strangers.
A man who hates others perishes in terms of both dharma and artha;
yet a single evildoer makes his own virtues manifest in the world.
But the second [type] draws away from virtue and friendliness established in the world.
Thus, all these are known as difficult to endure, the progeny of consumption (yakṣman),
of evil conduct, by whom the entire world is pervaded.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Birth of Duḥsaha," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-Two:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Such was this creation of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, characterized by darkness (tāmasa).
I shall now proclaim the creation of Rudra; listen as I speak of it.
Likewise, there were eight daughters, wives, and sons;
for at the beginning of the kalpa, the Lord meditated upon a son equal to himself.
Then, O best of the twice-born, a blue-and-red boy appeared upon his lap; he then cried out with a sweet voice and ran about.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā replied, "Why do you weep? Then he replied to the Lord of the World, "Grant me a name."
"You are Rudra, O God; by name you are so called, so do not weep, but summon fortitude.
Having been addressed thus, he then wept seven times.
Then the Lord gave him seven other names,
as well as the stations for these eight, their wives, and their sons, O twice-born one.
The Lord Grandfather spoke thus to Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Bhīma, Ugra, and Mahādeva.
He established these names accordingly and assigned these locations for them:
the sun, water, earth, fire, wind, and space.
The initiated Brāhmaṇa, Soma—these are his bodies in sequence;
likewise Suvarcalā, Umā, Vikeśī, and the other, Svadhā.
O best of the twice-born, Svāhā, Diś, Dīkṣā, and Rohiṇī follow in due order as the wives of Sūrya and the others,
together with their names beginning with Rudra.
Śanaiścara, Śukra, Lohitāṅga, Manojava,
Skanda, Sarga, Santāna, and Budha were their sons in due order.
Rudra, being of such a nature, obtained Satī as his wife;
however, due to Dakṣa’s wrath, that Satī cast off her own body.
O best of the twice-born, she became the daughter of Himavat by Menā;
her brother was Maināka, the peerless friend of the ocean.
The Blessed Lord Bhava married her again, as she was devoted to no other;
and Khyāti gave birth to the two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ from Bhr̥gu.
And Śrī, who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods,
as well as Āyāti and Niyati, the two daughters of the high-souled Meru.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ had two wives, and from them were born two sons:
Prāṇa and Mṛkaṇḍu, my father of great renown.
From that [Manu], my son Vedaśiras was born of Manasvinī;
now learn from me also concerning Prāṇa’s son born of Dhūmravatī.
A radiant son was born to Prāṇa, and his own son was Ajaras;
they had many sons and grandsons.
Marīci’s wife, Sambhūti, gave birth to Paurṇamāsa;
Virajas and Parvata were the two sons of that high-souled one.
O twice-born one, I shall now describe their sons in the recitation of the lineage:
Smṛti was the wife of Aṅgiras, and she gave birth to daughters.
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, Bhānumatī, and likewise Anasūyā—these faultless daughters were born to Atri. Among them, she gave birth to sons who were free from blemish.
Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya were born;
furthermore, another son named Datta was born to Pulastya’s wife Prīti.
In a previous birth during the Svāyambhuva interval, he was known as Agastya;
Kardama, Cārvavīra, and Sahiṣṇu were his three sons.
Kṣamā, the wife of the progenitor Pulaha, gave birth [to the Kṣamācyutas]; Sannati, the wife of Kratu, however, gave birth to the Bālakhilyas.
Of the sixty thousand rishis who were perpetual celibates,
seven sons were indeed born to Vasiṣṭha through Ūrjā.
Rajogātra, Ūrdhvabāhu, Sabala, Anagha, Sutapas, and Śukla— these are all remembered as the seven ṛṣis.
O twice-born one, from that Agni, the presiding deity who was the first-born son of Brahmā,
Svāhā obtained three sons of noble splendor.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Śuci, and also Jalāśin;
their descendants were forty-five others.
These are frequently spoken of as the father and his three sons;
thus, the forty-nine Durjaya demons are proclaimed.
The ancestors were created by Brahmā, as I have described to you;
they are the Agniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣadas, those who are without fire and those who possess fire.
From them, O twice-born one, Svadhā gave birth to Sūtā and likewise to Menā and Dhāriṇī; both of them were exponents of the Veda and both were practitioners of yoga.
Endowed with supreme knowledge and possessed of all virtues—
thus has this progeny of the daughters of Dakṣa been described.
A man of faith who constantly remembers this is born with offspring.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Creation of Rudra," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-three— 53—
Krauṣṭuki said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear correctly that which has been described by you as this Svāyambhuva Manvantara; let it be told.
O Blessed One, [tell me] the measure of a Manvantara, as well as the gods, the celestial sages, those who are lords of the earth,
and likewise he who is the Lord of the Gods.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "The number of Manvantaras is indeed seventy-one and more;
listen to me regarding the duration of a Manvantara according to human measurement."
The number is calculated as thirty crores, twenty thousand,
and sixty-seven lakhs.
And the measure of a Manvantara, excluding the additional period,
is recorded as eight hundred thousand [years] by divine reckoning.
There were fifty-two thousand others as well;
first was Svāyambhuva Manu, and then Svārociṣa Manu.
Auttami, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa—
these six Manus have passed away, and now it is the Vaivasvata Manu.
These are Sāvarṇi, the five Raucyas, and the Bhautyas who are yet to come;
their detailed account shall be given further in the description of the future Manvantaras.
O Brahmin, I shall declare the origin and the summary account of the gods, the ṛṣis, the lords of the yakṣas, and those who are the ancestors;
listen now to their lineage.
And that which was their field became the field of those high-souled sons;
Svāyambhuva Manu had ten sons who were equal to him.
By whom this entire earth— with its seven continents, its mountains,
its oceans, and its mines— was established anew every year.
In that same manner, during the Tretā Yuga, the earth together with its oceans and mines was [ruled] year by year by those sons and grandsons of Priyavrata and Svāyambhuva.
From Priyavrata and Prajāvatī, a daughter was born to Vīra;
that highly fortunate maiden became the wife of the progenitor Kardama.
Two daughters and ten sons, as well as Samrāṭ and Kukṣi—these two were their [wives];
from them were born ten heroic brothers equal to Prajāpati.
Āgnīdhra, Medhātithi, and another named Vapuṣmat, as well as Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Bhavya, and Savana— these seven indeed were they.
Priyavrata consecrated those seven as kings over the seven continents according to that dharma; learn from me now concerning those continents as well.
Likewise, in Jambūdvīpa, his father made Agnīdhra the king;
and in Plakṣadvīpa, Medhātithi was made the sovereign by him.
In Śālmala he is Vapuṣmant; in the land called Kuśa, Jyotiṣmant;
in Krauñcadvīpa, Dyutimant; and in the lordship of the land called Śāka, Bhavya.
And he also begot a son named Savana;
Mahāvīta and Dhātaki were the two sons of Puṣkarādhipati.
Having divided his realm into two parts, he settled one in Puṣkara;
Bhavya had seven sons—learn of them from me by name.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra,
Manīvaka, Kuśottara, Medhāvī, and Mahādruma as the seventh.
He established regions in Śākadvīpa named after those [sons];
likewise, Dyutimat had seven sons—learn of them from me.
Kuśala, Manuja, Uṣṇa, Prākara, Arthakāraka,
Muni, and Dundubhi are proclaimed as the seven [kings].
Their respective names became the names of the regions in Krauñcadvīpa; likewise, in Kuśadvīpa, they were indeed marked by the names of the sons of Jyotiṣmān.
There too, for seven years, listen to their names from me:
Udbhida, Vaiṣṇava, Suratha, and likewise Lambana.
Dhṛtimat, Prākara, and Kāpila as the seventh—
these were the seven sons of Vapuṣmat, the son of Śālmali.
Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita,
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Ketumān as the seventh.
In the same way, there are indeed seven regions of Śālmala with names identical to theirs;
these are the seven sons of Medhātithi, the lord of Plakṣadvīpa.
Plakṣadvīpa is divided into seven regions by the years marked with their names;
first is the region born of Śāka, and then Śiśira, which brings about happiness.
Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka,
and Dhruva likewise [reigned] over the lands beginning with Plakṣadvīpa and ending with Śākadvīpa.
The duty arising from the divisions of caste and stage of life is to be known as fivefold:
it is eternal, inherent, and augmented by the rule of non-violence.
O twice-born one, among these five sons, the father first gave Jambūdvīpa to Agnīdhra as his common share.
He indeed had nine sons who were equal to the Prajāpatis;
the eldest was known as Nābhi, and his younger brother was Kimpuruṣa.
Harivarṣa was the third, while Ilāvṛta was the fourth;
Vaśya was the fifth son, and Hiraṇya is said to be the sixth.
Kuru is the seventh among them, and Bhadrāśva is recorded as the eighth;
the ninth is Ketumāla, and the arrangement of the regions is according to those names.
Excluding those regions such as Kimpuruṣa and others, with the exception of the one called Himavat,
their success is achieved through their own inherent nature, consisting mostly of happiness and requiring no effort.
For them there is no perversion, nor is there the fear of old age and death;
for them neither merit nor demerit exists, nor are there superior, inferior, or middling states.
Indeed, there was no state of the four ages, nor were there seasons according to the seasons;
yet, O twice-born one, from the navel of Āgnīdhrasūnu, Ṛṣabha became his son.
From Ṛṣabha was born Bharata, a hero who was the best among his hundred sons;
having consecrated his son, Ṛṣabha undertook the great renunciation.
The illustrious father performed austerities while residing in the hermitage of Pulaha;
he gave the southern region of the Himalayas to Bharata.
Therefore, that region of Bhārata was named after that great-souled one;
and Bhaṭa also had a righteous son named Sumati.
Having entrusted the kingdom to him, Bharata also went to the forest;
by their sons and grandsons, the earth with its seven continents was ruled.
O best of the twice-born, after the sons of Priyavrata had enjoyed [the earth] during the Svāyambhuva interval,
this creation of Svāyambhuva has been recounted to you.
In the previous Manvantara, what else may I tell you correctly?
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Manvantaras," in the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Chapter Fifty-Four:
Krauṣṭuki said:
O twice-born one, how many continents, oceans, or mountains are there?
And how many regions are there, O Sage, and what are their rivers?
The dimensions of the great elements, as well as the illumination of the world, its inversions,
its measurements, and even the course of the moon and the sun.
Tell me all of this in detail, O Great Sage.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O twice-born one, the earth has an extent of fifty crores [yojanas] in its entirety;
hear now as I describe every part of it to you.
O twice-born one, O illustrious one, listen again to the detailed account of those continents beginning with Jambudvīpa and ending with Puṣkara that have been described by me.
Each continent is twice the size of the preceding one: Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmala, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara-dvīpa.
They are surrounded on all sides by the oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water, each increasing double the size of the preceding one.
I shall describe the configuration of Jambūdvīpa; listen to me:
it is one hundred thousand yojanas in circumference, both in width and in length.
Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Ṛṣabha, Meru,
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin— these are the seven mountain ranges in this region.
In the middle there are two great mountains, each two hundred thousand yojanas in extent;
those which are to the south of them and likewise those which are to the north are mountains.
Each of these is ten thousand leagues less than the one preceding it;
they are all two thousand leagues in height and as many in width.
Six mountain ranges enter this [continent] from the edge of the ocean;
the land slopes down toward the north and south, while in the middle it rises up in a long ridge.
On the southern half of Vedyardha there are three regions, and likewise three on the northern;
between them lies Ilāvṛta, situated in the shape of a half-moon.
To the east of that is Bhadrāśva, and to the west is Ketumāla;
in the center of Ilāvṛta stands Meru, the golden mountain.
The height of that great mountain is eighty-four thousand [yojanas];
it enters sixteen thousand below, and its width is likewise sixteen thousand.
And because it rests upon a shallow bowl, it extends across the thirty-two heads;
it is white, yellow, black, and red, respectively, in the directions starting from the east.
The Brahmin, the Vaiśya, the Śūdra, and the Kṣatriya [reside] according to their respective castes;
likewise, above him, there are eight cities in the cardinal directions in due order.
In the midst of those [worlds] of Indra and the other world-protectors is the assembly hall of Brahmā,
which rises fourteen thousand yojanas in height.
Ten thousand yojanas in height and equal in width at their base,
Mandara and Gandhamādana stand respectively in the east and other directions.
Vipula and Supārśva are adorned with banner-trees;
Kadamba is the banner on Mandara, and Jambu is on Gandhamādana.
On Vipula there is likewise an Aśvattha tree, and on Supārśva a great Vaṭa tree;
these mountains are eleven hundred yojanas in extent.
The mountains Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are in the eastern direction;
Ānīla and Niṣadha meet each other without any interval between them.
Niṣadha and Pāriyātra are on the western side of Meru;
these two are as long as the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains are on the eastern side.
Kailāsa and Himavat are two great mountains to the south;
these two extend from east to west and are situated within the ocean.
Śṛṅgavān and Jārudhi, as well as the northern mountain,
are situated in the same manner within the oceans on the southern side.
O best of the twice-born, these eight mountains are called the boundary-mountains (maryādāparvata) that lie between the Himavat,
Hemakūṭa, and the other mountain ranges.
To the east, north, south, and west of Meru, within the region of Ilāvṛta, there is an extent of nine thousand yojanas in each direction.
Indeed, those fruits of the Jambu tree on Mount Gandhamādana,
which are as large as the body of an elephant, fall upon the summit of the mountain.
From their flow arises that which is known as the river Jambū,
where the gold named Jāmbūnada is produced.
Having circled Mount Meru, O tiger among the twice-born, that river flows again to the foot of the Jambū tree,
being drunk by those people.
In Bhadrāśva Viṣṇu has the form of a horse-headed one; in Bhārata he is established as a tortoise;
in Ketumāla he is a boar; and likewise in the northern region, he is in the form of a fish.
O best of the twice-born, within those [regions], the territories are established according to the arrangement of the lunar mansions; they are all four, O foremost of brahmins,
which indicate the subjugation by the planets.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of Jambūdvīpa," in the Bhuvanakośa section of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-Five.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of the twice-born, learn from me also about the four winds and the four lakes that exist upon the four mountains, beginning with Mandara.
To the east is the grove named Caitraratha, to the south is the Nandana grove,
on the western mountain is Vaibhrāja, and on the northern peak is Sāvitra.
To the east of Meru is Lake Aruṇoda, and likewise Mānasa to the south;
Śītoda is to the west, and Mahābhadra is to the north.
Śītārta, Cakramuñja, Kulīra, then Sukaṅkavān,
Maṇiśaila, Vṛṣavān, Mahānīla, and Bhavācala.
Sūbindu, Mandara, Veṇu, Tāmasa, Niṣadha,
and Devaśaila— these great mountains lie to the east of Mandara.
Then there are the mountains Trikaṭaśikhara, Kaliṅga, Pataṅgaka,
Rucaka, Sānumant, Tāmraka, and Viśākhavant.
Śvetodara, Samūla, Vasudhāra, Ratnavān,
Ekaśṛṅga, Mahāśaila, Rājaśāla, and Pipāṭhaka.
Pañcaśaila, Kailāsa, and Himavat, the best of mountains—
these are declared to be the great mountains on the southern side of Meru.
Surakṣa, Śiśirākṣa, Vaidūrya, Kapila,
Piñjara, Mahābhadra, Surasa, Piṅgala, and Madhu.
Añjana, Kukkuta, Kṛṣṇa, Pāṇḍara, and Cālottama; Sahasraśikhara, the mountain Pāriyātra, and Śṛṅgavān.
Likewise, to the west of Meru, outside the western diameter, these mountains are declared;
now hear of the others to the north.
Then Śaṅkhakūṭa, Vṛṣabha, Haṃsanābha, and likewise Acala; Kapilendra, the mountain Sānumant, and Nīla as well.
Svarṇaśṛṅgī, Śātaśṛṅgī, Puṣpaka, Meghaparvata,
Virajākṣa, Varāhādri, Mayūra, and likewise Jārudhi.
Thus, O Brahmin, these mountains to the north of Meru have been described;
the plateaus (*drauṇyaḥ*) of these mountains are exceedingly beautiful.
Adorned with forests and lakes of pure water,
O best of the twice-born, it is there that meritorious men take birth.
O best of the twice-born, these earthly realms are heavens that possess even greater heavenly qualities; in them,
there is no acquisition of new merit or demerit.
O best of the twice-born, even for the gods, those very same [pleasures] consisting of the enjoyment of merit exist in those regions, such as Śītānta and the other mountains.
The great abodes of the Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, as well as the splendid dwellings of the Devas and Gandharvas.
Possessing great merit, they are always endowed with delightful groves,
charming lakes, and winds that grant happiness in all seasons.
And among these, humans never experience any mental distress whatsoever.
Thus, O King, I have described this four-petaled lotus.
And its petals in the four directions are Bhadrāśva and the others;
that which I have described as the southern region is called Bhārata.
That is the land of action; elsewhere there is no attainment of merit or sin.
This should be known as the primary [realm], wherein everything is established.
Therefore, O twice-born one, a man indeed attains heaven and liberation, as well as the human state or the state of hell, or even the condition of an animal, or whatever else there may be.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the Bhuvanakośa of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-six:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The goddess Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, originated from the earth-supporting foot of Nārāyaṇa, the source of the world.
Having entered the source of nectar, the moon— the reservoir of waters—
she is then purified by contact with the rays of the sun that are being joined with her.
It fell upon the summit of Meru and then split into four parts;
falling from the edges of the peaks of Meru, it was turned back.
With its waters being scattered, that [mountain] fell unsupported,
its waters evenly distributed across the foothills of Mount Mandara and the others.
O Sītā, she fell into four [oceans], her mountain-like feet split apart by the waters;
she became widely known as Pūrvā and went to the Caitraratha forest.
Having flooded that [region], he went to the Varuṇoda lake and the Śītānta mountain, and from there, in succession, to other mountains.
Having gone and reached the earth from Bhadrāśva, it flows into the ocean;
likewise, the river named Alakanandā flows on the southern side of Gandhamādana.
Having gone to Merupādavana and Nandana, the delight of the gods,
he flooded Lake Mānasa with great speed.
Having reached the king of mountains and its delightful peak,
he likewise [overlooked] all the mountains situated to the south.
Having inundated them, she reached the great mountain Himavat;
there Śambhu, whose banner is the bull, held her fast and did not release her.
The Lord was propitiated there by Bhagīratha through fasts and hymns of praise;
and Śarva released [the Gaṅgā] there into the southern ocean in seven streams.
The great river entered the eastern ocean in three ways, flowing by one of its currents toward the south, following the track of Bhagīratha’s chariot.
In the same way, that great river flowed through the vast western foot [of the mountain], and being renowned as Sucakṣus, it went toward the Vaibhrāja mountain;
from there, the great river overflowed into Lake Śītoda. 56.13.
Sucakṣu reached Parvata, and from there she went to Triśikha.
Therefore, having fallen successively upon the peaks of the mountains,
she reached Ketumāla and entered the salt ocean.
In that same manner, she went to the mountain Supārśva, which is indeed a foothill of Meru;
there, known as Somā (the auspicious one), she proceeded to the forest of Savitṛ.
Purifying them, that great river reached the Mahābhadra lake,
and from there she proceeded indeed to Śaṅkhakūṭa.
And from that mountain Vṛṣabha, having reached the mountains in succession,
she reached the great ocean after flooding the Northern Kurus.
Thus, O bull among the twice-born, have I described to you this Gaṅgā,
as well as the layout of Jambūdvīpa and its regions exactly as they are.
In all of those regions, beginning with Kimpuruṣa, the subjects dwell in a state of great happiness, free from affliction, and devoid of both deficiency and excess.
In each of the nine continents as well, there are seven mountain ranges;
likewise, in each region, there are rivers flowing forth from those mountains.
O best of the twice-born, in those eight regions beginning with Kimpuruṣa, the waters arise from the earth; here in Bhārata, however, they are the rain from the clouds.
For men, these eight kinds of supernatural powers— arising from trees, natural, regional, born of water, mental, and born of karma— are perfected within these respective years.
From trees that grant desires, the success derived from trees is born of their own nature;
it is declared to be natural, as well as satisfying, demonstrable, and instructional.
And because of the subtlety of the waters, that which arises from water and is endowed with meditation is called "mental" (mānasī);
furthermore, because it results in the performance of worship and other rites, it is also described as being "born of dharma."
Nor do the conditions of the ages (yugas), nor fears, nor diseases exist among them;
O best of the twice-born, there is no undertaking of merit or demerit among them at all.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-seven:
Krauṣṭuki said:
O Blessed One, this Jambūdvīpa has been described by you in brief;
as it has been stated by you, merit-yielding action bears fruit nowhere else.
Or for the sake of merit, O illustrious one,
with the exception of the *Bhārata*,
from this [work] heaven, liberation, the intermediate state, and the ultimate goal are attained.
"Indeed, no other duty is prescribed for mortals on earth than this;
therefore, O Brahmin, recount to me this Bhārata in detail."
O tiger among the twice-born, its divisions, their number, and how they are situated, as well as the regions and mountains within it— this is the year. (MarkP 57.4)

Learn from me the nine divisions of this land of Bhārata;
they are known to be separated by oceans and inaccessible to one another.
Indradvīpa, Kaśerumān, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, as well as Saumya, Gāndharva, and Vāruṇa.
Among them, however, the ninth island is surrounded by the ocean;
this island measures one thousand yojanas from south to north.
O twice-born one, the Kirātas dwell on its eastern edge, and likewise the Yavanas on its western;
while the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras reside within it.
"Purified by such activities as sacrificing, studying, and trading,
their social interaction is intended to be conducted through these very occupations."
At that time, there was the attainment of heaven and liberation, as well as merit and sin;
[there were also] Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and the Ṛkṣa mountain.
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges here;
and there are thousands of other mountains that lie adjacent to them.
There are delightful, vast plateaus here, wide in extent and height:
Kolāhala, Savaibhrāja, Mandara, and the mountain Dardura.
Vātasvana, Vaidyuta, Maināka, Svarasa,
Tuṅgaprastha, Nāgagiri, Rocana, and Pāṇḍarācala.

The Ambalas, Mālavas, Madras, Veṇukas, and Savadantikas;
the Piṅgalas, Mānakalahas, Hūṇas, and likewise the Kohalakas.
The Māṇḍavyas, the Bhūtiyuvakas, the Śātakas, the Hematārakas, the Yaśomatyas along with the Gāndhāras, and the Kharasāgararāśis; 58.46.
The Yaudheyas, the Dāsameyas, the Rājanyas, the Śyāmakas,
and the Kṣemadhūrtas likewise took refuge on the left side of the tortoise's belly.
And here the lunar mansion is Vāruṇa; therein are the two Proṣṭhapadas, by which [the regions of] Kinnararājya, Puṣpavāla, and Sakīcaka are governed.
Likewise, the kingdom of Kaśmīra, the people of Abhisāra,
the Davadās, the Aṅganās, the Kulaṭās, and the Vanarāṣṭrakas.
The Sairiṣṭhas, the Brahmapurakas, and likewise the Vanabāhyakas; the Kirātas, Kauśikas, Nandas, and the Pahnavas and Lolas.
The Dārvādās, the Marakas, the Kuraṭas, the Annadārakas,
the Ekapādas, the Khaśas, and the Ghoṣas— these blameless ones dwell on earth as if in heaven.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, there are the Sayavanas, the Hiṅgas, those who wear garments of bark, the Trinetras, the Pauravas, and the Gandharvas.
These three— the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī (the deity of the Aśvins), and Bharaṇī (the deity of Yama)— are situated upon the forefeet of the Tortoise in the northeast.
In that regard, O best of sages, these have been declared for cooking on the foot;
and these constellations also, O twice-born one, apply to these regions.
O Brahmin, these aforementioned regions suffer from this affliction;
however, they attain prosperity when the planets are properly situated.
O best of sages, whatever constellation a planet presides over, fear arises from that [planet] for that region;
conversely, when it is exalted, there is the arrival of auspiciousness.
O best of the twice-born, for each region there arises a common danger to the world arising from the conjunctions of lunar mansions and planets, which may be either auspicious or inauspicious.
When the planets are in their own asterisms but are inauspicious, it brings fear common to all living beings;
it produces inauspicious suffering arising from the planets with little effort.

In the same way, even an auspicious planetary configuration becomes one of little benefit for men when the planets are situated in unfavorable positions, unless it is understood by wise men who know the local conditions and their own circumstances.
When a planet is in an unfavorable position, even for meritorious men, there is fear regarding wealth, the cow-pen, servants, friends, sons, or the wife.
Thus, those of little merit have fear within themselves, and those who are great sinners everywhere;
for those who are truly without sin, there is never fear anywhere at all.
A man experiences good and evil fortune that is common to his region, country, and people; common to kings; and common to the stars and planets.
And mutual protection arises from the unfavorable state of the planets; likewise,
O best of Brahmins,
there is a loss of auspiciousness through these very same inauspicious ones.
This which has been described by me among the constellations as being shaped like a tortoise is the general configuration of the regions, both inauspicious and auspicious.

Therefore, O best of beings, having understood the planetary afflictions concerning one's country, the lunar mansion, and oneself, a wise person should perform propitiatory rites and heed the common sayings of the world.
From the sky, the deities, and the Daityas and others, their longings fall upon the earth; these are heard of in the world as "worldly rumors" (lokavādas).
A wise man should act in that very same way; he should not neglect worldly conventions.
By acting accordingly toward those people, the destruction of their arrival at evil is appropriate.
O best of the twice-born, they bring about the destruction of merit and the increase of evils;
they cause the loss of wisdom and the depletion of wealth and other possessions.
Therefore, a wise person devoted to peace, as well as one intent on worldly discourse,
should perform both worldly rites and rites for peace during afflictions caused by the planets.
Abstaining from malice, observing fasts, venerating shrines and the like,
as well as recitation, fire-offerings, giving gifts, bathing, and the avoidance of anger and other such passions are recommended.
The wise person should practice non-malice toward all beings and cultivate friendliness;
likewise, they should avoid untruthful speech as well as excessive or contentious talk.
In all afflictions caused by the planets, a person should perform worship of the planets;
thus, O best of the twice-born, all terrible calamities are pacified without exception.
For men who are diligent, all [the afflictions] arising from the planets and constellations [are removed];
this tortoise has been described by me as the omnipresent Lord in Bhārata.
For Nārāyaṇa is the inconceivable Self in whom everything is established;
there all the gods reside, taking refuge in the various lunar mansions.
Likewise, O twice-born one, fire is in the middle, as are earth and the moon;
three signs beginning with Aries are in the middle, while two beginning with Gemini are at the mouth.
Likewise, Cancer and Leo are situated at the front right foot;
and the three zodiac signs—Leo, Virgo, and Libra—are situated in the belly.
Libra and Scorpio are both situated in the southwestern quarter;
and Sagittarius stands at the back together with Scorpio.
In its northwest quarter (vāyavya) are the three beginning with the Archer (Sagittarius);
likewise, Aquarius and Pisces are situated upon its northern flank.
O best of the twice-born,
Pisces and Aries are situated in the north-eastern quarter;
likewise, O twice-born one, there are regions and asterisms within these very regions on the back of the tortoise.
Likewise, the zodiacal signs are situated within the constellations and the planetary signs;
therefore, one should predict affliction for a country when there is affliction of the planets and constellations.
Having bathed there, one should perform the rites of giving, fire-offerings, and so forth.
This indeed is the Vaiṣṇava foot, which is Brahmā situated in the center of the planetary sphere;
it is the one named Nārāyaṇa, the inconceivable self, the cause, and the Lord of the universe.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Settlement of Kūrma," in the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Chapter Fifty-nine:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus, O Sage, the land of Bhārata-varṣa has been described to you exactly as it is, along with its four ages:
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and likewise Kali.
In this very [Kṛta] age, O twice-born one, the lifespan of the four castes is indeed four hundred,
three hundred, two hundred, and likewise one hundred years.
O Brahmin, men live here in succession during the Kṛta, Tretā,
and other ages on the eastern side of the great mountain-king Devakūṭa.
Learn from me concerning Bhadrāśva, the region situated to the east:
there are the excellent mountains Śvetaparṇa, Nīla, and Śaivāla.
Kaurañja, Parṇa, Śālāgra—these five are the principal mountain ranges (kulācala);
from them are born the many other minor mountains.
By them were distinguished thousands of regions of various forms;
thereafter [appeared those] resembling white water-lilies, possessing pure ridges and auspiciousness.
In this manner, there are hundreds and thousands of others as well,
such as Sītā, Śaṅkhāvatī, Bhadrā, Cakrāvartā, and so forth.
Moreover, there are many broad rivers carrying floods of cool water;
in this region, men possess a radiance like that of pure conch shells and gold.
Those who possess divine unions are meritorious and have a lifespan of one thousand years;
among them, there are neither the dull-witted nor the superior, for they all possess equal vision.
By nature, they are endowed with the eight qualities beginning with forbearance (*titikṣā*);
there too resides the four-armed Lord Janārdana, whose head is that of a horse.
Endowed with a head, heart, anus, genitals, feet, and hands, as well as the three eyes—
these should be understood as the sense objects of that Lord of the World.
Now learn from me concerning Ketumāla, the western region:
Viśāla, Kambala, Kṛṣṇa, Jayanta, and Hariparvata.
Viśoka and Vardhamāna—these seven are the principal mountain ranges;
there are thousands of other mountains upon which the multitude of worlds rests.
Their chiefs are Mahākāya, Śāka, Potaka, and Kambhaka; and there dwell hundreds of people, headed by Aṅgula.
Those who drink from the great rivers— the Vaṅkṣu, the Śyāmā, the Sakambalā,
the Amoghā, the Kāminī, and likewise the Śyāmā and thousands of others— [attain their desires].
Here too, the lifespan is equal to that of the previous [kalpas]; here also the Blessed Lord Hari, in the form of the Boar, [manifested] from his feet, mouth, heart, back, and sides.
In the region joined by three constellations, the constellations are auspicious;
this, O best of sages, has been described to you as Ketumāla.
Beyond this, I shall describe the Northern Kurus; listen now to my account of them.
There, the trees bear honey-sweet fruit and are always laden with flowers and fruit.
And from their fruits are produced garments and ornaments;
for they indeed grant all desires and bestow the fruits of every wish.
The ground there is made of jewels, and the wind is fragrant and always pleasant;
men who have descended from the world of the gods are born there.
Pairs are born that remain together for an equal duration of time;
they are mutually devoted to one another, resembling ruddy geese.
Their duration is indeed fourteen thousand and five hundred [years].
There is the lord of mountains Candrakānta, and another, Sūryakānta.
In that region between the two Kulaparvatas,
the great river Bhadrasomā flows across the earth, carrying a flood of pure and meritorious waters.
Likewise, there are thousands of other rivers even in the northern region;
similarly, there are others that carry milk and others that carry clarified butter.
There were lakes of curd, as well as other mountains nearby,
and various fruits whose taste was almost like that of nectar.
In those forests and those regions by the hundreds and thousands,
there too the Blessed Viṣṇu, in the form of a fish, had his head facing the east.
O Brahmin, the constellations are divided ninefold,
three for each [quarter];
likewise, O best of sages, the directions are also divided ninefold.
Candradvīpa is in the ocean, and Bhadradvīpa is another;
there too, O great sage, is the famous and meritorious region within the sea.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have described Kuruvārṣa to you; now hear from me as I speak of Kimpuruṣa and the other regions.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Uttarakuru," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O twice-born one, I shall now describe that region of Kimpuruṣa,
where the lifespan of the well-formed men is ten thousand years.
For there the men and likewise the women are free from disease and free from sorrow;
and there is said to be a vast grove of Plakṣa trees, equal to the Nandana garden.
Those men who constantly drink the juice of that fruit always possess stable youth, and the women have the fragrance of blue lotuses.
Beyond this, after Kimpuruṣa, Harivarṣa is described;
there, human beings are born resembling great silver.
All those who have descended from the world of the gods, possessing entirely divine forms,
all the men in Harivarṣa drink the auspicious juice of sugarcane.
There, old age does not afflict them, nor do they ever grow old;
for all that time they live free from disease.
I have described Meruvarṣa as the central region, which is Ilāvṛta;
there the sun does not scorch, nor do those humans age.
The rays of the sun and moon, as well as those of the stars and planets, do not attain their own manifestation there; for on that [mountain], Meru possesses supreme splendor.
The humans born there possess the luster of lotuses, the fragrance of lotuses, and subsist on the juice of jambu fruits; their eyes are as broad as lotus petals.
There too, the lifespan is thirteen thousand years;
the arrangement in the shape of a shallow bowl is situated in Ilāvṛta in the middle of Meru.
There lies the great mountain Meru; that region is called Ilāvṛta.
Beyond this, I shall describe the region of Ramyaka; learn about it.
And there too stands a lofty banyan tree with green foliage;
indeed, they subsist by drinking the juice of its fruit.
There, the humans have a lifespan of ten thousand years and enjoy the fruits thereof;
they are preeminent in pleasure, pure, and free from old age and foul odors.
Therefore, the region to the north is known by the name Hiraṇmaya,
where the river Hiraṇvatī flows, radiant with abundant lotuses.
There, human beings are born with great strength and splendor;
they possess large bodies, great courage, wealth, and are pleasing to behold.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Varṣas of Kiṃpuruṣa and Others," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-One.
Krauṣṭuki said:
O Great Sage, you have correctly explained that which you were asked:
the configuration of the earth, oceans, and so forth, as well as their dimensions and the planets.
The dimensions of those very [planets] and the configuration of the stars, as well as the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ and all the netherworlds (pātāla) as well; MarkP_61.2 //
O Sage, the Manvantara known as Svāyambhuva is thus declared to be mine;
I wish to hear indeed about those other intervening Manvantaras.
The gods who are lords of the manvantaras, the sages, and their sons, the kings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: I have described to you the Manvantara of Svāyambhuva;
now hear from me the one called Svārociṣa, which follows immediately after that.
In the city of Aruṇāspada, on the bank of the Varuṇā, there was a certain preeminent brahmin, a learned man whose beauty surpassed even that of the two Aśvins.
Gentle by nature and of virtuous conduct, he had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
he was always fond of guests and provided refuge to those who arrived even at night.
This thought occurred to him: "I shall behold the earth, with its exceedingly beautiful forests and gardens, adorned with various cities."
Then, at one time, a certain guest arrived at his house,
who was knowledgeable regarding the powers of various medicinal herbs and skilled in the sciences of mantras.
Thus entreated by him with a mind purified by faith,
he described to him various regions and delightful cities.
Then, filled with wonder at the forests, rivers, mountains, and sacred shrines, he spoke to that best of the twice-born.
Having seen many lands, you are overcome with great fatigue;
you are neither too old in years nor have you passed beyond youth.
O twice-born one, how is it that you traverse the earth in such a short time?
The Brahmin said:
"O Brahmins, by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, my movement is unimpeded;
indeed, I travel a thousand yojanas in half a day."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then that brahmin, full of faith in the words of that wise brahmin, replied to him once more with great respect.
O Blessed One, grant me your grace arising from the power of your mantra;
a desire to behold this earth of mine arises within me as if it were great.
That noble-minded brahmin gave him an ointment for the feet and consecrated it with mantras, and he also diligently pointed out the direction to him.
Then, O best of the twice-born, that brahmin, his feet anointed with it,
went to see the Himavat mountain, which is endowed with various springs.
Thinking, "Since I travel a thousand yojanas in half a day,
I shall return in the other half," he indeed departed.
O twice-born one, having reached the ridge of the Himalayas with his body not yet overly exhausted,
he then wandered there upon the surface of the snowy mountain.
Then, as the frost was trodden upon by his foot and began to melt,
the foot-ointment produced from the supreme medicinal herbs was washed away.
Then, moving with a sluggish gait and wandering here and there,
he beheld the most enchanting plateaus of the snowy mountain.
In various places here and there, there were delightful pleasure gardens frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, and cherished by Kinnaras, belonging to the gods and other celestial beings.
Beholding those places crowded with hundreds of hosts of divine apsarases,
that best of the twice-born was not satiated, O Sage, his hair standing on end with thrill.
In some places it was enchanting with waterfalls cascading from springs,
and in other places it resounded with the cries of dancing peacocks.
In some places it was filled with the exceedingly charming calls of gallinules, lapwings, and other birds, accompanied by the sweet, melodious warbling of male cuckoos that captivated the ear.
Fanned by winds scented with the fragrance of blossoming trees,
he beheld the great mountain Himavat, filled with joy.
Having seen this great mountain Himavat, the son of the twice-born resolved upon his home, thinking, "I shall see it tomorrow."
Then, his foot-ointment having worn off and his gait becoming sluggish after a long time, he reflected: "What is this that I have performed out of ignorance?"
"If my ointment has been destroyed, dissolved by the water of the snows,
this mountain is exceedingly difficult to traverse and I have come here from afar."
"I shall depart; how shall I perform my religious duties, such as tending the sacred fire, now that this great crisis has arrived? (MarkP 61.29)
"This is delightful, this is delightful"— with such a view toward this excellent mountain, I shall not reach satiety even in hundreds of years.
The sweet-voiced songs of the kinnaras, enchanting to the ear from all sides,
and the fragrance of blossoming trees reach the sense of smell to an extreme degree.
The wind is pleasant to the touch, the fruits are succulent,
and the lakes, so delightful to the mind, forcibly captivate the heart.
If, while things stand thus, I should behold some treasure of asceticism,
he might instruct me in the path for returning home.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thinking thus, that brahmin wandered upon the Himālayas;
his strength from foot-herbs having failed, he fell into a state of extreme despondency.
The highly fortunate and beautiful Varāpsarā, a Mauleyā woman, saw that best of sages wandering about with his army.
Upon seeing that best of brahmins,
the army at that very moment became filled with passion, their hearts drawn by love.
He reflected: "Who indeed is this one of such most beautiful form?
My birth would be fruitful if he does not disregard me."
"Oh, the sweetness of his form! Oh, the grace of his gait!
Oh, the profundity of his gaze! Whence on earth could there be one equal to him?"
Gods, Daityas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas have been seen by me;
yet not even one exists who is equal in form to this Great-Souled One.
If he were to be as full of passion for me as I am for him,
then I would perform the accumulation of merit resulting from that.
If he should cast upon me today a gaze so full of affection,
then no woman in the three worlds would possess greater merit than I.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus reflecting, that divine woman, afflicted by love,
revealed herself in her most beautiful form.
Seeing that beautiful Varūthinī, the son of the twice-born approached her with courtesy and spoke these words.
"Who are you, O lady with the luster of the interior of a lotus, to whom do you belong, and what are you doing here?
I am a brahmin who has come here from the city of Aruṇāspada."
"O lady with intoxicating eyes, my foot-ointment has been washed away and dissolved here by the water of the Himavat; it was through its power that I came here."
Varūthinī said:
"O illustrious one, I am a native of this place, known by the name Varūthinī;
I always wander here upon this delightful great mountain."
O Brahmin, by the sight of you I have fallen into a state beyond description due to desire;
instruct me as to what I must do, for I am now subject to your will.
The Brahmin said:
"O lady of pure smiles, tell me that means by which I may go to my own home, O auspicious one; otherwise, there will be a loss of all our religious merits."
"O blessed lady, a great loss of the obligatory and occasional rites will befall me, a twice-born;
therefore, deliver me from the Himalayas."
"Travel abroad is never praised for Brahmins;
O timid one, it was not out of a desire to see the country that I committed an offense against you."
In the house of a preeminent Brahmin who is mindful, there is the successful completion of all rites—
both daily and occasional— but for one living abroad, there is only their neglect.
Therefore, O illustrious lady, what is the use of saying more? Act in such a way that I may behold my own home before the sun has set.
Varūthinī said: "Do not speak thus, O illustrious one;
let that day never come to me."
"Wherever you go, having abandoned me, to your own home," [MarkP_61.53]
"O joy of the twice-born, heaven is not more delightful than this;
therefore, having abandoned that abode of the gods, we remain here."
Therefore, O beloved, sporting here with me on this lovely snowy mountain, you shall not remember your mortal kinsmen.
"I shall give you garlands, garments, ornaments, enjoyments, food, and ointments;
for I have been carried away here, brought under your control by the God of Love."
The song of the kinnaras, with its sound like that of the lute and the flute, was enchanting;
the wind brought refreshment to the limbs, and the water was warm and pure.
O illustrious one, for one who does not exist here [in this world], what more is there in his own home than a bed desired by the mind and fragrant ointment?
For one who is not present here, old age will never occur;
this is the realm of the Thirty-three, which bestows the increase of youth.
Having spoken thus, that lotus-eyed woman, full of passion and agitated in mind, suddenly embraced him while saying softly, "Be gracious."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Do not touch me; go elsewhere, O wicked woman! You who are like yourself, you have been solicited by me in one way, yet you approach me in quite another."
The oblation offered in the evening and in the morning bestows eternal worlds;
this entire triple-world, O foolish one, is established upon the sacrificial offering.
Varūthinī said:
"O Brahmin, am I not dear to you?
Is this mountain not delightful?"
Indeed, having set aside the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others, who is it that you desire?
"Without doubt, you shall return from this place to your own abode;
meanwhile, enjoy for a short time with me those pleasures that are so difficult to obtain."
The Brahmin said:
"O twice-born one, among those eight qualities of the self, compassion comes first;
why do you not show it toward me, O protector of the true dharma?"
"Released by you, I shall not live, for I am so full of love for you;
I do not speak this falsely, so be gracious, O delighter of your lineage."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"If you speak to me truthfully out of affection, and not merely as a formal courtesy,
then tell me the means by which I may go to my own abode."
Varūthinī said:
"Without doubt, you will return to your own abode from this place;
meanwhile, enjoy with me for a short time those pleasures that are so difficult to obtain."
The Brahmin said:
Indeed, an army is not praised for the sake of the enjoyment of Brahmins;
for the exertion of Brahmins in this world leads only to suffering and yields no fruit after death.
Varūthinī said:
"By providing protection for me as I am dying,
you will obtain the fruit of merit in the hereafter, and enjoyments in another birth."
And thus, both of these will be the cause of your own ruin here:
by rejecting me, you shall incur death, and I shall incur sin.
The Brahmin said:
"One should not desire another's wife," so my teachers have told me;
therefore, I do not long for you—lament as you wish, or wither away.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, that illustrious one, being restrained and pure after touching water,
prostrated before the Gārhapatya fire and spoke these words in a low voice.
O Blessed One, you are the source of all ritual acts for the householder’s fire;
from you alone come the Āhavanīya and Dakṣiṇa fires, and not from any other.
Through being nourished by you, the gods become the cause of rain, grain, and so forth;
from grain, the entire world comes into being, and not otherwise.
"By that very truth by which this world exists through you,
may I behold my own home today while the sun still shines."
"Just as indeed Vedic ritual was never abandoned by me at its proper time,
by that truth may I, though now a householder, behold the sun today."
And just as my mind has never at any time been inclined toward another's property or another's wife with desire, may this [vow] of mine attain fulfillment.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Words of the Brāhmaṇa," in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-two:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
As that son of a twice-born spoke thus,
the Gārhapatya fire then established its presence within his body.
Then, presided over by him and standing in the midst of a circle of light,
he illuminated that region like the embodied fire-god.
But as that celestial woman gazed upon the brahmin of such form, her passion for him there became all the more intense.
Then, having been empowered by that bearer of oblations at that very moment,
the son of the twice-born set out to travel just as he had before.
And he departed with haste, watched by that goddess,
whose slender-limbed form made her neck tremble with sighs from the moment his gaze fell upon her.
Then, having reached his own home in that very moment,
that best of brahmins performed all the rites exactly as they had been described.
Then she, whose every limb was beautiful, with her soul and mind attached to him there, spent the remainder of the day and likewise the night, devoted almost entirely to sighing.
Sighing, the faultless-limbed one with intoxicating eyes wept repeatedly, crying "Alas! Alas! and reproached herself, saying, "I am ill-fated."
At that time, she found no delight in the monastery, nor in pleasant food, nor in the forest,
nor even in lovely mountain caves.
And as she took delight, she felt envy for a pair of ruddy geese;
thus released by him, the woman of beautiful hips reproached her own youth.
Where have I come to this mountain, compelled by the force of adverse fate?
And where has such a man as that come within the range of my sight?
If that illustrious one does not come to my side today,
then this unbearable fire of desire will surely consume me.
That very place which was once so delightful, resounding with the calls of male cuckoos,
now seems utterly to consume me, being utterly bereft of them.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus, O best of sages, she went forth possessed by passion,
and her lust for him increased at every moment.
A Gandharva named Kali, who had previously been rejected by her despite being full of passion,
then beheld her in that state.
Then he thought: "What indeed is this army, moving like an elephant, withered by the wind of its sighs, upon this mountain?"
Has she perhaps incurred the curse of a sage, or has she been insulted by someone,
since her face is thus drenched with tears?
Then Kali reflected upon that matter for a very long time out of curiosity;
and by the power of his meditative absorption, he came to know it exactly as it was.
Having understood that, Kali reflected again:
"This has been well bestowed upon me by my previously performed merits."
"Though she was repeatedly entreated by me with passion, she rejected me; yet today, she shall become mine."
"She will undoubtedly take delight in me, a human being who possesses passion and assumes that very form; what can I do about that in the course of time?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, by his own power, having assumed the form of that twice-born man,
he moved about where that army was stationed.
Seeing him, that woman of beautiful hips and slender limbs, her eyes slightly blossoming with joy, approached and said again and again, "Be gracious!"
If I am abandoned by you, I shall undoubtedly give up my life;
in that case, there will be a most grievous unrighteousness and a failure in my religious duties.
Having come together with me in this delightful cave of the great mountain,
you shall certainly attain the merit born of my protection.
"O Great-minded One, there is indeed a remainder of my lifespan;
it is because of that that you have surely returned, bringing joy to my heart."
Kali said:
"What shall I do? Here, the performance of my duties is being neglected by you, even though I am present; yet you, O slender-waisted one, speak such words."
Therefore, I have fallen into a dilemma: do what I tell you;
if there is to be a union with you today, it shall not be otherwise.
Varūthinī said:
"Be gracious; I shall do exactly what you say, for it shall not be in vain for you.
I speak this without hesitation regarding that which must now be performed by me."
Kali said:
"O fair-browed one, you must not see me today in the forest at the time of our union; your contact with me shall take place while your eyes are closed."
Varūthinī said:
"So be it; may it be well with you. Let it be exactly as you wish.
For from now on, I shall remain under your control in every respect."
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the Svārociṣa Manvantara of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-three—63.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then he sported with her upon the mountain ridges and by the delightful lakes, which were charming with their blossoming forests.
And in delightful caves, on the sandy banks of rivers,
and in other such charming places, the twice-born one remained joyful.
Because of the splendor of his form as he was presided over by Fire,
she closed her eyes during the time of enjoyment, for she could not contemplate it.
Then, O best of sages, in the course of time she conceived a child from the seed of the Gandharva and from the contemplation of the form of that twice-born one.
Then, having consoled Varūthinī who was carrying a child in her womb, he,
assuming the form of a brahmin, departed, having been dismissed by her with affection.
That boy was born resplendent, like a blazing fire,
illuminating all directions with his own radiance just as the sun does.
Because that boy shone with his own radiance like the sun,
he became renowned by the name Svarocis.
And the illustrious one grew day by day in age,
as well as in a multitude of virtues, just as the moon, marked with a hare, waxes in its digits.
Then, having reached the prime of youth, that highly fortunate one mastered the science of archery, the Vedas, and all branches of knowledge in their proper order.
Once, while wandering on Mount Mandara with his graceful movements,
he then beheld a maiden on a mountain plateau, overcome with fear.
Looking at him, she then spoke these words: "Save me! He, for his part, said to her whose eyes were overwhelmed with fear, "Do not be afraid."
When the high-souled Vīra had spoken these words, "What is this?",
she then related the account, her syllables faltering and overwhelmed by gasps for breath.
The maiden said:
"I am indeed the daughter of the Vidyādhara named Indīvara;
I was born by the name Manoramā from the daughter of Marudhanvan."
My companion Vibhāvarī was born from the Vidyādhara Mandāra,
and Kalāvatī was the daughter of the sage Pāra.
Together with those two, I went to the excellent slopes of Kailāsa;
there I saw a certain sage whose form was exceedingly emaciated by ascetic penance.
With his throat parched by hunger, devoid of luster, and his pupils far-sunken, he was mocked by me; enraged, he then cursed me. (MarkP 63.16)
"O ignoble and wicked ascetic, because you have mocked me with your voice so exceedingly feeble and your sprout-like lower lip slightly distorted."
"Therefore, before long, a Rākṣasa will overcome you.
When he had thus pronounced the curse upon me, that sage was rebuked by my two friends.
Fie on your Brahminhood! Because of your lack of forbearance, all your ascetic merit has been taken away;
you have been overcome by those who cannot endure provocation, and you were not sufficiently refined by your penance.
"Brahminhood indeed has patience as its foundation, and austerity consists in the restraint of anger.
Having heard this, he of immeasurable luster uttered a curse upon those two as well.
In one woman there was leprosy on her limbs, while in the other there was consumption;
for both of them, that which had been described by him arose at that very moment.
In my case as well, this great Rakshasa approaches, following my footsteps;
yet you do not hear his mighty roar, even though he is shouting not far away.
Today is the third day that [this knowledge] has not left my back;
today I have become the knower of the heart of your entire collection of weapons.
"I give these to you; protect me from this demon, O high-minded one!
In the beginning, Rudra himself, the wielder of the Pināka bow, bestowed them upon Svāyambhuva."
Svāyambhuva gave it to Vasiṣṭha, the best of the perfected ones;
he, in turn, gave it to Citrāyudha, the father of my mother.
That father-in-law himself also bestowed a dowry upon my father;
and I too, O hero, was instructed by my father while still a child.
This is the heart-mantra of all weapons, the destroyer of every enemy;
let it be taken up quickly, for it is the ultimate resort of all missiles.
Therefore, slay this evil-minded rākṣasa who has come here.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When he had spoken thus, the other then touched the water for purification and bestowed upon him the heart-mantra of those weapons, along with the secret methods for their withdrawal.
In the meantime, that Rākṣasa of terrifying form arrived in great haste, uttering a mighty roar.
"Overpowered by me, what protection can you find? Come quickly to me! Why do you delay?"—he saw him speaking thus as he was about to devour him.
Seeing that he had arrived, Svarocis reflected:
"May he accept the truthful word of that great sage, 'Let it be so for her.'"
That Rākṣasa also approached her with haste and seized her, as she, slender-waisted, was piteously crying out, "Save me! Save me!"
Then Svarocis, filled with rage, fixed his gaze upon that Rākṣasa and beheld him with unblinking eyes, having discharged a most terrifying and fierce weapon.
Overwhelmed by that, the night-stalker then abandoned her and said, "Be gracious;
let this weapon be stilled, and let my words be heard."
O one of great splendor, I have been liberated by you from that most terrible curse,
which had been pronounced by the wise Brahmamitra with extreme severity.
O highly fortunate one, there is no other benefactor to me greater than you,
by whom I have been liberated from this most grievous and great curse.
Svarocis said:
For what reason were you cursed by the high-souled sage Brahmamitra, and of what nature was the curse that was given in the past?
The Rākṣasa said:
The twice-born Brahmamitra studied the Āyurveda divided into eight parts, having mastered the thirteen sections of the Atharvaveda.
And I was known by the name Indīvara, and I became the father of this girl; I am the son of Nalanābha Khaṅgin, the lord of the Vidyādharas.
Previously, I requested the sage Brahmitra:
"O Blessed One, you ought to grant me the entirety of Āyurveda."
But when, O hero, though I had bowed with great humility and repeatedly entreated him, he would not grant me the knowledge consisting of Āyurveda that I requested.
O sinless one, as he was bestowing [the knowledge] upon his disciples, I then received from him the science consisting of Āyurveda by means of my power of invisibility.
Once the vidyā had been acquired within eight months,
I laughed again and again with extreme joy.
Recognizing me with a laugh, the sage, filled with anger and his neck trembling, spoke these harsh words to me: MarkP_63.45 //
"O evil-minded one, since my spells were stolen by you, a Rākṣasa, while you remained invisible, and you have indeed treated me with contempt through mockery."
Therefore, O sinful Rākṣasa, you shall be cast out by my curse;
in seven nights you will become a terrible being, of this there is no doubt.
When this was said, that brahmin, having been propitiated by prostrations and other marks of reverence,
immediately spoke to me again with a gentle mind.
O Gandharva, that which I have spoken must necessarily come to pass; it cannot be otherwise.
However, having become a Rākṣasa, you shall regain your own body once again.
When, with your memory lost and filled with rage, you desire to devour your own offspring,
you shall then attain the state of a night-stalker, tormented by the fire of weapons.
Having regained consciousness once more, you shall obtain your own body and likewise your own abode in the world known as Gandharva.
Thus, O illustrious hero, I have been delivered by you from this great danger of being a night-stalker.
Therefore, fulfill my prayer.
"I give you this daughter as a wife; accept her.
And take also, O high-minded one, the entire Ayurveda in its eight branches, which was obtained by me from that sage."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, he, radiant in divine garments, wearing garlands and ornaments, and assuming a divine and ancient form, bestowed the knowledge upon him.
Having bestowed the lore, he then proceeded to give away his daughter;
at that time, the maiden spoke to her progenitor, who stood before her in his true form.
"Father, my affection for this great-souled man has also arisen intensely;
indeed, it was born at the very first sight of him, especially since he has been so helpful."
But this friend of mine and she herself are tormented by grief on my account;
therefore, I have no desire to enjoy pleasures together with him.
Even men are not capable of committing such cruelty;
how then could a woman like me, who naturally delights in such things, do so?
O father, just as those two daughters of mine are afflicted with grief on my account,
so shall I remain in that same sorrow, tormented by the fire of their lamentation.
Svarocis said:
"By the grace of Ayurveda, I shall restore you both to youth;
O slender-waisted one, cast away your great sorrow."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, on that mountain, Svarocis married that maiden named Cārunetrā, who had been given to him by her father himself according to the prescribed rites.
Having then bestowed that maiden upon him and consecrated the beautiful woman with blessings,
the Gandharva departed for his own city by means of a divine course.
Accompanied by that slender maiden, he then went to that excellent garden where the pair of maidens lay afflicted by the disease arising from the curse.
Then he, the knower of reality, Svarocis Aparājita, rendered the bodies of those two free from disease by means of medicines and elixirs that destroy illness.
Then, once those two most beautiful and auspicious maidens were liberated from their affliction,
they illuminated the quarters of the sky with their own radiance and that great mountain.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the Svārociṣa Manvantara of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-four:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus freed from her ailment, the maiden, filled with joy, spoke these words to Svarociṣ: "Listen to my words, O Lord. (MarkP 64.1)
Born of the Vidyādhara Mandāra, she was renowned by the name Vibhāvarī.
"O benefactor! I offer myself to you; accept me."
And I shall grant you the knowledge of the cries of all beings, by which they will become manifest; be filled with serene confidence.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When Svarocis, the knower of dharma, had replied, "So be it," the second daughter then spoke these words.
My father was named Pāra; he was a celibate from his youth, a highly illustrious brahmin seer who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Formerly, during the springtime, which was as enchanting as the song of the male cuckoo,
the celebrated Apsaras Puñjikasthalā came into his presence.
At that time, that bull among sages was led into a state where desire must be expressed;
through union with her, I was born here on this great mountain.
And that mother of mine has departed, leaving me alone— a mere child— upon the surface of the earth in this desolate forest teeming with beasts of prey and wild animals.
Then, O best of beings, as the digits of the moon increase at the end of the day,
being replenished day after day, I shall attain growth.
Then, O noble-souled one, my father, the Gandharva, gave me this auspicious name, Kalāvatī, because he had taken hold of me. MarkP_64.10.
"I was not given away by that high-souled one when he was entreated;
therefore, my father, who was sleeping, was killed by that enemy of the gods."
Then, out of extreme despondency, as I was intent on taking my own life,
I was restrained by Satī, the consort of Śambhu, who was true to her promise.
"Do not grieve, O fair-browed one;
your husband shall be highly fortunate,
and he shall have a son named Svarocis who will become a Manu."
And all the treasures will carry out your command with respect;
O auspicious one, they will bestow upon you wealth according to your desire.
"O child, receive from me that spell by whose power [this is possible];
this spell, named Padminī, is honored by Mahāpadma."
"Thus spoke Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, who is devoted to truth:
'O Goddess Svarocis, you are certainly Dhruva; she would not speak otherwise.'"
Therefore, O giver of life, I now bestow that lore as well as my own body;
please accept them, being well-disposed toward me with favor.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"So be it," he said to that maiden Kalāvatī,
being encouraged by the affectionate glance of Vibhāvarī, the mother of Kalāvatī.
Then, while celestial instruments resounded and the Apsarases danced, he of divine splendor took hold of their two hands.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Svārociṣa Manvantara.
Chapter Sixty-Five.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, accompanied by those wives, he of celestial splendor took his pleasure upon that king of mountains, which possessed lovely forests and waterfalls.
All kinds of precious objects of enjoyment, honey, and sweet things,
as well as treasures, brought themselves to the lotus-lake that was under his control.
Garments, ornaments, and fragrant ointments rich with scent;
and seats that are exceedingly bright and made of gold, according to their desire.
O highly fortunate one, there were golden water-pots and vessels,
as well as various kinds of beds provided with divine coverlets.
Thus, accompanied by them on that excellent mountain, which was perfumed with divine fragrances and illuminated by his own radiant splendors, he took his delight.
And they too, together with him, experienced supreme joy on that mountain peak,
sporting there just as they do in heaven.
A female swan, longing for a charming union with him and with them, spoke to a certain female ruddy goose who was staying in the water.
"Blessed is this man, and most meritorious is he, who, within the domain of youth,
enjoys his desired pleasures together with these beloved women."
There are those who possess praiseworthy youth, yet their wives are not very beautiful;
in this world, there are few wives who are both excellent and have husbands who are exceedingly handsome.
