A beloved woman is desired by someone, and a beloved man is sought after by someone;
a conjugal union rich in mutual affection is exceedingly rare.
"Blessed is this man, beloved by his wife, for she too is exceedingly dear to him;
indeed, mutual affection arises only among those who are blessed."
Having heard these words uttered by the female swan,
the female ruddy goose, her mind not greatly astonished, spoke to her.
This man is not fortunate, since he feels no shame from the proximity of another's wife;
he enjoys one woman while his mind is not fixed upon all of them.
"Since his affection for the mind is fixed upon a single object, O friend,
how indeed will he come to feel love for his wives?"
These women are not beloved by their husband, nor is the husband beloved by them;
they are merely for diversion, just like any other servant.
If he is beloved by these women, why does he not give up his life? For he embraces another beloved woman while being meditated upon by yet another beloved.
For he has been sold like a servant for the price of the gift of knowledge;
indeed, love does not abide equally among many.
"O Kalahaṃsī, my husband is blessed and I too am blessed,
since for such a long time his mind has been fixed on me alone and mine has remained fixed on him alone."
Knowing the cries of all sentient beings, Svarocis, who was invincible, heard this and, feeling ashamed, reflected: "This is indeed the truth, not a falsehood."
Then, when a hundred years had passed, while he was sporting on the great mountain together with them,
he beheld a deer before him as he was enjoying himself.
With limbs exceedingly smooth and full,
he was wandering with herds of deer and surrounded by beautiful female deer.
Then, as those female deer, their nostrils drawn back, were sniffing [the scent],
that male deer said to the women, "Go, casting aside your shame."
"I am not Svarocis, nor do I possess his character, nor am I Sulocanā;
there are many shameless people like that who go there."
Just as a single woman, though following many men, becomes an object of laughter among people,
so too is a single being perceived through the vision of the awakened ones as manifold.
Day by day his performance of religious duties declines;
he is always attached to the wives of others and ever intent on the desires of others.
"Whoever else is such as that—possessing his character and averse to the next world—desire him; may it be well with you, for I am not his equal in my own radiance."
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the Svārociṣa Manvantara of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa. [The Lord said: "I shall describe the future, as well as the past and the present in their entirety."
When he said, "Consider this and then give the command," I understood that matter as well;
therefore, I did not offer you the price according to the prescribed rule.
"It is true, O King;
you are worthy of honor in the lineage of Svāyambhuva.
Nevertheless, we consider you, though most excellent, not yet fit for the guest-offering."
The king said:
"O Brahmin, what indeed have I done, whether knowingly or even unknowingly?"
Because of you, I am worthy of honor, for I have come as a guest after a long time.
The sage said:
"Have you forgotten that your wife was abandoned by you in the forest? By abandoning her, you have abandoned all dharma, O King."
By the neglect of ritual action for a fortnight, a man falls into a state of touchlessness;
he whose neglect of the daily rites lasts for a year becomes one who is defiled by excrement and urine.
A wife should be favorable toward her husband, O Lord of Men, even if he is ill-behaved;
likewise, even an ill-behaved wife must be supported.
For that wife who was abducted was indeed repugnant to that brahmin;
nevertheless, O King, desiring to fulfill his duty, he caused you to be revealed.
O lord of the earth, you establish others who are wavering in their own duties;
who else will establish you when you have strayed from your own duty?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been told "He is to be shunned" by that wise one, the protector of the earth replied,
"So be it," and then questioned [the sage] regarding the abducted wife of the twice-born man.
"O Blessed One, by whom was that brahmin’s wife led away, or to where?
You know the past and the future in this world without error."
The sage said:
"A Rākṣasa named Balāka, the son of a mountain, carried her away;
and you shall see her today, O King."
In the forest of Utpalāvataka.
"Go, O best of the twice-born, and quickly reunite with your wife;
let her not become a vessel for sin day by day, just as you have."
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter in the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Auttama Manvantara.
Chapter Seventy: Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having prostrated before the great sage, he ascended his own chariot;
and having been instructed by him regarding the forest, he set out for Utpalāvatī.
Then the lord of men saw that wife of the twice-born man, whose true nature had been described by her husband, devouring wood-apples (śrīphala).
And he asked: "How have you come to this forest, O blessed lady?
Speak clearly; you are the wife of Suśarman from Vaiśālī."
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"I am the daughter of a forest-dwelling twice-born man named Atirātra, who has many sons; he is the husband whose name was mentioned by you."
I, having fallen asleep within the palace, was forcibly abducted by the evil-minded Rākṣasa Balāka, separated from my brothers and mother.
May that Rākṣasa be reduced to ashes by whom I have been thus separated from my mother, my brothers, and others; I remain here in great misery.
"In this extremely dense forest, I was brought by him and abandoned;
I do not know what the reason for that is, since he neither enjoys me nor eats me."
The king said:
"Is it known where that Rākṣasa has gone after abandoning you?
O daughter of a twice-born man, I have been sent here by your husband himself."
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"That night-stalker stands right at the edge of this very forest;
enter and see him, if you do not fear him."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having entered along the path shown by her,
he beheld the Rākṣasa accompanied by his retinue.
Then, as soon as he was seen, that Rākṣasa, hurrying,
approached the vicinity of his feet while touching the earth with his head from afar.
The Rākṣasa said: "By coming here to my home, you have shown me great favor. Command me; what shall I do? I shall dwell within your domain."
"Please accept this water for the feet and remain upon this seat;
we are your servants and you are our master—command me firmly."
The king said:
"O night-stalker, you have already performed all the duties of hospitality;
for what purpose have you brought this Brahmin woman here?"
"She is not beautiful; there are others. If she was taken by you for the sake of a wife, or if she was taken for the sake of food, why was she not eaten? Tell me this."
The Rākṣasa said:
"O King, we are not those other Rākṣasas who subsist on human flesh;
rather, O King, we consume only the fruit of our own well-performed deeds."
We partake of the very nature of men and women, whether they treat us with contempt or honor; we are not devourers of living creatures.
When we show patience toward men, they then become angry;
yet when their wicked nature has been experienced, they even become virtuous.
"O King, we have women here who are equal in beauty to the Apsarases;
while these Rākṣasīs are present, how can you find pleasure in mere human women? (MarkP 70.19)
The king said:
"O night-stalker, if she was not for your enjoyment nor for food,
then why did you enter the house of the brahmin and carry her off?"
The Rākṣasa said:
"O King, that best of the twice-born is a knower of mantras; by reciting mantras that destroy Rākṣasas at every sacrifice I attend, he effects my expulsion."
We have been starved by his rite of incantation-eradication;
where shall we go? For that twice-born man serves as the officiating priest at all sacrifices.
Then we brought about this deficiency for him:
that a man, without a wife, does not become fit for the performance of sacrificial rites.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Due to the faltering pronunciation of that high-minded Brahmin,
the king then became exceedingly despondent.
"By speaking thus of my deficiency, that best of sages reproaches me alone; he even says of me that I am unworthy of honor."
The Rākṣasa also told me of that Brahmin’s deficiency;
because of his lack of a wife, I have fallen into great distress.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Sage, while he was reflecting thus, the Rākṣasa spoke again to the king, bowing low in salutation with his palms joined in reverence.
"By granting the command of a lord of men, please show favor to me,
your servant who bows before you and dwells within your realm."
The king said:
"O night-stalker, we eat according to our own nature as you have described;
we are seekers of that purpose for which [we act], so hear it from me."
"Today, let this Brahmin woman experience the misconduct that was committed by you,
so that she may be disciplined by the very misconduct she has taken upon herself."
"O night-stalker, let her be led to the house of him to whom she belongs;
once this is done for me, who have come to your home, everything will be accomplished."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then that Rākṣasa, having entered her interior by means of his own magic power,
devoured Dauḥśilya by his own might at the king’s command.
Due to his exceedingly fierce misconduct, the wife of that twice-born man was abandoned by him; she then spoke to that lord of the earth.
Through the ripening of the fruit of my own karma, I was separated from that high-souled husband; this night-stalker was the cause of that.
Neither is this his fault, nor that of my high-souled husband;
it is my own fault alone, for no one else experiences the fruit of their own deeds.
"In some other birth, a separation must have been caused by me to someone; that very same [consequence] has now come upon me. What fault is there in this great-souled one?"
The Rākṣasa said: "O Lord, at your command I shall convey you to this husband's home;
O King, command whatever else is to be done by me."
The king said:
"O night-walker, by doing this, you have accomplished everything for me. And you must come back, O hero!"
By me, when remembered at the time of need.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having said "So be it," that Rākṣasa took the brahmin’s wife—
pure because her wickedness had departed— and led her to her husband's home.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Auttama Manvantara.
Chapter seventy-one—71.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having sent that woman back to her husband’s house, the king too, sighing deeply, reflected: "What would be the best course of action here?"
"Alas! That high-minded one told me that I am unfit for an invaluable [price];
likewise, this night-stalker spoke thus regarding the Brahmin's deficiency."
"How then shall I act, for that wife has indeed been abandoned by me?
Or rather, I shall ask that best of sages regarding the vision of knowledge."
Having reflected thus, that protector of the earth mounted the chariot and went to where that righteous-souled, great sage, the knower of the three times, was located.
Then, having descended from his chariot, he approached him, bowed down,
and related exactly what had occurred regarding his encounter with the Rākṣasa.
The sight of a Brāhmaṇa woman, as well as the departure from immorality,
the sending [of gifts] to the husband's house, and whatever duty is required upon her arrival.
The sage said:
"O lord of men, all that you have done previously, and the entire purpose for which you have come into my presence, is already known to me."
"Ask me here what must be done by me," he said with an anxious mind;
"O protector of the earth, now that you have arrived,
hear what the task is that you must perform."
A wife is the powerful cause for men’s dharma, artha, and kāma, especially for dharma; for he who abandons her truly abandons dharma itself.
O King, a man without a wife— whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra— is unfit for his own duties. (MarkP 71.10)
By abandoning your wife, you have not done what is right;
for just as a husband is not to be abandoned by women, so too is a wife not to be abandoned by men.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, what shall I do? This is the ripening of my own actions; because she was neither favorable nor unfavorable, she was therefore abandoned by me."
Whatever he does,
O Blessed One, is done with a burning heart and an inner self terrified by the pain of separation from her.
But now that she has been abandoned in the forest, I do not know where she has gone;
perhaps she has even been devoured in the woods by lions, tigers, or night-stalking demons.
The sage said:
"O protector of the earth, she was not devoured by lions, tigers, or night-stalkers."
She, however, with her conduct unimpaired, is now in the subterranean realm (rasātala).
The king said:
"By whom was she taken to the netherworld (pātāla), and how did she remain there defiled?
This is most wonderful, O Brahmin!"
You ought to speak according to the truth.
The sage said:
"In the netherworld (pātāla) there is a renowned king of serpents named Kapotaka;
by him you were seen as you were wandering in the great forest, abandoned [by your husband]."
O King, that beautiful young woman was then led to Pātāla by that passionate man who had understood her purpose.
Then, O lord of the earth, that wise king of the *nāgas* had a daughter named Nandā, who was fair-browed, and he also had a charming wife.
Thinking, "She will become a co-wife to my mother," that beautiful woman was seen by her,
brought to her own home, and kept hidden within the inner apartments.
But when Nandā, though entreated, did not give the king's reply,
her father then said to his daughter, "You shall become mute."
O King, having been thus cursed by him, that virtuous daughter remained there,
led away by that lord of serpents and held captive by his daughter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the king, having attained supreme joy,
questioned that best of the twice-born regarding the cause of his own misfortune with respect to his beloved wife.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, all the world has unsurpassed affection for me;
what then is the cause by which my own wife is not excessively fond of me?"
"And she is exceedingly dear to me, O Great Sage, even more than my own life;
yet she is ill-behaved toward me. Tell me the reason for this, O twice-born one."
The sage said:
"At the time of your marriage, you were gazed upon by the Sun, Mars, Saturn,
Venus, and Jupiter as they looked toward your wife."
At that very moment, O King, Candrā became her son Soma; thereafter,
those two were exceedingly hostile toward one another.
Therefore, go and protect the earth according to your own duty;
accompanied by your wife, perform all religious rites in accordance with dharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When this had been said, Uttama, that protector of the earth, prostrated before him, ascended the chariot,
and then departed for his own city.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter in the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Auttama Manvantara.
Chapter Seventy-two:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having reached his own city, the king saw that brahmin accompanied by his virtuous wife Śīlavatī, filled with joy.
The Brahmin said:
"O best of kings, I have achieved my purpose, since dharma has indeed been protected by you here,
who know dharma, by bringing back my wife."
The king said:
"O best of the twice-born, you have achieved your purpose through the faithful observance of your own duty."
O Brahmin, we are in distress,
for our wives are not in our homes.
The brahmin said:
"O lord of men, if she was indeed devoured by beasts of prey in the forest, what is the use of another woman? Why do you not take her hand?"
Having fallen under the sway of anger, you did not protect the Dharma.
The king said:
"My beloved has not been devoured by wild beasts; for she still lives.
Since her conduct remains untainted, how can I do this?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"If your wife is alive and not unfaithful,
then why do you commit the sin of living as one without a wife?"
The king said:
"O Brahmin, even though she was brought here,
she has always been hostile toward me."
Her love for me is neither for my suffering nor for my happiness;
therefore, exert such effort on my behalf that she becomes subject to my will.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"For your pleasure, a sacrifice for boons that is beneficial to her is being performed by those desiring a friend; I shall perform that which is called Mitravindā."
O lord of men, she is indeed the supreme progenitor who brings joy to those who are estranged; I shall perform for you the *tāntava* sacrifice for husband and wife.
"O lord of the earth, let that fair-browed wife of yours, wherever she may be, be brought back to you; she will bring you the highest joy."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed, that lord of the earth brought all the necessary materials without exception,
and that best of the twice-born performed the sacrifice.
Then, for the sake of providing a wife for that king, that best of the twice-born performed the sacrifice again and again for seven times.
When the great sage considered that artificial friendliness toward his own master, the brahmin then spoke to that lord of men: MarkP_72.13 //
"O best of men, let her who is dear to you be brought into your presence; enjoy pleasures together with her and perform sacrifices with due reverence. (MarkP 72.14)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus by that brahmin, the king was then struck with wonder and remembered that night-stalker of great prowess and true resolve.
Then, being summoned by him, that great sage immediately approached the lord of men and, having prostrated himself, said, "What shall I do? O Great Sage.
Then, when this had been related in detail by that lord of men,
he went to the underworld, took the king’s wife, and returned.
Brought there with great affection, she then beheld her husband and,
filled with joy, said again and again, "Be gracious!"
Then that king, having impetuously embraced the proud lady, said:
"My dear, I am indeed pleased; why do you speak thus once again?"
The wife said:
"O lord of men, if your mind is inclined toward me with favor,"
Therefore, I entreat you for this; perform that which is worthy of me.
The king said:
"Speak without hesitation whatever you desire from me;
there is nothing unattainable for you, O timid one."
I am subject to you; it is not otherwise.
The wife said: "For my sake, that Naga cursed my friend, my daughter, saying,
'You shall become mute,' and she has indeed fallen into muteness."
If you are able, out of affection, to provide a remedy for that,
then what has not already been accomplished for me by the pacification of this obstruction of speech?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that king said to the brahmin, "What kind of ritual is this?
And he [the brahmin] spoke to the monarch in order to dispel his state of muteness.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, at your word I shall perform the Sārasvata sacrifice;
let this wife of yours attain freedom from her debt through the commencement of that speech."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
For that purpose, that best of the twice-born performed a Sarasvatī sacrifice and,
with a concentrated mind, recited the hymns dedicated to Sarasvatī.
Then, when her speech had come to an end, Garga spoke in the netherworld:
"This exceedingly difficult service has been performed for you by your friend's husband."
Having thus acquired this knowledge, Nandā, the daughter of a serpent, moved swiftly toward the city; there, the snake-born woman embraced her friend, the queen.
Having praised that protector of the earth again and again with auspicious words,
the Nāga woman, having taken her seat, spoke sweetly.
O Hero, a service has been rendered to me by you just now;
my heart is drawn to you by that, so listen to what I say.
"O lord of men, your son shall be of great heroism;
therefore, his wheel shall be unimpeded upon this earth."
He who knows the truth of all treatises on worldly affairs, who is devoted to the practice of dharma,
and who is a wise lord of a Manvantara— he indeed shall become Manu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Sage, having thus granted him the boon, the daughter of the Naga king then embraced her friend and departed for Pātāla.
While that lord of the earth was thus enjoying himself with her there,
a very great length of time passed as he protected his subjects.
Then, a son was born to that high-souled king from her,
like the lovely moon with its full orb on a full-moon night.
When that great-souled one was born, all the subjects attained joy;
the celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
Having seen his lovely form and his future character,
the assembled sages gave him the name Auttama.
He has been born into this most excellent lineage at this most excellent time;
because his limbs are so excellent, he shall therefore be known as Auttama.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, the son of Uttama was likewise known by the name Auttama;
he became Manu. O Bhāguri, hear from me an account of his power.
He who constantly hears this entire narrative of Uttama and the birth of Uttama never falls into enmity.
Never shall he experience separation from beloved wives, sons, or kinsmen, whether he merely hears or even recites this.
O Brahmin, listen as I describe his Manvantara;
hear who was the Indra there, as well as the gods and the sages.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter in the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Auttama Manvantara.
Chapter Seventy-three:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In this third Manvantara of the Prajāpati Auttama, learn from me as I speak of the gods, Indra, the Ṛṣis, and the kings.
Likewise, the gods are named according to their own powers;
and there is another group of thirty-three deities, the second of which is called Satya.
But in the third group, O best of sages, are the gods known as the Śivas;
they are called Śivas because of their very nature, and they are heard to be the destroyers of sin.
And the host of gods named Pratardana, O best of sages,
is declared there as the fourth in the interval of the Manu Auttama.
O twice-born one, O great sage, all the Vaśavartin gods in that fifth group are exactly as their nature has been described.
These five groups of gods are likewise remembered as the consumers of the sacrifice;
during the Manvantara of the best of Manus, all these groups consist of twelve members each.
Among them, the illustrious Indra shall become the preceptor of the three worlds;
having performed a hundred sacrifices, he shall be known by the name Suśānti.
Even today on this earth, men sing the verse adorned with his name for the destruction of calamities.
The beloved King of the Gods, Śuśānti, bestows peace;
he does so together with Śiva, Satya, and the others who are likewise under his command.
Aja was born, divine, pure as fire, and possessed of great strength and prowess;
his sons were known as the Manus, who were like the gods.
The earth was protected by the lords of men born from his lineage for as long as the *manvantara* of that Manu of supreme splendor lasted.
The number of four-yuga cycles is indeed seventy-one and more,
which have been described by me as the ages known by the names Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth.
Indeed, by the power of his own asceticism, the seven sons of that great-souled one, the most eminent of ascetics, became the Seven Sages within that interval.
This third Manvantara has been described to you by me;
now the fourth Manvantara of Tāmasa is being told.
O Brahmin, hear from me as I recount the birth of that Manu, by whose glory the world was illuminated, even though he was born from a non-womb.
Likewise, the conduct of all the Manus, which transcends the senses,
as well as their births and the power of those great-souled ones, should be understood.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Auttama Manvantara.
Chapter Seventy-four:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
There was a king renowned by the name Svarāṣṭra, who was heroic,
wise, a performer of many sacrifices, and unconquered in battles.
O twice-born one, the Sun, propitiated by his minister, granted him a very long life and a hundred blessed wives.
O Sage, although he was long-lived, his wives did not live very long;
in the course of time, they as well as his servants and ministers passed away.
Accompanied by his wives and his servants born with him, he,
with an anxious mind, suffered a loss of vigor day and night.
Then his neighbor, the one named Vimarda, deposed from the kingdom that man who was devoid of vigor, abandoned by his discreet servants, and deeply distressed.
Having fallen from his kingdom and gone to the forest with a despondent mind, he,
O illustrious lady, performed austerities while staying on the bank of the Vitastā.
In summer he remained as one who has reached the fifth state; in the rainy season he stayed under the open sky;
in the cold season he slept in water; and, firm in his vows, he remained without food.
Then, while he was performing austerities, during the rainy season there occurred a great flood,
with clouds raining continuously day after day.
Neither east nor south, nor west nor north could be discerned;
everything became as if smeared with darkness.
Then, by the excessive flood of the river, that king was driven toward the bank; though he cried out, the lord of the earth could not reach it as he was being swept away.
Then, being carried away by the flood of water at a distance,
the lord of the earth encountered a rohī fish in the water and seized it by its tail.
Carried along by that raft upon the surface of the earth,
he moved here and there in the darkness until he reached a riverbank.
Crossing that vast and exceedingly difficult-to-traverse mire,
the king reached yet another beautiful forest while being drawn along in that very same manner.
There, in that darkness, that Rohiṇī dragged the lord of the earth, who was clinging to her tail—
highly fortunate, yet emaciated with his veins standing out.
And from her touch, I experienced supreme joy;
yet, with my mind drawn by passion, I wandered further in the darkness.
Perceiving that the king was full of passion and intent on touching her back,
that female deer spoke to him within the depths of that forest.
"Why do you touch my back with a trembling hand?
O King, the outcome of this matter has turned out quite otherwise."
Your mind has not wandered to an improper place, nor am I unapproachable by you, O Lord;
however, this fickle one creates an obstacle for me in our union.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the doe, the lord of the earth,
filled with curiosity, spoke these words to Rauhī.
"Tell me, who are you? Why does a doe speak words like a human?
And who is this fickle one who creates an obstacle for me in your company?"
The doe said: "O King,
I was formerly your beloved, named Utpalāvatī."
The wife was Śatāgrā, the chief queen, and the daughter of Dṛḍhadhanvan.
The king said: "But what deed was performed by which she came to this birth—
she who was devoted to her husband, intent on dharma, and yet became such as this?"
The female deer said: "When I was a young girl in my father’s house, I went to the forest with my friends to play;
there I saw a male deer who had come together with a female deer."
Then, as she was nearby, I struck that doe;
terrified by me, she fled elsewhere, and thereupon the enraged deer said:
"O foolish woman, why are you so intoxicated? Shame on such wickedness!
For this very reason, the time for our union has been rendered fruitless by you."
Then, having heard the speech of him who spoke like a human being, I was terrified and said to him: "Who are you that have entered this womb?"
Then he said: "I am the son of the seer Nirvṛticakṣus, named Sutapas; once, out of desire for a doe, I became a deer."
"O wicked woman, since you have been followed by me with affection in the forest and desired by her,
yet you have separated her from you, I therefore pronounce a curse upon you."
And I said: "O Sage, this offense was committed by me through ignorance;
please show me favor, for you ought not to pronounce a curse upon me."
Thus addressed, O lord of the earth, that sage also spoke to me in this way:
"I shall not pronounce a curse upon you, provided that you give yourself to me."
And I said: "I am not a doe, O one who assumes the form of a deer in the forest;
you shall find another doe, so let your affection for me be withdrawn."
Thus addressed, his eyes red with anger and his lower lip quivering, he said:
"O fool, you have not been called a 'deer' by me; rather, you shall become a deer! (MarkP 74.32)
Then, deeply distressed, I bowed to the sage who stood in his true form and was exceedingly wrathful, and said to him again and again, "Be gracious!"
Because children are ignorant of speech, this was said by me:
for when a father is no longer present, a woman chooses a husband for herself.
"O best of sages, while my father is still alive, how could I choose [another]? Or rather, O Lord, I am at fault; be gracious and I bow before your feet."
"Be gracious, be gracious," [she cried] as she bowed down, O Great-minded One;
to her who was thus lamenting, that bull among sages spoke.
My word, once spoken, never becomes otherwise;
you shall become a doe, dead in this very forest in this very birth.
"And in his state as a deer,
O beautiful lady, the mighty-armed son of the sage Siddhavīrya, named Lola, shall enter your womb."
When he has entered the womb, you will become a rememberer of your past lives;
having regained your memory, you will likewise utter human speech.
"Once this has occurred, you shall be released from your state as a doe and honored by your husband;
you will attain those worlds which are not reached by those of evil deeds."
He too, the restless and very powerful one, having indeed struck down his father's enemies and conquered the entire earth, will then become Manu.
Having thus received this curse, I died and entered the state of an animal;
and through contact with you, this embryo has been conceived within my womb.
Therefore I say: your mind has not been directed toward me inappropriately; nor am I one who should not be approached, for this restless child within my womb is creating an obstacle.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus, the king then attained supreme joy,
thinking, "My son, having conquered his enemies, shall become the Manu on earth."
Then that doe gave birth to a son endowed with auspicious marks;
and upon his birth, all living beings experienced great joy.
And especially because this son was born with great strength,
that doe was released from the curse and attained the unsurpassed worlds.
Then, O best of sages, all those seers assembled together and,
beholding the future prosperity of that great-souled one, bestowed a name upon him.
He was born from his mother into a womb that partook of darkness;
since the world is enveloped by darkness, he will be characterized by darkness.
Then, having been raised in the forest by his father, that son of Tamas,
his intellect having awakened, spoke these words to his father, O best of sages.
"Who are you, dear father? And how am I your son? Who is my mother? For what purpose have you come? Tell me this truly."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the father, the lord of the earth with mighty arms, related to his son everything as it had happened, beginning with his fall from his own kingdom.
Having heard all that and having propitiated the Sun-god,
he too obtained the divine weapons in their entirety, along with the methods for their withdrawal.
Having mastered the use of weapons, he defeated those enemies and brought them before his father;
then, permitted by that sage, he established himself in his own dharma.
His father also, having cast off his body, attained his own worlds acquired through austerity and sacrifice, and beheld his son’s face with joy.
Having conquered the entire earth, that king named Tāmasa became the Manu known as Tāmasa; hear now of his Manvantara.
Those gods, and he who is the Lord of the Gods (Indra), and likewise those sages, and those sons of Manu who were the protectors of the earth; // MarkP_74.56 //
O Sage, there are likewise other wise ones, Satyas, Surūpas, and Haris; these groups of deities there number twenty-seven.
Possessed of great strength and great heroism, distinguished by a hundred sacrifices,
Śikhin was the sovereign Indra among those gods.
Jyotirdharmā, Pṛthu, Kāvya, Caitra, Agni, Valaka, and likewise Pīvara, O Brahmin—
these were the seven great ṛṣis.
Nara, Kṣānti, Śānta, Dānta, Jānu, Jaṅgha, and others were the sons of Tāmasa; they were kings of exceedingly great strength.
O Brahmin, this Manvantara has been described as tāmasa;
whoever reads or even hears it shall not be afflicted by darkness.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter in the Tāmasa Manvantara of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-Five:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Brahmin, the fifth Manu, renowned by the name Raivata, is also well-known;
listen as I describe his origin to you in detail.
There was a highly fortunate seer renowned as Ṛtavāk;
at the end of the Revatī era, a son was born to that great-souled man who had been childless.
He performed for him the birth rites and other ceremonies according to the prescribed rules, as well as the initiation ceremony and the rest; yet, O Sage, he remained devoid of virtuous conduct.
From the moment that he was born, from that very time on,
that seer, the bull among sages, suffered from the affliction of a chronic disease.
His mother was in extreme agony, afflicted by leprosy and other diseases;
his father also went there and, being distressed, reflected [upon the situation].
"What is this? thought even his son, who was exceedingly wicked-minded;
he seized the wife of another sage's son as she stood before him.
Then, with a dejected mind, Ṛtavāk said this:
"For human beings, childlessness is better than having a bad son."
A bad son always causes distress to his father's heart and to his mother's;
he causes even his ancestors, who reside in heaven, to fall below.
Fie on the birth of that evildoer, which brings no benefit to friends, no satisfaction to the ancestors, and only sorrow to his own parents!
Blessed are those sons who are esteemed by all the world,
who act for the benefit of others, who are tranquil, and who are devoted to virtuous deeds.
Likewise, a birth dependent on a bad son is unpeaceful, dull, averse to the next world, leading to hell rather than a good rebirth.
A wicked son certainly brings misery to his friends and joy to his enemies,
and he prematurely causes old age for his parents.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus, with his mental state burning due to the conduct of his exceedingly wicked son, the sage questioned Garga about his past life.
Ṛtavāk said:
"In former times, the Vedas were duly received by me through my observance of excellent vows;
having duly completed the study of the Vedas, I took a wife."
"O great sage, until this day, no Vedic or Smārta rites, nor any utterances of *vaṣaṭ*, have been performed by me with my wife; none of them have been left incomplete."
O Sage, this son was begotten for the sake of a male heir, not out of desire, and certainly not by one who fears the name "sonless" (punnāman), according to the prescribed rite of conception.
O Sage, has this man come to bring us sorrow through his own fault or through mine,
becoming a source of grief for our kinsmen due to his immoral conduct?
"O best of sages, this son of yours was born at the end of the Revatī asterism;
therefore, he has been born for your sorrow, because he was born at an ill-fated time."
This was not your fault, nor that of your mother, nor of this family;
rather, the cause of his misconduct has reached its limit in Revatī.
Ṛtavāk said:
"Since this wickedness has arisen from my only son, Revatī, let that Revatī fall down immediately."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When that curse had been thus uttered, the constellation Revatī fell down while all the world looked on, their minds overcome with wonder.
And the constellation Revatī fell upon Mount Kumuda on all sides,
suddenly transforming it into forest caves and waterfalls.
And from its falling, the mountain Kumuda became known as Raivataka;
it was an exceedingly beautiful mountain, the most delightful on the entire earth.
From the luster of that bear which had arisen in the lotus-lake,
a maiden was then born who was exceedingly beautiful in form.
Seeing her, who was born from the splendor of Revatī, the sage Pramuca gave her this name:
"O Bhārgava, she is named Revatī."
And that illustrious Pramuca nourished her, who had been born near his own hermitage,
on that very same great mountain.
Seeing that young girl, Kānyakā, endowed with beauty, the sage reflected: "Who might become her husband?"
As he was reflecting in this manner, O Sage, a great deal of time passed;
yet the great sage did not find a suitable bridegroom for her.
Then, in order to ask her for a boon, the sage Pramuca entered the fire-chamber; thereupon the consumer of oblations spoke to the questioner.
Possessing great strength and great heroism, pleasant of speech and devoted to righteousness,
the lord of the earth named Durgama shall indeed become his husband.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O sage, immediately thereafter, that wise lord of men, while engaged in the pursuit of hunting, arrived at his hermitage, which was difficult to reach.
Born in the lineage of Priyavrata, possessed of great strength and prowess,
he was the son of Vikramaśīla, born from the womb of Kālindī.
Having entered the hermitage and not seeing that slender woman or the sage, the lord of the earth called out "My dear! and questioned her.
The king said:
"O beautiful one, where has the Blessed One, that bull among sages, gone from this hermitage? I wish to bring him back here; therefore, tell me that."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard his speech and the address "O dear one," the brahmin went to the fire-sanctuary and departed in great haste.
The sage beheld the high-souled king, who was difficult to approach,
standing before him accompanied by the insignia of royalty and bowed down with humility.
When he had seen him, he then said to his disciple Gautama:
"Gautama, let an offering of hospitality (argha) be brought quickly for this lord of the world."
"First of all, O King, this man has arrived after a long time; moreover, as my son-in-law, he is especially in my view worthy of the arghya offering."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the king reflected upon the matter concerning his son-in-law;
however, the silent sage did not reveal it, and the king accepted the water-offering (arghya).
When he had taken his seat and accepted the guest-offering, the great sage, the brahmin, said to the lord of kings: "Welcome; is all well in your home?"
O Lord of Men, O mighty-armed one, [one should look] at the treasury, the army, the friends, the servants, the ministers,
and likewise at oneself, wherein everything is established.
And your wife is well, since she remains right where she is;
therefore, I inquire after her welfare, for no others among your kin are as well.
The king said:
"O you of noble vows, by your grace no misfortune has ever befallen me anywhere;
yet, O sage, my curiosity is aroused—tell me, who is this woman here who is my wife?"
The sage said:
"O King, do you not know that Revatī, your wife of noble form, who is highly blessed and the most beautiful even in the three worlds?"
The king said:
"O Lord, [I shall give you] Subhadrā, the daughter of Śāntanu, the daughter of Kāverī,
the one born in Surāṣṭra, Sujātā, Kadambā, and Varūthajā."
“O twice-born one, I know Vipāṭhā and Nandinī as my wives at home;
they remain there with me, O Blessed One, but I do not know Revatī—whom she is.”
The sage said:
"O King, have you forgotten that which was just now spoken by you, 'O fair-complexioned one, [I am] dear'?"
This wife of yours is praiseworthy.
The king said:
"O sage, what I have spoken is true; however, my disposition was not wicked. Since you have been entreated by us, you ought not to feel anger toward us."
The seer said:
"O protector of the earth, you speak the truth; your disposition is not corrupted."
"O King, impelled by Agni, you have spoken this."
"O King, when I asked the Fire-god who her husband would be,
he replied that you yourself would indeed be the bridegroom this very day."
"Therefore, O lord of men, accept this maiden given by me to you;
she has been addressed as 'Priyā' (the Beloved), so why do you hesitate?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then that lord of the earth became silent when addressed by him;
the sage likewise prepared to perform the marriage rite for her.
O great sage, as her father was thus prepared for the marriage,
the maiden, with her face bowed down in humility, said something to him.
"O father, if you are pleased with me, you ought to grant me this favor:
having been propitiated, let him perform my marriage during the asterism of Revatī."
The sage said:
"O blessed lady, the constellation Revatī is not currently in conjunction with the moon;
O fair-browed one, there are other constellations suitable for your marriage."
The maiden said:
"Father, without him, time seems fruitless to me;
how could a marriage for one such as I take place at a fruitless time?"
The sage said:
"The ascetic renowned as Ṛtavāk became enraged toward Revatī;
by him, in his anger, a bear was struck down."
"And I have promised this intoxicating-eyed woman to him as his wife;
if you do not desire the marriage, a great crisis has come upon us."
The maiden said:
"O father, that sage was a speaker of truth; why did he perform such ascetic penance?
Am I not the daughter of your father, but rather the daughter of a mere Brahmin outcaste?"
The sage said: "O child, you are not the daughter of a mere Brahmin, nor indeed of an ascetic;
you are my own daughter, I who am capable of creating other gods."
The maiden said:
"If my father is an ascetic, then why is this star in the sky being used as the bridegroom for me? Is my marriage not to be performed with that very star?"
The sage said:
"So be it; may you be blessed, O auspicious lady, and be filled with joy.
For your sake, I shall place the constellation Revatī into the path of the moon."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O best of the twice-born, by the power of his asceticism, the great sage restored the constellation Revatī to its former state as being conjoined with the Moon.
Having duly performed his daughter’s marriage according to the ritual application of mantras, he,
being full of joy, then spoke again to his son-in-law:
"O protector of the earth, tell me what I may give you for your marriage;
I shall grant even that which is difficult to obtain, for my ascetic power is unimpeded."
The king said:
"O sage, I am born in the lineage of the self-existent Manu;
by your grace, I choose you as my son to be the sovereign of a manvantara."
The sage said:
"O King, this desire of yours shall be fulfilled; your son Manu will enjoy the entire earth and he shall be a knower of dharma."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Taking her with him, the king then went to his own city;
from her, Revatī gave birth to a son, Raivata Manu.
Endowed with all human virtues, unconquered by men,
he was a knower of the meaning of all scriptures, learned in the Vedas, the sciences, and the treatises on worldly affairs.
O Brahmin, listen with full concentration as I describe the gods, sages, lords of the gods, and kings of his Manvantara. MarkP_75.70.
O twice-born one, there are fourteen gods of great wisdom and likewise fourteen sovereigns— Vaikuṇṭha and Amitābha among them.
Among those four groups of gods,
the one who was their leader was Indra by name, known as Vibhu and characterized by the performance of a hundred sacrifices.
Hiraṇyaloma, Vedaśrī, and another named Ūrdhvabāhu;
Vedabāhu, Sudhāman, and the great sage Parjanya.
And the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta—
these were the seven ṛṣis during the interval of the Manu Raivata.
Balabandhu, Mahāvīrya, and Suyaṣṭavya were others;
likewise, Satyaka and the rest were the sons of Raivata Manu.
Those Manus ending with Raivata whom I have described to you are all dependent upon Svāyambhuva, with the exception of Svārociṣa.
Whoever should constantly hear or recite this supreme narrative,
being liberated from all sins, attains his desired world.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter in the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Raivata Manvantara.
Chapter seventy-six—76.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus has this fifth Manvantara of yours been told to you;
now hear this sixth interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
O twice-born one, because he was born from the eye of Parameṣṭhin in another birth,
he is therefore called Cākṣuṣa even in this birth.
Having placed the newborn upon her own lap and cradling him,
the mother embraces him with deep affection and then rocks him again.
Having been born with the memory of his former lives, he indeed sat upon his mother’s lap;
at that time, his mother laughed at him and spoke these words in anger.
"I am afraid; what is this, my child, that there is a smile upon your face?
Has an untimely awakening occurred? Do you see something auspicious?"
The son said:
"Do you not see that the female cat desires to eat me here before you? And this second one, who carries off newborns, has become invisible?"
And out of affection for her son, you look upon me with kindness,
for you embrace me again and again, many times over.
With my hair standing on end from the arising of affection and my eyes clouded with tears, laughter then came over me; hear now the reason for this.
The female cat, intent on her own purpose, gazes at me as I am intent on mine;
likewise, there is another, who moves invisibly and carries away newborns.
Just as these [beings] have hearts full of affection toward me for their own sake,
so too do you appear to me to be acting, having resorted to your own self-interest.
But a female cat is a stealer of newborns for her own enjoyment;
you, however, desire from me a fruit that is to be enjoyed gradually.
"No one knows who I am, nor have I done any harm;
our meeting was not long ago, having occurred only five or seven days hence."
Nevertheless, you dote on me with tears and embrace me too closely; you address me without guile as "Father," "Child," and "Noble Lady."
The mother said:
"O child, I embrace you not for the sake of some service, but out of affection."
If this were not so, I would have been abandoned by you for the sake of your pleasure.
"I have renounced my own self-interest, whatever that may be for you," she said, and having abandoned him, she departed from the maternity chamber.
Then Sā, having become a "stealer of life," carried off him who had been abandoned— his limbs and external senses rendered inert, yet his inner self remaining pure.
Having then stolen that boy from King Vikrānta,
she placed him on the bed of the queen Prasūtā and took his own son.
Having led him as well to another house and seized his son, she,
who habitually carried off newborns, devoured that third one in due order.
Having repeatedly stolen it, that exceedingly merciless woman eats the third [portion];
she indeed performs this daily, while the other two portions are merely exchanged.
Then the lord of the earth had the consecration rites performed for that son of his, which are the rites that pertain to a member of the royal caste.
And that valiant lord of men, filled with supreme joy, duly gave him the name Ānanda.
Once the initiation ceremony had been performed, the preceptor said to the youth:
"First, perform the attendance upon and salutation of your mother."
Having heard those words of his teacher, he laughed and then spoke thus:
"Which mother of mine is to be revered—is it the one who gave birth, or rather the one who nourishes?"
The Guru said:
"O fortunate one, this is not your mother, nor is she the daughter of Ruci."
The chief queen of Vikrānta was known by the name Haiminī.
Ānanda said:
"This is the mother of Caitra, who dwells at Viśālagrama and is the son of Bodha, the foremost of brahmins; he was born of her by another man."
The Guru said:
"O Ānanda, tell me, where have you come from? Who is this Caitra who is being mentioned by you?"
A great peril appears; tell me, where were you born here, and what do you say?
Ānanda said:
"O twice-born one, I was born in the house of a kṣatriya lord of the earth;
from his wife Giribhadrā, I was taken up by a *jātahāriṇī*."
Having been released there by that Haiminī, she took her son and led him back once more to the house of the eminent brahmin Bodha.
And he devoured the son of that brahmin;
there, the son of Haiminī was consecrated with the sacraments of a twice-born.
"O illustrious one, we have been refined here by you, our teacher.
O teacher, which of your words shall I now carry out?"
The Guru said:
"O child, this is exceedingly profound;
a great crisis has arrived."
I know nothing at all; for my faculties are as if wandering due to delusion.
Ānanda said:
"When the world is established in this manner, what occasion is there here for delusion?
O brahmin-sage, who is whose son?"
Or who, indeed, is the kinsman of whom?
O Brahmin, those relatives who are connected to men from the time of their birth are turned away by death; other relatives [are likewise lost].
Even here, for one who has been born, whatever connection he has with his kinsmen—that too ceases when the body has set; such is the entire sequence.
Therefore I say: for one dwelling in saṃsāra, who is not a kinsman?
Or who indeed is a constant relative? Why is your mind so bewildered?
Indeed, two fathers have been obtained by me in this very birth, and likewise two mothers; what is there surprising about anything else that arises from the body?
Therefore, I shall perform penance; for you must bring here the son of this king from Viśālagrāma, named Caitra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the king, filled with wonder, together with his wife and kinsmen,
turned away from that sense of possessiveness toward him and consented to his departure for the forest.
Having brought back his son Caitra, he made him fit for the kingdom,
after having honored the brahmin by whom he had been protected as if he were his own son.
That Ānanda also, while still a child, performed austerities in the great forest for the sake of destroying those actions that stand as obstacles to liberation.
Then the god Prajāpati spoke to him as he was performing penance: "For what purpose, my child, do you perform such intense austerity? Tell me that."
Ānanda said: "O Blessed One, desiring the purification of my self, I perform austerities,
being intent upon the exhaustion of those actions of mine which lead to bondage."
Brahmā said:
"One whose office has expired becomes fit for liberation and no longer possesses karma;
since you possess the authority of *sattva*, you shall therefore attain liberation."
"You must become Manu as the sixth; go and do that.
When that is accomplished, you will attain liberation through penance."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been thus addressed by Brahmā, that high-minded one replied, "So be it," and turning toward that task, he desisted from his ascetic penance.
Brahmā addressed him as "Cākṣuṣa," turning him away from his asceticism;
thereafter, he became renowned by that former name as Cākṣuṣa Manu.
He married Vidarbha, the daughter of King Ugra,
and through her he begot sons of renowned prowess.
O twice-born one, hear now of those gods, the sages, Indra, and his sons who belong to that Manvantara-lord.
O Brahmin, among those gods known as the Āpyas, one group consists of eight members; this is the assembly of those of celebrated deeds who consume the oblations at the sacrifice.
And the second group of gods consists of eight known as the Prasūtas, whose strength and heroism are renowned and whose circles of radiance are difficult to behold.
In the same way, there is another group of eight deities called the Bhavyas;
and the fourth group there consists of those called the Yūthakas, likewise numbering eight.
Likewise, O twice-born one, there were others known as Lekhasaṃjñas in that Manvantara;
and in the fifth group of gods, they were indeed called Amṛtāśinas.
Having brought together a hundred sacrifices, he became their sovereign;
likewise, Indra, who is swift as thought, is reckoned as a partaker of the sacrificial portion.
Sumedhas, Virajas, Haviṣmat, Unnata, Madhu,
Atināman, and Sahiṣṇu— these were the seven ṛṣis.
Ūrupuru, Śatadyumna, and others of great strength were the sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu who became lords of the earth.
Thus, O twice-born one, I have related to you this sixth Manvantara,
as well as the birth and the life-story of the high-souled Cākṣuṣa.
Now, hear from me concerning those gods and others who belong to this seventh interval (antara) of the Manu named Vaivasvata who exists at present.
The wise person who recites this account of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara on earth,
or hears it, shall obtain sons, health, happiness, and prosperity.
Thus ends the sixth Manvantara in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa;
Chapter Seventy-six;
Chapter Seventy-seven—77.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O illustrious one, Mārtaṇḍa’s wife was named Saṃjñā, the daughter of Viśvakarman; upon her, Bhānu begot [his sons].
Because he was the son of Vivasvat, that Manu— renowned for his fame and having reached the further shore of manifold knowledge— is therefore called Vaivasvata.
When Saṃjñā was seen by Ravi, she closed her eyes;
therefore, the Sun, filled with wrath, spoke harshly to Saṃjñā.
"Since you always restrain your gaze upon seeing me,
therefore, O foolish woman, you shall give birth to Yama, the restrainer of living beings."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then that goddess, overwhelmed by fear, cast a flickering glance;
seeing her with her eyes darting about, Ravi spoke to her again.
"Since your gaze has now become unsteady upon seeing me,
you shall therefore give birth to a daughter, a river named Vilolā."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, by that very curse of her husband,
there were born to her Yama and this Yamunā, the world-renowned great river.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? And where, having gone, will there be peace for me? How can my husband not bring back the sun of his anger?"
Having reflected thus in many ways, the daughter of Prajāpati,
that highly fortunate lady, then considered taking refuge with her father alone as the best course.
Then, having resolved to go to her father’s house, the illustrious lady created for herself a shadow-form as a beloved body of the Sun.
And he said to them: "Just as you have behaved toward me here in the house of Bhanu, so must you behave properly toward my offspring, just as toward the Sun himself."
Even when questioned, this departure of mine should not be spoken of;
one should always say these words: "I am indeed that very same person named Saṃjñā."
Chāyāsaṃjñā said: "O Queen, from the grasping of your hair down to the tips of your toes, all these words are yours."
I shall perform and narrate the account from the time of the extraction of the curse.
Having been addressed thus, the goddess then went to her father’s abode;
there she beheld Tvaṣṭṛ, whose impurities had been washed away by ascetic penance.
And out of great respect, she was honored by Viśvakarman as well;
thus that blameless woman remained in her father’s house for some time.
Then her father spoke to that fair-limbed girl, who had not been with him for very long,
having praised his daughter with affection and great respect.
O child, though many days pass for me while gazing upon you, they shall be equal to half a moment; yet, dharma is being violated.
For women, a long residence among kinsmen is not conducive to their reputation;
rather, the desire of their relatives is for the woman’s stay in her husband’s house.
"O daughter, you who have been united with your husband Sūrya, the lord of the three worlds, ought not to remain for long in your father's house."
Go then to your husband’s house; I am pleased with you and have been honored by you. O auspicious one, you must come back again to see me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been thus addressed by her father, O sage, she replied, "So be it," and after honoring her father, she departed for the Northern Kurus.
Disliking the heat of the sun and fearing its brilliance,
she performed austerities there as well, assuming the form of a mare.
Thinking, "This is Saṃjñā," Bṛhaspati begot upon her two sons and one beautiful daughter.
Just as Chāyā was exceedingly affectionate toward her own offspring,
Saṃjñā’s daughter did not behave in that same way toward her two sons.
Day after day, Manu tolerated her particular fondness for luxuries such as being pampered,
but Yama could not endure it.
And indeed, out of anger, he raised his foot to strike her;
yet, being patient, he did not let it fall upon her body.
Then, O twice-born one, Chāyāsaṃjñā, her lips quivering slightly and her sprout-like hands trembling, cursed Yama out of anger.
"Since you, my father's wife, have transgressed all bounds by threatening me with your foot,
therefore this very foot of yours shall fall upon the earth this very day."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard this curse uttered by his mother, Yama, overcome with fear,
approached his father and spoke to him after first prostrating himself.
Yama said: "O father, this is a great marvel that has never been seen by anyone:
that a mother, casting aside her maternal affection, should utter a curse upon her own son."
Just as Manu declares, this view is not mine;
even toward sons who are devoid of virtue, a mother does not herself become devoid of virtue.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of Yama, the Blessed One, the dispeller of darkness,
summoned Chāyā-Saṃjñā and asked her, "Where has she gone?"
And she said, "I am Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, O Vibhāvasu;
I am your wife, and these offspring were begotten by you upon me."
When she did not speak, despite being questioned thus many times by Vivasvat,
the radiant one became enraged and prepared to curse her.
Then she related everything exactly as it had happened regarding Vivasvat;
and the Blessed One, having understood the matter, went to the abode of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Then he worshipped with supreme devotion that radiant one, who is honored by the three worlds, as he arrived at his own home.
When asked about his name, the Creator of the Universe then said to him:
"I have indeed come here to my own abode, sent by you."
Then Divākara, established in meditative absorption, beheld her performing austerities in the form of a mare in the northern Kuru region.
The Sun perceived her intention for her ascetic penance: "May my husband have a gentle form and an auspicious appearance."
"Let my splendor be diminished today," said the Sun to Viśvakarman, the father of Saṃjñā, O twice-born one. (MarkP 77.41)
Then, while he was wandering for a year, Viśvakarman fashioned [the wheel] and dulled his splendor as he was being praised by the gods.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Vaivasvata Manvantara.
Chapter seventy-eight:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the gods and the celestial sages, having assembled from the entire three worlds, praised that Sun with words of praise.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you who are the embodiment of the Ṛgveda; salutations to you who are the embodiment of the Sāmaveda;
salutations to you whose form is the embodiment of the Yajurveda, and who possess the abode of the Sāmans."
Homage to him who is the sole abode of knowledge, from whom all darkness has been dispelled;
who is pure light by nature, perfectly purified, and of stainless essence.
Salutation to the most excellent, the one worthy of choice, the supreme Supreme Self,
whose nature pervades the entire universe and who is the embodiment of the Self.
This beautiful, supreme hymn should be heard with faith by men;
having become a disciple and established in meditative concentration, one should also give what is to be given to the teacher.
This should not be heard by those whose elements are void; however, it shall be fruitful for those whose minds possess knowledge, which is the ultimate state of all causal factors.
Homage to you who are the very form of the sun, whose nature is light;
homage to you, Bhāskara, and likewise homage to the maker of day.
Salutations to you, the cause of the night and the creator of the twilight and moonlight!
O Blessed One, this entire world is whirled about by you.
The entire cosmic egg, including all that is moving and unmoving, revolves in confusion;
yet when touched by your rays, it all becomes pure.
The purification of water and other substances is brought about by the touch of your hands;
yet religious acts such as burnt offerings and gifts do not result in any benefit [for you].
As long as this world is not pervaded by your rays,
these are indeed all the *ṛc*s, and these others are the *yajus* verses.
And all the *sāman* chants descend from your body;
O Lord of the World, you consist of the *ṛc*,
and you alone consist of the *yajus*.
Since you consist of the Sāman, O Lord,
you therefore consist of the three Vedas;
you alone are the form of Brahman, both the higher and the lower.
Manifest and unmanifest, subtle as well as existing in gross form, consisting of moments, *kāṣṭhās*, and so forth, you are time itself, whose nature is decay.
Be gracious; by your own will, pacify your own fiery form.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus being praised by the gods and the celestial rishis,
that imperishable mass of splendor then released his own radiance.
By that splendor of his which consists of the Ṛgveda, the earth shall be pervaded;
by that which consists of the Yajurveda, the sky; and by that which consists of the Sāmaveda, the solar heaven of the Sun.
Those fifteen portions of splendor which had been cut off by Tvaṣṭṛ were used by that great-souled Tvaṣṭṛ himself to fashion the trident of Śarva.
The discus of Viṣṇu and the Vasus, as well as the most terrible spikes;
likewise the spear of Pāvaka and the palanquin of Dhanada.
Whatever fierce weapons belonged to other enemies of the Asuras,
as well as those of the Yakṣas and Vidyādharas, the Creator of All fashioned them for him.
And thereafter, the all-pervading Lord bears a sixteenth part;
that splendor was divided into fifteen parts by Viśvakarman.
Then Bhānu, assuming the form of a horse, went to the northern Kurus;
there he found Saṃjñā, who had likewise assumed the form of a mare.
And seeing him approaching, she, suspecting him to be another man,
went out to meet him, intent on protecting her back.
Then, as those two were united there,
the two sons, Nāsatya and Dasra, emerged from the mouth of Aśvinī through the union of their noses.
And at the end of Retas appeared Revanta, bearing a sword and clad in armor;
mounted upon a horse, he was equipped with arrows and a quiver.
Then the Sun-god revealed his incomparable true form;
and having beheld his true form, she was filled with joy.
And Bhāskara, the stealer of waters, brought back to his own abode this Saṃjñā, his beloved wife, who had assumed her own true form.
Then, her first-born son became Manu Vaivasvata;
and the second son, Yama, through the power of the curse, became one whose vision was fixed upon dharma.
"May worms take his flesh and fall from his foot onto the surface of the earth"—
thus his father himself set the limit to his curse.
Since he possessed the vision of Dharma and was thus impartial toward friend and foe alike,
the Dispeller of Darkness then appointed him to that office.
And the river Yamunā was born, flowing through the interior of Kalinda;
and the two Aśvins were made the physicians of the gods by their high-souled father.
Revanta was also appointed to the position of Lord of the Guhyakas;
now hear from me the appointment of the sons of Chāyā and Saṃjñā.
The first-born son of Chāyā, equal to his elder brother Manu,
thereafter obtained the name Sāvarṇika as the son of Ravi.
When he shall become Manu, and Bali likewise Indra,
then Śanaiścara was appointed by his father among the planets.
The third daughter of those two, named Tapatī,
obtained from King Saṃvaraṇa a son, a lord of men, O Kuru.
I shall now describe the seventh interval of that Vaivasvata Manu, including his sons who were kings, the ṛṣis, the gods, and the lord of the deities.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Origin of Vaivasvata," in the Sāvarṇika Manvantara of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter seventy-nine:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, the hosts of Maruts,
the Bhṛgus, and the Aṅgirases— these are remembered as the eight classes of gods who dwell there.
The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras are to be known as the sons of Kaśyapa;
the Sādhyas, Maruts, and Viśvedevas are the three groups who are the sons of Dharma.
The Bhṛgus were the sons of Bhṛgu, and the gods were the sons of Aṅgiras;
this is to be known as the lineage of Mārīca, whose current sovereign is [Dakṣa].
And the great-souled Indra, named Ūrjasvin, who partakes in the sacrificial portion,
[knows] those who have passed away, those who are yet to come, and those who exist at present.
All of them should be known as lords of the thirty-three gods, possessing identical characteristics;
they are all thousand-eyed, wielders of the thunderbolt, and Purandaras.
All of them were bountiful, bulls among men, horned, and possessed the gait of elephants;
they were all masters of a hundred powers, with splendor capable of overwhelming all beings.

"O twice-born one, listen to these three: those who, through pure causes such as dharma and the like, are endowed with the quality of sovereignty, and are the lords of the past, the future, and the present."
This world is known as Bhūrloka; the intermediate space is remembered as Bhuvarloka, and that which is called Divi is likewise Svargaloka; these three together are termed Trailokya.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and the great ṛṣi Kāśyapa;
Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and Kauśika.
Likewise, the son of the high-souled Ṛcīka was the venerable Jamadagni; these seven sages were present here during that interval.
Ikṣvāku, Nābhaga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti,
the renowned Nariṣyanta, and Nābhāgāriṣṭa.
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and Vasumān, world-renowned—
these are proclaimed as the nine sons of Vaivasvata Manu.
O Brahman, this account of Vaivasvata has been narrated by me to you;
O best of beings, upon hearing and reciting it, a person is immediately purified.
He is liberated from all sins and partakes of great merit.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Glorification of Vaivasvata," in the Sāvarṇika Manvantara of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty:
Krauṣṭuki said:
These seven Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva have been described by me;
as well as the gods, kings, and sages who existed during their respective intervals.
O Great Sage, please describe those seven other Manus who will appear in this kalpa, as well as the gods and others who will exist.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Sāvarṇi, who is the son of Chāyāsaṃjñā, has been described to you;
he will be the eighth Manu, equal to his elder brother Manu.
Rāma, Vyāsa, the radiant Gālava, Kṛpa,
as well as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and Droṇa— these were the seven sages there.
The Sutas, the Amitābhas, and the Mukhyas are the three classes of gods;
for these three, the group is said to consist of twenty multiplied by three.
Tapaḥtapta, Śakra, Dyuti, Jyotis, Prabhākara, Prabhāsa, Dayita, Dharma, Tejas, Raśmi, and Cirakratu.
The group of twenty gods beginning with Sutapas,
and likewise another group of twenty beginning with Prabhu, Vibhu, and Vibhāsa, [are the Viśvedevas].
Listen now to me regarding the third group of the immeasurable gods:
Dama, Dānta, Ṛta, Soma, and Vittādi—these twenty.
For these are declared to be the principal gods who preside over the Manvantaras;
they are the sons of Kaśyapa, the Prajāpati, the son of Marīci.
And they shall exist during the interval of Manu Sāvarṇa;
O Sage, Bali Vairocana shall be their Indra.
The Daitya who remains even today bound by his vow in Pātāla—
Viraja, Cārvavīra, Nirmoha, Satyavāk, and Kṛti—
and Viṣṇu and the others shall be the sons of Sāvarṇi Manu, the kings.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chapter eighty-one:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen as I describe in detail the origin of Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun, who is called the eighth Manu. MarkP_81.1 //
Through the power of Mahāmāyā, that illustrious son of Ravi became Sāvarṇi, the lord of a Manvantara.
Formerly, in the Svārociṣa interval, there was a king named Suratha, born of the lineage of Caitra, who ruled over the entire circle of the earth.
While he was thus properly protecting his subjects like his own biological sons,
there arose kings who were his enemies, such as the Kolāvidhvaṃsins.
A battle took place between him, who wielded an exceedingly powerful staff, and them;
though they were fewer in number, he was defeated in the fight by those Kolās, who were capable of destruction.
Then, having returned to his own city, that illustrious one became the ruler of his own land;
yet he was subsequently assailed by those powerful enemies.
Then, by powerful, wicked, and evil-minded ministers,
both the treasury and the army of that weak king were seized from within his own city.
Then, under the pretext of hunting, that lord of men, deprived of his sovereignty,
mounted a horse alone and went into the dense forest.
There he beheld the hermitage of Medhā, the best of the twice-born;
it was filled with peaceful wild beasts and graced by the disciples of the sage.
Honored by that sage, he remained there for some time,
wandering here and there within that hermitage of the best of sages.
Then, his mind drawn by the sense of "mine," he thought there:
"That city was formerly protected by my ancestors;
now that it is bereft of me, will it be protected according to dharma by those wicked servants of mine? (MarkP 81.11)
I do not know what enjoyments my preeminent and heroic elephant Sadāmada will obtain now that he has fallen under the power of my enemies.
Those who have always followed me with gifts of favor, wealth, and food,
will today certainly attend upon other monarchs.
Because they are habituated to improper expenditure and constantly squander it,
that treasury which was accumulated with great difficulty will go to ruin.
The king constantly reflected upon this and other matters;
there, in the vicinity of a brahmin’s hermitage, he beheld a certain vaiśya.
Being questioned by him, he said: "Who are you, sir, and what is the reason for your coming here?
Why do you appear as if filled with grief, as though troubled in mind?"
Having heard these words spoken with affection by the king,
that merchant, bowing low with humility, replied to the monarch.
The Vaiśya said: "I am a Vaiśya named Samādhi, born into a family of wealthy men;
yet, out of greed for wealth, I was cast out by my wicked sons and wife."
Deprived of wealth, wives, and sons, having taken my riches,
he has come to the forest in misery, cast out by his trusted kinsmen and friends.
Therefore, staying here, I do not know the conduct— whether virtuous or non-virtuous— of my sons, nor of my kinsmen and wives.
Is there security or insecurity in their homes right now? How are they? Are my sons well-behaved or ill-behaved? (MarkP 81.21)
The king said:
"Regarding those greedy sons, wives, wealth, and so forth by whom you were cast out—
why does your mind continue to cling with affection to them?"

Alas, my heart is fixed upon those very people by whom I was cast out— driven away by greed for wealth, having abandoned affection for their father and the love of their husband and kinsmen.
O Mahāmati, even though I know it, I do not understand this: why is it that the mind is inclined toward affection even for kinsmen who are devoid of virtue?
On their account, sighs and dejection arise within me;

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, O Brahmin, that Vaiśya named Samādhi and that best of kings approached that sage together.

The king said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to ask you one thing;

O best of sages, why is it that this man— who has lost his kingdom and knows all the constituent elements of sovereignty to be as nothing— still possesses a sense of "mine" regarding them, like one who is ignorant?
Though he has been treated with deceit by his sons, abandoned by his wife and servants,
and forsaken by his own kinsmen, he nevertheless maintains such great affection for them.
In this way, both he and I were utterly miserable,
our minds drawn by the sense of "mine" toward objects that had been seen to be full of faults.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, what is this that causes delusion even for two men of knowledge— this state of ignorance which belongs both to me and to him who is blind to discernment?
The sage said:
"O illustrious one, every living being possesses knowledge regarding the sphere of sense objects, and the sense object likewise proceeds toward each individual in this manner."
Some living beings are blind by day, while others are blind at night;
some beings have equal vision both by day and at night.
Human beings are truly wise, yet they are not the only ones;
for all animals, birds, beasts, and so forth, are also wise.
The knowledge of those humans is the same as that of those deer and birds;
likewise, everything else regarding those humans is equal for both.
Even though you possess knowledge, behold these insects at the tips of the young birds' beaks;
though they are being tormented by hunger, they remain devoted to the release of the grain out of delusion.
O tiger among men, do you not see that human beings, out of desire for their sons and through greed, act toward them with longing for the sake of receiving a return?
Nevertheless, they have been cast into the whirlpool of "mine-ness" and the pit of delusion by the power of great illusion, which maintains the cycle of existence.
Therefore, no wonder should be felt here regarding the yogic sleep of the Lord of the World;
for this is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) of Hari, by which the world is thus deluded.
For that divine and blessed Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) forcibly draws away even the minds of the wise and delivers them over to delusion.
By her this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is emitted;

That supreme, eternal Vidyā is the cause of liberation;

The sage said:
That form of the world is eternal; by it all this is pervaded.

When the world had been turned into a single ocean at the end of the eon, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, spread out Śeṣa and resorted to yogic sleep.

Brahmā said:
[He praised] the Goddess Nidrā, the sovereign of the universe, the sustainer of the world, the cause of its preservation and destruction,

You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, for you are the Vaṣaṭkāra; you are the essence of the sacred sound (Svar). You are the nectar of immortality (Sudhā) abiding in the threefold measure within the eternal, imperishable syllable.
You abide as the eternal half-measure, who is especially beyond utterance;

By you alone is everything sustained; by you this world is created;

O you who consist of the universe, at the time of emission you are the form of creation, during preservation you are the form of maintenance, and likewise at the end of this world you are the form of withdrawal.

Khaḍginī, Śūlinī, Ghorā, Gadinī, and likewise Cakriṇī;

Gentle, more gentle than all other gentle beings, and exceedingly beautiful,

O Goddess, being thus praised with these noble powers of yours,

"Let Acyuta, the Lord of the world, be quickly awakened;

The sage said:

And Janārdana, the Lord of the World, released by her, rose up from his serpent-bed in the single ocean; and then he beheld those two.
The two evil-minded ones, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, possessed of extreme heroism and prowess,

Then, having risen up, the Lord Hari, the omnipresent one whose weapons are his arms, fought with those two for five thousand years.
Those two as well, intoxicated by their excessive strength and deluded by great illusion,
said to Keśava, "Let a boon be chosen from us."
The Blessed One said:
"O Bhava, since both of these are to be slain by me today for my satisfaction, what need is there for any other boon? This much alone has been requested by me."
The sage said:
Then, having perceived that the entire world consisted of water, those two who felt deceived spoke to the lotus-eyed Blessed One.
"Kill us both before your thighs are submerged by water;

The sage said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
severed their heads and hips with his discus.
Thus has she arisen, personally praised by Brahmā himself;
hear further from me as I describe the power of this goddess.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the Devīmāhātmya of the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Chapter Eighty-two.
The Sage said:
In ancient times, there was a battle between the gods and the asuras lasting for a full hundred years,

There, the army of the gods was defeated by the Asuras of great prowess;

The gods related to them exactly what had occurred, detailing the conduct of Mahiṣāsura and the full extent of his victory over the deities.
He himself presides over the offices of the Sun, Indra, Agni, Vāyu, and the Moon, as well as those of Yama, Varuṇa, and others.
Excluded from heaven by that evil-minded Mahiṣa, all the hosts of gods wander upon the earth like mortals.
All this activity of the enemies of the immortals has been told to you;

and jeweled rings upon all his fingers.

Himavat gave him a lion as a vehicle and various kinds of jewels;
the Lord of Wealth gave him a drinking vessel filled with divine liquor.
And Śeṣa, the lord of all nāgas, gave her a nāga-necklace adorned with great jewels,
which supports this earth.
Honored by other gods as well with ornaments and weapons, the Goddess let out a loud roar with a boisterous laugh again and again.
By her terrible cry, the entire sky was filled;
through its immense length, a great echo arose.
All the worlds were agitated, and the oceans trembled;
the earth shook, and all the mountains moved.
"Victory! the gods joyfully said to her as she rode upon the lion;
and the sages, their bodies bowed with devotion, offered praise to her.

those enemies of the immortals rose up with all their armies arrayed and weapons uplifted.
"Āḥ! What is this? exclaiming thus in anger, Mahiṣāsura, surrounded by all the asuras, rushed toward that sound.
Then he beheld the Goddess, pervading the three worlds with her radiance,
bending the earth beneath the tread of her feet and scraping the sky with her crown.
With the twang of his bowstring, he caused the entire underworld to tremble;

Then a battle commenced between that goddess and the enemies of the gods,
