The great asura named Cikṣu, the commander-in-chief of Mahiṣāsura’s army,
fought along with Cāmara and others, accompanied by a fourfold force.
The great asura named Udagra fought with sixty thousand chariots,
and Mahāhanu fought with ten million.
The great asura Asiloma fought in the battle with fifty million [demons],
and Vāṣkala fought with six hundred thousand myriads.
Surrounded by many thousands of fierce-looking elephants and horses,
as well as ten million chariots, he fought in that battle with a formidable appearance.
Then Biḍālākṣa, surrounded by fifty myriads of chariots, fought there in that battle against another fifty myriads.
Surrounded by fifty myriads of chariots,
he fought there in that battle, encircled by an equal number.
And there, tens of thousands of other great asuras, surrounded by chariots, elephants, and horses, fought with the goddess in that battle.
Surrounded in that battle by thousands of millions of chariots, as well as elephants and horses, Mahiṣāsura was present there.
They fought with the Goddess in battle using tomaras, bhindipālas, śaktis, and mūsala clubs, as well as swords, axes, and paṭṭiśa spears.
Some hurled spears, others likewise threw nooses;
they set about trying to kill the goddess with blows from their swords.
Then the goddess Caṇḍikā, raining down her own weapons and missiles, effortlessly cut those weapons and missiles to pieces.
The goddess Anāyastānanā, being praised by the celestial rishis,
released weapons and missiles from the bodies of the asuras, O Lord.
Enraged, that lion with a shaggy mane, the mount of the goddess,
roamed through the armies of the asuras like a fire in the forests.
And those very breaths which Ambikā released while fighting in battle immediately became hosts of attendants by the hundreds of thousands.
Strengthened by the power of the Goddess, they fought with axes, slings, swords, and spears, destroying the hosts of asuras.
In that great festival of battle, some groups sounded kettledrums, others likewise blew conchs, and still others played clay drums.
Then the goddess struck the great asuras by the hundreds with her trident, mace, showers of spears, and other weapons such as the ṣaḍga.
He caused others to fall, bewildered by the sound of his bell,
and having bound other asuras to the ground with his noose, he dragged them away.
Some were cut in two by sharp sword-strokes,
while others lay prostrate on the ground, crushed by the falling of maces.
Some, violently struck by the mace, vomited blood;
others, pierced in the chest by the spear, fell to the ground.
Some among the harassers of the gods, rendered continuous by the flood of arrows on the field of battle,
released their lives like falling crags.
The arms of some were severed, others had their necks cut off;
the heads of some fell, while others were split asunder in the middle.
Other great asuras fell upon the earth with their shanks severed;
some, having only one arm, eye, or foot, were split in two by the Goddess.
Even when their heads were severed, others fell down and rose up again;

And others there in that battle, headless trunks with severed torsos, holding swords, spears, and double-edged blades in their hands, danced to the rhythm of musical instruments.
"Stay! Stay! cried out the other great asuras to the goddess in that hair-raising battle, their limbs drenched in streams of blood.
With fallen chariots, elephants, horses, and asuras,
that earth where the great battle took place became impassable.
Great rivers of blood immediately flowed forth there from the midst of the asura army— of elephants, asuras, and horses.
In an instant, Ambikā brought that great army of the asuras to destruction,
just as fire consumes a vast heap of grass and wood.
And that lion, shaking his mane and letting out a great roar,
seemed to pluck away the lives from the bodies of the enemies of the immortals.
A battle was waged there by the Goddess and her hosts against those asuras,
such that the gods in heaven were so gratified that they released a rain of flowers.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Slaying of Mahiṣāsura’s Army," in the Devīmāhātmya of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Chapter Eighty-three: The Sage said:
Beholding that army being slaughtered,
the great asura general Cikshura then went forth in anger to fight Ambika.
In that battle, the asura showered the goddess with a rain of arrows,

Then the goddess, having effortlessly severed his volleys of arrows,
struck down the horses and the driver of the steeds with her shafts.
He immediately cut his bow and his exceedingly lofty banner,
and pierced him in his limbs with swift arrows once his bow was severed.
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,

Having struck the lion on the head with his sharp-edged sword, he,
possessing great speed, also struck the goddess on her left arm.

thereupon, with eyes red with rage, he seized a trident.
Then that great asura hurled it at Bhadrakālī;

Seeing that spear as it was falling upon him, the goddess discharged her own spear;

When that highly heroic general of Mahiṣa had been slain, Cāmara,

Then the lion, springing up and standing between the frontal globes of the elephant,

The Supreme Goddess struck Ugrāsya, Ugravīrya, and likewise Mahāhanu with her trident; she who has three eyes.

With extremely fierce sword-strokes, she struck Agradaśana;

Seeing that great asura approaching, puffed up with rage,

O Goddess, the virtuous man always performs all his righteous duties with great devotion every day;
and because of your grace, he goes to heaven from there.
O Goddess, it is surely because of that [mantra] that you grant fruits even throughout the three worlds.
O Durgā, when remembered, you take away the fear of all living beings; when remembered by those established in well-being, you grant them most auspicious wisdom.
O remover of poverty, suffering, and fear—who else is there besides you?
Her heart is always moist with compassion for the sake of performing every kind of assistance.
When these are slain, the world attains happiness;
let them indeed commit sin for a long time in hell,
so that by meeting death in battle they may go to heaven.
Thinking thus, O Goddess, you surely destroy those who are unfriendly.
Why does your ladyship not reduce all the asuras to ashes merely by seeing them, since you hurl your weapon at your enemies? Let even your foes go to the higher worlds, purified by your weapon.
In this way, your mind toward them also becomes exceedingly virtuous.
That the eyes of the asuras did not dissolve away by the radiance flashing from the mass of sword-blades, nor by the intense collection of light from the tips of spears,
was due to the fragments of the sun and moon.
This is that very face of yours, as it appears to those who behold it with a worthy disposition.
O Goddess, your conduct pacifies the behavior of the wicked;
likewise, this form of yours is inconceivable and incomparable to others;
and your prowess is a slayer of those who have stolen the valor of the gods.
Thus, compassion has been manifested by you even toward your enemies.
What comparison can there be for this prowess of yours?
Where is this form that so captivates even enemies with fear? Compassion is seen in your heart, yet ruthlessness in battle.
O Goddess, granter of boons, [there is none] even throughout the three worlds but you.
This entire triple world has been protected by you through the destruction of the enemy; having slain them at the head of the battle,
those hosts of foes have been led to heaven, and even fear has been cast away.
Salutations to you, who arose from the intoxication of the enemy of the gods.
Protect us with your trident, O Goddess; protect us with your sword, O Ambikā;
protect us with the sound of your bell and with the twang of your bowstring.
Protect me in the east and in the west, O Caṇḍikā; protect me in the south, and likewise in the north, O Īśvarī, by the whirling of your own trident.
Whatever gentle forms wander through the three worlds,
and whatever forms are exceedingly terrible— with those, protect us as well as this earth.
O Mother, with those weapons such as the sword, the trident,
and the mace that rest upon your sprout-like hands, protect us from all sides.
The sage said: Thus praised by the gods with divine flowers grown in the Nandana grove,
the Mother of the Worlds was likewise honored with fragrant ointments and unguents.
Incensed with devotion by all the gods and celestial beings with divine incenses,
she, her face radiant with grace, spoke to all the prostrate deities.
The Goddess said:
"O all you gods, let that which is desired from me be chosen;
being well-honored by these hymns of praise, I shall grant it with great affection."
"And we do not know what other difficult task remains to be done," having heard these words of the goddess, those dwellers of heaven replied.
The gods said:
"Everything has been accomplished by the Blessed Lady; nothing remains.
For this enemy of ours, Mahiṣāsura, has been slain."
And if a boon is to be granted by you to us, O Maheśvarī,
then whenever we remember you, you shall surely ward off our greatest calamities.

O Ambika of stainless countenance, may you always be pleased with this mortal who praises you with these hymns, so that for the increase of his wealth, prosperity, power, and the abundance of wives and other riches, you may grant him success through this [praise].
The sage said:
Thus propitiated by the gods for the sake of the world as well as for their own,
Bhadrakālī, having replied "So be it," vanished, O King.
Thus has been told, O King, how that Goddess, seeking the welfare of the three worlds, was born in ancient times from the bodies of the gods.
And furthermore, she was born from the body of Gaurī in such a manner as to bring about the destruction of the wicked Daityas, namely Śumbha and Niśumbha.
And for the protection of the worlds, she is a benefactor to the gods;
listen to that as I recount it to you exactly as I have been told.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the *Devīmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Sāvarṇika Manvantara*.
Chapter Eighty-five: The Sage said:
In former times, the three worlds and the sacrificial portions were seized from the Lord of Śacī by the two asuras, Śumbha and Niśumbha, who relied upon the power of their intoxication.
In that same manner, those two established their respective jurisdictions over the solar realm, as well as over the realms of the Moon,
Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa.
They alone performed the functions of the wind and the power of the ocean, as well as the work of fire;
he himself presided over the offices of others.
Consequently, the gods were cast out, deprived of their kingdom, and defeated.
Deprived of their authority and all cast out by those two great asuras,
the gods remembered that unconquerable goddess.
By her a boon was granted to us: "Whenever you are remembered in times of distress, I shall instantly destroy all your supreme calamities. (MarkP 85.5)
Having thus resolved their minds, the gods went to Himavat, the lord of mountains,
and there they offered praise to the goddess Viṣṇumāyā.
The gods said:
"Salutations to the Goddess, to Mahādevī; constant salutations to Śivā. Salutations to Prakṛti, to Bhadrā; being self-restrained, we bow down before her."
Salutations to Raudrī, to the Eternal One; salutations again and again to Gaurī and Dhātrī.
Salutations to the Goddess who is the foundation of the world; salutations again and again to Kṛtyā.
Constant salutations to Dyotstrā, who has the form of the moon, and to Sukhā;
we offer repeated salutations to Kalyāṇī, to Vṛddhi, and to Siddhi, who are bowed down to by us.
Salutations again and again to you, Nairṛtī, the Fortune of the mountains, and Śarvāṇī;
to Durgā, who carries one across difficulties, the Essence, and the Performer of all deeds;
likewise, constant salutations to Khyāti, Kṛṣṇā, and Dhūmrā.
Salutations again and again to her who is both exceedingly gentle and exceedingly fierce;
salutations again and again to the Goddess Kṛtyā, the mind and the foundation of the world.
To that Goddess who, among all beings, is designated by the name Viṣṇumāyā—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who is designated as "consciousness" within all beings—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of the intellect—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
Salutation to that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of sleep; salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her; homage to the mind!
To that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of hunger,
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of a shadow—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of power—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of craving—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of patience—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of birth—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of modesty—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of peace—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that goddess who abides in all beings in the form of faith—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! MarkP_85.24 //
To that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of beauty,
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of Lakṣmī—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her; homage, homage!
Salutations to that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of fortitude; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, repeated salutations!
To that Goddess who is established in all beings in the form of their vital function—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of mindfulness—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! MarkP_85.29 //
To that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of compassion—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her; homage again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of policy (nīti),
salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again!
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of contentment—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! MarkP_85.32 //
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of nourishment—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of a mother—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
Salutation to that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of delusion; salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again!
Salutations again and again to that pervasive Goddess, who is the presiding power over the senses and over all beings, and who is eternally present within every creature.
Salutations to her who, in the form of consciousness, stands pervading this entire world; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again.
May that Sovereign Lady, who was formerly praised by the gods for providing their desired refuge and likewise served day after day by the Lord of the Asuras,
be the cause of our auspiciousness.
May auspicious and blessed things strike down all calamities.
She who is now being worshipped by us gods, who are tormented by the arrogant Daityas, and she who,
when remembered, instantly destroys our [suffering].
All calamities [are warded off] by those whose forms are bowed in devotion.
The sage said: O prince, while the gods were thus engaged in hymns of praise and other rites, Pārvatī approached the waters of the Jāhnavī there to bathe.
That woman of beautiful brows said to those gods, "Who is being praised here by you?
And Śivā, who had emerged from the cavity of her body, replied.
This hymn is being offered to me by the gods, who were defeated in battle by Niśumbha and driven away by the Daitya Śumbha, though they remain united.
Because Ambikā emerged from the body-casket of that Pārvatī,
she is therefore celebrated in all the worlds as Kauśikī.
When she had departed, Pārvatī herself became dark;
taking refuge with Himācala, she was known as Kālikā.
Then Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the two servants of Śumbha and Niśumbha, beheld Ambikā, who was assuming a supreme and most enchanting form.
They reported to Śumbha that there was a certain exceedingly beautiful woman staying there, O Great King, illuminating the Himalaya mountain.
"Never before has such a supreme form been seen anywhere by anyone;
let it be known that she is some goddess, O Lord of Asuras, and let her be seized!"
O Lord of Daityas, that jewel among women, with her exceedingly beautiful limbs, stands there illuminating the quarters with her radiance; you ought to see her.
O Lord, whatever jewels, gems, elephants, horses,
and so forth exist throughout the three worlds, they all now shine within your home.
Airāvata, the jewel among elephants, was brought from Purandara;
likewise, this Pārijāta tree and the horse Uccaiḥśravas were brought.
"This celestial chariot, yoked with swans, stands in your courtyard;
it was brought here as a jewel, that wonderful creation of the Creator."
This great treasure, Mahāpadma, has been brought here from the Lord of Wealth;
and the Ocean gave me a garland of lotuses with filaments, whose blossoms never fade.
In your house stands the umbrella of Varuṇa, dripping with gold;
likewise, here is that most excellent chariot which formerly belonged to Prajāpati.
O Lord, the power of Death known as Utkrāntidā has been taken away by you;
the noose of your brother, the King of Waters, has been placed in your keeping.
Niśumbha gave you all varieties of gems produced from the ocean,
and Agni also gave you two garments as pure as fire.
"O Lord of Daityas, all these jewels have been brought by you;
why is this auspicious jewel among women not accepted by you? (MarkP 85.56)
The sage said:
Having heard these words of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
the great asura Śumbha then dispatched Sugrīva as a messenger to the goddess.
Śumbha said:
"Having gone there at my command, she must be told 'this' and 'that';
you must act quickly so that she approaches with affection."
Having gone there to that most beautiful mountain region where she was staying,
he then spoke to the goddess in gentle and sweet words.
The messenger said:
"O Goddess, Śumbha, the lord of the Daityas and supreme sovereign of the three worlds, has sent me as his messenger; I have come here into your presence."
Listen to that which he has said— he whose command is never thwarted among all the divine races, and who has utterly conquered the enemies, the Daityas.
"The entire three worlds are mine; the gods are subject to my will.
I partake of all the sacrificial portions, each one individually."
"Whatever excellent jewels exist in the three worlds, all of them without exception shall be under my control;
likewise, having seized the jewel among elephants, the vehicle of the Lord of the Gods."
Having prostrated before me, the gods presented to me that jewel among horses named Uccaiḥśravas, which had emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
And whatever other beings exist among the gods, the Gandharvas,
and the Uragas who are like jewels, O beautiful one, they reside in me alone.
"O Goddess, we consider you to be a jewel among women in this world;
therefore, come to us, for we are enjoyers of jewels."
"O lady of tremulous glances, resort to me or my younger brother Niśumbha of vast prowess; for you are indeed a jewel."
Through my acceptance of you, you shall attain incomparable and supreme sovereignty;
having reflected upon this with your intellect, enter into the state of being my consort.
The sage said: Thus addressed, the goddess Durgā, the blessed and auspicious one by whom this world is sustained, then spoke with a deep inner smile.
The Goddess said: "What you have spoken is true; nothing false has been uttered by you.
Sumbha is the lord of the three worlds, and Niśumbha is likewise."
But how can that which was promised here be made false?
Listen to how that promise was formerly made out of limited intelligence.
"He who conquers me in battle, he who dispels my pride,
and he who is my equal in the world— he shall become my husband."
Therefore, let Śumbha or Niśumbha, the great asura, come here;
having conquered me, why delay? Let him take my hand quickly.
The messenger said:
"O Goddess, do not speak thus with such arrogance before me.
What man in the three worlds could stand before Śumbha and Niśumbha?"
O Goddess, all the gods cannot even stand before other Daityas in battle face-to-face; how much less so you, a single woman?
All the gods, beginning with Indra, stood their ground in battle against Śumbha and his hosts;
how then will you, a mere woman, go before them?
Go, therefore, as commanded by me, to the side of Śumbha and Niśumbha;
do not go there with your dignity shaken by the dragging of your hair.
The Goddess said:
"It is even so; Śumbha is powerful and Niśumbha is exceedingly heroic.
What can I do, since my vow was made previously without due reflection?"
Therefore, go and respectfully communicate all this that has been told to you to the Lord of the Asuras; let him do what is appropriate.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Goddess," in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, within the account of the *Ṛṣabha-sāvarṇika Manvantara*. The Sage said:
Having heard these words of the goddess, that messenger, filled with indignation,
returned and related everything in detail to the king of the Daityas.
Having heard those words of the messenger,
the king of the asuras then spoke with anger to Dhūmralocana, the lord of the daityas.
"O Dhūmralocana, you, surrounded by your own army,
must quickly bring that wicked woman here by force, while she is overwhelmed by the pulling of her hair."
If anyone else should arise to protect him,
he must be slain, whether he be an immortal, a yakṣa, or even a gandharva.
The sage said:
Commanded by him, that Daitya Dhūmralocana then quickly departed,
surrounded by sixty thousand asuras.
Having seen that goddess stationed upon the Snowy Mountain, he then spoke aloud: "Go to the abode of Śumbha and Niśumbha! (MarkPurāṇa 86.6)
"If she does not become pleased with my husband,
then I shall take her away by force, while she is overwhelmed by the pulling of her hair."
The Goddess said:
"Sent by the Lord of the Daityas, you, powerful and surrounded by an army, are carrying me away by force; what then shall I do for you?"
The sage said:
Thus addressed, that demon Dhūmralocana rushed toward her;
then Ambikā reduced him to ashes with a mere *huṃ* sound.
Then Ambikā showered sharp arrows, as well as spears and battle-axes, upon the enraged great army of the Asuras.
Then the lion, the goddess’s own mount, with his mane bristling from rage, let out a most terrifying roar and fell upon the army of the asuras.
He struck some of the great asuras with a blow of his hand, others with his mouth,
and still others by seizing them with his lower lip.
The lion tore open the bellies of some with his claws,
and likewise, by striking them with his palms, he severed their heads from their bodies.
Others likewise had their arms and heads severed by him as they fled; and he, his mane shaking, drank the blood from the bellies of others.
In an instant, that entire army was brought to destruction by that high-souled lion,
the mount of the Goddess, who was exceedingly enraged.
Then, having heard that the Asura Dhūmralocana had been slain by the Goddess,
and that the entire army had been destroyed by the Goddess’s lion, [the demons were struck with fear].
Śumbha, the lord of the Daityas, grew enraged with his lips quivering;
he then commanded those two great Asuras, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
"O Caṇḍa, O Muṇḍa, surrounded by many forces, go there;
and having gone, let her be brought back quickly."
If you have any doubt in battle, whether by pulling them by the hair or binding them,
then let all the asuras be slain with every weapon remaining.
When that wicked woman has been slain and the lion has been struck down,
come quickly, having bound and seized that Ambikā.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Dhūmralocana," in the Devīmāhātmya of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Chapter Eighty-seven: The Sage said:
Then those Daityas, led by Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, having been thus commanded,
set out with their fourfold army, their weapons raised.
Then they beheld the Goddess standing there with a slight smile upon a great golden peak of the lord of mountains, atop a lion.
Seeing them, others who were nearby drew their bows and took up swords, exerting themselves with intent to seize her.
Then Ambikā directed a great rage toward those enemies;
and by that anger, her face then became the color of ink.
From her forehead-slab, which was furrowed with a frown,
there suddenly emerged Kālī, with a terrifying face, bearing a sword and a noose.
She carries a variegated khaṭvāṅga staff, is adorned with garlands of human heads,
wears a garment of tiger skin, has withered flesh, and is most terrifying.
With an exceedingly wide mouth, terrifying as she lolls her tongue,
with sunken and bloodshot eyes, she fills the quarters of the sky with her roar.
Rushing forward with speed and slaughtering the great asuras,
she devoured that army of the enemies of the gods.
Seizing with one hand elephants equipped with rear-guards, goads, riders, and bells, he threw them into his mouth.
In the same way, having seized a warrior along with his horses and charioteer,
they cast them into their mouths and chew them most terrifyingly with their teeth.
One he seized by the hair, another by the neck;
having trampled one with his foot, he crushed another with his chest.
And the weapons and great missiles released by those asuras,
he seized with his mouth in a rage, even as they were being crushed by his teeth.
He crushed all that strength of the powerful, evil-minded asuras;
he devoured some, struck others, and likewise beat down yet others.
Some were slain by the sword, some were struck by the khaṭvāṅga staff, and others were crushed by the tips of his tusks; thus did the asuras meet their destruction in battle.
Seeing that great army of the asuras struck down in an instant,
the great asura Caṇḍa rushed toward Bhīmākṣī.
The great asura Muṇḍa covered that woman with terrible eyes with showers of arrows and with thousands of hurled discs, all most fearsome.
Those many wheels, entering his mouth,
appeared like numerous solar disks entering the interior of a thick cloud.
Then Kālī, laughing with great fury and uttering a terrifying roar, her mouth gaping wide and her blazing teeth visible within, addressed Bhīma.
And having risen, the queen rushed violently toward the great lion;
seizing him by the hair, she cut off his head with that sword.
When his head was severed, the lord of the Daityas let out a most terrifying roar;
by that great roar, the three worlds were struck with fear.
Then, seeing Caṇḍa struck down, Muṇḍa rushed toward her;
she, enraged, struck him with her sword and felled him to the ground as well.
Then, seeing Caṇḍa struck down and the exceedingly heroic Muṇḍa as well, the remainder of the army, overcome with fear, fled in all directions.
Having seized the head and the skull of Caṇḍa,
Kālī approached Caṇḍikā and spoke with a loud, piercing laugh.
I have brought here for you the two great sacrificial animals, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa;
you yourself shall slay Śumbha and Niśumbha in this sacrifice of battle.
The sage said:
Having seen that the two great asuras, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, had been brought there,
the auspicious Caṇḍikā spoke these graceful words to Kālī.
The Goddess said:
"Since you have come here having seized Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
O Goddess, you shall therefore become renowned in the world as Cāmuṇḍā."
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa," in the Devīmāhātmya of the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Chapter Eighty-Eight: The Sage said:
When the Daitya Caṇḍa had been slain and Muṇḍa had been struck down,
and when many armies had been destroyed, the Lord of the Asuras [acted].
Then the powerful Śumbha, his mind overcome by anger,
issued orders for all the Daitya armies to prepare for battle.
Today, let the eighty-six Daityas with uplifted weapons and the eighty-four Kambus, surrounded by their own forces, march forth with all their armies.
By my command, let fifty families of asuras possessing ten millionfold vigor,
and one hundred families of the Dhaumras, come forth.
Let the Kālakas, Daurhṛdas, Mauryas, and the Kālakeyas, as well as the Asuras,
go forth quickly at my command, prepared for battle.
Having thus issued his command, Śumbha, the lord of the Asuras and the fierce commander,
set forth surrounded by many thousands of great armies.
Seeing that most terrifying army approaching, Caṇḍikā filled the space between earth and sky with the sounds of her bowstring.
And that lion let out a truly great roar, O King;
Ambikā also amplified that roar with the sound of her bell.
With her mouth wide open, Kālī, filling the quarters of the sky with the sounds of bowstrings, lion-bells,
and her own terrifying roars, triumphed.
Hearing that roar from the Daitya armies on all four sides,
the Goddess, the Lion, and Kālī were surrounded by those filled with rage.
In the meantime, O King, there arose beings endowed with extreme heroism and strength for the destruction of the enemies of the gods and for the welfare of the lions among the immortals.
The powers of Brahmā, Īśa, Guha, Viṣṇu, and likewise of Indra,
having emerged from their bodies, went to Caṇḍikā in those very forms.
Whatever was the form, ornaments, and vehicle of each god,
his Śakti indeed appeared in that very same manner to fight the Asuras.
Seated at the front of a celestial chariot drawn by swans, holding a rosary and a water-pot,
she who has arrived as the power (śakti) of Brahmā is designated as Brahmāṇī.
Māheśvarī, mounted upon a bull, holding a trident and granting boons,
arrived with great serpent-bracelets and adorned with a crescent moon.
Kaumārī, with a spear in her hand and mounted upon a noble peacock,
Ambikā in the form of Guha advanced to fight the Daityas.
In the same way, the power of Viṣṇu, seated upon Garuḍa and holding in her hands the conch,
the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the sword, approached.
She who, as the power (śakti) of Hari, had assumed the incomparable form of a boar, was born there as Vārāhī,
assuming a boar-like body.
Nārasiṃhī, assuming a body resembling that of Nṛsiṃha,
arrived there, scattering the clusters of stars with the tossing of her mane.
Likewise, Vajrahastā and Aindrī are seated upon the king of elephants;
having attained a thousand eyes, she is just like Śakra himself.
Then, surrounded by those divine powers (devaśakti),
Īśāna said to Caṇḍikā, "Let the Asuras be slain quickly for my pleasure."
Then, from the body of the God, there emerged the exceedingly terrifying power of Caṇḍikā,
most fierce and resounding with a hundred howls of Śivā.
And Aparājitā said to the smoke-crested Īśāna:
"O Blessed One, go as a messenger to the side of Śumbha and Niśumbha."
"Speak to Śumbha and Niśumbha, who are exceedingly proud among the Dānavas,
and to whatever other Dānavas are present there for the sake of battle."
"Let Indra obtain the three worlds; let the gods be the consumers of the oblations.
You all go to Pātāla, if you wish to live! (MarkP 88.25)
If, out of pride in your strength, you now desire battle, then come;
let my dogs be satiated with your flesh.
Since Śiva himself was appointed as a messenger by that goddess,
she consequently attained renown in this world as Śivadūtī.
Having heard those words spoken by the goddess Śarvā, those great asuras,
filled with indignation, went to where Kātyāyanī was stationed.
Then, at the very outset, the enemies of the gods, their fury aroused, rained down showers of arrows, spears, and double-edged swords upon that goddess.
And she effortlessly severed those dispatched arrows, spears, javelins,
and axes with great shafts released from her drawn bow.
In front of him, Kālī then moved about, rending her enemies with the fall of her trident and crushing them with her skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
And Brahmāṇī rendered her enemies powerless and drained of their vital energy by the discharge of water from her water-pot, wherever she might run.
Māheśvarī struck the Daityas with her trident, Vaiṣṇavī with her discus,
and the exceedingly wrathful Kaumārī with her spear.
By the fall of Indra’s thunderbolt, hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas fell to the earth, torn asunder and raining down torrents of blood.
Shattered by the blows of his snout, their chests mangled by the tips of his tusks,
they fell down, torn apart by his discus in the form of a boar.
Tearing apart other great asuras with her claws and devouring them,
the Nārasiṃhī roamed the battlefield, filling the quarters of the sky with her roar.
Corrupted by the fierce, loud laughter of the messengers of Śiva, the asuras fell to the earth;
then she devoured them as they lay prostrate.
Seeing the enraged host of Mothers thus crushing the great Asuras, the soldiers of the enemies of the gods could not prevail despite various stratagems.
Seeing the Daityas intent on flight and tormented by the hosts of Mothers,
the great Asura Raktabīja advanced in a rage to fight.
Whenever a drop of blood falls from his body onto the ground,
a great asura of that same size springs up from the earth.
That great asura fought with Indra’s spear while holding a mace in his hand;
then Indrī struck Raktabīja with her own thunderbolt.
When struck by the thunderbolt, much blood flowed forth quickly;
from that, warriors arose who possessed his very form and his prowess.
As many drops of blood as fell from his body,
so many men were born, possessing his own vigor, strength, and prowess.
And those men born of blood also fought there together with their mothers, a scene most terrifying due to the falling of extremely fierce weapons.
And again, when his head was wounded by the fall of the thunderbolt,
blood flowed forth, and from it thousands of men were born.
In the battle, Vaiṣṇavī struck him with her discus,
and Aindrī struck that lord of the asuras with her mace.
The world was pervaded by thousands of great asuras, equal in size to him, who had emerged from the flow of blood produced when he was pierced by Viṣṇu’s discus.
Kaumārī struck the great asura Raktabīja with her spear, Vārāhī likewise with her sword, and Māheśvarī with her trident.
And that great asura Raktabīja, his mother overcome with rage, struck each and every one of them individually with his mace.
When that invincible one was struck in many ways upon the earth with spears, tridents, and other weapons,
a torrent of blood fell from him, by which hundreds of asuras were slain.
The entire world was pervaded by those asuras born from the blood of the asuras;
consequently, the gods were seized by the greatest fear.
Seeing those gods despondent, Caṇḍikā spoke in haste;
she said to Kālī, "O Cāmuṇḍā, open your mouth wide!"
"Receive these great asuras, who are drops of blood produced by the falling of my sword, with this swift mouth of yours, O Raktabindu! (Markandeya Purana 88.53)
"Roam through the battlefield devouring the great asuras born there;
in this way, this Daitya will go to his destruction, his blood exhausted.
And while being devoured by you, these fierce ones shall not be reborn as others."
The seer said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess then struck him with her trident;
Kālī seized the blood of Raktabīja with her mouth.
Then he struck Caṇḍikā there with his mace;
yet the blow of the mace did not cause her even the slightest pain.
From the body of that slain one, much blood flowed out;
from here and there, Vāmuṇḍā received it with her own mouth.
The great asuras who emerged from her mouth due to the falling of his blood—
those Cāmuṇḍā devoured, and she drank his blood.
The Goddess struck that Raktabīja with her trident, discus, arrows, swords, and spears; and Cāmuṇḍā drank his blood.
Struck down by the impact of the weapons,
that great asura Raktabīja fell upon the surface of the earth, O protector of the earth, his blood having been drained.
Then, O King, those thirty gods attained incomparable joy;
their host of mothers, intoxicated with blood and pride, began to dance.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Raktabīja," in the Devīmāhātmya of the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Chapter Eighty-nine:
The King said:
O Blessed One, this wondrous account of the greatness of the Goddess’s deeds, centered upon the slaying of Raktabīja, has been related by you to me.
Furthermore, I wish to hear what deeds Śumbha and the exceedingly wrathful Niśumbha performed after Raktabīja had been struck down.
The sage said: When Raktabīja had been struck down, and Śumbha and Niśumbha were slain along with the others in battle, the asura [Śumbha] conceived incomparable anger.
Beholding his great army being slaughtered, Niśumbha, filled with indignation,
then charged forward at the head of the principal asura host.
Before her, behind her, and on both her sides, the great asuras approached in a rage, their lips bitten together, intent on slaying the goddess.
The immensely powerful Śumbha also arrived, surrounded by his own forces,
out of anger to slay Caṇḍikā, having already engaged in battle with the Mothers.
Then there occurred a most intense battle between the Goddess and Śumbha and Niśumbha,
with a torrent of arrows as fierce as two raining clouds.
Caṇḍikā cut those arrows apart with her own volleys of shafts,
and struck the two lords of the asuras on their limbs with floods of weapons.
Niśumbha, seizing a sharp sword and a radiant shield,
struck the lion, the supreme mount of the Goddess, upon its head.
Niśumbha, seizing a sharpened sword and a radiant shield,
struck the lion, the supreme mount of the Goddess, upon its head.
When his shield and sword were severed, that asura hurled a spear; he [Viṣṇu], for his part, cut that spear also into two pieces with his discus as it came toward him.
Then the Dānava Niśumbha, inflated with rage, seized his trident;
as it came toward him, the Goddess pulverized it with a blow of her fist.
Then he too, taking up a mace, hurled it at Caṇḍikā;
that [mace] was shattered by the Goddess’s trident and reduced to ashes.
Then, as that bull among the Daityas approached with an axe in hand,
the Goddess struck him with a flood of arrows and felled him to the ground.
When Niśumbha of terrible prowess had fallen to the ground,
his brother, exceedingly enraged, advanced to slay Ambikā.
Standing upon his chariot, he shone as he pervaded the entire sky with his eight incomparable arms, which held supreme weapons raised very high.
Beholding him approaching, the goddess sounded her conch and also made the sound of her bowstring exceedingly unbearable.
And he filled the quarters of the sky with the sound of his own bells,
which served to destroy the splendor of the entire army of the Daityas.
Then the lion, with his great roars that caused the elephants to shed their vast rut-fluids,
filled the sky, the earth, and likewise the ten directions.
Then Kālī, leaping up into the sky, struck the earth with her two hands; by that sound, those previous noises were eclipsed.
Śivadūtī let out a most inauspicious, piercing laugh;
at those sounds the asuras trembled, and Śumbha fell into a state of supreme rage.
When Ambikā cried out, "Wicked one! Stay!
Stay!", the gods stationed in the sky then exclaimed, "Victory! (Jaya!).
The extremely terrifying flame of power that was released by Śumbha as he approached—
shining like a mass of fire— it was warded off by a great meteor.
O lord of the earth, the space between the three worlds was pervaded by Śumbha’s lion-roar, which was as terrible as the sound of a thunderclap; he had been conquered.
The Goddess cut down the arrows released by Śumbha, and Śumbha’s arrows dispatched by her,
with her own fierce shafts by the hundreds and thousands.
Then Caṇḍikā, enraged, struck him with her trident;
thus assailed, he fell to the ground in a swoon.
Then Niśumbha, having regained consciousness and taken up his bow,
struck the goddess Kālī as well as the lion with arrows.
Furthermore, having created ten thousand arms,
the lord of the Danujas, that son of Diti, covered Caṇḍikā with his discus-weapon.
Then the Blessed Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of the distressed, became enraged and cut those discs and those arrows with her own shafts.
Then Niśumbha, surrounded by the army of the Daityas, seized his mace with speed and rushed toward Caṇḍikā in order to slay her.
As he was rushing forward, Caṇḍikā swiftly cut his mace with her sharp-edged sword,
and he took up a trident.
As Niśumbha, the tormentor of the immortals, approached with a trident in his hand,
Caṇḍikā pierced him in the heart with her trident, which she had hurled with great force.
When he was pierced by the spear, another [being] emerged from his heart—a man of great strength and great heroism, saying, "Stay! (tiṣṭha).
As he was departing, the goddess laughed and then severed his head with her sword; thereupon he fell to the ground.
Then the lion devoured those fierce asuras, their necks crushed by his fangs; likewise did Kālī, Śivadūtī, and others devour the rest.
Some great asuras perished, pierced by the power of Kaumārī;
others were repelled by water consecrated with the mantra of Brahmāṇī.
Others, pierced by the trident of Māheśvarī, fell down;
some were ground to powder on the earth by the blow of Vārāhī’s snout.
The Dānavas were reduced to pieces by the discus of Vaiṣṇava,
and others likewise by the thunderbolt released from the hand of Indra.
Some asuras perished, some were destroyed in the great battle,
and others were devoured by Kālī, the messengers of Śiva, and the lords of beasts.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Niśumbha," in the *Devīmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Sāvarṇika Manvantara*.
Chapter Ninety— 90 The Sage said:
Seeing his brother Niśumbha, who was as dear to him as his own life, slain, and seeing his army being slaughtered, Śumbha spoke these words in a rage: MarkP_90.1 //
"O wicked Durgā, do not harbor pride out of an overweening sense of power;
you fight by relying on the strength of others, O woman of excessive conceit."
The Goddess said: "I alone am here in this world; who else could be my second?
Look, O wicked one, at these manifestations of mine entering into me."
The sage said:
Then all those goddesses, headed by Brahmāṇī, entered into dissolution within the body of that goddess; at that time, Ambikā alone remained.
The Goddess said:
"When I was present here with many forms through my manifold power, I withdrew them all and remain as one alone; be steadfast in battle."
The sage said:
Then a fierce battle commenced between the Goddess and Śumbha,
while all the gods and asuras looked on.
With showers of sharp arrows, as well as weapons and most terrible missiles,
a battle once again took place between them, causing fear to all the worlds.
The lord of the Daityas shattered with counter-weapons those hundreds of divine missiles which Ambikā had released.
O Supreme Goddess, she effortlessly shattered those divine weapons discharged by him through the utterance of fierce *huṃkāras* and other means.
Then that asura covered the goddess with hundreds of arrows;
and the goddess, enraged by that, cut his bow apart with her shafts.
When his bow was severed, the lord of the Daityas then took up a spear;
the Goddess, with her discus, cut that too from his hand as it remained there.
Then, taking up his sword and his radiant shield marked with a hundred moons,
the lord of the Daityas rushed toward the goddess.
As he was falling upon her, Caṇḍikā swiftly cut off his sword with sharp arrows released from her bow,
and his shield, which was as bright as the rays of the sun.
He felled the horses along with the charioteer and the chariot;
then that Daitya, his horses slain, his bow severed, and deprived of his charioteer,
seized a terrible mallet, intent on the destruction of Ambikā.
He cut down the mallet as it was falling with sharpened arrows;
nevertheless, the powerful one rushed forward, raising his fist.
That bull among the Daityas struck a blow with his fist at the heart of the goddess,
and the goddess in turn struck him on the chest with her palm.
Struck by that blow of the palm,
the king of the Daityas fell to the surface of the earth, yet he rose up again instantly in that same manner.
Having leaped up and seized the goddess, he ascended high into the sky;
even there, being without support, Caṇḍikā fought with him.
Then, in the sky, the Daitya and Caṇḍikā engaged in a wrestling match with one another; it was the first such feat, which caused wonder even to the perfected sages.
Then, after wrestling with Ambikā for a very long time,
he lifted her up, whirled her around, and hurled her onto the surface of the earth.
Having been thrown down and reached the ground, that evil-minded one, rising up with his fist and acting with speed,
rushed forward with the desire to slay Caṇḍikā.
Then the goddess, having pierced him— the lord of all the Daitya hosts—
as he approached with her trident in the chest, cast him down upon the earth.
Wounded by the tip of the goddess’s trident, he fell lifeless upon the earth,
shaking the entire world with its oceans, islands, and mountains.
Then, when that evil-minded one was slain, the entire world became serene and attained extreme well-being, and the sky became stainless.
The portentous clouds accompanied by meteors that had appeared in the east subsided;
likewise, the rivers that flowed out of their courses returned to their proper paths once he had been struck down.
Then all the hosts of gods became filled with hearts overflowing with joy;
once he was slain, the Gandharvas sang merrily.
Likewise, other hosts of Apsarases played instruments and danced;
holy winds blew, and the sun became radiant with light.
The fires blazed peacefully, and the sounds arising from the quarters became calm.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śumbha," in the Devī-Māhātmya of the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Chapter Ninety-one.
The sage said:
When that great lord of the asuras had been slain there by the goddess, the gods, led by Indra and preceded by Agni, [approached her].
Having obtained their desired object, they praised Kātyāyanī,
their lotus-like faces blooming and illuminating all directions.
The gods said: O Goddess, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, be gracious, be gracious, O Mother of the entire world!
Be gracious, O Sovereign of the Universe; protect the universe, for you, O Goddess, are the Mistress of all that is moving and unmoving.
Since you abide in the form of the earth, you alone are the sole support of the world;
by you, who exist in the form of the waters, this [world] is sustained.
He is nourished by that which possesses entirely invincible power.
You are indeed the power of Viṣṇu, possessed of infinite valor; you are the supreme Māyā, the seed of the universe. O Goddess, all this has been utterly deluded by you.
Thus, indeed, faith on earth is the cause of liberation.
O Goddess, all branches of knowledge are your manifestations; all women throughout the worlds are your parts.
This entire universe has been filled by you alone, O Mother.
What praise can there be for you, who are beyond all that is praiseworthy, and whose speech is directed toward the transcendent?
O Goddess, since you bestow both heaven and liberation upon all beings, what other supreme words could there be for your praise when you have already been extolled?
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who abides in the hearts of all people in the form of their intellect and who bestows both heaven and liberation— salutations be unto you!
O Nārāyaṇī, who brings about transformation in the form of moments, divisions of time, and so forth, and who is the power that brings the universe to rest— salutations be to you!
O you who are the most auspicious among all that is auspicious, O Śivā, the accomplisher of all goals,
O refuge, O Tryambakā, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
O eternal one, who has become the power for creation, maintenance, and destruction;
O refuge of the qualities, composed of the qualities, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who are solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge, the wretched, and the afflicted; O Goddess, who removes the suffering of all—salutations be unto you!
O Goddess who dwells in a celestial chariot yoked with swans, who assumes the form of Brahmāṇī, who pours forth the waters of Kauśāmbī; O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you!
O you who bear the trident, the moon, and the serpent; O you who ride upon the great bull;
O Nārāyaṇī, who possess the very form of Māheśvarī—homage be to you!
O you who are surrounded by peacocks and cocks, O wielder of the great spear,
O you who abide in the form of Kaumārī, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
O you who hold the supreme weapons—the conch, the discus, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow—be gracious, O you in the form of Vaiṣṇavī; O Nārāyaṇī, homage be unto you!
O you who held up the great mountain with your tusk, O you who lifted the earth with your fang,
O auspicious one in the form of a boar, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
O Nārāyaṇī, who are endowed with the protection of the three worlds and have exerted yourself to slay the Daityas with your fierce form as the Man-Lion, salutations be to you!
O wearer of the diadem, wielder of the great thunderbolt, blazing with a thousand eyes,
destroyer of Vṛtra’s life, O son of Indrāṇī, O Nārāyaṇa, homage be to you!
O you who have slain the great strength of the Daityas in the form of Śivadūtī,
O you of terrible form and great roar, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you!
O Cāmuṇḍā, whose mouth is terrifying with fangs, who is adorned with a garland of heads,
who crushes the skulls [of enemies], O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
O Lakṣmī, O Lajjā, O Mahāvidyā, O Śraddhā, O Puṣṭi, O Svadhā, O Dhruvā,
O Mahārātri, O Mahāmāyā, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
O Medhā, O Sarasvatī, O Excellent One, O Prosperity, O Daughter of Babhru, O Tāmasī,
O Self-Restrained One, O Sovereign, O Nārāyaṇī— salutations be unto you!
O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be to you, whose hands and feet extend everywhere, whose eyes, heads, and faces are everywhere, and whose ears and nostrils are everywhere.
O Goddess who possesses every form, O Sovereign of all, endowed with all powers; protect us from fears, O Goddess Durgā; homage be to you!
May this gentle face of yours, adorned with three eyes, protect us from all fears; O Kātyāyanī, homage be to you!
May the trident—fierce, terrifying with its flames, and the destroyer of all asuras—protect us from fear; O Bhadrakālī, homage be to you!
O Goddess, may that bell protect us from sins— she who, filling the world with her sound, destroys the splendors of the Daityas, as she would protect her own children.
O Caṇḍikā, may this radiant sword of yours, smeared with the mud of the blood and fat of Asuras, lead to our welfare; we bow down before you.
When pleased, you destroy all diseases without exception; when angered, however, [you grant] all desired objects to those who have taken refuge in you and whose lives are failing.
For those who have taken refuge in you attain the state of being a refuge themselves.
O Goddess, this slaughter of the great asuras who hate righteousness, which you have performed today by manifesting your own form in many ways through various bodies— this was accomplished by you.
O Mother, having performed that, what else could she possibly do?
In the sciences, in the treatises, in the lamps of discernment,
and in the primordial utterances— who else but you exists within the bottomless pit of possessiveness, its darkness so profound?
It causes this entire universe to whirl excessively.
Where there are rākṣasas and nāgas with fierce venom, where there are enemies and the forces of bandits,
where there is a forest fire, and likewise in the midst of the ocean—
Abiding there, you protect the entire universe.
O Sovereign of the Universe, you protect the universe;
as the soul of the universe, you sustain the universe. You are the one worshipped by the Lord of the Universe, and so do all beings exist.
Those who take refuge in all things and are bowed down by devotion toward you.
O Goddess, be gracious and protect us forever from fear, just as you have just now immediately [protected us] from the slaughter of the Asuras;
quickly bring the evils of all living beings to rest.
And the great calamities produced by portents and the ripening of karma.
Be gracious to those who bow before you, O Goddess, you who remove the suffering of the universe; O one praised by the inhabitants of the three worlds, become the bestower of boons upon the worlds.
The illustrious Goddess said: "I am the giver of boons; O hosts of gods, choose whatever boon you desire in your hearts. Grant it to me, for I shall bestow that which is beneficial to the worlds."
The gods said:
"O Sovereign of the entire triple world, you must act in this very way to pacify all afflictions of the three worlds and to destroy our enemies."
The Goddess said: When the Vaivasvata interval has arrived, in the twenty-eighth yuga,
two other great asuras, Śumbha and Niśumbha, will arise.
Born in the house of Nandagopa, originating from the womb of Yaśodā—
I, dwelling on the Vindhya mountains, shall therefore destroy those two.
Furthermore, descending to the surface of the earth in an exceedingly fierce form,
I shall slay the Vaipracitta Dānavas.
And as they devour those fierce sons of Vipracitti, the great Dānavas,
their teeth will become red, resembling the blossoms of the pomegranate tree.
Then, in heaven the deities and in the mortal world men shall constantly proclaim my name, praising me as Raktadantikā.
Furthermore, during a hundred-year drought when there is no water,
I shall be born upon the earth from no womb, as praised by the sages.
Then, with a hundred eyes, I shall behold those sages whom men will thereafter proclaim as "the Hundred-eyed One" (Śatākṣī).
Then, O gods, I shall sustain the entire world with vegetables produced from my own body, which will serve as the support of life during the drought.
"Then I shall attain renown on earth as Śākambharī;
and right there I shall slay the great Asura named Durga,
and my name shall become celebrated as the goddess Durgā."
And again, when I assume a terrifying form on the Himālaya mountains and devour the rākṣasas for the sake of protecting the birds, [I shall do so].
Then all the sages, with bodies bowed in reverence, shall praise me;
thus my name shall become renowned as Bhīmā Devī.
When he who is named Aruṇa shall cause great affliction in the three worlds,
then I, having assumed the form of a bee with innumerable bees, [will act].
"For the sake of the welfare of the three worlds, I shall slay the great asura;
and then they will praise me everywhere, calling me 'Bhrāmarī'."
Thus, whenever there shall be oppression arising from the Dānavas,
at each such time I will descend and bring about the destruction of my enemies.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Hymn to Nārāyaṇa by the Gods," in the *Devīmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Chapter Ninety-Two. The Goddess said:
Whoever, with a concentrated mind, shall constantly praise me with these hymns, I will undoubtedly destroy all of his afflictions. (MarkP 92.1)
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth day, those who, with one-pointed minds and devotion, shall praise my supreme majesty; (MarkP 92.3)
For them there shall be no misdeed whatsoever, nor calamities arising from misdeeds;
there shall be no poverty, nor indeed any separation from what is beloved.
He shall have no fear from enemies, nor from bandits, nor from kings;
never shall there be danger for him from weapons, fire, or floods of water.
Therefore, this majesty of mine should be recited together with those who seek my welfare;
it should always be heard with devotion, for it is a supreme and great means of securing well-being.
May my majesty pacify all calamities arising from great pestilence, as well as the threefold portents.
Wherever this is recited properly and constantly in my temple, I shall never abandon that place; my presence remains there forever.
In the offering of oblations, in worship, in the fire-ritual, and at great festivals,
all this conduct of mine must be recited and indeed heard.
Whether done knowingly or unknowingly,
I shall graciously accept this offering of bali-worship as well as the oblation into the fire thus performed.
In the autumn season, the great annual festival is performed;
having heard this majesty of mine during that occasion, one should be endowed with devotion.
Freed from all afflictions and endowed with wealth and grain, that man shall come to be through my grace; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this majesty of mine, as well as my various auspicious origins and my prowess in battles, a man becomes fearless.
Enemies go to destruction and prosperity arises;
the family of those men who hear of my greatness rejoices.
In all rites for pacification, as well as upon seeing an evil dream,
and during fierce afflictions by planetary spirits, one should hear my majesty.
Calamities subside, as do the terrible afflictions caused by malevolent planets;
and the bad dreams seen by men turn into auspicious dreams.
It brings peace to children overcome by infantile seizures,
and it is the supreme means for creating friendship among men who are divided by factions.
It is the supreme destroyer of the strength of all those of evil conduct;
it brings about the destruction of Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas by the mere recitation [of it].
All this majesty of mine brings about my presence.
With animals, flowers, water-offerings, and incense, as well as with excellent perfumes and lamps,
by feeding Brahmins with gold, and with sprinkling-water, [he should worship] day and night.
The pleasure that is produced by various other enjoyments and gifts over the course of a year is produced by this single instance of hearing well-spoken verses.
Hearing this account of my births removes sins, bestows health, and provides protection from malevolent spirits. (MarkP 92.22)
When men hear of my conduct in battles— the destruction of the wicked Daityas— fear caused by enemies does not arise within them.
Whatever hymns have been composed by you, those made by the Brahman-sages,
and those created by Brahmā— these indeed bestow an auspicious state of existence.
Whether in a forest or a wilderness, surrounded by a forest fire,
or beset by bandits in a desolate place, or even captured by enemies;
Or followed by lions and tigers in the forest, or with wild elephants;
or commanded by an angry king to be executed, or even while held in captivity.
Whether the ship is tossed about by the wind upon the great ocean,
or while weapons are falling in an exceedingly terrible battle.
Even when afflicted by all manner of terrible diseases or overwhelmed by painful sensations,
a person who remembers this conduct of mine shall be liberated from distress.
By my power, lions and other beasts, as well as robbers and enemies,
flee far away at the mere thought of my deeds.
The sage said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed goddess Caṇḍikā, of fierce prowess,
vanished right there while the gods were looking on.
They too, freed from fear by the Goddess and with their enemies destroyed, all resumed their respective offices as before, partaking in the sacrificial portions.

When Śumbha, the enemy of the gods, that destroyer of the world, most fierce and of incomparable prowess, had been slain in battle by the Goddess, and Niśumbha too, of great heroism, the remaining Daityas fled to the netherworld (pātāla).
Thus, O King, that Blessed Goddess, though eternal, repeatedly manifests and performs the protection of the world.
By her this entire universe is deluded; she herself gives birth to the universe.
When entreated, she bestows wisdom; when pleased, she grants supernatural power.
O lord of men, this entire cosmic egg is pervaded by that Mahākālī,
who, at the time of the Great Dissolution (mahākāla), takes the form of Mahākārī.
At the proper time, she herself becomes the great pestilence; she herself is the unborn creation;
and at the proper time, that eternal one brings about the maintenance of all beings.
In times of prosperity, that very same thing brings increase of fortune to men in their home;
yet in times of adversity, it likewise becomes misfortune, leading to destruction.
When praised and worshipped with flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth,
she bestows wealth, sons, intelligence regarding the Dharma, and an auspicious state of rebirth.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Words of the Goddess," in the *Devīmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, within the *Sāvarṇika Manvantara*.
Chapter Ninety-three: The Sage said:
Thus has this supreme majesty of the Goddess been told to you, O King;
such is the power of that Goddess by whom this entire world is sustained.
In that very same way, knowledge is brought about by the illusory power (māyā) of Lord Viṣṇu;
likewise you, this Vaiśya, and other discerning men are deluded— some have been deluded, some are being deluded, and others will be deluded.
Go for refuge, O Great King, to her, the Supreme Goddess;
when propitiated, she alone bestows upon men worldly enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of his, King Suratha prostrated before that illustrious ṛṣi of celebrated vows.
O great sage, both he and that Vaiśya, being despondent due to their excessive attachment and the seizure of their kingdom, immediately departed for asceticism.
Staying on the sandy bank of a river for the purpose of seeing his mother,
that Vaiśya performed austerities while reciting the supreme Devīsūkta.
Having fashioned an earthen image of the Goddess upon that mound,
the two of them performed her worship with offerings of flowers, incense, and fire-oblations.
Abstaining from food, self-controlled, with their minds fixed on Him and composed in meditation,
the two of them offered as an oblation even the blood flowing from their own limbs.
When they had thus propitiated her for three years with self-restraint,
Caṇḍikā, the sustainer of the world, being well-pleased, spoke to them face to face.
The Goddess said:
"O King, O delighter of your lineage, whatever is requested by you from me—may all that be obtained; being well-pleased, I grant it."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the king chose that he might regain his kingdom in another birth,
and that his own kingdom here should be regained by force, with the power of his enemies destroyed.
Then that Vaiśya, his mind filled with world-weariness, requested knowledge from him—
the wise man who brings about the cessation of attachment to the notions of "mine" and "I."
The Goddess said: "O King, within a few days you shall regain your own kingdom;
having slain your enemies, your sovereignty there shall be unimpeded."
And having died, you shall again obtain birth from the god Vivasvat;
you will become the Manu named Sāvarṇika on earth.
"O best of Vaiśyas, whatever boon you desire from us, I grant it for the sake of your complete success; you shall possess knowledge."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus granted them the boon as they desired, the Goddess,
praised by them with devotion, instantly vanished from sight.
Thus, having obtained a boon from the Goddess, Suratha, that bull among Kṣatriyas,
shall take birth from the Sun and become Sāvarṇi Manu.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons," in the Devī-māhātmya of the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
